The authors give lower and upper bounds for the general case. Specific classes receive closer treatment, including trees and graphs of bounded degree or degeneracy. They also study graphs growing by one edge swap per step. Results hold even online, when future snapshots are unknown while coloring proceeds.
arxiv-2505-12707:
Yingchen He, Christian Weilbach, Martyna Wojciechowska, Yuxuan Zhang, and Frank Wood release PLAICraft, in a 2025 preprint, a huge dataset of people playing Minecraft together. Training believable embodied agents needs data with sight, sound, action, and social play in sync. Such data barely existed. PLAICraft records five streams at once: screen video, game audio, microphone audio, mouse moves, and key presses. Every stream is stamped to the millisecond. The world is open-ended and multiplayer, so behavior stays rich and social.

The haul exceeds ten thousand hours from over ten thousand players worldwide. A test suite ships with it, covering object recognition, spatial sense, language grounding, and long-term memory. The authors argue this is the raw material agents need to act with purpose in real time. Other teams can now train and grade embodied models on the same ground. The platform keeps collecting, so the dataset can keep growing.
arxiv-2505-13307:
Qiguang Chen, Libo Qin, and colleagues examine the limits of step-by-step reasoning in large language models in a 2025 study. Writing out intermediate steps helps models on hard tasks, but users lack clear measures of how far that help extends. Unmeasurable skills, such as perception across image and text, are even harder to assess.

Their framework defines a reasoning boundary as the top level that stepwise reasoning can reach. A combination law lets them analyze how boundaries interact across tasks. For unmeasurable skills they add assessment methods suited to cases without clean scores. The aim is practical guidance for improving reasoning rather than blind trial and error.
arxiv-2505-15607:
David Dinucu-Jianu, Mrinmaya Sachan, and four co-authors train language models to teach, not just solve. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, starts from a clash. Models tuned to answer at once make poor tutors, since good teaching holds back the answer. Their method uses trial chats with a fake student to shape the tutor by reward.

A mid-size tutor trained this way matched big paid models on teaching tests. No human labels were needed for the training. A dial trades teaching support against student success, tracing a clear frontier. The tutor keeps its raw reasoning skill better than plain fine-tuned rivals. Optional thinking tags expose its plan, which aids trust.
arxiv-2505-18707:
Khalifa and Breuer wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, with given names Ali and Michael in its text. It watches clumps of sticky particles break apart in churned flow, in a simulation that resolves each grain.

One clump of hundreds of like spheres is set in even, swirling turbulence. An immersed boundary method tracks the flow, and a soft-sphere model tracks the grains and their glue. Flow strength and glue strength are swept across ranges. Strain-led zones start the wear and drive it on. The breakup is mostly erosion, grain by grain, not a sudden split. The break rate falls off with the glue gauge in a power law like past reports. Shards fly out along the flow's stretch-squeeze plane.
arxiv-2505-22507:
Marco Bee and Flavio Santi build a statistical model for data that bunch near zero yet stretch into a long, heavy tail. Insurance losses behave this way: many small claims, a few huge ones. A lognormal curve fits the body of such data well but falls too fast at the top. Their model grafts a Pareto-style tail onto that body.

Because the tail starts at zero on its own scale, no cutoff point must be picked by hand. The model is fully unsupervised in that sense. Fitting runs through a standard expectation-maximization routine. Tests on made-up data and real car claims show fit as good as two rival models, with simpler fitting. The authors ship the method as a free R package. Risk teams can use it to price extreme losses with less guesswork.
arxiv-2505-23107:
Pushapdeep Singh and four co-authors build a shared tool for brain signal work in twenty twenty-five. EEG records electrical activity from the scalp and is widely used to decode mental states. But data is usually gathered for one task at a time. Devices also differ in how many channels they record, which breaks a single fixed pipeline.

Their framework, EAD, learns embeddings of EEG signals that travel across tasks. The aim is one pipeline that works even when channel counts vary between samples. Older pipelines lean on preprocessing plus deep models tied to a set channel count. A flexible adapter could serve many decoding tasks from mixed sources. Readers get a step toward unified EEG classification.
arxiv-2505-23607:
Carolina Fortuna, Gregor Cerar, and colleagues design data models for explainable learning in electricity systems in a 2025 study. Smart grids, renewable growth, and price shocks have pushed power companies toward machine learning, but most models eat a single measurement stream and cannot explain themselves. Metadata and extra measurements could enrich them, yet no structured study had mapped what that richer data should look like.

The authors set out the data model design that explainable applications need. Clear data structure is a precondition for models whose reasoning grid operators can audit before acting on a forecast or alarm.
arxiv-2505-23907:
Amirhossein Alimohammadi and five co-authors edit images with big structural changes while keeping textures true. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Diffusion editors are fast, but bending shapes or moving objects trips them. Few-step editors often smear in irrelevant texture. Key traits of the source, like pose, get lost. Their Cora framework attacks both failure modes.

Semantic correspondence links source and target regions. A noise correction step uses that alignment during generation. Interpolated attention maps guide where new content may appear. Texture transfers where it should, and fresh content fills true gaps. Users control the balance between keeping and generating. Visual effects and graphics work stand to gain.
arxiv-2506-01407:
Olga Zamaraeva, Dan Flickinger, Francis Bond, and Carlos Gomez-Rodriguez wrote this linguistics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on how machine writing differs from human writing at the level of grammar. They compare New York Times-style text from six large language models with real Times prose.

The lens is a formal grammar theory, Head-driven Phrase Structure Grammar, which parses each sentence into a detailed structure. Counting which grammar types show up, and how often, exposes systematic gaps between the two kinds of text. The models' writing leans on a narrower slice of the grammar than the humans' does. The authors say such counts give a sharper picture than surface word checks. The study speaks to both language model builders and students of human style.
arxiv-2506-02307:
Ruoyu Guo compares two measures of complexity for a family of algebras built from quivers in a 2025 math study. Serial quiver algebras, whose representations string together in a simple chain-like way, have finite values for both the delooping level and the finitistic dimension. The first can be computed by a short algorithm. The question is when the two numbers coincide.

For right serial algebras the right finitistic dimension equals the left delooping level outright. For left serial algebras the equality needs extra conditions, and examples show where it fails. Sub-versions of the delooping level round out the comparison.
arxiv-2506-05007:
Rui Zhang and a large team present a system that aims to design a complete processor chip, hardware and software, automatically. Chip design faces fabrication limits, ballooning resource demands, and fragmenting ecosystems. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team builds the system in three layers. At the bottom sits a domain-specific large model for processor design, engineered around the field's knowledge gaps, scarce data, correctness demands, and huge solution space. Above it, a hardware design agent and a software agent use that model's knowledge and inference to do the actual design work.

The ambition is full automation of the stack, from architecture to the code that runs on it. The paper lays out the layered architecture and the special training and inference choices behind the chip model. It is a position-and-system paper from a major computer architecture group.
arxiv-2506-08207:
Alejandro Peña-Torres, Michail Stamatakis, and Hannes Jónsson explain why silver atoms pair up on a silicon surface even when deposited in deep cold, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Experiments had seen silver dimers form on the Si(100) surface at temperatures as low as one hundred forty kelvin, which seemed far too cold for atoms to wander.

The surface is corrugated into rows of silicon dimers. The authors simulate deposition with classical dynamics, hunt down the energy saddles between sites, and run kinetic Monte Carlo over long times. Silver atoms, they find, glide easily along the tops of the silicon dimer rows. Once an atom drops into a snug site between rows, it stops moving. The rival idea, that landing energy briefly melts a hot spot and boosts motion, contributes little. Easy row-top migration plus sticky valleys explains the low-temperature pairing.
arxiv-2506-08707:
Anshu Gautam and six co-authors study D mesons in nuclear matter in two thousand twenty five. Pseudoscalar and vector D mesons change inside dense nuclei. Isospin asymmetry of the medium shapes those changes. A hybrid model couples two frameworks for the task.

In medium quark masses come from a chiral SU(3) mean field model. A light front quark model then computes meson traits. Masses, decay constants, and distribution shapes all shift. Mesons with up or down quarks move most. Strange quark mesons respond less to the medium. Baryon density outweighs temperature and asymmetry effects.
arxiv-2506-09207:
William Anderson, Seung Whan Chung, and Youngsoo Choi boosted a fast stand-in modeling method in 2025. Solving partial differential equations at full fidelity is slow, so reduced-order models learn a squeezed stand-in. The method they extend squeezes data through an autoencoder into a small latent space. It then learns normal differential equations that move the squeezed state through time. New forecasts come from evolving the cheap equations and reading the state back out.

The strain shows in complex or rapidly oscillating problems. There one autoencoder must both reconstruct the data faithfully and keep its latent space obedient to simple motion, two demands that fight. The multi-stage version trains several autoencoders in sequence, each stage cleaning up what the previous one missed. The authors argue the staged design keeps the first method's speed while extending its reach to harder physics.
arxiv-2506-09407:
Harbir Antil, Daiki Mizuno, and Ken Shirakawa study how to steer the motion of grain boundaries in materials by optimal control, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Grain boundaries are the seams between crystals inside a metal or ceramic, and their motion reshapes the material's strength and behavior.

Their model is the KWC system, a standard phase-field framework written as a downhill flow of a free energy. Plain KWC models resist control theory because their solutions may not be unique. The authors recently added a pseudo-parabolic twist that keeps the energy flow while restoring uniqueness. Building on that fix, this paper sets up an optimization problem governed by the improved system. Its main theorems cover when optimal controls exist, how they depend on the data, and what conditions they must satisfy. The work opens a rigorous path to controlling microstructure.
arxiv-2506-12407:
Yunqing Huang and Shangyou Zhang prove superconvergence for a quadratic finite element in two thousand twenty-five. The mesh is uniform and built of tetrahedra in three dimensions. Their core step is a direct computation with interpolation. They show a key projection trait holds on each local patch.

From that trait, convergence in two norms follows at a lifted rate. A standard cubic interpolation then lifts the solution to near best cubic form. The lift works cube by cube across the mesh. Numeric tests confirm the theory. The paper is a tight piece of numerical analysis.
arxiv-2506-12507:
Pablo Gonzalez-Oliveras, Olov Engwall, and Ali Reza Majlesi test how a social robot sways high school students in two thousand twenty-five. The robot argued answers to true or false questions on electric circuits. It was right on most items and wrong on two. Students had learned the topic in class.

Most students were swayed past their own expected level, for good or ill. Students who used language models more were swayed even more. The robot showed three levels of certainty through words, voice, and face. Students matched its stance most when it seemed certain. They also rated it most convincing then. The team urges care in how robots show certainty.
arxiv-2506-12607:
Christodoulos Constantinides, Shuxin Lin, and Dhaval Patel build embedding models to help engineers who keep plant gear in repair. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The aim is to guide an engineer's picks and cut the time gear sits idle. Each task is a plain-words ask tied to a named asset, with queries on how it fails. The tool must find the right items, such as sensors, and stretch to kin assets. The team built a vetted base of facts and nine task sets, one per asset. They enrich each task with short notes made by a large model. The embeddings then feed an agent that plans and acts.
arxiv-2506-17107:
Dong and co-authors sense background methane at a distance by catching scattered light in a nonlinear interferometer. Such interferometers serve sensing, spectroscopy, and imaging, but most need mirrors and exact alignment. That limits their use outdoors.

Their setup probes methane with mid-infrared light but detects near-infrared photons on a silicon camera. The probe light bounces diffusely off a matte surface, losing much of its strength. A two-lens confocal scheme matched the beams well enough to work anyway. They sensed background methane at 4.6 meters under sixty decibels of loss. Glass, brushed metal, and a leaf all worked as targets.
arxiv-2506-18207:
Horatio Boedihardjo, Xi Geng, and Sheng Wang attack a conjecture in rough path theory in a twenty twenty-five paper. Rough paths describe paths too jagged for classic calculus. Each path has a signature, a tower of integrals, and a log signature that packs the same data more tightly.

Lyons and Sidorova guessed that only straight lines can have a log signature with an infinite radius of convergence. The team proves that such a case forces the signature to obey an endless system of rigid algebraic rules, phrased with integrals along complex forms. In a stronger form, where the trait holds on every sub-interval, they prove the path must indeed be a straight line.
arxiv-2506-18507:
Florin Ambro matched two gauges of how bad a singularity is in a 2025 paper. Symbol-based geometers quantify singularities with invariants such as the minimal log discrepancy, which probes a singularity from inside. The log canonical threshold, which tests it against a cutting hyperplane. Ambro studies whether the two quantities approach zero jointly. Comparing the minimal log discrepancy of a singularity with the threshold of its general hyperplane section.

The equivalence question matters because the two invariants are worked out very differently, and agreement near zero would let results transfer between them. The paper sits in the minimal model program's long effort to sort singularities. The actions of these numbers governs conjectures about which singular spaces can appear in groups.
arxiv-2506-19107:
Ruiwei Xiao and colleagues teach computer science students to ask chatbots questions that help them learn, instead of questions that hand over answers. They call the skill pedagogical prompting. Misuse of language models by students is a documented drag on learning. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team first surveyed dozens of instructors of introductory courses to learn what classrooms actually need. They then built an interactive training system with scenario-based lessons. A study with novice students measured skills before and after, using mixed methods.

Students' pedagogical help-seeking improved significantly, by the authors report. Attitudes toward the system were positive, and willingness to use such prompts in the future rose. The contributions include a theoretical framework for pedagogical prompting and the tested intervention itself. The work treats prompting as a teachable study skill, not a trick.
arxiv-2506-21707:
Anirudh Lanka, Shashank Hegde, and Todd Brun wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It uses machine learning to tune continuous-time quantum error correction for any noise, even noise with memory.

In this mode of guarding, checks and fixes run all the time, not in rounds. Given a space and a noise process, which may link errors across place and time, the protocol learns both the code space and the fix map that best guard the stored state. The score is the mean fidelity of the logical state. The aim is fix plans grown for the true noise of a real device, not a stock guess.
arxiv-2506-22707:
Kaiser, Sugeet Sunder, Ajey Jacob, and Akhilesh Jaiswal build memory that computes where it sits, in light: X-pSRAM, a photonic SRAM cell with XOR logic inside. Their paper from twenty twenty-five attacks the von Neumann bottleneck, the costly shuttling between memory and processor. Cross-coupled microring resonators hold the bits electro-optically. Differential photodiodes read them without leaving the optical domain.

Read, write, and XOR compute all run at ten gigahertz or better. Wavelength multiplexing packs many bits into one shot, so wide XORs finish together. On a GlobalFoundries photonic node, each XOR bit costs a sliver of energy. The authors aim the cell at cryptography, hyperdimensional computing, and neural nets. Light-speed memory math is the pitch.
arxiv-2507-04007:
Kai Liang counted independent sets on grid graphs with tensor network methods in a 2025 combinatorics paper. An independent set picks points on a grid so that no two touch, like a hard-core gas where particles refuse to sit side by side. Counting such sets gives an entropy constant prized by physicists and mathematicians, but exact counts grow explosively with grid size.

Tensor contraction pushed counts far beyond earlier reach, on square and triangular grids, king graphs, and cylinders alike. Surface and parity effects showed clearly in the numbers, and Liang derived bounds for the entropy and surface terms. Several integer sequences gained many new terms, and the hard square entropy estimate improved on the best known accuracy.
arxiv-2507-06607:
Liliang Ren and a large team build SambaY, a model build that shares memory across layers to make long text cheap to write. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

State-space models give a swift way to read long chains. Past mixed builds joined them with focus parts, or stacked two decoders. None had mined the gain from shared memory states across layers. The team adds a small gated unit that lets layers share what they read out of memory. Put in a cross-decoder over a state-space self-decoder, it lifts how fast long text is made. The work aims at thought tasks that need long output.
arxiv-2507-06707:
Asaf Abas and Nir Sharon study approximation in a twenty twenty-five paper. Their method builds estimates level by level, correcting errors at each scale. The goal is to cut bias, the steady part of error that does not wash out with more data. They judge estimators by the bias ratio, the share of total error due to bias.

For a plain case with zero-mean noise, they show the method's bias matches the leftover error of the correction scheme. A condition on how that leftover shrinks then gives bias reduction. A spectral model shows the bias ratio never rises as levels are added. The work covers both plain number-valued and manifold-valued functions. Readers get a reason why multiscale steps help.
arxiv-2507-07107:
Yimin Du builds a trading system for Chinese stocks in this two thousand twenty-five paper. He starts by naming a bug. A-share markets cap daily price moves, so some closing prices could never be traded. Pipelines take those prices in before filtering, poisoning moving averages, correlations, and ranks. Du calls this contamination. It swelled predictive power while cutting realized performance, as the model learned to call returns that can not be traded.

The fix is a mask-first design: a tradability mask is built at data load and threaded through all sums. On that base sit a GPU-vectorized engine computing two hundred-plus factors, a loss function punishing wrong-sign predictions eleven times harder than size errors, bootstrap-based augmentation, and optimized construction. Tests that drop one part showed the mask gave more than a model or loss choice. The build is released under an MIT license.
arxiv-2507-10607:
Qian Qi wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It founds a field the author calls Measure Learning, in which neural networks drive the equations behind nonlinear expectations.

Expectations of this kind model deep doubt, where no one probability law is trusted. The operators here solve backward stochastic equations whose drivers are neural nets. The main theorem proves such equations are well set under a local smoothness term and square growth, far laxer than the classic global rule. That covers common nets such as ReLU builds. Ways to bake traits like convexity into the net are given, and the theory stretches to coupled systems and big particle crowds.
arxiv-2507-13407:
Vinu Sankar Sadasivan, Mehrdad Saberi, and Soheil Feizi proposed IConMark in twenty twenty-five, a watermark for AI-generated images that a human can read. Provenance marks usually hide in noise-like perturbations and crumble under attack. IConMark instead embeds meaningful semantic concepts into the image itself — attributes a person can see and verify with their own eyes.

The watermark survives common image augmentations while leaving quality intact. In detection tests it beat the best baseline by about eleven points of area under the curve. Hybrid versions grafting it onto two existing watermarking systems gained roughly fifteen points each. The authors present interpretable watermarking as a first step toward marks that stay meaningful — and checkable — without special software, a property pure signal-processing schemes cannot offer.
arxiv-2507-13807:
H. Koehn and co-authors put out a software package in 2025 that makes the study of cosmic explosions dramatically cheaper. When two neutron stars merge, the gamma-ray burst afterglow and the glowing kilonova that follow encode the merger's physics. From the equation of state of dense matter to the expansion of the universe. Extracting that information means Bayesian sampling over an actual model's settings, and each likelihood testing with a detailed model is costly enough to dominate the whole study.

Their package, fiesta, trains machine learning surrogates that imitate the state-of-the-art afterglow codes at a fraction of the cost, so samplers can afford the millions of tests they crave. Extensive surrogates are provided for the leading afterglow models named in the paper. And the method broadens to kilonova models as well, putting careful inference within reach of normal computing budgets.
arxiv-2507-16107:
Trung Phung, Kyle Reese, Ilya Shpitser, and Rohit Bhattacharya wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It fills gaps in data that are missing not at random, without leaning on the shaky guesses that standard tools bake in.

Tools like MICE assume gaps are random and smooth over patterns the data never shows. That skews all that follows. The team gives a fresh account of the full data law in graphical models of missingness. The account is constructive, and yields fill-in laws for both random and not-at-random gaps. Their method, MISPR, samples in rounds like MICE but stays true under both regimes. In tests it ties MICE on random gaps and beats it, with less bias, when gaps bite.
arxiv-2507-16907:
Amir Michaelis and Hagai Perets argue that the single-degenerate channel produces Type Iax supernovae rather than normal Type Ia events, in a two thousand twenty-five astrophysics paper. Type Ia supernovae anchor cosmic distance measurements, yet their progenitor systems remain unsettled.

In the single-degenerate picture a white dwarf gains mass from a companion star. Three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations show most such white dwarfs ignite early, below the Chandrasekhar mass, giving weak, incomplete explosions matching Type Iax events. Only dwarfs reaching a narrow threshold near 1.37 solar masses fully disrupt. This safety valve could explain missing progenitor signatures and pushes normal Type Ia origins toward other channels.
arxiv-2507-20907:
Jeongun Ryu and co-authors wrote this medical imaging paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on a quiet threat to AI diagnosis: the scanner itself. Tissue slides scanned on different machines come out looking slightly different, and a model can learn the machine instead of the disease.

The team built SCORPION, a data set of four hundred eighty tissue samples, each scanned on five scanners, giving twenty-four hundred aligned patches. Because the tissue is held fixed, any wobble in a model's answers is the scanner's fault. They also propose SimCons, a training scheme that pairs data augmentation with a consistency loss that punishes scanner-dependent answers. It improved consistency without hurting task accuracy. The data set and method are offered as a new reliability standard for pathology AI.
arxiv-2508-01307:
Fahimeh Ahmadi, Zahra Moradimanesh, Reza Khosrowabadi, and Reza Jafari wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, with the last name in fuller form in its text. It tracks how opposed brain networks grow apart, or fail to, as a child becomes an adult.

The team reads resting brain scans through structural balance theory, which sorts triples of regions by their signed ties. In childhood the pattern is local and blocky. In the teen years it turns loose and reshuffling. In adults it is split and specialized, with strong opposition between the default mode and frontoparietal networks. That split lets inner thought and outer focus take turns with less clash. The weaker teen links show the split is built, not born.
arxiv-2508-05007:
Jeehyun Yang and three co-authors measure Jupiter's deep oxygen in twenty twenty-five. What Jupiter is made of constrains how it, and the solar nebula, formed. Oxygen hides deep in the atmosphere, so it must be inferred. They use carbon monoxide as a proxy tracer for the deep abundance.

Their approach couples two models. One-dimensional kinetic-transport chemistry meets two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulation. A large chemical network from a reaction mechanism generator supplies the rates. An often-neglected reaction involving methanol proves significant for the chemistry. The coupled result supports a modest oxygen enrichment, about one to one and a half times the solar value. They also derive the atmosphere's eddy diffusion range from the simulations.
arxiv-2508-06207:
Andrea Dal Prete and seven co-authors make back-support exoskeletons smarter by letting them see the load before the lift begins. Current devices react to sensors after strain starts, so help arrives late and cannot adapt to context. Their design predicts the payload with computer vision instead.

Experiments with twelve subjects first mapped how muscle activity, discomfort, and user preference trade off across assistance levels. A fine-tuned vision transformer with depth sensing then estimated payloads before lifting, reaching about eighty-two percent accuracy in a second group. The adaptive strategy cut peak back muscle activation by up to twenty-three percent. Average offloading also improved without adding discomfort.
arxiv-2508-09007:
Sanjana Paul sets out principles for environmental justice in technology, arguing that how tools are built should serve repair and shared flourishing rather than speed and profit alone. The framework is modeled on the landmark nineteen ninety-one principles of environmental justice and extends their commitments into computing and engineering. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Paul places the proposal among neighboring movements: environmental justice, design justice, and post-growth computing. The principles stress interdependence among people and ecosystems, repair of past harm, and community self-determination over local technology choices.

The aim is practical as well as moral: a shared values infrastructure that builders, funders, and communities can cite when resisting extractive defaults. Paul frames the piece as support for collective efforts to change not only what gets built, but how, why, and for whom.
arxiv-2508-10107:
Themba Hodge, Philipp Frey, and Stephan Rachel showed in 2025 how measurements rescue topological quantum computing as it scales. The approach stores information in exotic particles called non-Abelian anyons and computes by braiding them, which resists local disturbance. But the authors highlight an overlooked wall: beyond two qubits, braiding alone cannot even produce the full Clifford gate set, so the machine stalls short of universality.

Adding projective measurements lets the system switch between different qubit encodings, restoring full computational power. In many-body simulations of braiding with measurement-based switching, the team prepared entangled states of two and five qubits and ran a random circuit on five qubits with fidelity above ninety-nine percent. Fidelity stayed that high under moderate disorder, evidence that the architecture keeps its promised fault tolerance while scaling.
arxiv-2508-10307:
Zhaoming Kong, Jiahuan Zhang, and Xiaowei Yang present a fast image denoising method that cleans noise in one pass by exploiting how image patches repeat. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Cameras keep improving, yet the flood of images still demands cleaning that is both quick and gentle on detail. Many top methods learn local building blocks, which costs time.

Their method, Haar-tSVD, views patch groups through a tensor lens tied to the Haar transform. That link lets one projection capture both wide and local correlations at once. No learned patch bases are needed, so the filter stays simple and highly parallel. A small neural estimator gauges the noise level and adapts the cleaning. Tests on real-world tasks confirm speed with strong detail keeping. Code and data are shared in public.
arxiv-2508-11107:
Adam Binswanger and colleagues presented a numerical method in 2025 for flows where two immiscible fluids meet, such as oil and water, governed by the two-phase Navier-Stokes equations. Accuracy lives or dies at the interface, where pressure and velocity jump; smearing those jumps ruins the physics. Their solver keeps the interface sharp by construction.

Working on adaptive quadtree and octree grids that refine where needed, with every variable stored at the grid nodes themselves, the authors built new spatial and time discretizations around that collocated layout. A hybrid finite difference and finite volume treatment enforces the boundary and interface jump conditions exactly rather than approximately. Canonical test problems in two and three dimensions demonstrate the accuracy, and the authors sketch extensions to richer physics, arguing the simpler data structures suit both research and engineering use.
arxiv-2508-12007:
Sabrina Aufiero, Silvia Bartolucci, Fabio Caccioli, and Pierpaolo Vivo review systemic risk in old and new finance in two thousand twenty-five. The old world is banks and markets, the new is decentralized finance on chains. The pair of worlds now touch more and more. The review maps how risk forms and spreads in each.

For old finance they sketch a model from leverage cycles and liquidity crises. For new finance they stress traits like composability and code flaws. Some risks share roots but move in distinct ways. They coin a term for two way spread between the worlds. Lessons aim at policy makers and market actors.
arxiv-2508-12407:
Zhuorui Liu, Chen Zhang, and Dawei Song redesigned attention in 2025 so language models can read long documents without drowning in memory. Long contexts are expensive mainly because the key-value cache grows with every token. Research shows attention heads split into types: retrieval heads that fetch distant facts, and streaming heads that mostly watch nearby words. Streaming heads can shed much of their cache with little loss.

Simply splitting each layer's computation into two passes creates its own overhead, though. ZigzagAttention reorganizes the work so retrieval and streaming heads are handled exclusively and efficiently. The aim is long-context inference that fits realistic hardware while keeping the model's grip on distant information. For applications like book-length question answering or code repository analysis, memory savings of this kind decide whether the feature ships at all.
arxiv-2508-13107:
Figarri Keisha and a team of co-authors build an adaptive retrieval pipeline for legal research. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses retrieval-augmented generation, which grounds model answers in fetched texts. Law is a field where stray claims are costly, so grounding counts double. Three upgrades drive their gains over past baselines.

A query translator splits cited documents from plain questions. It also tunes search depth and answer style to the asker's skill and detail. Open-source embedding tools, SBERT and GTE, match paid rivals at lower cost. Scoring mixes RAGAS, BERTScore, and ROUGE to weigh sense match and faithfulness. A legal-grounded prompt beat plain prompts on faithfulness and fit. The authors argue that task-aware tuning at each part yields sound, cheap legal help.
arxiv-2508-15207:
Arjun Srinivasan, Anubhav Paras, and Aniket Bera train hostile drivers to stress-test self-driving systems in a 2025 study. Safety training usually surrounds the learner with rule-following traffic that behaves politely. Real danger comes from other road users who cut in, brake oddly, or block, and simple car-following models miss that variety.

Their deep reinforcement learning method learns adversarial behavior for the surrounding agents, aiming to provoke failures in the driving policy. The adversary is evaluated against the standard rule-based agents used in simulators. Finding failure scenarios in simulation is far cheaper than meeting them on real roads.
arxiv-2508-16107:
Amir Bouziane and Huseyin Arslan design a radio waveform that can talk and sense at once without straining cheap hardware. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Standard waveforms for such dual use swing wildly in power. Those swings force amplifiers to back off, which shortens the sensing range.

Their scheme wraps the standard signal in frequency modulation, holding its strength flat. A flat signal lets the amplifier run at full power without warping the output. The authors work out the math for channels that shift in both time and frequency. They also design a receiver that reads speed from slow phase changes. Tests under strict bandwidth rules beat rival waveforms. The scheme kept detection sharp and error rates low even at top power and high speeds. It suits small, cheap dual-use radios.
arxiv-2508-16207:
Thinesh Thiyakesan Ponbagavathi, Kunyu Peng, and Alina Roitberg tackle a practical weakness of driver monitoring systems: they fail when the camera moves. Deep learning foundation models generalize well when adapted lightly, by probing their final layers. But their robustness to unseen camera viewpoints was underexplored.

The authors adapt image foundation models to driver monitoring using a single training view, then evaluate directly on unseen perspectives with no further adaptation. They benchmark linear probes and advanced probing strategies for two foundation models against heavier fine-tuning approaches. Building on the results, they introduce T-Mask, an image-to-video probing method that masks temporal tokens to emphasize dynamic video regions. On a public driver activity dataset, T-Mask improved cross-view accuracy over strong probing baselines and over parameter-efficient fine-tuning, while adding no parameters. Gains were largest for underrepresented secondary activities.
arxiv-2508-17307:
Zikun Lin and a large team of astronomers report new behavior from the black hole binary candidate IGR J17091-3624 during its twenty twenty-five outburst. The outburst stayed in the hard state. Observations with the IXPE telescope revealed a series of intermittent X-ray dips spanning about a day in total.

Follow-up observations with NICER, the Einstein Probe, NuSTAR, and Swift showed the dips recur with a period of about two point eight days, accompanied by increased spectral hardness. Such quasi-periodic dipping had never been seen in this source before. Spectral analysis attributes the dips to obscuration by an ionized absorber, likely material in the outer accretion disk modulated by the binary's orbital period. If that period is orbital, the donor star is probably a partially stripped giant rather than a standard main-sequence star. The team also examined the optical band for related signals.
arxiv-2509-00107:
Chuanbo Liu and Jin Wang propose in 2025 that deep networks learn through joint action of a key set of neurons. Networks now beat humans on many hard tasks, yet how training works inside them stays murky. The authors argue that strongly active, task-bound neurons, called critical neurons, couple in step to drive learning.

That coupling yields Hebbian-like correlation graphs, where linked firing strengthens links. Early in training, the graph passes a sharp shift in how it connects. Weights among critical neurons are reinforced and shuffled at once, which strikes a fine balance. The picture frames training as self-organization in an adaptive system, not mere curve fitting. Such insight could guide leaner network designs.
arxiv-2509-00707:
Daehoon Gwak leads seven authors in total, with Minseo Jung, Junwoo Park, Minho Park, ChaeHun Park, Junha Hyung, and Jaegul Choo, in improving masked diffusion language models. Such models generate text by unmasking tokens in parallel, a non-autoregressive approach, meaning tokens are not produced strictly one by one, yet standard decoding often falls back into a sequential order.

Gwak and his co-authors propose Reward-Weighted Sampling, which uses an external reward model to judge each whole intermediate sequence during generation. The scores rescale token logits, the model's raw preferences, boosting tokens that support global coherence. Theory shows the scaling induces helpful rank reversals and raises expected reward, and experiments improve both non-autoregressive order and overall metrics.
arxiv-2509-00907:
Jediah Tau and one co-author, John T Whelan, investigate hardware injections in LIGO's third observing run. Simulated continuous gravitational wave signals were physically added to the detectors through auxiliary laser actuation on test-mass mirrors, before any data cleaning, to validate search methods.

Two periodic signals mimicked a spinning neutron star in a low-mass X-ray binary like Scorpius X-1. Tau and Whelan searched with the model-based cross-correlation pipeline, using an orbital parameter region sized like the plausible range for Scorpius X-1 but containing each injection. Their self-blinded analysis confidently detected one injection. The other, made with lower amplitude in a costlier frequency region, was not detected, though a deeper targeted search at its true parameters verified its imprint.
arxiv-2509-01307:
How fast a galaxy turns gas into stars follows a known relation, but its fine detail inside galaxy centers is less clear. K Sruthi, with five co-authors, examines that relation in three nearby barred spiral galaxies that host active nuclei. They combine ultraviolet images from AstroSat with carbon monoxide maps from the ALMA telescope array.

The data trace recent star formation and molecular gas at a sharp scale of about one hundred twenty to one hundred thirty-two parsecs. The fitted relation was sublinear in all three galaxies, with slopes from about zero point one seven to zero point seven one in plain terms. One galaxy showed a firm relation matching past work, while the other two were weaker, likely due to fewer star-forming regions and dense central gas. The study refines how gas feeds stars near galaxy cores.
arxiv-2509-01407:
A phylogenetic tree maps how species are related through evolution, and gene sequences give molecular evidence for building such trees. S M Rafiuddin proposes a model that fuses existing tree-building methods with a genetic algorithm, a population-based search that breeds candidate solutions toward better ones. The goal is an independent platform for estimating trees from sequence data.

Gene data are drawn from the NCBI Entrez databases, a major public store of biological records. A modular parallel design handles the data set efficiently, splitting the work across parts that can run at once. Benchmark approaches for tree populations supply the search techniques to be combined. Rafiuddin presents the model as a way to search the huge space of possible trees and settle on the best estimate for a given set of gene sequences.
arxiv-2509-01707:
Ao Sun, Zhihan Wang, and Jinxin Xue study the singular set of mean curvature flow, a process that moves a surface by its bending. Singular points are spots where the flow breaks down and the shape pinches. The authors focus on singular sets shaped like cylinders in higher dimensions. They ask how smooth and structured those sets must be.

The team proves the sets sit inside a smooth curved sheet of the same dimension, once thin lower parts are removed. When the set itself forms such a sheet, its bending is fixed by the flow shape near the pinch. They also give a close profile of the flow and a size estimate near these points. The proof rests on a new distance bound that filters out slow fading modes.
arxiv-2509-01807:
Smbat Grigoryan extends a model he built for particle spectra from collider crashes to also cover sideways flow patterns. The model blends a blast wave picture, where matter expands like an explosion, with flexible statistical terms. Earlier work fit how many particles emerge at each sideways momentum in Large Hadron Collider data. The extension now targets elliptic flow, which measures how flow strength varies with direction.

The extended model fits both spectra and flow for many particle types, from light pions to heavy charmed states. Data cover lead and xenon crashes at several energies and crash alignments. Predictions for oxygen crashes at a stated energy are also given. The model even works at much lower energies from an older collider, widening its reach.
arxiv-2509-02007:
Shreyash Adappanavar leads four co-authors with mFARM, a fairness audit for language models in clinical decision support. Models in high stakes medical use can inherit and amplify social biases. Simple fairness metrics miss the multi sided nature of medical harm. Worse, they can reward models that stay clinically inert and safe but wrong.

Two large controlled benchmarks are built from a public intensive care database. Each holds tens of thousands of prompts varied by race and gender across context tiers. The audit scores allocational, stability, and latent disparity, then blends them into one mark. A balance score pairs fairness with accuracy to expose trade-offs. Four open models and tuned variants are tested under compression and context cuts.
arxiv-2509-02107:
Shaoshuai Chu and Michael Herty build high order schemes for random flow laws that keep mass and push. Such laws rule how fluids move, and random inputs add doubt to the flow. Young measures are tools that can hold wavy, spiky answers to those laws. A past first order scheme turned the task into a straight equation solved by linear programming.

A second order form comes from straight line rebuilds of point values on each side. A fifth order form adapts a weighted scheme that steers clear of fake waves. Tests on both random and fixed cases show much more sharp breaks in the flow. Cases span Burgers flow, Euler flow for light gas, and gas with no push. The new forms keep the good build of the first scheme.
arxiv-2509-02707:
Daciberg Lima Gonçalves, John Guaschi, and Carolina de Miranda e Pereiro wrote a 2025 topology paper. It studies mixed braid groups. Such groups describe braids whose strands come in several labelled families on a surface. They ask when a classic exact sequence for such braids splits.

The surfaces treated are the torus and the Klein bottle. Splitting means a projection admits a consistent way back, called a section. For projections that drop the last family, a section exists exactly when the first family's strand count divides every other family's count. Other cases get partial conclusions. The proofs compute suitable mixed braid groups and key quotient groups. Splitting questions reveal how braid groups decompose into simpler pieces.
arxiv-2509-03307:
Marta Silva and 3 co-authors tested machine learning inference for hunting anomalous Higgs couplings in 2025. The Higgs boson's links to W bosons could hide deviations from the Standard Model, and such deviations might relate to the cosmic surplus of matter over antimatter. The authors study one Higgs production channel ending in a lepton, a neutrino, and bottom quarks.

Two simulation-based inference methods are compared: one estimates a likelihood ratio for each event, the other builds an optimized observable for the target parameters. Both are also checked against traditional histograms of motion and angle variables. The learning methods beat one-dimensional histograms and matched two-dimensional ones. Cutting to a cleaner signal region sharpened sensitivity to one class of couplings without losing the other. Robustness fixes for the ratio method are a clear next step.
arxiv-2509-03607:
Ignacio Magaña Hernandez and one co-author's 2025 research paper measures cosmic expansion with spectral sirens, gravitational-wave events whose distance comes from the waves alone. Most sirens need a visible counterpart or a complete galaxy catalogue to fix redshift, the stretching of light by expansion. Spectral sirens instead use bumps in the black hole mass distribution as a ruler.

Their data come from GWTC-4.0, the latest gravitational-wave transient catalogue, holding 153 strong binary black hole candidates. Three population models are fitted: two parametric shapes with power laws and peaks, and a flexible Gaussian process model that lets the data draw the shape. All give broadly consistent values for the Hubble constant, which sets the expansion rate. The Gaussian process result, combined with the bright event GW170817, reaches about ten percent precision, the tightest in the study.
arxiv-2509-03907:
Subhojit Roy and three co-authors' 2025 physics paper takes up a pairing mechanism for unconventional superconductivity in single layers of transition metal dichalcogenides. These atom-thin materials show several odd traits under Ising spin-orbit coupling, where electron spins are pinned by the lattice. Experiments report collective Leggett modes, a nodal energy gap, an unusually large in-plane critical field, and a twofold gap anisotropy.

Their mechanism pairs electrons through spin and charge fluctuations. For monolayer tantalum disulfide, they identify its dominant instability. An added electron-phonon term is then tested against experiments. The theory stabilises a ground state whose density of states looks nodal, matching tunnelling microscope results. The large in-plane critical field follows from Ising coupling combined with mixing of even and odd parity pairing. A magnetic field applied in the plane splits the ground state's degeneracy, yielding the twofold pattern behind the anisotropy.
arxiv-2509-04107:
Ozgu Goksu and one co-author, Nicolas Pugeault, tackle uneven training data in federated learning for a 2025 computer science paper. Federated learning trains one shared model across many devices without gathering their private data in one place. Trouble starts when each device sees very different examples, or only a few, so merged models generalize poorly. Their method, FedQuad, works directly on how examples are arranged inside the model.

Similar examples are pulled closer together while different classes are pushed farther apart, across all devices. That tidier layout reduces the damage done when local models are averaged. Tested on two standard image data sets under many lopsided splits, FedQuad beat earlier approaches. The authors also map where this style of training helps most.
arxiv-2509-04407:
Roman Krcmar and two co-authors calculate the magnetic field made by straight wires spread across a hyperboloid in a 2025 physics paper. A hyperboloid is a saddle-like surface curving away in opposite directions. Currents run steadily, or nearly so, along identical wires placed at equal spacings on that surface. The authors work out how the resulting magnetic field distributes through space, and what force each wire feels from all the others.

A dense limit, where wires crowd into a continuous sheet, receives the same treatment. The discussion closes with an application: shaping current paths this hyperbolic way as a route to generating high magnetic fields. Magnet designers gain a new geometry to consider.
arxiv-2509-05707:
Families of hyperbolic complex manifolds can change only in an all-or-nothing way, Mu-Lin Li, Sheng Rao, and Mengjiao Wang prove in a 2025 complex geometry paper. A hyperbolic complex manifold is one whose geometry forbids certain maps from the complex plane, making it rigid in spirit.

For a smooth family over a disk, the set of parameters where the fibre equals a fixed hyperbolic manifold is either discrete or the whole base. Over a compact Riemann surface the set is finite or everything. For the projective line and elliptic curves the authors conjecture the set is empty or everything. Deformation questions of this kind measure how special hyperbolic manifolds are among all complex manifolds.
arxiv-2509-05907:
Offloading computing tasks from moving vehicles to roadside edge servers is optimized in a 2025 paper by Qianren Li and three co-authors. Vehicles hand jobs to base stations, which pass them to an edge server, but random speeds make future positions unknowable. Planning must therefore balance cell choice, upload time, and throughput under uncertainty.

The authors frame a scheduling period as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and solve it on two time scales. At the start of each super slot, deterministic optimization yields a reference plan and an approximate value function. Within the super slot, each small slot improves its action against that approximation, a scheme with a proven cost bound. Tests driven by a high-fidelity traffic simulator show clear gains over baseline schedulers.
arxiv-2509-06207:
Families of sets where the biggest intersecting subfamilies sit at single points are the Erdős-Ko-Rado property, and J. B. Ebrahimi and A. Taherkhani prove it by composition in a 2025 paper. Their framework builds the property for large systems from smaller subfamilies already known to have it, including the strong form where point stars are the only maxima.

The method streamlines proofs of classic results from Katona's cycle method, admissible orderings, permutations, and perfect matchings. Its new power shows on copies of a fixed hypergraph inside a complete hypergraph: for large enough ground sets, that family has the strong property. Cycle families in complete and complete bipartite graphs get a series of related results.
arxiv-2509-06807:
Safer language models that stay useful instead of refusing everything are the target of a 2025 paper led by Yanrui Du, with five co-authors. Security tuning often makes models overly conservative, trading usability away. The authors aim to push the balance point itself, the Pareto frontier, rather than slide along it.

Their framework, MoGU, routes each layer's work between a security-tuned and a usability-tuned variant, with routers that sense hidden states and allocate weights dynamically. The second version tightens that coupling: routers sit only in layers carrying clear security features, and backbone modules join router training for two-way adaptation. Results hold across mainstream, on-device, and reasoning models. Even after instruction fine-tuning weakens safety, a simple data-mixing step restores security without losing task gains.
arxiv-2509-07007:
Pradosh Keshav MV and Arun Kenath study what phase changes do to black hole horizons in a 2025 paper. A horizon is the edge of a black hole, past which light cannot escape. How it acts under stress, such as near collapse or at a phase change, is still poorly known. That is all the more true for soft hair and for a slow growth effect found at extreme horizons.

The pair show that when conformal symmetry, a scale symmetry of the field laws, breaks as a black hole sheds its hair, the horizon's layout is reshaped. That shift brings wild growth in entropy terms and new pressure-like terms. Those terms grow by set scaling laws, much like phase changes in condensed matter, with the most extreme holes acting as critical points. With mild boundary rules, the horizon can be kept stable with no ad hoc fixes, they argue.
arxiv-2509-07107:
Yingjia Li and 3 co-authors study how to steer an exciton with an electric field in a 2025 paper. An exciton is a bound pair, an electron tied to the hole it left behind in a semiconductor, and it can carry energy. They tune a time-dependent electric field to control where it goes.

A stripe-like gate acts on the exciton and drives its quantum dipole moment, which changes over time. The authors offer a search method that needs far less computing than a brute-force hunt. It still finds good control settings efficiently. With those settings, the exciton can be placed precisely, with a chosen final velocity, after a set time of travel. The results point toward control of exciton flows and populations. They also point toward shaping where light is emitted, place by place, in flat semiconducting structures.
arxiv-2509-07207:
Mack Dowell Komba Moudoumou and 2 co-authors give a new variational principle in 2025 for a gas of sticky particles that start out accelerating. Sticky particle models track grains or matter clumps that merge when they collide, forming clusters. Such models help solve pressureless gas equations, a system where particles move without pressure pushing them apart, even under an outside force.

The authors characterize clusters that form when the acceleration function decreases over time. Their principle rests on how mass is spread over particle velocities and on the shape of that acceleration. Momentum conservation requires care, since the force on each particle must be counted as clusters form. The result gives a fresh solution route for the forced pressureless gas system. It may help model flows where outside forcing and clumping act together.
arxiv-2509-07507:
Saad Lahlali and 4 co-authors present MVAT in 2025, a method for detecting 3D objects when only 2D box labels are available. Labeling 3D data is costly, while 2D boxes drawn on camera images are far cheaper. The catch is projection ambiguity: one 2D box can match many 3D poses, and a single viewpoint often hides part of an object.

MVAT aggregates object point clouds across time in sequential data to build fuller 3D representations. A teacher network learns from single views but is trained toward targets built from those aggregated objects. The teacher then creates high-quality pseudo-labels, stand-in labels, that a student learns to predict from one view for both still and moving objects. A multi-view projection loss ties predicted 3D boxes to all 2D labels. Tests use the nuScenes and Waymo Open driving datasets.
arxiv-2509-08307:
Julian A. Lawn and 2 co-authors compute how long a DNA strand can survive as a wire in a 2025 paper. The strand is held between two electrodes, and a current runs through it. The current does more than carry charge. It reshapes the energy landscape the strand sits in. It adds a drag force and random kicks.

The team follows the strand's main bending motion with a dynamics method built for open quantum systems. They time how long the junction lasts before it breaks. Even low voltages hurt. The safe spot shifts toward the breaking point, and the guard barrier shrinks. DNA-based circuits are a real hope for tiny electronics. This work sets honest limits on the currents they can take.
arxiv-2509-08607:
Mapping gravity around asteroids and comets is the goal of Pietro Fanti and 1 co-author in a 2025 paper introducing MasconCube. Spacecraft fly close to these irregular bodies, where older spherical models fail. Polyhedral models assume even density, and neural methods can be slow to train.

MasconCube places point masses, called mascons, on a regular three-dimensional grid and learns their values directly. Known shape data limits the possible answers. Tests on Bennu, Eros, Itokawa, and synthetic bodies beat rival methods on several measures. Training runs about forty times faster than GeodesyNets, while the mass layout stays easy to read.
arxiv-2509-08707:
Ada Fang and 3 co-authors introduce Igloo, a tokenizer for antibody loops, in a 2025 paper. Antibody loops called CDRs bind to antigens and shape new drug design. Older grouping methods cover only part of loop diversity and fit poorly with protein foundation models.

Igloo encodes both backbone angles and sequence, trained so similar loops sit close in latent space. It retrieves matching loops better than prior methods and assigns tokens to all loops. Added to protein language models, it improves binding prediction on most targets tested. It also samples new loops that are diverse in sequence yet consistent in structure.
arxiv-2509-09007:
A supersolid flows like a superfluid while keeping a crystal's order, and it has only been made with ultracold atoms. J. L. Figueiredo, J. T. Mendonça, and H. Terças predict a version made of light in a 2025 research paper. Their setting is a semiconductor microcavity filled with plasma. Inside it, photons gain effective mass and interact through the plasma.

The authors derive the governing equation with a tunable photon-photon interaction. Under steady laser driving, the cavity light can crystallize spontaneously into a supersolid lattice through an instability. The effect needs only weak light-matter coupling and no hybrid light-matter particles. They identify realistic electron densities and light intensities for an experiment. A photonic supersolid would give physicists a new, comparatively accessible platform for studying quantum order that usually demands extreme cooling.
arxiv-2509-09107:
Pritam Sen and 2 co-authors present CryptGNN for secure inference with graph neural networks in a 2025 paper. Clients may use a third party graph model in the cloud as a service. Input data, graph structure, and model parameters all need protection from other parties.

Secure message passing and feature transformation layers use distributed secure multi-party computation. No trusted server is required, and the system works with any number of computing parties. Security is proved even if all but one party collude. Analysis and experiments demonstrate both security and efficiency. The design lets sensitive graph data be used without exposing it to the cloud.
arxiv-2509-09307:
Zhengzhao Lai and 7 co-authors present MatCha, a benchmark for materials characterization image understanding, in a 2025 paper. Characterization images reveal links between processing, microstructure, and properties in materials. Multimodal models show promise in materials science, but their grasp of real characterization data was untested.

MatCha holds fifteen hundred questions demanding expert level knowledge across four research stages and twenty-one tasks. Leading multimodal models score far below human experts. Performance degrades further on questions needing higher expertise and finer visual perception. Few-shot and chain of thought prompting do not close the gap. The benchmark aims to spur work on material discovery and autonomous science agents.
arxiv-2509-09607:
Erini Lambrides and 52 co-authors report iron emission lines in 2025 from a distant compact red source seen by the James Webb Space Telescope. These so-called Little Red Dots, found in surprising numbers in the early universe, show odd spectra with broad hydrogen lines. Guesses about them range from black holes buried in dense gas to extremely packed star systems, with large stakes for early galaxy growth.

Lambrides and colleagues found several rare multiply ionised iron features, plus a possible highly ionised iron line, in a source from the universe's first eight hundred million years. Such signatures strongly favour an actively feeding supermassive black hole. Balmer absorption details, narrow and comparatively shallow, add further clues about the gas around it.
arxiv-2509-09907:
Diane Donovan and 2 co-authors build fresh families of Heffter arrays in a 2025 combinatorics paper. Such an array fills a square grid with signed whole numbers. Each row and each column sums to zero. Each line holds a fixed count of entries. The values cover a cyclic group in plus and minus pairs. A small subgroup is left out. Open cases for such arrays are many.

The authors build two new endless families. The new arrays have one extra virtue. They are strippable, so they can be peeled apart in a set way. With those families in hand, one case is now closed in full. That case has three entries per line. Its grid size is prime. It is a tidy end for one corner of the field.
arxiv-2509-10007:
Samuli Soutukorva and 3 co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a system for teaching robots paths by showing them. Rather than code a route, a person demonstrates a path shape, and the system stores it as a Gaussian path model, a statistical summary of the curve. Many such models, of many shapes, form a library the robot can draw on.

New demonstrations can be matched against the library to classify which known path a person is showing. The authors also give a way to reshape an existing model through a fresh demonstration, using geometric analysis of the new path. The aim is intuitive motion programming: people who cannot code can still teach a robot how to move.
arxiv-2509-10107:
Dmitrii S. Bespalov and 60 co-authors benchmark how scientists read X-ray scattering data from warm dense matter in this 2025 paper. Warm dense aluminium, squeezed to extreme pressure, is hard to diagnose, and the standard analysis leans on uniform electron gas models. The team fired femtosecond X-ray pulses through aluminium shocked to high pressure at the European XFEL facility and recorded scattering over many angles.

The measured plasmon signal showed the standard models overshoot the resonance energy by a clear margin. A first-principles treatment matched the data within error, once the disorder created by the shock was taken into account. The authors conclude that reliable readings of such experiments need that fuller treatment, at least for aluminium in this state.
arxiv-2509-10607:
Nahuel Mirón-Granese and Claudia G. Scóccola study a subtle bias in cosmology measurements in this 2025 paper. The tensor-to-scalar ratio, usually called r, measures the strength of gravitational waves from the early universe, read from polarization patterns in the cosmic microwave background. Dark radiation that interacts with itself can quietly change that pattern.

In their model the dark radiation behaves like a light particle with self-interactions. Those interactions reduce the damping of gravitational waves, which boosts the expected signal. Running mock data through standard analysis, they find that ignoring the interactions can shift the inferred r by about as much as the error bars of coming experiments. Careful modeling, they argue, is essential for unbiased results.
arxiv-2509-10707:
Sajjad Abdoli and 2 co-authors study how AI models judge each other's work in this 2025 paper. Their test material was image descriptions written by a vision-language model, graded by three members of the GPT family. The question was whether each grader has a stable style of its own, an evaluation personality, rather than a neutral yardstick.

Clear personalities emerged. One model graded with tight consistency, one was best at catching errors, and the largest was strict yet erratic. Control tests with a different model writing the questions confirmed the styles belong to the graders. The GPT models also showed a shared tilt toward negative judgments, about two to one, which did not appear in the other family tested.
arxiv-2509-11407:
Syed Emad Uddin Shubha and Tasnuva Farheen map a stealthy attack on shared quantum computers. This 2025 quantum security paper treats multi-tenant hardware. One user's pulses can leak into a neighbor's qubits. The leak path is crosstalk. An attacker can inject chosen errors across the tenant line.

The team built the first pipeline that tracks such an attack end to end. It starts at raw pulses. It ends at a clear logical error channel. Density-matrix simulation does one stage. Quantum process tomography does another. A new isometry-based step pulls out an equivalent circuit. On a three-qubit chain, two roles emerged. One hostile qubit drives the induced rotation. A second acts as a catalyst and sharpens it. The team proposes watching for the attack's signs.
arxiv-2509-11507:
Jared Zhu and Junde Wu design an agent-based operating layer for digital health in a 2025 paper called MedicalOS. Clinical software has eased routine work, yet clinicians still juggle many tools, repeat manual steps, and work through complex screens instead of caring for patients.

MedicalOS turns plain language orders into predefined health commands that follow trusted clinical rules. Tasks such as patient inquiry, history lookup, exam handling, report writing, referrals, and treatment planning are wrapped as ready-made tools. The authors checked the system on hundreds of patient cases across many specialties. It showed high diagnostic scores, sound exam requests, and steady structured reports and medication advice. The design aims at trustworthy, scalable workflow automation.
arxiv-2509-11607:
Jun Wu and twenty-seven co-authors survey wireless networks for a coming low-altitude economy. This 2025 review looks at the drone age. Swarms of drones promise new services. Their airspace is dynamic and interference-prone. Yesterday's aerial systems cannot cover it well.

The authors describe the low-altitude wireless network frame. It folds many jobs into one design. Communication is one job. Sensing, computation, control, energy delivery, and air traffic management are others. The survey covers the frame's basics and how its functions grew. It covers the metrics used to judge performance. Privacy and security worries of an open-air network get a section. The newest work on airspace structure and traffic control closes the survey.
arxiv-2509-12107:
Asking questions back, in the Socratic style, versus telling rich stories: which makes a better AI coach for teachers? Si Chen and six co-authors compare the two conversational designs in 2025 through TeaPT, a language model built for instructors' professional growth.

Forty-one higher-education instructors tried both versions in a mixed-method study. The Socratic mode, which guides reflection through questions, drew greater engagement. The Narrative mode, which offers elaborated suggestions, won when people wanted concrete guidance they could act on. Experience and attitude split the preferences further: newer, AI-optimistic instructors leaned Socratic, while seasoned, AI-cautious ones chose Narrative. The authors draw design lessons for teaching-focused AI that adapts its conversational stance to the instructor in front of it.
arxiv-2509-12407:
Some random graph models look the same after nodes are merged into groups. That property is called discrete scale invariance. It turns up in network renormalization. Alessio Catanzaro and two co-authors work out the spectrum of such a graph in 2025. Node fitness follows a heavy-tailed Pareto law. Its mean is infinite.

The leading eigenvalues all grow like the square root of the node count. They alternate in sign. They sit where the real axis meets a logarithmic spiral in the complex plane. The Gamma function describes that spiral. Their eigenvectors show complex scaling exponents and log-periodic wiggles. Those are the fingerprints of the scale symmetry. Ordinary random graphs behave quite differently.
arxiv-2509-12507:
Anna Deichler and 3 co-authors teach embodied agents to point, in a 2025 paper. Talking with people in a shared physical space takes more than words. Gestures matter, and pointing is one of the most useful. Their system creates such pointing gestures for conversational agents that share a setting with their users.

The method mixes two kinds of learning. From motion capture examples it imitates how people point. It then improves by reinforcement, earning rewards for doing the job well. The training set of captured motion was small. Still, the learned motor control policy produced gestures that are physically valid and look natural. The points also landed on their targets with high accuracy. The team scored the system with plain objective measures. They also ran a referential game in virtual reality with human players. The authors report higher naturalness and accuracy than leading supervised models achieved.
arxiv-2509-12807:
Ankur Mahesh, William Collins and three co-authors set a physics bound in 2025 for how much heat and moisture atmospheric rivers carry toward the poles. These long, wet wind bands shape floods and water supply, but rival detectors disagree on their counts and strength.

The team computes fast swirls of moist air moving poleward, a flow that physics caps from above. That cap checks the spread of detector results for count, strength, and change over time. In past climate the cap sits near the peak band in north winter. In a warmer future run both the flow and its swings grow. The bound gives forecasts a firm check.
arxiv-2509-13207:
Zucheng Gao, Azadeh Moradinezhad Dizgah and Zvonimir Vlah compress in 2025 the parity-odd part of galaxy four-point signals into two one-way spectra. Parity breach on cosmic scales would hint at new physics. Scalar galaxy data forces use of the bulky trispectrum.

Kurto spectra pair weighted squared fields, or a linear with a cubic field. An FFTLog pipe gives fast theory values. Tests on perturbed and full N-body fields validate the gauges, with and without odd starts. Phase-matched subtraction tames even noise for matter. Halo noise needs weight and cross tricks. A Euclid-like forecast is given.
arxiv-2509-13307:
Toby Lovick and 4 co-authors demonstrate GPU-accelerated Bayesian model comparison in cosmology in a 2025 paper. Comparing cosmological models requires computing Bayesian evidence, a measure of how well a model explains data, in high-dimensional parameter spaces. Nested sampling is a reliable method for that computation but can be slow on CPUs.

Using neural emulators and likelihoods built with JAX for cosmic microwave background and cosmic shear analyses, their framework provides parameter constraints and direct evidence calculation. In a thirty-nine dimensional analysis comparing two dark energy models, they produced Bayes factors with a robust error bar in just two days on a single high-end GPU, without loss of accuracy. Interpolation in the matter power spectrum gave a further speed-up with consistent results.
arxiv-2509-13407:
Gal Shavit explains in 2025 why nematic order boosts superconductivity in layered graphene via quantum geometry. Layered graphene hosts linked phases from superconductivity to Hall states. Nematic breaks, where threefold symmetry breaks on its own, often sit beside robust superconducting phases.

Symmetry breaking reshapes Bloch waves near the Fermi level. The quantum metric, a gauge of wave overlap, grows and spreads in response. Pairing via the geometric Kohn-Luttinger path then amplifies sharply. Coupling rises in ranges that labs probe. Geometry takes center stage, and nematic tuning offers a knob for stronger exotic states.
arxiv-2509-13507:
Artem Savkin, Thomas Lapotre and three co-authors add fake walkers to Cityscapes in 2025 to help self-driving cars spot people. Fake data can cover rare street cases that cars must handle. A gap in look and light still splits fake streets from real ones.

The team builds a pipe that places virtual walkers in custom scenes. A new net learns the light of the data set in an adversarial way, meaning it trains against a critic. That step lifts how real the added walkers look. Scores on two tasks, pixel tagging and object splits, test the pipe. The gains back light-aware adds for walker training.
arxiv-2509-13607:
S. Hutschenreuter and seven co-authors map the motions of the Scorpius-Centaurus OB association in a 2025 astronomy paper. Sco-Cen is the nearest large group of young, massive stars, and its three-dimensional velocity field records how stellar feedback has pushed the group apart over time.

Working from Gaia DR3 positions and radial velocities, the team reconstructs the field without assuming a fixed shape, using information field theory on a fine grid. They find a main field plus a younger component in Upper Scorpius and Lupus, clear signs of feedback-driven expansion, and only a minor role for galactic rotation. Gas in nearby clouds moves in broadly similar patterns but with offsets of a few kilometers per second, suggesting young stars and gas partly drift apart.
arxiv-2509-13907:
Jiyun Im and three co-authors improve few-shot three-dimensional point cloud segmentation in a 2025 computer vision paper. The task labels every point of a new scene using only a handful of labeled examples, by building prototypes from the examples and matching points against them. The usual sampling method for picking prototype points is unstable, since its random choices swing the results.

The team replace it with attention-based prototype generation for stability, but find plain attention suffers a distribution gap between prototype tokens and support features. Their module, WARM, wraps cross-attention with whitening before attention and coloring after it, realigning distributions in both directions. It set a new best result by a wide margin on the S3DIS dataset and stayed competitive on ScanNet.
arxiv-2509-14007:
Karim Elbakly and four co-authors map how entropy patches behave at a choked nozzle in a 2025 fluid mechanics paper. A patch of hotter gas convecting through a nozzle throat, as in a jet engine, generates sound that travels upstream, part of the indirect noise behind combustion instability. Which simplified model predicts that sound depends on the patch in ways nobody had charted.

Two-dimensional Euler simulations revealed two regimes separated by one ratio: the patch's streamwise length against the throat height. Short patches obey an inertial model; longer patches obey a quasi-steady matching-condition model. Patch shape mattered little. A second ratio, perturbation energy against upstream energy, showed both linear models hold only for weak patches. The result is a practical selection map for engine noise modeling.
arxiv-2509-14107:
Joan Llobera-Querol, Sascha Husa, and Maria de Lluc Planas construct hybrid waveforms for precessing binaries in a 2025 paper. Waveform models must cover the full inspiral, merger, and ringdown. Full relativity simulations are the most accurate source, but they are too short because they are so expensive. Hybridization stitches a long analytic inspiral onto a short numerical merger. Precession, the wobbling of the orbital plane, makes that stitching delicate.

Gauge loose ends, frame dependence, and spin dynamics all threaten the alignment step. The systems are precessing and quasi-circular. The authors' careful approach assumes little about the merger waveforms. It works in the quadrupole-aligned frame to suppress mode mixing. The result is a robust, broadly applicable recipe for building complete precessing waveforms. The uses are parameter estimation and model calibration.
arxiv-2509-15307:
Newlin C. Weatherford and Ana Bonaca warn that stellar stream measurements used to probe dark matter carry a selection effect in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Streams of stars torn from globular clusters get heated by passing dark matter subhalos, and their velocity spread is a favored dark matter probe. Standard stream models neglect strong encounters, retained black holes, and mass segregation inside the parent cluster.

Monte Carlo N-body simulations under Galactic tides generate realistic mock streams to test the omission. The velocity spread turns out to correlate with stellar mass, especially after core collapse expels the cluster's black holes. Kinematic cuts that observers routinely apply then bias the measured spread. Unless modelers include cluster-internal physics, dark matter inferences from stream heating risk reading a selection effect as a subhalo signal.
arxiv-2509-15507:
Shenghai Yuan leads a team that helps rescue workers see through walls. In a burning or ruined building, blocked views hide both victims and hazards. Their system, STARC, joins a ground robot's mapping with laser sensing worn by the responder. The robot scans wide areas and spots people in three dimensions.

The worn sensor is aligned to the robot's map by matching their poses. Found people and their point clouds then appear in the responder's view as an overlay, with low delay. Tests in mock runs, lab setups, and field trials show firm alignment and stable overlays. The team plan to release the code and design. The work aims to cut risk for first responders.
arxiv-2509-16107:
Words that could point to more than one thing force speakers to use shared context and common sense. Lukas Ellinger and Georg Groh test whether large language models can clear up such vague references in short chats. They built a new multi-language test set and checked five models with both machine and human judges.

Most models picked one reading or listed all options, rather than asking for more detail. Asking for simpler language made the problem worse, with less use of common sense. Extra training of one small model with a preference method improved its handling a lot. The gap shows a clear target for future tuning.
arxiv-2509-16407:
Hash tables on graphics chips speed up big data jobs, but most lack full support for tasks that run at the same time.
