Blessing A. Kyem leads a student team from North Dakota State University in teaching AI to narrate traffic safety videos. Understanding near-miss and crash footage in fine detail could help prevent accidents. Their 2025 arXiv paper pairs two vision-language models with divided labor. One model, VideoLLaMA, specializes in writing captions; the other, Qwen2.5-VL, answers questions about the footage.

The key insight is that training the two skills together makes them interfere. Trained separately, each model shines where it is strongest. VideoLLaMA proved especially good at temporal reasoning, earning the top captioning score, while Qwen2.5-VL led on visual question answering accuracy, at about sixty-one percent. On the WTS dataset the combined system placed tenth in the 2025 AI City Challenge's second track. Ablation tests confirmed the split strategy, beating joint training by about nine percent in question answering while keeping caption quality.
arxiv-2510-12207:
Thim and co-authors compute the ground state energies of the deuteron and triton in chiral effective field theory, in a 2025 arXiv nuclear theory paper. These are the bound nuclei of two and three nucleons, and their energies are basic tests of nuclear forces. The authors push earlier work to next to next to leading order, treating weaker interactions as small corrections rather than exactly.

Triton calculations use the no core shell model, a method that includes all nucleons actively. The team shows converged results for regulator cutoffs up to about twelve hundred mega electron volts, where the cutoff limits how much short range detail the theory keeps. They examine special cutoffs in two nucleon channels that cause unwanted cutoff dependence. Redefining the leading order wave function removes the effect in one channel for both nuclei, but in the other channel it fixes the deuteron and not the triton.
arxiv-2510-12307:
Bermudez and colleagues propose a numerical scheme for the coupled physics of porous media where stress changes how fluids diffuse, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Poroelasticity describes fluid filled porous solids, like tissues or rock, whose deformation and flow influence each other. Here diffusion is stress assisted, so compression alters the transport of a dissolved substance.

The method is a fully mixed virtual element scheme, meaning it solves directly for stresses and fluxes on meshes of general polygons. It enforces strong symmetry of the total stress via the Hellinger Reissner principle. A novelty is a weaker assumption on the stress assisted diffusion factor, handled by studying the perturbed diffusion equation in Banach spaces. The authors prove both problems solvable, adapting abstract theory for perturbed saddle point problems, and establish optimal error estimates. Numerical examples confirm the scheme's behavior and robustness across parameter values.
arxiv-2510-12607:
Heidari and Podolskij build a statistical test for whether a chosen volatility model actually fits a system of interacting particles, in a 2025 arXiv paper. McKean Vlasov equations describe large particle systems whose dynamics depend on the whole spread of particles, a mean field picture used in physics and finance. Volatility estimates in such systems are established, but formally testing one was largely unexplored.

Their test statistic uses discrete readings of the system, in a regime where both the count of particles and the sampling rate grow. The estimators involved are proven consistent: estimates settle on the truth as data accumulate. The statistic itself satisfies a central limit theorem. It converges to a centered Gaussian distribution, which is what makes usable critical values possible. The framework gives users a sound fit check for volatility choices in nonlinear diffusion and mean field models.
arxiv-2510-12907:
Aougab surveys how to study pseudo-Anosov surface maps through their mapping tori in this 2025 arXiv chapter. A pseudo-Anosov map stretches and folds a surface in a chaotic yet structured way. Its mapping torus is the three-dimensional space built by gluing the surface to itself through the map. That space encodes the map's dynamics geometrically. The chapter is written to be accessible with minimal background.

Aougab reviews the simplicial complexes attached to a surface, such as the curve, arc, and pants complexes, which organize its loops and decompositions into a network. He explains how a map's action on those networks mirrors its own dynamics and the hyperbolic geometry of its mapping torus. The chapter covers infinite-type analogs, then presents joint work with Futer and Taylor linking curve complex action to the minimum number of fixed points in a map's isotopy class.
arxiv-2510-13007:
Nakajima studies instantons on ALE spaces for classical groups in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Instantons are special field configurations from gauge theory. Their moduli spaces, the spaces listing all of them, connect geometry to representation theory. For orthogonal and symplectic gauge groups, these spaces appear as fixed point sets of involutions. An involution is an operation that, applied twice, returns to the start. The involutions act on quiver varieties.

Building on work by Yiqiang Li, Nakajima computes the K-matrices in examples. He matches the twisted Yangians arising there with versions studied in the literature. He also states the conditions needed for those algebras to be well-defined. These are coideal subalgebras of Yangians built through stable envelope methods. The work continues a program Nakajima began in the early 1990s, linking instanton geometry to quantum algebras.
arxiv-2510-13307:
Li, Wu, Zhang, and Han discover new object classes in 3D point clouds through causal reasoning in this 2025 arXiv paper. Point cloud segmentation labels every point in a 3D scan, but real deployments meet classes never labeled in training. Novel class discovery trains on labeled base classes only, then must segment unlabeled novel classes, and sloppy statistical correlations between representations and labels confuse that inference.

The authors re-formalize the task with a structural causal model and impose causal relationships as strong constraints on learning. They analyze hidden confounders in base class representations. They build causal representation prototypes with confounders removed. They then model causal links between base and novel prototypes as a graph, enabling reasoning from known to unknown classes. Extensive experiments and visualizations on 3D and 2D discovery segmentation benchmarks demonstrated the method's superiority.
arxiv-2510-13407:
Gfeller and colleagues study colexification, where one word carries several distinct meanings, as in words covering both hand and arm. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses this pattern to probe how word meanings change over time. Why some meaning pairs merge while others stay separate remains only partly understood. The data come from dictionaries gathered across many languages in each family.

The team applies family-tree models to dictionary data from three language families. The families are Austronesian, Indo-European, and Uralic, which together span wide regions. They test three predictors: how close two concepts feel, how borrowable a word is, and how often it is used. Closely related concept pairs were colexified more widely and changed more slowly. Frequent and borrow-prone pairs changed faster and were colexified less often. The families also differed, hinting that region and culture shape the pattern.
arxiv-2510-13607:
Doat and Vanrietvelde clarify a split between rival frameworks for quantum reference frames. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks what physics looks like from inside a quantum system. Two camps built frameworks that do not agree with each other. The split traces to one choice: how strongly symmetry constrains the system.

That choice maps to a plain question: can an inside observer measure the total charge? The weak choice, they show, leaves the momenta of a perspective unclear. It also bars reversible moves from one frame to the next. They define a perspective by what an observer can and cannot do. One simple scenario then hints that inside observers could gauge the global charge. It pairs a relativized interference test with classical messages sent between observers. The paper also weighs the older arguments that each camp has offered for its approach.
arxiv-2510-13807:
Simen and a large team pull machine learning traits out of data by letting it evolve inside many-body quantum spin systems. Their 2025 arXiv paper encodes data into spin-glass Hamiltonians, where terms capture single inputs and higher-order links at once. Counterdiabatic driving, a shortcut that speeds quantum evolution, steers the dynamics. The runs execute on an IBM processor with 156 qubits.

Means of simple and higher-order readouts become the new trait vectors for each data point. Those traits expose links in the data that plain prep steps struggle to reach. Tests cover hard tasks, from telling toxic molecules apart to image recognition. Trait checks show the quantum traits often add to the plain ones, and often beat them outright. Mixing both sources gave steady gains across the tasks tried, the authors report. The work argues near-term quantum hardware has real value in data work.
arxiv-2510-13907:
Wu and co-authors optimize prompts without any labelled data, letting prompts duel under an AI judge's pairwise preferences. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles automatic prompt optimization, which usually leans on gold validation labels. Collecting those labels is slow and expensive in real deployments. Yet a decent prompt is needed before large labelled sets even exist.

The Prompt Duel Optimizer frames the search as a dueling bandit problem. Double Thompson Sampling picks the most informative prompt matchups to judge. Winners then mutate under guidance from top performers, expanding the candidate pool cleverly. Partial labels, when available, can damp the judge's noise without being required. Experiments on BIG-bench Hard and MS MARCO beat baseline optimizers consistently. Ablations credit both the sampling strategy and the mutation step for the edge. The framework suits cold-start industrial classification especially well.
arxiv-2510-14007:
Bálint László Szarvas and Maksim Zhdanov improve a family of neural networks designed to respect the symmetries of physical equations, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Clifford-Steerable CNNs build in equivariance, the rule that rotating or boosting the input must transform the output in the matching way, for systems ranging from ordinary space to relativistic spacetime. Such networks are used to forecast partial differential equations, the equations governing fluids and fields.

The authors show that the kernel basis of these networks is incomplete, which caps what the models can express. Their fix, Conditional Clifford-Steerable Kernels, lets the convolutional kernels depend on the input field itself through additional equivariant features, and they show how to solve the resulting symmetry constraint efficiently. On forecasting tasks in fluid dynamics and relativistic electrodynamics, the conditional version outperformed the baseline methods.
arxiv-2510-14107:
Madeeha Nazish and Faisal Akram calculate how often a charm-beauty meson, the Bc meson, should be produced. They consider collisions at the Large Hadron Collider and at RHIC, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Bc meson is unique, built from both a charm and a beauty quark. Its excited states feed down into the ground state. That matters for experiments hunting undiscovered family members.

Earlier work ignored quark-antiquark annihilation diagrams and covered only the S states for lead and gold nuclei. The authors compute cross sections for both 1S and 1P states, including the previously neglected diagrams. They cover proton-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus collisions. Estimates are given for gold at RHIC and for lead and xenon at the LHC. They also give momentum distributions and nuclear modification factors. The results form a baseline for studies in the LHC's Run III and for finding undiscovered Bc states.
arxiv-2510-14507:
Qin Yi, Zeping Sui, and Zilong Liu study error rates and receiver design for a waveform called zero-padded affine frequency division multiplexing, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The waveform is meant for high-mobility communications, where fast-moving receivers smear signals; its zero padding gives the time-domain channel matrix a lower-triangular structure.

Using that structure, the authors propose two low-complexity detectors. One is a minimum mean square error detector that avoids full matrix inversion. The other is a maximum ratio combining detector working in the time domain. They also analyze the bit error rate of both the mean-square detector and the maximum likelihood detector, the gold standard, too costly to use. Simulations show the detectors achieve identical performance to the inversion-based detector with much reduced complexity, which matters for real-time receivers in vehicles and trains.
arxiv-2510-14707:
Del Piano and co-authors work, in a 2025 arXiv paper, on the problem of testing Einstein's theory with black holes whose shape might deviate from prediction. Several schemes describe such deformed black holes model-independently, each with its own parameters. The Johannsen-Psaltis, Rezzolla-Zhidenko, and Effective Metric Description frameworks are three of the most used. If they secretly describe the same physics, results in one should translate into the others.

The authors construct explicit transformation maps proving exactly that equivalence, for different patches of the spacetime. They then pick representative geometries and ask how many parameters each scheme needs to reproduce the black hole's wobble tones, called quasi-normal modes, to a chosen accuracy. In all three frameworks, a finite set of coefficients suffices for the observables considered. The paper closes by noting how each scheme's strengths probe complementary aspects of black hole physics.
arxiv-2510-14907:
So and Ma connect two questions about strategic behavior, in a 2025 arXiv paper, that are usually kept apart. Which equilibria can people actually learn? And are those equilibria good for everyone? They study learning dynamics where each player seeks only personal gain. Their focus is mixed Nash equilibria, where players randomize, that are stable in a strong uniform sense, not just in the limit.

The surprise is that learnability tracks collective rationality. Under mild conditions, a mixed equilibrium that is not uniformly stable cannot be weakly Pareto optimal: the players could jointly deviate and all do better. Conversely, a locally uniformly stable equilibrium must be weakly Pareto optimal, so no joint deviation improves everyone. Uniform stability also decides whether smoothed best-response dynamics converge on their final iterates. Unlike strict equilibria, which can lock in social inefficiency, self-interested learning near mixed equilibria leads to collective rationality.
arxiv-2510-15007:
Kou and a team argue, in a 2025 arXiv paper, that the field grades language model toxicity with the wrong answer key. Today's detectors are benchmarked on single-label data, one verdict per text. But toxic content is ambiguous and has many sides: a passage can be insulting, threatening, and identity-targeting at once. Single labels produce biased scores, missed detections, and false positives. And labeling fine-grained categories is very costly.

The team releases three multi-label benchmarks built from toxicity datasets, tagged against a fifteen-category scheme. They prove a theorem: on these datasets, training with generated pseudo-labels beats learning from single-label data. Their pseudo-label-based detector puts the idea to work. In experiments it surpassed baselines by a wide margin. The authors frame multi-label evaluation, not any detector, as the fix the field needs. Measure the dimensions separately, or keep misjudging all of them.
arxiv-2510-15107:
Ivan H. C. Shum presents a leaner recipe for preparing a key quantum error-correcting state in this 2025 arXiv paper. The target is the logical state of the two-dimensional toric code, a leading design for protecting quantum information spread across a grid of qubits. Fundamental physics limits how quickly such a state can be built, since influences spread at a bounded speed.

Shum gives an algorithm that encodes the state for a square grid using only two kinds of nearby operations, controlled-NOT and Hadamard gates, which are basic building blocks of quantum circuits. The circuit depth grows in a simple linear way with the grid size, beating earlier constructions that used only local Clifford gates. Rather than tracking the state directly, the method works in the Heisenberg picture, following how the operators themselves evolve backward through the circuit.
arxiv-2510-15207:
M. F. Ciappina reviews a fast-moving field where intense laser light drives solid materials to emit much higher-frequency light, a process called high-order harmonic generation. This 2025 survey covers how the effect has grown into a tool linking ultrafast spectroscopy, quantum optics, and condensed matter physics. Recent work has turned it toward questions about topology, magnetism-like Berry phases, and the control of bound electron pairs called excitons.

Among the advances Ciappina highlights are ways to produce nonclassical light using quantum or squeezed driving fields. Nanostructured platforms now boost the emission and tune its spectrum, while cryogenic tools resolve its phase on attosecond timescales. On the theory side, multiband models that include fading coherence and light propagation have clarified how electrons move both within and between energy bands. The review frames the field as a route toward quantum-engineered sources of ultrafast light.
arxiv-2510-15407:
Yuta Inoue, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, and Atsuyuki Miyashita prove a refinement of a classic coloring result for flat maps, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Any planar graph, a network drawable on paper without crossing edges, can be colored with five colors so that adjacent vertices differ. The team adds a balance condition on top of that guarantee.

They show five colors always suffice while keeping one chosen color class small, at most a sixth of all vertices. In other words, the vertices split into five independent sets, and the last set holds no more than one vertex in six. Their proof also yields an algorithm that finds such a coloring in quadratic time. Unlike the famous four color theorem, this proof needs no computer assistance and can be verified by hand. The result tightens knowledge of how evenly the color burden can be shared in planar graphs.
arxiv-2510-15607:
Spin of light is the twisting property that photonic chips might use to carry information. Mateusz Kędziora leads the Warsaw team behind this 2025 arXiv study of perovskite crystal wires. Perovskites that host polaritons work at room temperature and can be shaped into tiny structures easily. The group patterned single crystals into microwires that guide light without added mirrors. They report edge emission whose spin pattern shows the optical spin Hall effect clearly.

Above a threshold the wires emit spin-polarized laser light with chirality above eighty percent. That spin signal travels tens of micrometres along the wire. The result points to simple chips that move spin-coded information between components.
arxiv-2510-15707:
Martín de Frutos, Laura Botero-Bolívar, and Esteban Ferrer wrote a 2025 paper on sea noise from offshore wind farms. Turbine blades send pulsing noise into the water. That noise can disturb sea animals that steer and signal by sound. The team modelled three reference turbines of growing size. They used pitch control, which tilts each blade as it turns. The tilts were timed to the rhythm of the blades passing the tower.

Their tests cut the total sound level by up to five decibels. The pulsing quality of the noise fell by about a fifth. The pitch swings were small, around five degrees. The cost was a loss of five to ten percent of the energy captured. The authors call that an acceptable trade for wind farms already built.
arxiv-2510-15907:
Era Thaqi, Dennis Eigner, Arman Ferdowsi, and Ulrich Schmid compute circuit timing symbolically, so formulas replace repeated simulation. Timing analysis tells designers when each signal in a digital circuit will switch. Their method rests on recent closed-form delay formulas for two-input NOR, NAND, and Muller C gates developed by Ferdowsi and colleagues.

Given a fixed order for all input and internal transitions, the framework produces analytic expressions for every internal switching time. Those expressions depend on the input switching times and on gate parameters, both kept symbolic. Filling in values gives per-transition timing with no simulation at all. Better, differentiating a formula with respect to a parameter or input time yields sensitivity directly. The four authors implement the approach in SageMath and demonstrate it on the c17 benchmark circuit in its NOR form.
arxiv-2510-16007:
Ziao Yang, Longbo Huang, and Hongfu Liu estimate the value of each training sample while training is still running. Data-centred learning improves models by curating good samples rather than by redesigning networks, so sample influence must be scored. Past work scores influence once, on a finished model, and misses how a sample's worth shifts during optimisation.

Their layer-aware online estimator needs only gradients from loss to output, avoiding both per-parameter and full-network gradients. That design keeps the ranking of samples faithful while slashing the cost of repeated scoring. Across large language model pretraining, fine-tuning, and image classification, the method improves accuracy at much lower time and memory cost than earlier estimators. Dynamic curation thus becomes practical at scale, the three authors argue.
arxiv-2510-16207:
Mateus Pinto da Silva and four co-authors argue that mapping tropical agriculture from satellites is mainly a data problem, not a model problem. Persistent clouds, shifting crop calendars, scarce labeled examples, and high labeling costs all undermine the usual model-centric approach, which keeps tuning architectures while the training data stay weak.

Surveying the field from a data-centric standpoint, the authors assess twenty-five strategies, among them confident learning, core-set selection, augmentation, and active learning, rating each for readiness in large mapping pipelines. They finish with a practical pipeline built from the nine most mature and straightforward methods. The tutorial targets teams who need robust, scalable crop maps under real tropical conditions rather than laboratory benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-16307:
Paul Disberg and seven co-authors pin down how much metal a galaxy can hold and still host a long gamma-ray burst. Such bursts come from collapsing massive stars, and metal-rich stars shed spin through winds, which should block the burst. Where the cutoff sits, sharp or soft, was unsettled.

The team models cosmic star birth across galaxy masses and metal levels, with realistic scatter in each link. They then try burst efficiency curves of many shapes and compare with real bursts and their host galaxies. A sharp cutoff near sixty percent of the Sun's metal level fits the data best. A lower cutoff near thirty percent, favored in print, fits poorly. The high threshold clashes with most theory models, which now must explain how bursts survive in richer gas.
arxiv-2510-16407:
Achal Agrawal and Jeet Mukherjee tackle a clerical headache in research data: the same institute appears under many name forms. Sorting out which forms mean the same place is called institute disambiguation, and string matching alone misses many aliases. Their method ignores the names' spelling entirely and clusters by people instead.

The clue is co-occurrence: if the same authors keep appearing with two name forms, those forms likely name one institute. Working only from author and affiliation records in fifty thousand Crossref articles, the clustering gives encouraging results. Its catches differ from a leading string-matching method, so the two complement each other. Combined, they can supply aliases exactly where string matching fails. The code is open source, and the authors expect scale to sharpen it further.
arxiv-2510-17007:
Ignacio M. De la Jara and three co-authors test video feature choices in a 2025 paper. Temporal video grounding finds the moment matching a spoken query. A user describes an action, and the system locates it in video. Most research reuses only a few standard video encoders.

An encoder converts raw video into compact feature numbers. The team compared encoders based on three design families. Those families were convolutional networks, temporal reasoning models, and transformers. They tested on three well-known benchmark collections of videos. Simply swapping the encoder changed performance significantly. Clear error patterns tied to specific features also appeared. Different features seemed to complement each other. The study warns the field against overfitting to one favorite encoder.
arxiv-2510-17207:
Matteo Barbon, Nadir Ijaz, and Marco Peloso study gravity waves from early cosmos growth in this 2025 paper. Axion growth, a slow roll that puffs space fast, can amp gauge fields. Strong amping can leave a wave hum that tools might catch. It can also push back on the growth field itself.

Past work that smoothed the push-back found waves in the field speed. Grid sims of late cast doubt on that smooth view. The authors gauge the field's slope energy with math inside the smooth view. They find cases with a clear wave hum and low slope energy. In those cases the smooth view holds through the whole growth phase.
arxiv-2510-17607:
Yoel Groman compares two versions of a geometry invariant in a 2025 arXiv paper. The invariant is symplectic cohomology, an algebraic tool built from curves in certain curved spaces. One version depends on how a region sits inside a larger space. The other depends only on the region's own local shape. Groman asks how the two versions relate.

He proves their leading parts match once relative area is accounted for. Under a size condition called finite boundary depth, the ambient version is a controlled deformation of the intrinsic one. A new invariant measures the size of that deformation. It behaves predictably under changes of the region and its defining data. The results feed a local to global strategy for mirror symmetry.
arxiv-2510-17907:
Beatriz Villarroel, with five co-authors, lays out a low-cost search for alien probes inside our own solar system. Artifact hunting has drawn far less formal work than radio listening, partly for technical and social reasons. New surveys and imaging tools now make a real search possible, the authors argue.

Four search methods are described, and one is shown in action. Old sky photos from before the first satellites can reveal flashes from glinting objects. Other routes use space telescopes and the light spectra of Earth-orbit items. The paper gives SETI readers a practical plan for checking our neighborhood.
arxiv-2510-18007:
Ayrton Almada, with five co-authors, builds a live dashboard that judges power grid safety after sudden line faults. Standard checks look at steady states and miss the frequency swings that follow common faults. Their screen assumes a balanced grid, drops a random line for about a second, and flags cases where flows pass safe limits afterward.

A system-wide overload score sums the risk, and a linear-scaling method rates faults without brute-force simulation. Adaptive sampling focuses effort on the dangerous cases. Grid operators get a faster way to ask what-if questions while conditions change through the day.
arxiv-2510-18207:
Shu-Xu Yi, with seven co-authors, explains why some gamma-ray burst pulses keep the same shape across energy bands. Single clean pulses that rise fast and decay slowly come from one episode of the central engine, making them ideal test cases. Their shared shape, aligned subpulses, and hardening-then-softening spectra defy most radiation models.

The proposed model fires radiation sites in sequence as a magnetic disturbance travels outward. That one mechanism reproduces the self-similar profile, the aligned subpulses, the spectral drift, and the growing subpulse widths. Burst theorists get a physical story that ties a whole list of odd traits together.
arxiv-2510-18407:
Manjie Xu and his five co-authors present a learning setup modeled on how human teachers coach students. In ordinary self-play, two identical agents improve by competing, but that symmetry fits open-ended learning poorly. A teacher instead builds challenges matched to a learner's current level. The hard part is making an artificial teacher that invents the right tasks on its own, without a fixed ladder of lessons given in advance.

Their framework, Heterogeneous Adversarial Play, casts teaching and learning as a contest: a task-making instructor tries to press the learner, while the learner tries to master each new task. Both sides adapt through feedback, so task difficulty tracks the learner's real performance rather than a preset schedule. Across several multi-task domains, the framework matched leading baselines, and the courses it generated helped both artificial agents and human learners improve.
arxiv-2510-18607:
Stephen Griffeth and David Guevara compute a quantity in algebra connected to quaternionic reflection groups, special symmetry groups whose elements act like reflections but use quaternion numbers. Each such group leaves a set of hyperplanes fixed, and mathematicians study the space formed by removing those hyperplanes. The cohomology of that space, a graded algebraic summary of its shape, is what the authors determine.

Their main result gives the graded rank of that cohomology and shows it splits into irreducible pieces whose coefficients are all positive whole numbers. For an irreducible group, nearly every piece has the simplest, linear form. At most one piece is quadratic, and that exception happens for exactly three of the exceptional groups, a tidy pattern that the computation makes visible.
arxiv-2510-18907:
Atanu Manna and Suvra Kanti Chakraborty extend a traditional Indian floor art form into new mathematical territory. Hridaya Kolam patterns are drawn from a grid of dots connected by arms, and the classic theory assumes the dot count and arm count share no common factor. When they do share one, the single looping line of the classic pattern splits into several separate closed loops.

The authors propose an algorithm based on modular arithmetic that systematically generates these multi-loop patterns for any such pair of counts. Illustrative designs for various dot and arm combinations demonstrate the resulting structures. Beyond the mathematics, they note that multi-loop Kolam designs can inspire architectural motifs and ornamental patterns for floor plans, facades, and decorative elements, connecting a living folk tradition to contemporary design.
arxiv-2510-19107:
Aliakbar Mehdizadeh and Martin Hilbert study how peer pressure changes the stated opinions of large language model agents placed in social networks. Agents updated their views after seeing what peers around them thought, across topics where their starting commitment ranged from weak to strong.

Opinion change followed an S-shaped curve: steady under mild pressure, flipping sharply past a threshold, then leveling off. Thresholds differed by model, with one system needing a large majority against it while another shifted under a dissenting minority. Flipping from yes to no also took different effort than flipping back, an asymmetry the authors highlight.
arxiv-2510-19207:
Yizhu Wang and four co-authors present DataFilter, a defense against prompt injection attacks on language model agents. When an agent reads untrusted outside data, an attacker can hide instructions in that data and hijack the agent away from the user's task toward harmful actions.

DataFilter cleans the data before it reaches the main model, removing injected instructions at test time without needing model weights, heavy utility loss, or a rebuilt system. It is trained on simulated injections to recognize malicious text. A model-agnostic filter like this could be dropped in front of many existing agents to raise their security.
arxiv-2510-19407:
Vanshika Datta and C Nahak study sensor placement under uncertainty. They apply the radius of robust feasibility. The setting is directional sensor networks on uncertain terrain. A sensor probes its surroundings. Small errors in its position can break coverage. The radius measures how much error a placement can tolerate.

The authors give an exact formula for that radius. They pair it with a distributed greedy algorithm. The algorithm aims sensors at high-value coverage regions. Tests in changing environments show better efficiency and robustness. The guidance helps on real ground, where positions never match the plan exactly.
arxiv-2510-19507:
Demian Till and five co-authors test whether teaming several different language models beats asking one model the same question many times. Consistency methods fight hallucinations by sampling repeated answers and comparing them, but a single model shares its own blind spots. The authors call their multi-model variant consortium consistency.

They assemble teams from a pool of fifteen language models with different training data and designs, then measure detection and mitigation of made-up answers. Mixed teams often improved on single-model consistency by a wide margin. The gains frequently came with lower running costs, since fewer samples per model were needed to reach the same reliability.
arxiv-2510-19707:
Jounglag Lim, James Gossell, and Keri Ann Sather-Wagstaff introduce the open neighborhood ideal of a graph and study it for trees. The ideal is an algebraic object built from the graph's open neighborhoods, and the authors describe its minimal primary decomposition using the graph's minimal total dominating sets. The central question is when this ideal has the Cohen-Macaulay property, a strong regularity condition in commutative algebra.

For trees, they prove the ideal is Cohen-Macaulay exactly when the tree is well-totally dominated, a domination condition defined in the paper. They also compute the Cohen-Macaulay type in that case. The work links a graph's domination structure directly to the algebraic quality of an associated ideal.
arxiv-2510-19907:
Cesar A. Gallegos and three co-authors use large-scale numerical simulations to chart a phase transition in a triangular lattice model of electrons in a magnetic field. At weak interaction the system sits in an integer quantum Hall phase; at intermediate interaction it becomes a chiral spin liquid, an exotic magnetic state. The team studies both with density matrix renormalization group calculations on long cylinders.

Entanglement spectra, entropy, and charge and spin pumping under inserted flux all differ sharply between the phases. Scanning the interaction strength, the authors extract critical exponents from a bond-dimerization order parameter, and the behavior matches a one-plus-one-dimensional Ising transition. A neutral excitation tied to the order parameter loses its energy gap right at the critical point, while other excitations stay gapped.
arxiv-2510-20307:
Anastasios Papazafeiropoulos and three co-authors work out key rates for a stacked smart surface that aids MIMO links. Such stacks shape waves by pure spread and beat one layer on size. Two rates had not been worked out for this pair: mean mutual facts and the outage chance. The team gets the spread of mutual facts with large random matrix tools.

From channel stats they then derive a tight closed form for outage chance. A slope step cuts that chance down, and it runs faster than a swap-based rival with less load. Sim tests back the math. Gains over plain MIMO links and over the one-layer case stand out in the plots.
arxiv-2510-20607:
Alexandru Oarga and Yilun Du propose compositional energy minimization as a route to reasoning that generalizes to harder problems than those seen in training. End-to-end reasoning models learn useful heuristics but often fail outside their training distribution. Their approach instead learns energy landscapes over the solution spaces of smaller, tractable subproblems, one energy function per subproblem type.

At test time the subproblem energies combine into a global landscape for a full problem, and extra constraints can be added during inference to build landscapes for problems of growing difficulty. A parallel energy minimization procedure improves the quality of samples drawn from the combined landscape. Across a wide set of reasoning problems, the method outperforms leading rivals and generalizes to larger, more complex instances.
arxiv-2510-20707:
Xuyang Liu, Xiyan Gui, Yuchao Zhang, and Linfeng Zhang target a memory crunch in large vision language models, where storing key and value pairs for long image and text inputs swells fast. Shrinking that store is vital if such models are to run widely without huge hardware.

Most shrink methods keep only the pairs judged most important, yet the team shows that different attention heads repeat content to very different degrees. Keeping importance alone can drop whole strands of meaning held in less obvious pairs. Their MixKV method blends importance with diversity, tuned per head, and lifts scores over plain baselines across several models, with the clearest gains under extreme shrinking.
arxiv-2510-20907:
Victor Augias and one co-author introduce convex function ranges, families of convex functions pinned by level and slope constraints, as a tool for economic design. Such families arise by nature when joining limits depend on type or when two sided dominance constraints bind a mechanism.

Main results describe the extreme points of these families geometrically, give sufficient optimality conditions for linear programs over them. Supply nested optimization methods on the lower boundary, applicable to designing outside options. Four settings, including screening problems, show the machinery at work. The framework unifies scattered design problems under one convex analytic roof.
arxiv-2510-21107:
Yunuo Zhang leads four co-authors on ESCORT, a belief record method for partly seen decision problems. An agent must sum up its action and sighting history as a spread over hidden states. Realistic settings breed complex doubt that standard models capture poorly.

Combining Stein variational methods with sliced consistency optimization, ESCORT maintains temporal beliefs that stay faithful to complicated, high dimensional doubt shapes. Accurate beliefs drive better decisions under partial information, from robotics to dialogue. The work targets the representational bottleneck that limits how far planning under doubt can scale.
arxiv-2510-21407:
Kyungjun Min and three co-authors generate chip design code with large language models, targeting the register-transfer level where hardware behavior is written before fabrication. Language models often produce code that fails functional tests, and separate tuning for power, speed, and chip area tends to get stuck near local fixes.

Their framework, REvolution, breeds a population of candidate designs, each carrying a strategy, its code, and feedback from testing. Candidates split into two pools: failures get steered toward bug repair. While successes get steered toward better power, speed, and area, and a shifting rule favors whichever prompting strategy is currently winning. On two standard benchmarks, starting pass rates rose by up to twenty-four percentage points, and one model reached a final pass rate above ninety-five percent without extra training.
arxiv-2510-21607:
Yuan Zhong controls high-dimensional systems whose state must never go negative, a constraint that defines queueing networks, where waiting jobs pile up across many stations. Steering such networks well means solving a drift control problem over a finite horizon, yet exact dynamic programming collapses under the dimension of realistic systems.

His simulation-based scheme builds the value function and its gradient through multilevel Picard iterations, a recursive Monte Carlo method. The headline theorem says the method beats the curse of dimensionality. Reaching a chosen accuracy costs work that grows only polynomially with the number of dimensions and with the inverse accuracy. Numerical trials on heavy-traffic scheduling problems for parallel server systems stay feasible up to at least twenty dimensions, suggesting the approach can serve real network control.
arxiv-2510-22107:
Bailey Trang leads a nine-author team making image generators more honestly diverse. When a prompt is ambiguous, many different pictures could satisfy it. The usual tricks, changing the random seed or rewording the prompt, give variety that is either meaningless or limited to whatever words can express.

Their framework, Rainbow, splits the input condition into several latent descriptions, each capturing one strand of the uncertainty, and renders a distinct image from each. A latent graph steered by generative flow networks, a sampling method that rewards covering many good options rather than one best option, organizes those descriptions. The method wraps around any pretrained conditional image model rather than replacing it. The goal is diversity a viewer can interpret: visibly different, individually plausible readings of the same request.
arxiv-2510-22207:
Nnamdi Aghanya, Jun Li, and Kewei Wang compress text with a language model that is allowed to be wrong, within limits. Language models already compress losslessly near the theoretical floor by predicting what comes next. This study moves into lossy territory, where some fidelity is traded for size and the question becomes how to spend the error budget wisely.

Their codec, Error-Bounded Predictive Coding, masks part of the text and lets a masked language model guess the missing tokens at decompression time. Only when the model's top guess misses does the file store a compact, rank-based correction, creating a residual channel that dials the rate-versus-distortion balance continuously. Against simpler predictive masking and a vector quantization rival, the method delivered better fidelity at markedly lower bit rates under careful bit accounting, using the model's own knowledge more efficiently.
arxiv-2510-22707:
Ivan N Mikhailov wrote a short 2025 math note, and he wrote it alone. It deals with the Gromov-Hausdorff class of metric spaces. In that class, distance tells how alike two spaces are. He builds a geodesic line in that class. A geodesic is like a shortest path.

The real line sits inside his built line. It sits there as an interior point, not an end point. The real line has its natural metric, the usual gap between points. That is the whole claim of the note. It adds one new fact about the shape of this vast class.
arxiv-2510-22807:
Set theory axioms can force strong facts about trees and graphs. Carlos Martinez-Ranero and Lucas Polymeris study one such axiom in 2025. It is a variant of the Proper Forcing Axiom. The variant protects one almost Suslin tree. Krueger first introduced this axiom.

The pair extend its known consequence list. They prove it implies the Mapping Reflection Principle. It also implies the Open Graph Axiom. All special Aronszajn trees become club isomorphic under it. Yet not all almost Suslin trees do. Aronszajn trees are tall trees with no long branch. Club isomorphism is a strong form of sameness. The results sharpen what this axiom can and cannot do.
arxiv-2510-23307:
Jonathan Bauermann and David R Nelson study the genetic boundary between two species inside an expanding microbial colony. Microbes reproduce and diffuse both at the frontier and in the interior. Inside the bulk, the boundary between species is controlled simply by their interactions.

At the frontier, however, the interface width settles at a finite value for long times, for neutral strains and for antagonistic ones alike. Geometric effects cause this: interfaces drift toward local minima in the uneven frontier. The result shapes how mixed colonies sort themselves as they grow outward.
arxiv-2510-23607:
Yujia Zhang and six co-authors introduce Concerto, a learning scheme that teaches machines spatial understanding by mixing 2D images and 3D point clouds. People form concepts by combining senses, then can recall them from a single sense alone. Concerto copies that idea in minimal form, pairing self-teaching inside the 3D data with a joint embedding that ties 2D and 3D views together.

Even with simple probes, the learned features beat leading standalone 2D and 3D self-supervised models on 3D scene perception, and also beat just gluing the two feature sets together. With full fine-tuning, Concerto set new best results on several scene understanding benchmarks, including a top score on ScanNet. The team adds a variant for point clouds lifted from video, plus a translator that maps its features into the CLIP language space. That last step opens the door to open-world perception driven by words.
arxiv-2510-23907:
Eddison Pham and five co-authors present DynaStride, a pipeline that writes coherent captions for whole scenes in instructional videos. A good scene caption must follow both what is shown and how the action unfolds in time, since learners rely on that structure. Captions that miss it confuse rather than teach. The hard part is doing this without hand-cut scene boundaries.

Working from the YouCookII dataset, DynaStride samples frames adaptively and groups them into multimodal windows around key transitions. A multimodal chain-of-thought step proposes action-object pairs for each window. A dynamic stride selection algorithm then balances context against redundancy while fusing those pairs into one caption per scene. Against strong baselines including GPT-4o, the system won on word-overlap metrics and on semantic similarity scores alike. Human-facing checks also found its captions more coherent and informative.
arxiv-2510-24107:
Chanuka Karavita and three co-authors study how different learning speeds shape large patterns in social and economic networks. People learn at different rates, and networks also rewire as ties change, yet earlier work rarely treated both kinds of difference together. The team asks how this mix affects cooperation and structure over time.

They build a simulation based on the Prisoner's Dilemma and a model of noisy best response. Each agent has its own learning rate and the network has its own rewiring rate. Results show lower and more even learning rates favor scale free networks, with a few highly linked hubs. Higher or uneven rates lead to different structures, linking personal learning to network shape.
arxiv-2510-24407:
Christian Klein and two co-authors investigate the nonlinear Schrödinger equation inside a unit ball in one and two dimensions, with the wave forced to zero at the boundary. They focus on ground states, their limiting behavior, stability, and how perturbations evolve. Computations show the boundary has a stabilizing effect compared with the whole space case.

In subcritical and critical cases, the mass curves slope upward and perturbations recur near the ground state family rather than collapsing. In the critical case, ground state mass approaches the whole space value from below, which keeps perturbations stable. The supercritical case behaves differently, and the paper maps these regimes for bounded domain wave dynamics.
arxiv-2510-24507:
Győző Kovács and three co-authors study how finite size changes fluctuations near phase transitions in a chiral effective model. They build the model to include zero mode treatment, momentum discretization, and gradient effects through a finite volume profile. The fluctuations of the chiral order parameter and net baryon number, and their scaling, are examined near a critical point and a first order transition.

The team shows finite volume effects on the Binder cumulant and kurtosis along the phase boundary and near the freeze out line. These observables are used to hunt for the QCD critical point in heavy ion collisions, so size corrections matter for interpreting data. Phenomenological implications are explained.
arxiv-2510-24707:
Juraj Juraska and seven co-authors report two systems built for a shared test of translation grades. One task asks for a score of how good a translation is. The other asks for the spans of text where errors sit, with their type and weight marked.

Their score tool, MetricX-25, is a new take on a past tool, retrained on a large open weight model. Their span tool, GemSpanEval, writes out each error span plus the text near it, which helps keep spans true to source. The score tool beat its past form by a clear gap. The span tool matched a strong past base line.
arxiv-2510-24807:
Ziyao Cui, Minxing Zhang, and Jian Pei probe a weak spot in how data are shared in a chain over time. Most past safe work guards one data drop at a time. But firms and clinics drop fresh cuts of linked data again and again, and time links across drops can leak what one drop hides.

Their attack joins a hidden state model with a trial based learner that reads both ways in time. It can pull out hid facts from the chain, though each drop on its own met the usual safe rules. The flaw is in the chain, not one drop. The work warns teams that guard each drop to check the full run of drops.
arxiv-2510-24907:
Michal Stary, Julien Gaubil, Ayush Tewari, and Vincent Sitzmann open up multi view transformers, models that build three dimensional views in one pass. Such models have changed three dimensional work, but their inner steps are a black box. That blocks new gains past more data and hurts trust in safe use.

The team probes the left over streams that run through the model's layers and draws them as maps. On a known model kin, they track how the hid state grows block by block and what each layer adds. The model seems to refine point matches as its built shape grows. Their take sets it apart from old pipe lines with set pose steps.
arxiv-2510-25007:
Islam Nassar leads a team with ten co-authors who use large language models to code doctor visits for billing. Such codes, from a set list, log what a doctor did at a visit. Right codes help pay flow, but the task adds to the note load on doctors and is full of real world snags.

Their frame, ProFees, was built to face those snags head on. On a set of real cases picked by experts, it beat a sold code tool by a large gap in right codes. It also beat the team's best lone prompt base by a small gap. The work lays out the snags in full, then tests the fix on each.
arxiv-2510-25307:
Frederic Faure surveys how quantum dynamics can emerge from chaos. His 2025 paper reviews Anosov geodesic flows. Those flows are simple models of deterministic chaos. Deterministic chaos means motion follows rules yet stays unpredictable. The survey asks a surprising basic question. Can purely classical motion produce quantum-like behavior?

Faure explains that classical correlation functions can show it. The key tool is microlocal analysis, a fine-scale method. It reveals a discrete Pollicott-Ruelle spectrum for the flow. That spectrum naturally arranges into vertical bands. Sometimes the rightmost band stands apart by a gap. Then it governs an effective dynamics for correlations. That effective dynamics mirrors quantum evolution closely. The result links classical chaos and quantum theory. It gives readers a guided tour of recent work.
arxiv-2510-25407:
Timon J Vreman, Ad Lagendijk, and Willem L Vos study light output. Their 2025 physics paper concerns 3D photonic crystals. Spontaneous output depends on local density of states. Photonic band-gap crystals strongly modulate that density. They can therefore control spontaneous output rates. The authors compare two calculation methods carefully.

One method uses plane-wave expansion for infinite crystals. The other simulates dipole power in finite crystals. Finite-difference time-domain modeling supplies that second method. Both methods gave similar frequency-dependent trends overall. Relative differences stayed below twelve percent in comparisons. Edge settings explained most of those differences. Plane-wave results enabled distributions of output rates. Such distributions help interpret time-resolved decay tests directly. Emitters distributed inside crystals are common in tests. The authors expect results to aid optical design. Radiative density could become a product design tool.
arxiv-2510-25507:
Yuliang Xu, Yun Wei, and Li Ma propose testing generative models distributionally. Their 2025 paper presents a relative density ratio metric. Generative models produce samples meant to mimic real data. Judging distributional differences is central to testing. Their metric is function-valued rather than single-numbered. It characterizes differences between real and generated samples.

The relative density ratio preserves phi-divergence between distributions. Bounded range gives clear interpretability and numeric stability. Sample-level testing facilitates downstream feature-certain investigations. Estimation uses tuning on a variational form. Convergence rates are given for general estimators in theory. Neural network estimators get rates under Besov settings. Tests used MNIST and CelebA64 image data sets. American Gut microbiome data were also used. Estimated ratios enable effective comparison of competing models. They reveal goodness-of-fit nature in sample space. Support overlap, coverage, and fidelity can be assessed.
arxiv-2510-25607:
Xiaohong Chen, Zhenxiao Chen, and Wayne Yuan Gao study treatment assignment inference. Their 2025 economics paper covers welfare and value functionals. Optimal treatment assigns treatment when benefit is nonnegative. Their functionals depend on that nonparametric effect function. Estimation and inference theory are given here.

Only people with nonnegative effects receive treatment optimally. A variance formula in closed form is also given. More general value functionals behave differently in rates. Plug-in estimators converge at one-dimensional nonparametric rates usually. Edge populations explain the varied convergence rates. Welfare integrands vanish at zero-effect edges there. Monte Carlo runs show good finite-sample results. Job training program effectiveness supplies empirical use.
arxiv-2510-25707:
Loan Renaud led nine co-authors on hydrogen filled ice. Tomasz Poreba, Simone Di Cataldo, and Alasdair Nicholls helped. Leon Andriambariarijaona, Maria Rescigno, and Richard Gaal joined. Michele Casula, A Marco Saitta, and Livia Eleonora Bove joined. Their 2025 paper studies dual quantum locking in hydrates.

Filled ice forms show exceptionally strong host-guest effects. Ultra-short distances and one-to-one stoichiometry drive that. Two interpenetrated diamond-like sublattices form it. A dual-lattice quantum system emerges from that coupling. They explore pressure and temperature driven transitions. Lattice symmetry breaking and bond symmetrization also interplay. Computational modeling mixes classic and path-integral changes. Quantum embedding and high pressure tests complement modeling. Orientational ordering occurs at much lower pressures than hydrogen. Water and hydrogen changes couple more strongly then.
arxiv-2510-25907:
Marcos J. Hernandez, Bogar Diaz, and J. David Vergara apply resurgence methods to a geometric measure of quantum states. The quantum metric tensor describes how much a quantum state changes when a parameter shifts. For anharmonic oscillators, systems whose restoring force is not a simple spring, the series for this metric grows factorially and diverges, so plain perturbation theory fails at high order.

Hernandez and the team identify the non perturbative scales behind that growth in quartic, sextic, and higher dimensional models. They then rebuild the series with Borel Pade resummation, a method that tames divergent sums, and check it against exact numerical results. The rebuilt values are accurate, most clearly for the ground state, extending resurgence from energies to geometry.
arxiv-2510-26007:
Theresia Veronika Rampisela, Maria Maistro, Tuukka Ruotsalo, and Christina Lioma reflect on how to judge the judges of responsible AI. Responsible AI asks that systems be fair, safe, and accountable, and progress is often tracked with evaluation metrics. Yet the metrics themselves can be fragile, and far less work checks their robustness than uses them to score models.

Rampisela and the team draw on prior studies of fairness metrics for recommender systems, a concrete case where metric weakness has been probed. They distill the lessons into a set of practical, non exhaustive guidelines for building reliable responsible AI metrics. The guidelines are meant to apply broadly, including to AI used in science, where bad metrics can mislead high stakes work.
arxiv-2510-26207:
Luis Fredes and Jean-Francois Marckert give a combinatorial account of a famous constant for random walks on finite state spaces. For a Markov chain, a system that jumps between states with fixed probabilities. Kemeny proved that the expected time to hit a randomly chosen target state is the same no matter where the chain starts. That striking independence bears his name.

Fredes and Marckert show the property follows from a more general identity. They form a generating function that mixes hitting time distributions with determinants of matrices obtained by deleting one state at a time. They prove the whole sum does not depend on the start. The determinant factors at a special value recover the invariant measure, the long run state frequencies, and further results follow.
arxiv-2510-26407:
Ivan Razvorotnev, Marina Munkhoeva, and Evgeny Frolov build a recommender that guesses what a user will pick next. Such systems face sparse data, a pull toward popular items, and a clash between being right and being varied. Recent fixes learn by contrast, comparing good and bad pairs, but they need big batches and can boost popular items even more.

The three authors adapt Barlow Twins, a method that cuts overlap between learned features, into a Transformer model called BT-SR. It needs no fake data tweaks and no bad pairs to push against. On five public data sets it raised next-item accuracy, covered more rare items, and kept scores better balanced. One setting lets users trade accuracy against variety as they wish.
arxiv-2510-26507:
Anwesh Kumar Mishra, with five co-authors, surveys tools proposed for watching pulsating variable stars from the Mt Abu Observatory. These stars swell and shrink in a steady rhythm, and they have shaped much of modern astronomy. Big surveys such as OGLE and TESS now find them in huge numbers, which creates work for mid-size telescopes to follow up and pin down each star's traits.

Mishra and the team share early observations of type-II Cepheids, a class of old pulsating stars, from Mt Abu. They argue for dedicated observing runs on such stars. Then they present optical designs for several new instruments meant for the site. The designs stay fairly simple while using the site's telescopes and facilities well, and they aim to support steady follow-up work.
arxiv-2510-26607:
Maksim Maslov, Alexander Kugaevskikh, and Matthew Ivanov tackle regression over distributions, a learning task whose answers are whole probability curves rather than single numbers. Many current methods ignore the geometry of the space of distributions, or cost too much to run. The team wants a method that respects that geometry while staying practical.

Maslov and his two co-authors model the answer as a smooth trajectory of Gaussian curves, whose centre and spread are built from Bernstein polynomials of the input. Training minimises the Wasserstein distance, a geometry-aware gap between curves, averaged over the data. Tests on synthetic data with complex paths gave competitive scores on several measures, with the smoothest paths where change was strongly nonlinear. The explicit control points keep the model easy to read.
arxiv-2510-26707:
Mehar Bhatia, with six co-authors, traces how a language model's values form during post-training. After pre-training, models go through supervised fine-tuning on example answers and then preference optimisation, which rewards favoured replies. Most studies check the values of the finished model, not how those values arise.

Bhatia and the team measure the size and timing of value drifts across Llama-3 and Qwen-3 models of several sizes, and across popular data sets and algorithms. They find the fine-tuning phase generally sets a model's values, and later preference optimisation rarely moves them. With a synthetic preference data set that lets them dial values directly, they also show that different optimisation algorithms land on different value outcomes from the same data. The findings guide data curation and algorithm choice.
arxiv-2510-27207:
Hamed Najafi, Dongsheng Luo, and Jason Liu propose a geometric way to explain what a trained model has learned. Standard attribution methods give each feature one static score, which nonlinearity and interactions can distort. Their framework, feature-function curvature analysis, studies the shape of the learned function itself and gives each feature a four-part signature covering impact, volatility, nonlinearity, and interaction.

A dynamic extension tracks those signatures through training, moving from what was learned to how learning unfolded. Experiments give direct evidence of hierarchical learning, where simple linear effects appear before complex interactions. The dynamic view also flags insufficient model capacity and predicts overfitting onset. Together the tools turn explanation from a single number into a fuller, more trustworthy account of learning.
arxiv-2510-27507:
C. M. Newman and D. L. Stein study ground state stability in the Edwards-Anderson Ising spin glass in two and more dimensions. They perturb a single coupling and ask how ground states respond, reviewing critical droplets, flexibilities, and metastates along the way. A central result rules out a certain kind of critical droplet with space-filling boundary in ground states from coupling-independent boundary conditions, in any dimension.

From that result, if incongruent ground states exist, the variance of their energy difference over finite volumes scales with the volume itself. In two dimensions a metastate from periodic boundary conditions is then unique, supported on a single spin-reversed ground state pair. Excitations with a positive-density interface also have restricted-volume energy differences growing like the square root of volume.
arxiv-2510-27607:
John Won, Kyungmin Lee, Huiwon Jang, Dongyoung Kim, and Jinwoo Shin present DUST in 2025, a robot model that joins seeing, language, and action with a world model. A world model predicts how a scene will change. Joining that skill with action choice is hard, since sight data and move data differ a lot in form.

DUST keeps two streams, one for sight and one for action, inside one shared build. Each stream gets its own noise, and the loss keeps their causal links clear. Sampling at test time can then refine moves and views at distinct paces. Gains reach six points on sim tests and ten points on a real robot arm. Transfer to new tasks also improves.
arxiv-2511-00107:
Piyushkumar Patel presents MOVAI, a hierarchical approach for text-to-video generation aiming at temporal consistency, compositional knowledge, and fine control over visual narrative. Existing systems struggle to keep scenes coherent across time and to honor the structure in a prompt. A compositional scene parser decomposes text descriptions into hierarchical scene graphs with temporal structure.

Temporal-aware diffusion models then synthesize video from that parsed structure. Generative media readers get a design that plans a video's composition before rendering frames. Scene graphs give the generator clear objects and relations to respect, which should reduce the drifting and morphing that plague text-to-video systems.
arxiv-2511-00307:
Healey Kogan, Frederick Pardoe, and Helvi Witek simulate black holes that fly past each other rather than merge. During such a scattering encounter, each hole can reabsorb some of the energy and spin it radiates as gravitational waves, gaining mass and spinning faster. The team runs numerical relativity simulations for equal-mass holes with a wide range of starting spins and momenta.

Spin-up and mass gain peak near the angle that just avoids merger, with large momenta and spins pointing against the orbit. At that borderline angle, spin-up falls in a straight line as starting spin rises. Holes that start spinning fast sometimes even spin down, because mass gain outpaces spin gain. The largest effects seen were a spin-up of a substantial step and a mass increase of fifteen percent.
arxiv-2511-00607:
Tianyu Jiang, Yan Yang, Hongjin Liu, Runyu Han, Bo Ai, and Mohsen Guizani attack channel estimation for fast-moving millimeter-wave systems. A hybrid MIMO receiver must learn a high-dimensional channel that changes quickly as users move. The channel matrix is both low-rank and sparse, and the authors exploit each property in a separate phase of one compressed sensing framework.

First, an observation matrix is completed with a robust rank-one completion algorithm that updates the matrix and its rank together, no prior rank knowledge needed. Second, a rank-aware matching pursuit recovers the sparse channel with low latency. An autoregressive model tracks rank changes across time, exploiting their correlation between nearby instants. Simulations confirm state-of-the-art recovery accuracy with theoretical guarantees, a practical step for high-mobility millimeter-wave links.
arxiv-2511-00707:
Zoha Azimi, Reza Farahani, Vignesh Menon, and Christian Timmerer aim to stream high-resolution video with a smaller energy bill. Streaming dominates internet traffic, and ever-higher resolutions across many devices raise real carbon concerns. Measuring the energy of every encoding option at scale is infeasible, so the authors predict instead: cheap low-resolution anchor encodings stand in for the expensive full versions.

Encoding parameters such as resolution and quantization are then chosen automatically to save energy while holding perceptual quality, scored by VMAF, within acceptable limits. On one hundred ultra-high-definition sequences from the Inter4K dataset, encoded with the open VVenC encoder, the method saved just over half of encoding energy and a similar share of decoding energy. The average quality dip stayed below the just noticeable difference threshold.
arxiv-2511-01007:
M. Pandurovic estimates how well the planned International Linear Collider could measure the Higgs boson decaying into W boson pairs, when both W bosons decay into jets of hadrons. The Higgs is produced together with a Z boson, and the study uses detailed simulation of the ILD detector design.

Two collision energies are considered, with a large planned data set and strongly polarized beams, and machine learning methods carry out the analysis. Background from photon collisions producing hadrons is overlaid on every event. The expected relative statistical uncertainty comes out near four percent at the lower energy and about six and a half percent at the higher one. Such measurements test whether the Higgs couples to W bosons exactly as the Standard Model predicts.
arxiv-2511-01107:
Isabel Liu, Bowen Li, Benjamin Eysenbach, and Tom Silver teach robot planners to invent new moves. Task and motion planning solves long horizon problems by chaining abstract actions such as pick, place, and move. Those actions are hand defined by engineers, which limits what the robot can try.

Their method, SLAP, uses reinforcement learning inside the abstract planning graph to find shortcuts between states that the existing options already reach. Chaining a learned shortcut shortens plans, and the discovered moves are physical improvisations, such as slapping, wiggling, or wiping objects, quite unlike the programmed ones. In four simulated robot environments, SLAP cut overall plan lengths by more than half and beat both pure planning and flat and hierarchical reinforcement learning on success.
arxiv-2511-01507:
Muzaffar Rahmatullaev and Akbarkhuja Tukhtabaev study a hybrid spin model on a Cayley tree, an endlessly branching graph used as a laboratory for phase transitions. Their model mixes two classic systems: Ising spins, which point up or down, and Potts spins, which take several states, combined into a (2,q)-Ising-Potts model.

The authors derive a recurrence equation that produces a splitting Gibbs measure, the kind of equilibrium distribution built consistently from the tree's branching structure. They prove at least three translation-invariant splitting Gibbs measures exist for trees of order two or more. For the (2,3) model on the binary tree, under stated conditions, at least eight such measures appear, a sign of rich phase behavior.
arxiv-2511-01807:
Adewale Akinfaderin, Shreyas Subramanian, and Akarsha Sehwag teach language models to respect a word budget without retraining them. Length control matters from voice interfaces needing brevity to research summaries needing depth, yet existing solutions mostly fine-tune the model or bolt on inference-time tools.

Their method, Plan-and-Write, is pure prompt engineering: the prompt makes the model plan the answer's structure and count words deliberately as it writes, tracking the target length throughout. The testbed was document summarization across six state-of-the-art models. The method significantly improved length fidelity for several of them over standard prompting. Gains were largest at short-to-medium targets. Adherence rose by up to about 38 percent for some architectures. Quality checks found the outputs maintained or improved overall quality, making the technique immediately deployable.
arxiv-2511-02707:
Jadson Portela e Silva and four colleagues map the phases of a two-dimensional model where electrons and lattice vibrations shape each other. In their 2025 study of the optical Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, electron hopping depends on the gap between neighboring phonon positions. They ran quantum Monte Carlo simulations that avoid the sign problem, backed by mean-field checks.

Varying the coupling strength and phonon frequency revealed staggered and armchair valence bond solid phases, plus an antiferromagnetic phase with a wider symmetry. The bond solid phases formed at temperatures far higher than in models with local coupling, matching lighter polarons in the metal state. The result is a full phase map, at zero and finite temperature, for comparison with related materials.
arxiv-2511-03107:
Md Sakhawat Hossen, Md. Zashid Iqbal Borshon, and A. S. M. Badrudduza argue that classic machine learning can sort text nearly as well as deep learning, at a fraction of the energy cost. Deep models carry a heavy carbon footprint, a growing worry in text analytics. Their 2025 paper upgrades the standard TF-IDF weighting scheme into a variant they call CTF-IDF. It pairs that with a faster method for shrinking data dimensions.

The faster reduction step uses an IRLBA algorithm, keeping the pipeline light. In their experiments, the classic pipeline ran much faster and used far less compute than deep learning. Accuracy improved rather than falling for the methods tested, with only a minor compromise overall. The authors pitch the pairing as a greener route for everyday text classification.
arxiv-2511-03407:
Celian Ringwald and colleagues find why small language models stumble when pulling full fact graphs from text under shape rules. Guided by SHACL shapes, the models handle common simple facts well. Trouble starts with links between things and with rare properties, which appear too seldom in training for the models to learn.

Four fixes are tested: balanced sampling, weighted training loss, simply scaling data up, and synthetic examples built from templates. The winner is plain but strict: ensure every target property appears past a set threshold in training. Data, code, and results are released for others to check. The guidance helps teams that need complete graph extraction, not just the easy, frequent facts.
arxiv-2511-03907:
Liam Bakar and six colleagues designed SnappyMeal, a multimodal artificial intelligence app for logging food. Interviews with nutrition experts and regular trackers showed paper and app journals are inflexible, weakly followed, and often inaccurate. Flexible logging matters because diet records underpin links between food, medicine, fitness, and health.

SnappyMeal accepts several input types, asks goal-dependent follow-up questions when context is missing, and pulls detail from grocery receipts and nutrition databases. Benchmark tests were joined by a three-week real-world deployment with over five hundred logged items. Users praised the input options and perceived accuracy strongly, suggesting a more context-aware path for dietary tracking tools.
arxiv-2511-04007:
Zhiming Shuai, Xiangdong Zhang, and Gui-Rong Liang numerically study superradiance of a charged scalar field around charged black-bounce spacetimes. They cover both scattering setups and black hole bomb models, where a mirror traps amplified waves. A quantum parameter in the geometry shallows the effective potential.

That shallowing weakens superradiant amplification in both settings. Field mass suppresses gains at all frequencies, while black hole and field charge suppress low frequencies yet enhance high ones. In one bomb arrangement a distinct new eigenmode appears at large quantum parameter values, absent in a second arrangement. Heavy-field cases add another eigenfrequency at the same setting, without superradiant amplification.
arxiv-2511-04107:
Chengu Wang, writing alone, builds sorting networks of depth thirteen for twenty-seven and twenty-eight channels, improving the best known bound of fourteen. Sorting networks sort any input through a fixed pattern of comparators, and lowering depth for a given channel count is a long-running combinatorial contest.

The twenty-eight-channel network uses reflectional symmetry. High-quality prefixes from sixteen- and twelve-channel networks are combined, extended greedily one comparator at a time, and a SAT solver completes the remaining layers. Cutting one layer at these sizes is a concrete record step, and the hybrid hand-plus-solver construction shows how search can finish designs that pure greedy building stalls on.
arxiv-2511-04707:
Rishi Rajesh Shah leads six authors with NINJA, a jailbreak attack for long-context language models. Million-token inputs opened new powers, but their safety effects were unclear. NINJA hides a harmful goal inside a haystack of benign, model-written content.

Where the harmful goal sits in that long context turns out to matter greatly. Tests on the HarmBench suite raised attack success sharply across leading models. Open and proprietary systems alike were affected, including LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral, and Gemini. The finding warns that long context is not just a feature; it is also a new attack surface.
arxiv-2511-04807:
Matthew D. Kvalheim and his co-author map what topology allows and forbids in autoencoders. An autoencoder squeezes data through a small latent space and rebuilds it. The round trip should act like the identity on the data manifold itself.

Continuous encoder and decoder maps face hard topological limits, they show. Some manifolds simply cannot be compressed into a given latent shape faithfully. The authors also describe what autoencoders can do for dynamical systems. When the data manifold is invariant under the dynamics, those capabilities shape how learned models can track motion without leaving the manifold.
arxiv-2511-04907:
Lunjia Hu and co-authors speed up swap multicalibration, a fairness-linked test that asks if a forecast is right when checked within many overlapping groups. Prior work tied this test for a trait like a mean or median to whether that trait can be drawn out by regression.

In the online set-up, the known method reached its error bound but ran too slowly to use. The authors give a faster swap version and widen the result beyond group flags. Their work keeps the same style of error growth while it cuts the cost of each round.
arxiv-2511-05207:
Ryuji Hashimoto and co-authors build a market simulation where trader agents both learn and differ in taste, to see what price patterns emerge. Agent models have long split those two traits into rival camps, so their joint effect was unknown.

In their multi-agent learning frame, each trader has its own risk aversion, time discount, and access to information. Prices form from their linked choices, not from a set rule. The study checks which known market facts appear when both traits act at once, a step toward more true-to-life tests of market rules and shocks.
arxiv-2511-05307:
Akua Dickson and co-authors build a framework that keeps soft robot arms within safe force limits when they touch fragile things near them. Soft arms suit delicate work, but past obstacle methods track position only and ignore how hard the arm may push.

Their maps turn force safety rules from task space, points along the arm, into configuration space, the arm's joint angles. That lets the robot check force safety in real time as it moves. The work aims at safe use in homes, labs, and care sites where a hard push could do harm.
arxiv-2511-05407:
Yahui Fu and co-authors model user satisfaction in dialogue systems with an eye on minority users, whose ratings can differ from the crowd's for the same reply style. One-size alignment tends to fit the majority and miss those users.

Their frame learns both personal and group-level tastes for satisfaction scores. A chain of personalized reasoning feeds a preference-adaptive reinforcement step. The aim is a system that can tell when a minority user needs an unlike reply. It should not just grind toward broad consensus. That should lift fit for users at the edges of a user base.
arxiv-2511-05907:
Archit Agarwal, Meghali Garg, and Bibekananda Maji derive an exact formula for counting partitions that obey two restrictions at once. A partition splits a number into a sum of parts. Here the parts must avoid multiples of a fixed step, and each part may carry one of several colors.

The work extends a line running from Hardy and Ramanujan's circle method through Rademacher's exact series and later formulas for special partition families. Using the circle method, the authors get a Rademacher-type exact series for the combined family for any number of colors. As an application they prove higher-order Turán inequalities for the counting function. Bonus results cover colored distinct-part partitions and sums of minimal excludants over ordinary partitions and overpartitions.
arxiv-2511-06107:
David Kaplan and co-authors project whether countries will meet the United Nations goal for basic reading and math skills by 2030.
