Realizability plus Bellman completeness alone do not guarantee sample-efficient learning under partial coverage, shown via an information-theoretic lower bound. They then introduce a decision-estimation framework splitting complexity into decision and estimation parts. It yields the first epsilon-squared sample bound for soft Q-learning under partial coverage. It also gives the first learnability account for general low-Bellman-rank problems offline.
arxiv-2602-12207:
Studying online talk is hard when real platforms restrict data, ethics bar risky tests, and tools demand heavy coding. Emma Hoes led this work with two co-authors, presenting VIRENA, a virtual arena for controlled tests in lifelike social media settings. Several people can take part at once in copies of feed platforms and messaging apps, joined by language-model agents with set personas and human-like timing.

Researchers build tests in a visual tool with no coding: they set conditions, schedule posts, add moderation rules, assign people at random, and export results. The system supports hard-to-run designs, such as human-AI talk, moderation comparisons, and group debate over time. People and data stay under institutional control, with links to survey and recruitment tools.
arxiv-2602-12707:
Counting curves and related shapes in Landau-Ginzburg models has recently gained new foundations, and this survey pulls the progress together. Mark Gross, Tyler Kelly, and Ran Tessler explain how open enumerative invariants are defined as integrals over a moduli space with corners, using multisections of vector bundles with carefully set boundary rules. The survey walks through the ideas needed to make those definitions work.

It then covers the settings where the invariants obey recursion relations, fit into integrable hierarchies, or match mirror symmetry predictions. Along the way the authors flag what is known and what is not, closing with open questions for future work. Readers new to the area get a map of the foundations; specialists get a snapshot of where the theory stands.
arxiv-2602-12907:
Meter-class telescopes rarely attempt light interferometry, but a feasibility test can show whether the technique is viable on modest hardware. Km Nitu Rai and five co-authors test speckle interferometry on the 1.3-metre Devasthal Fast Light Telescope, now used for photometry. Using a sCMOS camera, they observed six binary stars and applied standard speckle recipes to the recorded images.

Individual speckle patterns varied strongly frame to frame, yet the analysis recovered the classic three-peak structure of wide binaries, yielding separations and position angles. Measured separations for gamma Leonis, gamma Virginis, and zeta Herculis match literature values closely. The study does not chase the diffraction limit; instead it validates instrumentation, acquisition, and analysis as a testbed for future interferometry on meter-class telescopes.
arxiv-2602-13507:
Remote Parkinson's screening by video could scale care, but which video foundation model works best for which clinical task was poorly understood. This large study uses a new data set from 1,888 participants, 727 with Parkinson's, spanning 32,847 videos across 16 standardized clinical tasks. It evaluates seven leading video foundation models by frozen embeddings with a linear classification head.

Task saliency proved highly model-dependent: VideoPrism led on visual speech and facial expressivity, V-JEPA on upper-limb motor tasks, and TimeSformer stayed competitive on rhythmic finger tapping. Overall AUCs ranged from 76.4 to 85.3 percent, with high specificity up to 90.3 percent but lower sensitivity, pointing to task-aware calibration and multi-task integration. Md Saiful Islam leads the work with thirteen co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13807:
Time series anomaly detection must find anomalous regions and support reliable decisions under complex settings. Yet most methods treat it as purely discriminative prediction with fixed features rather than an evidence-driven diagnostic process. They struggle when anomalies show strong context dependence, diverse patterns, or domain shifts across data sets. AnomaMind reframes detection as sequential decision-making through a coarse-to-fine workflow. It first finds suspicious intervals, then builds diagnostic evidence through tool interaction, and finally refines decisions through self-reflection.

A toolkit box combines knowledge memory and numerical diagnostics. Visual anomaly patterns and domain knowledge guide context, while statistical, value-based, change-based, and region-level operators supply measurable proof evidence. A hybrid inference setup pairs general-purpose reasoning with a detection-specific policy tuned by rule-based rewards for parsable outputs, F1 alignment, and false-positive control. Xiaoyu Tao leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14307:
Samuele Marro and ten co-authors confront a 2026 arXiv dilemma: what happens when benchmarks outrun human comprehension? Frontier models saturate new benchmarks soon after release, and humans may soon struggle to write discriminating tasks, supply ground truth, or judge complex solutions. The authors call that future the post-comprehension regime.

Their answer is Critique-Resilient Benchmarking, an adversarial framework for comparing models without full human understanding. An answer counts as correct when no adversary has convincingly refuted it. Humans act as bounded verifiers, checking localized claims rather than whole solutions. An itemized bipartite Bradley-Terry model then ranks models jointly on solving hard tasks and generating difficult ones.
arxiv-2602-14407:
Janet G. Johnson and four co-authors study a 2026 arXiv question: how does a generative AI agent's prominence shape group discussion? GenAI can now join spoken dialogue on video calls, but little is known about how its interface design affects group dynamics. The paper introduces interface-driven social prominence as a design lens for collaborative GenAI systems.

A conversational agent that engages in spoken dialogue during video calls was tested in three collaboration modes, varying its presence in shared space and user control over its participation. A mixed-method same-group study with 18 dyads in lifelike talks showed how talk patterns and haggling over the agent's sway shift with its setup. Findings guide design of GenAI that supports, rather than steers, group talk.
arxiv-2602-14907:
Moloud Arian Maram and others ease hull tuning by adjoint math, a strong tool for drag cuts that stalls on tricky drive gear. Tricky drives ask for long, fine-step time runs, with primal and adjoint runs read back in time, at high store and compute cost.

Their plan swaps in a learned drive stand-in, a conditional variational auto-code that mimics drive acts, so adjoint tuning can run where shops once balked. Hull drag cuts thus gain a workable path for ships with knotty drives. A hull with such a drive thus finds a route to adjoint tuning.
arxiv-2602-15107:
Levine and colleagues hunt barium stars across the Milky Way with the GALAH survey. Barium stars are unusually rich in barium, beyond what current Galactic chemical evolution models predict. Past work suggests two birth routes: mass transfer from a companion asymptotic giant branch star, or radiative levitation lifting heavy elements to the surface.

From roughly 450000 survey stars, the team identifies nearly 3000 new barium-rich stars, split into hot and cool groups. Cross-matching with Gaia DR3, they find about 48 percent of nearby barium stars show elevated RUWE, a binarity clue, against about 16 percent of field stars. That points to multiplicity shaping both groups. A subset of hot stars with low RUWE and low alpha enrichment supports levitation as well. Barium stars appear in the thin disk, thick disk, and halo, slightly favoring lower metallicities, with both formation routes at work across the Galaxy.
arxiv-2602-15207:
Kapoor and colleagues present a photon-pair source in ordinary optical fiber for quantum networks. Its output is photon pairs spanning telecommunication wavelengths and near-infrared wavelengths. The highly nondegenerate pairs sit 700 nanometres apart: one in the 1500 nanometre E- and S-band telecom range and the other in the 830 nanometre near-infrared range.

High non-degeneracy keeps the pairs far-detuned from Raman noise, giving a high coincidence-to-accidental ratio even at room temperature. Two phase-matched processes in the source stay separate in spectrum and in space, with little spectral cross-talk between them. Near-infrared light shows distinct transverse spatial modes, while telecom light shows a single fundamental spatial mode. Working at room temperature, using ready-made parts, and offering multiplexing, the source looks promising for quantum networks.
arxiv-2602-15307:
Kawamura and colleagues study inner codes of a general-purpose sound self-trained model from a neuron-level view. Though observed scores as tools are strong, the inner workings behind transfer of SSL sound models stay murky. Using a gears-level lens, they spot and study class neurons by watching firing shapes by context across varied tasks.

Their study shows SSL models grow the rise of class neurons giving wide reach across new task classes. These neurons show joint replies across different meaning groups and sound echoes, such as speech traits and music pitch. They also prove these neurons have a real effect on sorting scores. To their knowledge, this is the first full neuron-level study of a general-purpose sound SSL model, providing new views into its inner code.
arxiv-2602-15407:
Demir and colleagues offer uneven versions of well-known social dilemma worlds and study how gaps between agents shape teamwork. Sequential social dilemmas give a setup for probing how teamwork grows when single drives clash with good. In multi-agent teaching, these cases are tackled by adding inner urges that foster kindness. Most routes suppose agents face same drives in the dilemma and need reach to global data about other agents to judge fair play.

Their results show fair play routes falter under uneven terms by forcing sameness that wrongly rewards cheating. To fix this, they offer three tweaks: new fair play rules counting agents' pay spans, and an agent-based weighing trick to tame built-in gaps. Local signals make routes strong under part view without needing global data swapping. Findings show that in uneven scenes, their method speeds team plans versus routes, without losing growth.
arxiv-2602-15607:
Youngman and colleagues describe work in progress for a landmark policy moment. In June 2026 the United Kingdom sets its seventh carbon budget, covering 2038 to 2042. For the first time, the budget comes with a macroeconomic assessment of effects on growth, jobs, inflation, and inequality. Researchers at INET Oxford, working with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, build that assessment on a data-driven macroeconomic agent-based model.

Three work packages structure the effort. The first adapts a macro agent model prototype and builds a United Kingdom baseline from household microdata. The second models decarbonisation as a shock to financial flows and technical coefficients. It forces the model to follow Climate Change Committee green investment paths in time for the June decision. A third package will later build independent projections with social and technological learning, which may diverge from government plans.
arxiv-2602-15707:
Mahfuz and colleagues build a real-time conversational assistant for hands-busy procedural tasks that uses no video at all. Video input is costly and can compromise privacy, so the team relies only on light, privacy-preserving signals: audio and motion-sensor data from a wearable device. With a furniture assembly task and a cooking task, they show the assistant giving step-by-step guidance proactively and answering user questions.

The paper describes the data generation method and system design, plus an edge-device implementation with no cloud dependence. An off-the-shelf language model proves talkative but not always correct, so fine-tuning is tested: it cuts needless dialogue, raising answer precision by 50 percent, and lifts answer recall by 150 percent. The result is a private, on-device helper for manual work.
arxiv-2602-15807:
Working alone, Schwarz offers a fresh angle on the vertical lift's universality in tangent categories, via a categorified view of smooth-manifold dimension. That universality of the vertical lift counts as a central axiom for tangent categories, and the categorical dimension set out here clarifies what that property amounts to. Theorem 3.7, the main result, shows that when it exists, tangent-bundle dimension must meet an equation linking it with base dimension.

For a strong tangent dimension function, Theorem 3.8 shows tangent-bundle dimension comes out as either double base dimension or the same as base dimension. Many examples of dimension functions demonstrate the definition utility, and a consequence of Theorem 3.7 limits which functors may serve as tangent bundle endofunctors for a category. As an example, the paper shows sets admit no tangent structures except the trivial one.
arxiv-2602-16007:
Bonacci and colleagues build a statistical picture of how strong graphene is in every direction, straight from atomistic simulations. Large tensile tests across stress ratios and loading angles yield failure data, mapped from imposed strain rates to resulting stresses, but each full strength surface costs heavy sampling.

Their fix encodes each orientation dependent surface with smooth, low dimensional parameters, then compresses the fitted surfaces with principal component analysis. A Gaussian mixture model over that compact space captures defect driven variation, including rare outliers from clustered vacancies in defective graphene. Sampling the model creates new physically sound strength surfaces and confidence bands in both parameter and stress space, turning a small ensemble into a usable design tool.
arxiv-2602-16107:
Gerardo Morales-Navarrete and Jorge Cervantes-Cota test how the Symmetron modified gravity model shapes the growth of cosmic structure. They track how the growth rate changes with scale and study redshift-space distortion multipoles. Symmetron is set beside the Hu-Sawicki model and the standard Lambda-CDM model. The fk-PT approach, run in the FOLPS-nu code, gives the monopole and quadrupole multipoles.

At present day, the monopole of both modified gravity models sits below the standard model. Symmetron sits closer to it, while the quadrupole behaves in the opposite way. To check the pipeline, the team uses general relativity mock catalogs, since apt Symmetron simulations do not yet exist. A Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis recovers the expected general relativity limit from the Symmetron model on mock data. That result shows the method is ready for galaxy surveys, current and near-future.
arxiv-2602-16507:
Gaetan De Waele leads four coauthors on small molecule retrieval from tandem mass spectrometry. Identifying compounds behind output spectra is a central challenge in LC-MS/MS analysis. Deep learning methods now attack it by predicting a molecular fingerprint from a spectrum and searching a compound database for matches.

Many loss functions are used to train these models, but their effect on performance is poorly understood. The authors study common loss functions and derive new regret bounds showing when Bayes-optimal decisions for different objectives must diverge. They reveal a basic trade-off: better fingerprint predictions typically worsen retrieval, and vice versa, with the trade-off hinging on the similarity structure of candidate sets. The analysis guides loss and fingerprint choice.
arxiv-2602-16607:
Miguel Marques and a large team present CitiLink-Summ, a set of European Portuguese town meeting minutes. Minutes record local rule discussion and votes, but they are long, dense, and hard for residents to use. Auto summaries could help, yet study here is thin, above all in lower-resource tongues, and good hand-written summaries are scarce.

The set holds one hundred texts with over two thousand hand-written summaries, one per topic. Base scores use generative models such as BART and PRIMERA plus large language models, judged by word and sense scores. It is the first bench mark for town-domain summary work in European Portuguese, giving researchers data and base scores to build resident-friendly tools.
arxiv-2602-16807:
Duncan Soiffer and co-authors improve upper bounds for slicing the hypercube with hyperplanes. A set of hyperplanes slices all edges of the n-dimensional hypercube when each edge is cut in its interior by some hyperplane in the set. The minimum count needed is denoted S(n). Prior work from 1971 had bounded it near five-sixths of n.

The new proof shows S(n) is at most four-fifths of n, except when n is an odd multiple of five, where one extra hyperplane may be needed. New lower bounds are also given for the most edges sliceable with fewer than n hyperplanes. The upper bound rests on eight hyperplanes slicing the ten-dimensional cube, found with help from CPro1, an automated tool pairing reasoning models with tuning to search for mathematical constructions.
arxiv-2602-17007:
Peter Reinhard Hansen and Chen Tong bring in the Parabolic Mellin Transform, defined by an integral over a vertical line in the complex plane. Under substitution, that vertical line maps to a parabolic contour in the transformed plane. For the Gaussian kernel, the transform yields a parabolic-contour form of the classical Hankel representation for the reciprocal Gamma function.

The gain of that parametrization is that the contour integral becomes a Gaussian-damped vertical-line integral. Scaling, differentiation, and Dirichlet-composition identities are built for the transform and used to derive integral representations of the Hurwitz zeta, Riemann zeta, and Dirichlet eta functions. It gives a unified transform dictionary for Gamma-type and zeta-type special functions. It also yields new forms of the Riemann hypothesis and the Lindelof hypothesis in terms of zeros and growth of parabolic-contour integrals.
arxiv-2602-17207:
Martin Mäck led a three-author team asking whether a posited junction wobble survives in true-to-life molecular models. In molecular nanojunctions, current-driven vibration shapes stability. Beyond plain Joule heating, nonconservative current forces can trigger vibrational instability at low bias in multi-mode models, but past work used only harmonic nuclear potentials. The paper tests whether anharmonic potentials change the story.

Using a mixed quantum and classic approach built on electronic friction and Langevin dynamics, the authors run two-mode setups. They track how anharmonic effects shift wobbles from such forces, how junction breakup unfolds, and how steady-state observables like current respond. The results show whether the wobble mechanism, and its measurable fingerprints, persist once realistic models replace idealized springs.
arxiv-2602-17507:
Boscarino and Izzo present high-order semi-implicit Rosenbrock-type and multistep methods for evolutionary partial differential equations with higher-order derivatives. Their semi-implicit plan sits inside a Rosenbrock-type and IMEX linear multistep frame, aimed at a run of one-dimensional time-dependent equations with high-order spatial derivatives. That plan bends easily to these equations and yields plain implicit schemes with no Newton steps at all.

The schemes so built dodge the harsh time-step limits that explicit methods need to stay steady. Space is handled with finite difference schemes. The authors give sample methods up to order four and test them on dissipative, dispersive, and biharmonic-type equations. Trials show the schemes hold steady and hit their set orders.
arxiv-2602-17707:
Franziska Aurbach and team identify a tiny-scale origin of droplet line tension. How the resting droplet contact angle shifts with size is governed by line tension. Yet measured values change sign and span several orders of magnitude from nano-scale to milli-scale droplets, a multi-size puzzle.

Their mechanism adds a contribution from gravity effects and pressure-induced changes in surface tensions within an adsorption layer. The sign of the line tension is controlled by surface wetting, the initial volume fraction in the adsorption layer, and droplet size. Droplet size also strongly shapes its strength. Match with lab and simulation results supports a unified account of the observed shifts in both sign and strength.
arxiv-2602-17907:
Raymond Li and team improve topic modeling by distilling soft labels from language models. Traditional neural topic models optimize by copying bag-of-words codes, overlooking context information and struggling with data thinness. The new training frame, Distilling Soft Labels, constructs context-enriched copying signals. It maps next token odds, given a special prompt, onto a set word list. It trains topic models to copy soft labels using language model hidden states.

That approach yields higher-quality topics more closely aligned with the underlying theme structure of the corpus. Tests show large gains in topic clarity and sorting scores over existing baselines. A search-based metric introduced by the authors shows the approach clearly beating existing methods at identifying similar texts in meaning, highlighting power for search-focused uses. Readers gain a topic modeling method that uses language model knowledge without requiring full language model fine-tuning.
arxiv-2602-18007:
Jon Hu and colleagues present a technical solution for training large language models across mixed clusters of AMD and NVIDIA graphics processors. Growing compute and system demands have made single-vendor homogeneous clusters insufficient. Their compatibility-oriented approach uses CPU-forwarding communication, with different communication back ends chosen for different parallel groups and multi-network-interface parallel data transfer. A second, faster approach uses device-direct communication.

That approach adds a CPU-offloading peer-to-peer mechanism that moves data directly between graphics processors from different vendors without staging through host memory. In experiments on two large language models, device-direct communication reached up to ninety-eight percent of the throughput of a homogeneous NVIDIA system while preserving training stability and correctness. The work shows that mixed-vendor training can nearly match single-vendor speed without giving up reliability.
arxiv-2602-18107:
Andrew Parry and two co-authors built SuiteEval, a single tool for testing search systems the same way each time. Their 2026 paper starts from a known mess: test sets, scoring choices, and setup details vary so much that results are hard to compare. That problem bites hardest for new embedding models, which must work well on topics they were not trained on.

SuiteEval runs the whole test chain on its own, from loading data and building indexes to scoring and adding up results. It reuses stored indexes to save disk space and ships with support for five major test sets. A user only has to supply a way to build a pipeline, and a new test set can be added in one line. The goal is tests that other teams can rerun and trust.
arxiv-2602-18307:
Yutong Xin and three co-authors built VeriSoftBench, a benchmark for proving software correct in Lean. Their 2026 paper notes that language models shine at interactive theorem proving, but most benchmarks draw on mathematics from Mathlib, while software proofs live inside definition-rich codebases with large project-specific libraries. The benchmark gathers five hundred Lean 4 proof tasks from open-source formal-methods projects, keeping realistic repository context and cross-file links.

Tests of frontier models and specialized provers yield three lessons. Mathlib-tuned provers transfer poorly to this repository-centered setting. Success tracks transitive repository dependence: proofs drawing on large, multi-hop dependency closures fail more often. Curated context limited to a proof's dependency closure beats showing the whole repository, yet leaves much room to grow. Benchmark and evaluation suite are public.
arxiv-2602-18507:
Joseph Bingham and two co-authors personalize machine learning models the way brains learn: by pruning. Their 2026 paper notes deep neural networks take inspiration from the brain in neuron design, yet their training methods depart from biology. Backpropagation, the primary training method, requires substantial compute and fully labeled datasets, creating major bottlenecks.

The team returns to biomimicry, copying how the brain learns through pruning, to solve classical machine learning problems with far fewer resources and no labels. Experiments personalized several speech recognition and image classification models, ResNet50 on ImageNet among them, reaching about seventy percent sparsity while lifting accuracy to about ninety percent, all without backpropagation. The brain-inspired approach opens a promising path for efficient, personalized models in resource-constrained settings.
arxiv-2602-18707:
Robot policies trained in simulation often fail on real hardware because contact, above all collisions, is modelled too crudely. Haotian He, with four co-authors, presents CLASH in 2026, a hybrid simulator that learns a collision model from simulation and then corrects it with only a handful of real collisions.

A base model distilled from MuJoCo captures broad physical priors, then gradient-based identification of contact parameters and careful fine-tuning close the remaining gap without overfitting to the few real samples. The hybrid beats the base simulator on post-impact prediction, speeds collision-heavy search markedly. Doubles success in sequential pushing tasks when policies trained in it are moved to the real robot.
arxiv-2602-18807:
A chatbot that answers maths questions is not the same as a tutor that reviews a student's own proof. The difference may decide what students actually learn. Eason Chen, with twenty co-authors, evaluates GPTutor in 2026. It tutors undergraduates in discrete mathematics. It offers both a structured proof-review tool with embedded feedback and a general chatbot.

In a staggered-access study of 148 students, earlier access lifted homework performance while only the experimental group had the system. That gain did not carry over to exam scores. Students who doubted themselves and had lower prior exam marks used both tools more. Heavier chatbot use, especially answer-seeking, was negatively linked to later midterm performance. Proof-review use showed no such link. The lesson is that chat support alone may not reliably transfer to independent proof learning.
arxiv-2602-19207:
Federated learning lets several parties train one model together without handing over their raw data, which matters when privacy rules or business secrecy forbid sharing. Most methods assume data is split in only one way, either by different users or by different features. Real cases often split both ways at once, and standard methods handle that mix poorly.

Afsana Khan and three colleagues built HybridFL for exactly that mixed split, with users divided across parties and features divided as well. The paper tests it on financial crime detection, a setting where transaction records and related account details live with different holders. By training across the split without pooling the underlying data, the method aims to catch crime patterns that no single holder could see alone.
arxiv-2602-19307:
Checking whether a high-dimensional quantum state can be distilled usually demands full tomography, a measurement burden that grows costly fast. Christian Candeago and four co-authors study the first non-trivial case, a qubit-ququart system, and sort its states by the partial transpose test. States failing the test, called NPT, may be distillable, while states passing it, called PPT, are not. The paper asks whether machine learning can make that call from far fewer measurements.

The team tries support vector machines, random forests, and neural networks, using both fixed measurements and learnable observables. Learnable observables beat collective measurement witness methods, and every model separates PPT from NPT states. Telling NPT subclasses apart stays hard, a sign of the intricate geometry involved. Readers get an experimentally friendly route to checking distillability without reconstructing the full state.
arxiv-2602-19907:
Contrast-based learning on natural images picks positive and negative pairs by image tweaks, but in medical images random tweaks can warp the small regions that carry biomarkers. A 2026 arXiv paper by Kiran Kokilepersaud and four co-authors proposes a gentler selection strategy for OCT scans.

The method generates disease severity labels for unlabeled scans from gradient responses of an outlier detection algorithm. Samples with similar severity, which likely share structures tied to the course of disease, become the pairs for labelled contrast training. That training lifts marker accuracy above self-taught baselines for key diabetic retinopathy markers. The work shows that severity-aware pairing beats blind augmentation where detail is diagnostic.
arxiv-2602-20107:
Two questions haunt networks of dynamical systems. Do the signals excite the network enough for identification? Is the network identifiable in the first place? A 2026 arXiv paper by Anders Hansson and two co-authors answers both with algebra, using Gröbner bases.

For generic informativity, the paper gives a sufficient condition with two parts. The spectrum of external signals must be positive definite. The transfer function from external signals to predictor inputs must have full generic row rank. For identifiability in the algebraic sense, at the generic local level, the paper computes the dimension of the generic fiber of the closed-loop transfer function taking external measurable signals to measured outputs. The result is an algebraic toolkit for deciding when networks can be identified from data.
arxiv-2602-20307:
Shangqing Xu and three co-authors give time-series foundation models the ability to adapt to new tasks from context alone. Such models generalize well across datasets but are usually pre-trained for specific tasks and struggle with unseen tasks unless fine-tuned. This 2026 paper adds in-context learning, letting a model infer input-output relationships from examples supplied at test time. The method, called In-Context Time-series Pre-training, restructures pre-training data to build that ability into the backbone model.

Experiments show the approach lifts state-of-the-art time-series models by about eleven percent on unseen tasks, with no fine-tuning required. By adapting at inference time, the model turns context examples into task competence. The paper thus moves time-series foundation models closer to genuinely general tools rather than specialists tuned per task.
arxiv-2602-20407:
Shallow quantum circuits struggle to focus probability on low-energy states, a central limit for quantum optimization on noisy near-term hardware. Lucas A. M. Rattighieri and three co-authors offer measurement-guided initialization, a looping plan that reuses outcomes from earlier runs to set up later ones. The method reads single-qubit marginal chances from top results and sets a biased product-state start, with no classical tuning.

Applied to the feedback-based method, the approach is tested on weighted MaxCut problems. Tests show it improves shallow-depth circuit results and refines answers step by step toward high quality, while keeping it non-variational. Such readouts, the paper argues, can strengthen shallow quantum methods suited to near-term devices.
arxiv-2602-20507:
People recall files by when, where, and in what context they saw them, but retrieval systems force keyword searches across isolated silos. William Anthony Mason presents the Unified Personal Index in this dissertation, a memory-aligned architecture bridging that gap. The Indaleko prototype demonstrates feasibility on thirty-one million files spanning one hundred sixty terabytes across eight storage platforms, uniting temporal, spatial, and activity metadata in one graph database.

Indaleko answers natural language queries such as photos near a conference venue last spring, which existing systems cannot process, with sub-second responses through memory anchor indexing. It ends cross-platform search fragmentation and keeps perfect precision for well-specified memory patterns. Commercial systems tested all fail on memory-based queries, returning overwhelming results without contextual filtering. New data sources join in ten minutes to ten hours per provider, with privacy preserved through UUID-based semantic decoupling.
arxiv-2602-21107:
Cell-free massive MIMO networks promise uniform service, but active eavesdropping threatens their security. Junbin Yu, Tianyu Lu, Mohammadali Mohammadi, and Michail Matthaiou build a resilience framework for them in this 2026 arXiv paper. Protective partial zero-forcing at multi-antenna access points anchors the design, and a security-aware metric tracks performance during and after an outage through absorption, adaptation, and recovery.

A priority-aware power allocation problem minimizes the error between real-time and desired security efficiency, trading secrecy for one user against quality for all. A successive convex approximation algorithm solves it, choosing at each step the strategy with the best resilience score. Simulations show flexible adaptation between fast recovery and high-quality recovery as needs dictate.
arxiv-2602-21207:
Adding a third sign to the real numbers creates a system where addition can cancel in new ways. Jaehwan Kim introduces and studies that three-sign hypernumber system in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multiplication stays single-valued, while a hyperaddition encodes cancellation between positive and negative reals, and the classical reals embed as a genuine subfield.

Addition is almost associative but not a canonical hypergroup, and the paper pinpoints exactly where associativity fails. For a key triple form, a closed formula gives the associativity defect, matching the loss of absolute value when adding a number and its negative. An ambient cancellation monoid explains the behavior, though the system cannot be recovered from it by simple projection. Scalar multiplication distributes, and the sign layer admits a hypergroup envelope.
arxiv-2602-21307:
What functions do neural net parts truly learn? Elizabeth Tan, Adil Soubki, and Miles Cranmer answer with symbol-based boiling down in this 2026 arXiv paper, putting out the open-source SymTorch pack for the PyTorch world. The method states net parts as readable closed-form forms, baring learned working structure across designs.

Uses recover pairwise contact forces from graph nets and boil down exact closed-form answers of real systems with constants from sparse-data physics-based nets. They also uncover Lorenz chaotic motion from many-feature data, even beating the base net downstream. A symbol-based spread of the LIME clarity method beats LIME across eight yardsticks. Swapping attention-net layers with symbol-based stand-ins gains two to 19 percent throughput and nearly 19 percent memory savings.
arxiv-2602-21507:
Samuel Lai and three co-authors present independent Event Horizon Telescope imaging of Centaurus A and quasar 3C 279. Their tool, GenDIReCT, is a generative deep-learning framework built on conditional diffusion models that uses interferometric closure invariants as primary observables.

For Centaurus A, reconstruction reveals two prominent emission ridges along the jet sheath. Each ridge spans about 80 microarcseconds, with a brightness ratio near one and a half and an opening angle near 12 degrees. For 3C 279, three distinct components appear. Southern jet ejecta move about 5 microarcseconds over about 5 days, an apparent speed near 10 times light speed. The results match EHT Collaboration reports. Because closure-invariant imaging largely avoids calibration systematics, it offers a truly independent, calibration-free view at very high angular resolution, plus samples of plausible image solutions.
arxiv-2602-21607:
Taichi Ueyama and two co-authors show how pulsar timing arrays can gauge the direction of arrival of a gravitational wave. The paper tackles the inverse problem for four-pole moments of pulsar timings. Those moments come from gravity waves from a main lone source, such as a giant black hole pair, over an even random background.

Links between four-pole moments are discussed, with links between pulsar pairs over the full sky taken into account. Those links form a three-dimensional traceless matrix of rank 2, closely tied to a shadow tensor for the wave. The rank-2 matrix thereby allows arrival gauging. Looking ahead to the coming Square Kilometre Array, angular sharpness and arrival gauging errors are also examined.
arxiv-2602-21707:
Learned image reconstruction often leans on black-box modules whose inner logic is hard to read and whose robustness is in doubt. Joshua Schulz and four co-authors build on a method that embeds data-driven detail into a model-based convolutional dictionary through neural-network-inferred maps of local sparsity levels. Better network design and training extend the method so filter order no longer matters and the dictionary can be swapped at run time.

Tests on low-field MRI, including live human data, show the gain from switching dictionaries, and the method beats other recent deep learning methods there. On out-of-distribution data it degrades less than rivals, which the authors credit to its model-based core leaning less on training data.
arxiv-2602-21807:
Fatigue failure strikes when a solid faces repeated, cyclic loading. Swarnendu Maity and four co-authors study the distribution of fatigue failure times, rather than average times alone, in model glasses under cyclic shear and in an elasto-plastic model. Average cycles to failure diverge as strain amplitude approaches the fatigue limit from above, but the team asks how failure times spread.

In atomistic simulations, the standard deviation of the logarithm of failure times runs proportional to mean values, with the constant shrinking as system size grows, indicating a sharper distribution. A finite-element-based elasto-plastic model shows similar behavior, with the ratio of standard deviation to mean tending toward zero in the thermodynamic limit. The distributions appear to arise from intrinsic stochasticity of the failure process, analyzed through a stochastic damage accumulation model, rather than solely from sample disorder.
arxiv-2602-22207:
Multilingual model tests are only as good as their translations, and translated benchmarks often drift in meaning or drop context. Hanna Yukhymenko and two co-authors present a fully automated pipeline for translating benchmarks and datasets at scale without that decay. It adapts test-time compute scaling, including a method called Universal Self-Improvement and a new multi-round ranking method, T-RANK.

The pipeline preserves each benchmark's task structure and linguistic nuance during localization, and its outputs beat traditional pipelines on quality. The team applies it to popular benchmarks across eight Eastern and Southern European languages. Evaluators gain translated tests they can trust to measure models rather than translation errors.
arxiv-2602-22307:
Measuring cosmic time delays from light curves sounds routine, but Namu Kroupa and Will Handley identify a fundamental pathology in the likelihood itself. With Gaussian-process light-curve models, the likelihood generically develops a boundary-driven W-shape: a global maximum at the true delay, with gradual rises toward the edges of the observation window. Time-delay estimation, they note, is intrinsically extrapolative.

In practice, global samplers like nested sampling drift toward spurious edge modes unless strict convergence criteria are adopted, and the effect strengthens as data density grows over a fixed span. The authors advise concrete remedies, notably more live points. Methods favoring small delays, like optimizers and local MCMC, instead bias the Hubble constant upward. The paper clarifies failure modes that standard practice can miss.
arxiv-2602-22407:
Two famous active galaxies, NGC 4303 and NGC 1068, anchor studies of black-hole growth, but their distances need firm measurement. Madison Markham and four co-authors measure Cepheid-based distances from Hubble observations across a dozen visits per galaxy in two filters. They identify tens of thousands of point sources, with over a hundred strong Cepheid candidates in one galaxy and about fifty in the other.

Fitting the period-luminosity relation, calibrated on the Large Magellanic Cloud's geometric distance and corrected for metallicity, yields distance moduli of about thirty-one magnitudes for NGC 4303 and about thirty for NGC 1068. That puts NGC 4303 about sixteen and a half megaparsecs away. The measurements tighten the cosmic yardstick for two canonical active galaxies.
arxiv-2602-22507:
Generative AI now drafts floorplans, but fidelity goals borrowed from visual generators do not capture what floorplans are for: organizing spaces for use. Zhuoyang Jiang and three co-authors draw on space syntax, an established architectural design theory, to recover convex-space access graphs across varied formats. That theory-grounded shared representation, called a design container, supports evaluation and model understanding of spatial design.

Using the Space Syntax Integration Operator on four housing sets spanning fifteen countries reveals that public spaces score highest on linkage, with patterns that vary by set. Those patterns feed the RPLAN-SSI benchmark, which tests group-wide use-based profile match and within-plan public-space edge. Machine-made floorplans show a design gap: their public spaces enjoy a smaller linkage edge. Space Syntax-Guided Post-Training, using operator-derived reward signals, improves both scores across five diffusion backbones while keeping native workings.
arxiv-2602-22707:
Kai Li and six co-authors give exploring drones a lighter brain. Autonomous exploration in unknown places demands sensing, mapping, and deciding on the fly, but current methods lean on frequent global optimization. That brings heavy compute delays and wobbly paths, painful on small edge devices.

SCOPE builds a skeletal graph of the space piece by piece and reasons about unknown regions implicitly, skipping constant global replans. A proximal planner draws smooth, fast local paths, while a region-sequence planner wakes only when needed to order global visits. In simulation, SCOPE matched leading global planners while cutting compute cost by about eighty-seven percent. Real-world flights confirmed its robustness and low latency.
arxiv-2602-23007:
Fabian Grander and four co-authors study how zonal flows merge in gyrofluid resistive drift-wave turbulence, using the modified Hasegawa-Wakatani model. Merging of zonal flows and the chaotic development of the initial zonal flow pattern are explored, with conservation equations for zonal flow momentum and energy derived including consistent finite Larmor radius effects.

Those equations support a quantitative analysis of zonal flow mergers in numerical simulations. Nonlinear local Reynolds stress transfer, rather than viscous dissipation, emerges as the main cause of merging. The authors also discuss whether a phase transition in the strict thermodynamic sense applies to zonal flow transition hysteresis, weighing the concept against the simulated behaviour.
arxiv-2602-23107:
Pedro Lourenço proves structure theorems for locally compact modules over localizations of the integers. Given a multiplicatively closed subset of the integers, such modules admit theorems similar to those for locally compact abelian groups. The first theorem is the most notable. Every such module splits into a real vector part, a restricted product of p-adic vector parts over a set of primes determined by the subset, and a remainder. That remainder contains a compact open submodule.

As for locally compact abelian groups, the locally compact, compactly generated modules over the localized integers can be characterized, along with their Pontryagin duals, in the second and third structure theorems. The characterizations imply that any locally compact module of this kind is an inverse limit of modules from a specific family. As an elementary consequence, the first theorem yields a full classification of locally compact vector spaces over the rationals.
arxiv-2602-23207:
Spiros Argyros investigates the extreme points of the unit ball of the James Tree space, known as JT. Extreme points are the corners of a convex set, the points that cannot be split into averages of other points. Mapping them reveals the geometric shape of the space, and this note relates the structure of JT to the classical James space J.

The author gives partial characterizations of extremality built on the concept of separated vectors. For positive vectors the characterization becomes complete. He also establishes the equal sums property for positive extreme points, giving a clean test for extremality in that important special case and a foothold for the fuller picture.
arxiv-2602-23807:
Ryosuke Yoshii and Rio Oto study how a topological mass controls the Kondo scale in a chain of paired sites, the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. The 2026 paper looks at bound states that form at walls between two dimer patterns, once the chain couples to a metal and local repulsion acts.

The authors show, by analysis and numerics, that the Kondo temperature follows the topological mass that sets the bulk energy gap. Near the topological transition the scale falls in step with the mass, while keeping its sharp exponential response to coupling strength. That gives a minimal way for a bulk topological factor to set an emergent many-body energy. The result explains why soliton Kondo signals vary so strongly in graphene ribbons on gold, and it yields testable predictions for tunneling spectra.
arxiv-2602-24007:
Advaith Maddipatla and seven co-authors present an inference-time optimization framework for generating protein ensembles that match experimental data. The 2026 paper notes that protein function depends on dynamic ensembles, yet generative models often fail to match experiments. Guided generators suffer from fixed sampling horizons and sensitivity to initialization.

The framework optimizes over latent representations to maximize ensemble likelihood, removing dependence on diffusion length and initialization bias. Results beat leading guidance methods on diversity, physical energy, and agreement with X-ray and NMR data. In short, the team tunes the hidden settings, not the final shapes. The tuned shapes still match the lab data. That match is what makes the method useful. The work gives teams a steadier way to build protein shape sets from lab data.
arxiv-2602-24207:
Gabriele Farina and Juan Carlos Perdomo prove that any no-regret online algorithm deployed in prediction converges to a stable equilibrium. The 2026 paper addresses the feedback loop at the heart of performative prediction: deployed models shape the data distributions they later train on.

The main result is a reduction: no-regret algorithms converge to a mixed stable equilibrium, where models shape distributions so their own predictions look optimal in hindsight. Earlier results imposed strong restrictions on model influence. Using a martingale argument and allowing randomization, the authors avoid any assumption about how populations respond to predictions and sidestep hardness results for stable models. The connection also explains why common algorithms stabilize and prevent runaway feedback loops.
arxiv-2603-00007: Wang examines stability of the Betke-Henk-Wills conjecture, which bounds the lattice point count of a convex body by its successive minima. While the conjecture holds for orthogonal parallelotopes, general bodies in five or more dimensions remain open. He shows the inequality survives metric perturbations for integer boxes rotated within a calculated radius. He derives explicit geometry-invariant bounds on that radius from the operator norm. He also extends the analysis to Lp balls above a sharp threshold.
arxiv-2603-00207: Ghosal and colleagues present VisRef, a test-time scaling framework that re-injects a coreset of visual tokens into reasoning, keeping models grounded in images as textual reasoning extends. Extended text reasoning can degrade vision-dependent performance as attention drifts from visual tokens to textual priors alone. VisRef picks tokens that fit the reasoning context while staying diverse and globally representative of the image. Under fixed test-time compute budgets, it tops rival scaling approaches by up to 6.4% on three visual reasoning benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-00307: Korun tests a geometric classification of language-model hallucinations. It sorts failures into center drift, wrong-well convergence, and coverage gaps, induced in GPT-2. With fifteen prompts per group across twenty runs, he checks which failure types stand out in static embeddings and hidden states. Only coverage gaps stand out clearly, carried by vector size, not direction. The other two types do not stand out in either space. Token-level tests inflate significance several-fold by recounting the same material.
arxiv-2603-00807: Van Buskirk and five colleagues ask whether fields have settled the venue problem in similar ways. A survey of 3,510 US tenure track faculty, with 163,002 pairwise votes across 8,044 venues, finds fields span a wide accord spectrum. Economics, Chemistry, and Physics agree strongly on elite venues, while Computer Science and Engineering split across hundreds of outlets. Within fields, tastes track school rank and gender, and scholars realise own tastes more than field accord.
arxiv-2603-01007: Zhu and six colleagues improve 3D occupancy prediction for self-driving cars, where view transforms misalign geometry and semantic classes skew across space. Their Dr.Occ framework guides voxel alignment with dense depth cues and assigns region experts to different spatial areas, so depth fixes geometry while experts sharpen semantics. On the Occ3D-nuScenes benchmark it lifts the strong BEVDet4D baseline by about 7 percent on mean IoU and about 3 percent on IoU, using vision alone.
arxiv-2603-01207: Santra, Samanta, and Ghosh study the superconducting diode effect in multi-lane Rashba wires, where several transverse subbands make real devices richer than single-channel models. Both curved and box traps support uneven Fulde-Ferrell states driving strong one-way currents, with diode rates around 55 to 60 percent. Key: the current-driven Fulde-Ferrell state holds a topological phase with Majorana zero modes. Pair push follows fed-in current, giving direct control. Cross-lane coupling lets a transverse field alone produce a response.
arxiv-2603-01307: Goren and Soares analyze finality in the Filecoin network, the dynamic probabilistic guarantee that a tipset stays permanent in the canonical chain. Unlike static worst-case analyses, their method computes the error probability each round from live chain history. It needs only blocks from honest participants, so clients or off-chain apps can run it without changing Filecoin consensus. Under typical conditions the sought error probability of 2 to the power minus 30 is reached in about 30 rounds. That is a 30-fold improvement over the 900-round fixed threshold, speeding transactions and usability.
arxiv-2603-01407:
Saad Alqithami wrote this 2026 work on how smart agents can track what is true from many points of view. In groups of agents, each one sees a different scene and holds different beliefs. Older tools split time, place, and viewpoint into separate parts, which makes joint thought brittle and weak.

Alqithami joins all three in one math structure called the Observer-Situation Lattice. Each point in the grid pairs one observer with one scene, so beliefs sit in a single shared space. Two methods run on the grid: one spreads new facts step by step, and one finds and splits clashes. Proof checks and tests on mind-reading tasks show the frame is sound, fast, and clear for group agents.
arxiv-2603-01707:
Julien Hebraud, Floriane Arrouas, Bruno Peaudecerf, and colleagues study slow relaxation in a quantum kicked rotor. Their 2026 work uses a model where a quantum rotor gets periodic kicks, as in cold-atom lab tests. When the rotor starts from rest, the effective disorder gains a mirror symmetry.

That symmetry pairs up energy states at opposite momenta with tiny energy splits between partners. Tiny splits mean huge time scales, stacked in a hierarchy from fast to extremely slow. Scattering peaks then evolve in a non-monotonic way with lopsided contrasts. After that odd phase, both peaks relax toward a shared value at a logarithmic crawl. Such glass-like slowness from one symmetry, in a fully coherent system, links quantum order to slow dynamics.
arxiv-2603-02007:
Dongxue Liu, Jiaqin Dong, Yunxing Liu, and colleagues model how laser roughness imprints onto fusion targets. Their 2026 work serves direct-drive inertial confinement fusion, where lasers crush a fuel capsule directly. Tiny surface flaws can seed instabilities that spoil the implosion and its energy gain.

Their equivalent perturbation model maps laser imprinting into a matching target surface perturbation. Fabrication flaws and thermal smoothing in the plasma enter the same frame, widening past geometric views. A threshold ratio separates regimes: below it, target flaws dominate the outcome. Radiation-hydrodynamics simulations confirm that key timings and adiabat shifts stay small below that threshold. Omega experiments support the picture, so joint control of laser and target quality can guide stable high-gain designs.
arxiv-2603-02107:
Muhittin Evren Aydın and Rafael López extend a classic curve in this 2026 geometry paper. The classic curve is the catenary, the shape a hanging chain takes under gravity. They study a twin of that shape in the dual plane, a number system used in geometry. Their new curves are defined for a family set by one real value.

The authors define the new curves as points where an energy score stops changing. From that rule they derive the governing equations for the curves. For some values they solve those equations in closed form. They also describe the curves through their bend and their normal direction. The work gives dual geometry a firm analogue of a famous shape.
arxiv-2603-02407:
Ariel Edery studies a sudden pulse on a two-level quantum system in this 2026 paper. The system starts in a mix, called a superposition, of its two energy states. A delta-function pulse hits at a single instant, at time zero. Edery solves the coupled equations for the state's coefficients after the pulse.

Final coefficients depend on pulse strength and on the starting mix, both left as free inputs. A general formula gives the chance of landing in the second state. Curiously, that chance ignores the energy gap and the relative phase of the mix. At special pulse strengths, the system lands in one definite state with certainty. Edery reads that outcome as a form of collapse from superposition.
arxiv-2603-02507:
A Wood, D Rice, T Xie, and colleagues turn quantum spin into visible rotation in this 2026 paper. Diamond defects called NV centers hold spins that light can address. Their spins stay coherent at room temperature for long times. A levitated diamond hosts an ensemble of these spins in this experiment.

Laser and microwave pulses set the spins into a chosen quantum state. Spin-mechanical coupling then twists the host particle according to that state. The twist deflects a weak infrared laser beam, making the outcome macroscopic. Readout contrast exceeded seventy percent in their measurements. Pulsed control revealed Rabi oscillations, spin echoes, and relaxation effects mechanically. They timed the particle's turn from a vanishingly small spin torque. Levitated sensors and macroscopic quantum tests could follow.
arxiv-2603-02707:
Santhosh Kannan, Jainam Savla, and Madhuparna Karmakar chart what heat does to a strongly interacting magnetic material. Their 2026 paper is the first finite-temperature study of a d-wave altermagnet driven across the Mott transition, where electrons either flow or freeze in place. They use a non-perturbative numerical method, which avoids small-effect approximations.

The team maps the thermal phase diagram and gives concrete numbers for the transition scales. A frustration effect caused by the altermagnet order itself steadies a magnetic metal phase at finite heat. It also raises the magnetic transition scale across interaction strengths. Their results set the baseline picture of how heat and strong electron interactions jointly shape these new magnets.
arxiv-2603-03207:
Hirofumi Suzuki, Kentaro Kanamori, Takuya Takagi, and colleagues merge causal maps drawn from datasets that do not even share the same variables. Science often holds several studies of one system, each measuring a different subset of factors, with hidden confounders lurking. Learning one graph per dataset and overlapping them misses many real links.

Their method builds on causal additive models that retain information about unobserved variables in each graph. They prove the true causal graph stays structurally consistent with those per-dataset results. The integration algorithm then lists every graph compatible with all datasets, using an efficient combinatorial search. Tests against existing methods show the merged graphs recover relationships that overlap-based approaches cannot see.
arxiv-2603-03407:
Basil Hasan Khwaja and three colleagues trace where drug knowledge lives inside a language model. Models perform well on pharmacology tasks, but nobody knew how that knowledge is stored or fetched. Their 2026 study opens up Llama-based biomedical models with two tools. One is activation patching, which swaps internal signals to find what causes an answer. The other is linear probes, which test what each internal signal encodes.

Early layers turn out to matter most for drug-group knowledge. The strongest causal effects come from middle tokens inside a drug group's name, not its final token. Probes tell a matching story: single-token signals are weak, while pooled signals across tokens reach top accuracy, and traces exist already in the embedding layer. Drug meaning, the authors conclude, is spread across tokens rather than filed in one place.
arxiv-2603-03507:
Alessandro Salvatore, Stanislav Fort, and Surya Ganguli argue that adversarial examples are a geometry problem, not a glitch. Tiny invisible tweaks can flip a neural network's classification, and their 2026 paper asks why such tweaks are always nearby. They define a network's perceptual manifold for a concept: every input the network confidently assigns to that class.

Measured across networks, those manifolds are vastly higher-dimensional than human concepts. Volume grows exponentially with dimension, so machine concepts sprawl through input space, and almost any image sits close to one. That predicts robust accuracy should fall as manifold dimension rises. Tests on eighteen networks confirm both predictions. Even the most robust networks remain exponentially misaligned with human perception. Only the few manifolds near human dimensionality align well.
arxiv-2603-04007: Mukherjee and Moharir study best-arm identification under a fixed budget with feasibility constraints in grouped bandits. Each arm carries several independent attributes with random rewards, feasible only when every mean clears a threshold. The goal is the feasible arm of largest overall mean. The authors first derive a lower bound on error probability for any method in this setting. They then propose Feasibility Constrained Successive Rejects, identifying the best arm while ensuring feasibility, with near-optimal dependence. Empirically the method beats natural rivals while keeping feasibility guarantees.
arxiv-2603-04207: Costa and de Aguiar study Arnold tongues in the forced Kuramoto model with matrix coupling. Applying the Ott-Antonsen ansatz they obtain equations for the order parameter's module and phase. Since these equations depend explicitly on time, they run extensive numerical simulations to reveal the resonant modes and associated Arnold tongues and devil's staircases. This differs from the original forced Kuramoto model, where only one-to-one resonance is possible.
arxiv-2603-04307: Li and colleagues generate 3D avatars from text or image prompts without slow iterative optimization. They first assemble over 100,000 pairs across four modalities: detailed text, wild face photos, texture maps, and shapes. PromptAvatar pairs a texture diffusion model, guided by text or images, with a geometry diffusion model guided by text. Direct mapping from prompts to form yields lifelike avatars free of shading artifacts in under 10 seconds. Tests show it beats leading methods on quality, fine detail alignment, and speed.
arxiv-2603-04407: Rohan Saxena asks if semantic triggers alone compartmentalize emergent misalignment. Narrow harmful fine tuning causes failures far beyond training data. Prior work mixed mostly benign data with triggered harmful data. Saxena trains three model families on triggered harmful examples only, with zero benign data. Misalignment falls near zero without triggers at inference, but returns with triggers, and rephrased triggers keep the effect. Meaning, not surface wording, drives containment, so any framed harmful tuning creates hidden flaws standard tests miss.
arxiv-2603-04607: Fereydouni and colleagues study AI video in a public market. AI video tools have struggled in urban settings over privacy, ethics, and bias worries. A user-centric method puts trust and privacy safeguards first. It draws insights from abstract data forms without breaking ethical standards. Three signals drive Multi-Metric Behavioral Insights: flow, dwell, and movement patterns. Pose detection plus motion modeling stays robust under occlusion. Over 18 days, most visits last 3 to 4 minutes, while peaks lift the mean to 22 minutes. Over 60 percent of traffic crowds into 30 percent of space.
arxiv-2603-05007: Eric Duchêne and colleagues introduce s-of-k games, positional games scored by partial winning sets. Generalizing Maker-Breaker games to k-uniform games, they fix a threshold s: a player scores by claiming at least s elements of a set of size k. The paper studies the score under optimal play, denoted SC, and under pairing-restricted play, denoted SC_2, revealing the loss from limiting Maker to pairing strategies. General tools for both scores plus tailored strategies yield bounds on triangular, square, rhombus, and hexagonal grids.
arxiv-2603-05207: Jakir Hossain and Ahmet Erdem Sarıyüce replace Leiden grouping in GraphRAG with k-core decomposition for hierarchical document communities. On sparse knowledge graphs, modularity tuning lets exponentially many near-best partitions, making Leiden communities inherently non-reproducible. K-core decomposition instead gives a fixed, density-aware hierarchy, and lightweight heuristics shape it into size-bounded connected communities for retrieval and summarization, with token-budget-aware sampling cutting model costs. On earnings transcripts, news, and podcasts, the approach raises comprehensiveness and diversity of answers while reducing token usage.
arxiv-2603-05307: R. M. Bayazitov and team measure basic traits of HD 188101, a poorly studied weakly magnetic B9 star, spectroscopically and photometrically. Temperature and surface gravity are typical B9 values. Abundances of helium, carbon, oxygen, magnesium, silicon, titanium, and strontium include thermodynamic-balance departures. Silicon, titanium, and strontium exceed solar values, while helium is lower but within error limits. Beyond Kepler variability, absorption changes appear in helium, magnesium, silicon, and titanium, with same-element lines differing in abundance at the phase. It is a chemically peculiar He-weak SiTiSr star.
arxiv-2603-05607: Khan and team propose DreamCAD, a multi-modal framework that makes edge forms from point-level guidance alone, with no CAD-only annotations. Each edge form becomes a set of patches set by settings, such as Bézier faces, made through smooth tiling, for large-scale training with linked surfaces to edit. They also debut CADCap-1M, the largest CAD caption dataset, with over 1M notes made using GPT-5. DreamCAD leads on ABC and Objaverse across text, image, and point modes, with better shape trueness and passing 75% user liking.
arxiv-2603-06007: Liu and team present MASFactory, a graph-based frame running LLM multi-agent systems. Multi-agent workflows can be modeled as aimed graphs, where nodes run agents and edges hold links. Building complex graph workflows still needs manual effort and muddles outside context mixing. MASFactory gives Vibe Graphing, turning natural-language intent into an open plan and working graph. The frame also provides reuse parts and a viewer for layout previews, runtime traces, and contact. Tests on seven benchmarks back copying sameness and Vibe Graphing power.
arxiv-2603-06307: Alruwaili and his team compile cross section data for the oxygen-16 proton alpha nitrogen-13 reaction, which shapes alpha abundance and calcium to sulphur ratios in Type Ia supernovae. Recent work suggested a sevenfold rate enhancement over standard values to explain seen calcium to sulphur ratios, but low energy gaps clouded the picture. A first direct measurement at star energies with the MUSIC detector gives a rate about 1.5 times the REACLIB rate at 3 to 4 gigakelvin, with tighter error bars. That excludes the sevenfold lift.
arxiv-2603-06407: Arnold and Gröbner hunt for where a vision transformer realizes the Gestalt preference for convex over concave completions. With synthetic dart shapes, they mask regions admitting either completion equally and find BEiT reliably chooses the convex reading. Logit attribution into the discrete visual codebook traces that preference to identifiable units inside transformer substructures. Organization stays ambiguous early and midway before resolving sharply later. One head, L0H9, seeds a weak convex bias, and weakening it alone lets concave evidence steer completion.
arxiv-2603-06607: Wang and team cast vehicle radio allocation as multi-agent interference games in a hierarchy raising reinforcement learning challenges. Shift, coordination difficulty, large action spaces, partial sight, and robustness tangle. Old studies focus on new algorithms while testing and analyses remain limited, so the authors develop tasks and sets from made traces with layouts and clash conditions. Testing value-based, actor-critic, independent learning, and centralized-training plans, results identify toughness and reach across layouts as the dominant hurdle, cutting return by as much as 59 percentage points.
arxiv-2603-06807: Majdoub and Torebek study a parabolic equation that is both degenerate and singular, with a forcing term added. They seek critical exponents that divide global existence from blow-up. For one regime they prove no global solution exists for any exponent above one. For a second regime they show all weak solutions blow up in finite time below a critical exponent, given an integral of the forcing. Above that exponent, with initial data and forcing, they prove a global solution exists, using scaling, semigroup estimates and a fixed-point argument.
arxiv-2603-07207: Fu and colleagues study bidding in repeated first-price auctions under a hard budget with one-sided feedback: the top rival bid is seen after a loss but hidden after a win. The rival bid depends on impression context through an unknown coefficient plus noise of unknown distribution. A regression method based on conditional quantile invariance learns that model from censored observations. Combined with bid elimination and a dual update, it yields expected regret growing at most like the square root of the horizon, matching known lower bounds.
arxiv-2603-07307: Nguyen and colleagues tackle token merging for the Segment Anything family, where naive merging blurs boundaries and leaks prompt cues. Their StructSAM keeps resolution intact by merging only flat regions toward low-energy destinations, with explicit recovery of merged tokens. A spectral view shows the guided merges distort the graph spectrum only within bounds. Across natural and medical benchmarks it cuts encoder compute with small accuracy drops, beating rival merging methods at equal cost.
arxiv-2603-07407: Kulikov sharpens eigenvalue estimates for two localization operators, one time-frequency and one from the coherent-state transform. Both show the same plunge pattern: about as many eigenvalues near one as the area constant, then few in between, then the rest near zero. The paper pins down sharp uniform bounds just before the plunge and finds a real difference between the two cases. The coherent-state eigenvalues approach one much more slowly in the gap, a split the proofs draw from complex analysis.
arxiv-2603-07607: Hamzeh and Vahdatian close the strategic void in cloud-native autoscaling, where business policies detach from resource provisioning. Their MAS-H2 system splits control into three layers. A strategic agent turns policies into a global utility function, planning agents issue joint proactive pod-and-node scaling plans, and execution agents carry them out. Tested as a Kubernetes operator, it cuts sustained CPU stress and peak load versus native autoscalers and migrates strategies with zero downtime.
arxiv-2603-07707: Byzov and Pushkarev construct an infinite sequence of strongly regular digraphs from block matrices of circulant blocks with a packing step matching polynomial arithmetic. Computer search plus automorphism group analysis revealed a stable shape pattern, yielding an exact formula for the adjacency tables. Among the digraphs are examples with parameters where existence had before stayed open. A guess on the mirror groups of the sequence is also offered.
arxiv-2603-08607: Aditya Khan and Meredith Franklin propose RESAPLE, a one-step gauge of leftover spatial dependence in areal data. Moran's index and APLE miss the mark here, since neither targets dependence left after trends and controls are stripped out. Built from restricted-likelihood leftovers as a Rayleigh coefficient, RESAPLE stays cheap, clear, and true under middling dependence, and it also guides weight choice.
arxiv-2603-08707: Azul Garza and colleagues build Impermanent, a live test that scores forecasting models as time rolls on. Frozen train-test splits let models peek at test data or tune on test scores, puffing up their marks. Scoring forecasts in order over fresh GitHub activity streams tracks true staying power, drift, and stability, with daily updates over the top 400 repositories by stars.
arxiv-2603-08807: Yuly Billig studies time warping for series that live in any metric space. The stretching cost follows the Hellinger kernel, which sets how much a time stretch is penalized. To find the best match under that cost, he introduces the Elastic Time Warping algorithm, whose run time grows with the cube of the input size.
arxiv-2603-08907: Abhinaba Basu compares nine bound families for risk-controlled selective prediction. His Transfer-Informed Betting warm-starts a betting wealth process from a source domain's risk profile, tightening bounds when data is scarce. The wealth process stays a valid supermartingale under any source-target shift, dominates standard betting when domains match, and no data-free warm start can beat its convergence.
arxiv-2603-09007: Aishwarya Fursule and colleagues test gender fairness in audio deepfake detection. Fake voices grow ever more lifelike, raising fraud risks, yet gender bias in detection remains little studied. Training a ResNet-18 classifier on ASVspoof 5 with five fairness metrics, they find small overall error gaps between genders hide real disparities in error distribution that aggregate measures obscure.
arxiv-2603-09307: Zi Haur Pang and colleagues detect the right moment for emotional validation in Japanese empathetic spoken dialogue, working from speech alone without text context. Validation, a therapy technique that acknowledges another person's feelings, helps most when its timing and frequency are right. They fuse two HuBERT-based encoders, one tuned to paralinguistic cues and one to speech emotion, then fine-tune the pair on the timing task. Tests on an emotional storytelling corpus show clear gains.
arxiv-2603-09407: Yuki Minowa studies the topological complexity of spaces that are not simply connected, a number that gauges how unstable motion planning in the space is. Costa and Farber had introduced a cohomology class whose nilpotency bounds this number from below, and Farber and Mescher built a spectral sequence to evaluate it. Minowa extends both results along a group homomorphism. As an application, the topological complexity of some 3-manifolds whose fundamental group is nonabelian is determined.
arxiv-2603-09607: L. G. Chej and colleagues investigate a slip and no-slip wall pattern designed to stir swirl flow inside a straight microchannel. Microchannel heat sinks cool high-power electronics well, but many heat transfer boosts cost extra pumping power. Slip patterns can raise flow and convective removal with no added energy, and swirling motion promotes mixing. They assess the hydrodynamic and thermal performance of their pattern under laminar cooling conditions and find suitably arranged regions do induce the swirl.
arxiv-2603-09907: Siddhartha Das, Alexander Yosifov and Jinzhao Sun propose hysteretic squashed entanglement, a new measure of true quantum links in many body systems. It gauges how strongly two regions are quantum linked once a third region is taken into account. The measure shows wanted traits such as monogamy, convexity and faithfulness, and sits below conditional mutual information. In a quenched Ising chain it strips out classical parts and reveals real quantum links.
arxiv-2603-10007: Khamis reports a GATech entry to a shared task on spotting machine generated Arabic text. He fine tunes the multilingual E5 large encoder to sort text as human or machine written, and tries several ways to pool token vectors. Weighted layer pooling, attention pooling and gated fusion all lost to plain mean pooling, he finds. A side pattern helps explain the task: human written texts run much longer than machine ones.
arxiv-2603-10107: Moritz S. Fischer and coauthors describe how self interacting dark matter was added to the OpenGadget3 cosmology code, now released publicly. Such interactions could ease small scale tensions of cold dark matter, and N body simulations are the main tool for testing them. The implementation handles elastic scattering for many cross sections, including strongly directional ones, plus a two species model. Test problems, scaling runs and remaining challenges are all reported.
arxiv-2603-10207: Vincent Fiorino, Sean D. Lawley and Alan E. Lindsay study how a single cell senses direction from extremely faint chemical signals. At low concentration, receptor binding is discrete and choices happen long before steady profiles form. They derive the joint distribution of binding times and places given the source position. Early binding events carry far more directional information than later ones, so estimates built from the earliest impacts prove accurate with few events.
arxiv-2603-10607: Zhihong He and co-authors report a binary open cluster inside the high-velocity cloud Complex H, the first stellar tracer for such a cloud. The young, metal-poor clusters pin the cloud's distance and show it on a prograde orbit, running south to north through the outer Galactic disk. Its outer layers slow as they merge into the disk, in a slow-fast-slow velocity pattern. Orbit work suggests the clusters formed in an internal cloud-cloud collision. The find shows the circumgalactic medium can sustain star formation.
arxiv-2603-10807: Fabrizio Dimino, Bhaskarjit Sarmah, and Stefano Pasquali introduce a risk-adjusted harm score for automated red teaming of language models in finance. Binary attack-success rates and generic checklists miss failures that come through plausible framing, a real risk for banks and insurers. Their score blends how severe a disclosure is, how far disclaimers soften it, and how much the judges agree. A companion benchmark holds nearly a thousand prompts across seven risk areas, judged by three models checked against human experts. Multi-turn pressure produces more severe disclosures.
arxiv-2603-11107: Nathan Sudermann-Merx attacks Heilbronn's triangle problem with mixed-integer nonlinear programming. Points go in the unit square to make the smallest triangle area they form as large as can be. A symmetry-breaking strategy based on boundary structure strengthens the model. The nine-point case reaches certified near-global optimality in fifteen minutes on a desktop, versus about a day before. Numerical certification plus exact symbolic computation recovers coordinates matching all best-known configurations up to nine points. Their areas cluster around few values.
arxiv-2603-11307: Rickard Brännvall conditions a single global federated model on each client's own training data statistics, sidestepping the usual trade between ignoring client differences and paying for clusters or per-client models. Each client computes principal component statistics of its local data locally, so the conditioning costs zero extra communication. Across ninety-seven configurations spanning four heterogeneity types, four datasets, and seven baselines, the method matches an oracle knowing the true clusters. It beats the oracle under combined heterogeneity and stays uniquely robust when data are sparse.
arxiv-2603-11507: Dong, Liang, and Zhang give one shared theory for back-action-evading (BAE) measurements and quantum non-demolition (QND) variables in linear quantum systems. The core rule pairs a purely imaginary Hamiltonian with a coupling operator that is real or imaginary. Meet it, and conjugate observables can be read with no back action. Symmetric coupling goes further and yields QND variables by itself. When a system misses the rule, coherent feedback can engineer the effect. The rule also promotes the coupling operator to a QND observable.
arxiv-2603-11607: Zhao and co-authors present DyWeight, a learned multi-step solver that speeds up diffusion sampling. Diffusion models sample slowly, needing hundreds of evaluations per output. Newer solvers reuse past gradients, yet their handcrafted coefficients cannot track shifting sampling dynamics. DyWeight learns time-varying weights that gather gradients and scale the step size on their own. This calibration lines the solver's path up with the model's denoising dynamics, even at large steps. Across image benchmarks and text-to-image models, it wins on fidelity and stability with fewer evaluations.
