Independent upstream and downstream volumes plus tight leak, temperature, and pressure control yield steady results, with open data processing so runs can be traced. Tests on 316 stainless steel and AISI 1018 steel from 100 to 600 degrees Celsius show Arrhenius behavior matching published data.
arxiv-2604-15507: Ben Naveed and three colleagues tackle safe trajectory planning under model uncertainty with Dual-gatekeeper, a framework joining robust planning to active exploration. Exploration runs only when it yields a verifiable gain without breaking safety or a mission cost budget, weighing task scores against long-term uncertainty cuts. Two safety variants prove out on drone flights and self-driving car races with unknown parameters.
arxiv-2604-15607: Cohen and eight colleagues compare how human traits and AI design traits shape imperfectly cooperative human-AI interactions, where goals only partly align. Across 2,000 simulations and 290 human participants in hiring negotiations and AI transactions with possible concealment, simulations weight personality and AI traits evenly. With real people, AI traits, above all transparency, matter far more. The gaps vary by scenario and context.
arxiv-2604-15907: Oyejide and four colleagues propose a reconfigurable pneumatic joint for vine-inspired robots, which grow by turning inside out at the tip to reach cluttered spaces. Free-space use is limited by low axial stiffness, weak load bearing, and poor shape retention during steering. Each joint module uses symmetric air chambers that stiffen locally when pressurized, separating global flexibility from local rigidity. Tests show better shape retention, less sag under load, cascading retraction, and payload hauls up to 202 g in free space.
arxiv-2604-16007: Wu and 18 colleagues present MemExplorer, a memory synthesizer for heterogeneous NPUs serving agentic workloads. Prefill and decode need different memory, and SRAM, HBM, LPDDR, GDDR, and high-bandwidth flash trade capacity and power. MemExplorer models options and picks a heterogeneous system alongside NPU choices. Under budget, it reaches up to 2.3 times the baseline NPU's efficiency and over three times the H100's in prefill work. In decode work, it delivers nearly twice the baseline NPU's efficiency and over two and a half times the H100's at equal performance.
arxiv-2604-16207: Wang and seven colleagues present AIFIND, a method for face forgery detection that keeps learning as new forgery types appear. Older methods lean on replayed data or coarse labels, and their features drift badly, causing forgotten earlier tasks. AIFIND anchors learning with stable semantic anchors built from low-level forgery cues, aligns shifting visual features to those anchors, and keeps classifiers consistent across tasks.
arxiv-2604-16707: Bittner builds a shape account of response in spin systems, applied to the flat Ising model. With heat and field strength as axes, the mixed field tracks field and heat links. Runs reveal a ridge rising from the point into the crossing regime. Susceptibility, specific heat and mixed maxima scale apart across field, heat and mixed sectors. In axes, paths at varied fields collapse onto a common curve, bound by susceptibility. That collapse points to a thin manifold and an account of crossing.
arxiv-2604-17007: Kumar and three colleagues present MobileAgeNet, a lightweight age-estimation model built for phones. It pairs a pretrained MobileNetV3-Large backbone with a compact regression head, reaching an average error of 4.65 years on the UTKFace test set. With 3,230,000 parameters and on-device runs of about 14 milliseconds, the pipeline moves from PyTorch training through ONNX export to TensorFlow Lite conversion without measurable loss of accuracy.
arxiv-2604-17107: Hamdan and nine colleagues combine multi-dimensional MRI of tissue composition with a neural network for prostate cancer detection. Their two-stage HBR-Net-18 first smooths intensity unevenness across six maps with a Hadamard U-Net, then sorts patches with a residual network. Using overlapping 11-by-11 patches with both within-slice and between-slice information, it beats standard radiomics and baseline convolutional models, showing even sensitivity and specificity.
arxiv-2604-17207: Kang argues that greedy alignment methods outperform existing regret guarantees, because KL regret and reward learning are different targets. KL regret tracks recovery of the aligned policy, while practitioners often only need the reward inducing the correct best response. Isolating reward learning via temperature-zero regret, which scores only the top response, Kang proves reference-logged offline RLHF reaches exponentially small expected regret, needing only logarithmically many comparisons for regret at most epsilon. Greedy online RLHF achieves bounded temperature-zero regret, extending to its pairwise online DPO form.
arxiv-2604-17507: Amblard and Drezet sketch a test that could expose a hidden layer of relativistic Bohmian mechanics. That theory adds a preferred foliation, a cosmic order of simultaneity, to spacetime, long thought undetectable once quantum equilibrium holds. From arrival-time predictions for spin-1/2 particles, they show that in an EPRB-type setup with distant spin and arrival-time readings, seen timing patterns hinge on the order of readings relative to the foliation. Such a link would mark the foliation and even allow superluminal signaling.
arxiv-2604-17607: Rather, Aouchiche, and Bovdi obtain the characteristic polynomials of the Laplacian and distance Laplacian matrices of power graphs of groups of order pqr, where p, q, and r are primes. They also give these polynomials for proper power graphs of cyclic and dicyclic groups. The paper further presents inequalities for the zeros of the distance Laplacian characteristic polynomials of power graphs of finite groups, in comments.
arxiv-2604-17707: Cacioli applies validity scaling from clinical personality assessment to data probing 20 frontier models across 524 items. LLM evaluation screens nothing before interpreting substantive scales. Six indices are used: L for keeping confidence on errors, K for betting on errors, F for dropping agreed items, and Fp for dropping correct answers. RBS covers flipped watching; TRIN covers fixed answers. A tiered system finds four models construct-invalid and two elevated. Valid-profile models show item-linked confidence with mean r of 0.18, while invalid-profile models do not, at -0.20.
arxiv-2604-18107: Zang and six colleagues address a weakness of vision-language-action models. These robot brains turn images and words into actions, but they overfit memorized patterns and stumble on small changes in object pose. Their PDF method adapts such models at test time without retraining. It uses uncertainty-guided augmentation, action voting, and a small perturbation module tuned by delayed feedback, lifting success on LIBERO and Atari benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-18307: Nikankin, Tutek, Ashuach, Rosenfeld, and Belinkov ask whether reasoning models know which of their own steps matter. Long reasoning chains mix crucial steps with removable ones, and the team tests whether model activations or surface tokens better flag importance. Probes trained on activations predict step importance even before later steps are generated, and importance signals agree strongly across models. The signal spreads across layers and ignores surface cues such as position or length, showing internals reveal what tokens hide.
arxiv-2604-18707: Çakmak and three colleagues study synchronization in a chain of qubits hit by amplitude-damping noise at chosen sites. They show the noise-free subspace follows a simple rule from number theory, based on the noise sites and the chain length. Stable sync of the edge qubits for any start state holds just when that subspace holds one single-excitation state, and the same rule also locks in lasting entanglement between the edges.
arxiv-2604-18907: Macfarlane and three colleagues bridge symbolic and neural program induction with a Neural Language Interpreter. Symbolic methods generalize in new ways and use data well, but scale poorly. Neural networks learn well yet generalize poorly on new tasks. The interpreter learns its own discrete language end to end. It discovers primitive operations and runs variable length sequences with a neural executor. A Gumbel-Softmax relaxation makes the structures trainable and enables test time tuning. The model outperforms in context learning and test time training on combinatorial tasks.
arxiv-2604-19107: Mukhia, Ansari, and Nurujjaman identify a structural signature of G5 markets in shocks. Using random matrix theory, they define the complexity gap as normalized largest eigenvalue minus average correlation. The gap shows three phases: positive before shocks, near zero during shocks, and nonmonotonic recovery with false widening, recollapse, and sustained restoration. The pattern holds for the tariff event, the COVID crisis, and shocks in Japan and China. Ordinal entropy confirms it. Lower gap values predict higher volatility after shocks, making the gap a risk indicator.
arxiv-2604-19507: Hook argues that framing scholarly infrastructure as openness versus commercial enclosure distorts policy and practice. The real tension is the cost of refining structured metadata under deep technological friction. Different communities also demand different data quality, focus, and granularity. He names the innovation annulus for the zone between free structured data and the advancing frontier of commercial products. The paper recasts the debate around costs and demands rather than free data alone. That zone, he argues, will not go away.
arxiv-2604-19607: McNamara and colleagues test whether turbulence dissipation in hot cluster atmospheres can offset radiative cooling flows. Jets and bubbles inject turbulence into these atmospheres. No trends appear between atmospheric velocity dispersion and either the kinetic-to-thermal energy ratio or jet power over four decades of jet power. Jets seem to disperse energy gently at roughly constant energy per gram of gas. If velocity dispersions at Perseus, Virgo, and Hydra A centers reflect jetted turbulence, up to roughly half the bubble enthalpy could be dissipated by turbulent motion.
arxiv-2604-19707: Kumar and Marto argue that in quadratic gravity with a Weyl squared coefficient above zero, the extra spin-2 sector behaves as a dual inverted harmonic oscillator rather than a ghost. Using the Wightman spectrum condition, they prove the associated spectral density vanishes, fixing the propagator to a principal value form as a theorem rather than a prescription. The optical theorem holds, the dual sector never appears as an asymptotic state, and unitarity survives with renormalizability.
arxiv-2604-20007: Castellucci and four colleagues model a gas current fed into a curved axisymmetric porous channel, a toy model of buried storage in domes. Thinness yields an equation for how the gas-liquid interface evolves, with a simpler form for weakly curved channels. In Gaussian channels buoyancy keeps acting because the flow keeps slowing, while in parabolic channels rising slope lets buoyancy win over time. The parabolic flow shows five time regimes, and reduced models match full simulations, with lessons for hydrogen and carbon dioxide storage safety and efficiency.
arxiv-2604-20807: Abdulaziz, Ammer, and Madlener are building Isabelle/HOL tools for formalising primal-dual arguments: a framework plus a library. They discuss example formalisations from matching theory, covering classic methods like the Hungarian Method, widely seen as the first primal-dual method. They also cover modern methods like the Adwords method, which models giving search queries to advertisers in search engines.
arxiv-2604-21007: Kakimoto and colleagues confirm crowded regions of massive quiescent galaxies in the early Universe with JWST spectroscopy, finding three such galaxies near the Jekyll and Hyde pair at redshift 3.71 and two near SXDS-27434. Number-density analysis shows both neighborhoods run three to four times denser than their fields, and spectral fitting gives the galaxies matching formation and quenching epochs. The same pattern in other proto-clusters points to large-scale environment driving quenching, likely through mergers, gas flows, and black-hole feedback.
arxiv-2604-21107: Cody Baker and six colleagues derive a closed formula counting 2-bridge knots by crossing number and signature, extending earlier work on their average signature. From that count they show the signatures spread toward a bell-shaped normal curve as the crossing number grows without bound. The result is a central limit theorem for a knot invariant, giving the distribution of signatures a precise large-scale shape.
arxiv-2604-21307: Wenzhao Wei and 16 colleagues report a 13-liter purified liquid argon test stand at Wellesley College built to support detector research on charge and light readout. A single-pass liquid-phase column drives impurities to sub-part-per-billion levels, and a double-gridded purity monitor tracks electron lifetime. The system holds about one-fifth of a part per billion of oxygen-equivalent impurity steady over 20 hours, corresponding to an electron lifetime of 1.6 milliseconds at a drift field of 500 volts per centimeter.
arxiv-2604-21507: Nikhil Raghav explains DiariZen, the leading open-source speaker diarization system, in a self-contained guide. Speaker diarization answers who spoke when in a multi-speaker audio stream. DiariZen joins a pruned WavLM-Large encoder, a Conformer backend with powerset tagging, and VBx clustering. The guide covers seven stages: loading and sliding-window segmentation, feature extraction, tagging, aggregation, embedding extraction, VBx clustering, and reconstruction with RTTM output. Each block gives reasons, code links, tensor shapes, and marked pictures on a 30-second AMI excerpt, with scripts and a notebook online.
arxiv-2604-21707: Hunt and four colleagues ask how changing drone-swarm size affects the human operator watching over the mission, since robots may join or leave after failures or redeployment. In two studies with 34 people monitoring simulated swarms, small size increases stayed manageable while small decreases left workload strangely elevated, a residue effect. Large changes in either direction wiped out those patterns, suggesting a cognitive reset.
arxiv-2604-21807: Hsiao, Liu, and Reinhart show that treatment history, often ignored in alloy design, can be recovered from text and put to work. A language model turns annealing treatment text into vectors. Those vectors recover treatment settings with R2 above 0.99 overall. Using the vectors as features for high-entropy alloy hardness then improves forecasts by 20 percent. Text descriptions of treatment, the authors argue, carry real value for alloy properties.
arxiv-2604-21907: Lockwood presents Equity Bias, a framework joining philosophy and practice to build fairer, smarter AI. It starts from hermeneutic philosophy and epistemic injustice theory, treating bias as a mirror of whose knowledge gets encoded, not as a defect to erase. Traditional approaches aim to cut or remove bias. The framework instead makes bias transparent and contestable, broadening whose perspectives shape AI and viewing AI systems as interpretive agents. Its three-phase AI Life Cycle covers Equity Archaeology, Co-Creating Meaning, and Ongoing Accountability.
arxiv-2604-22007: Andrenšek investigates equations in Kiselman's semigroup Kn, generated by a1 through an. Let f denote the zero element of Kn. He proves that if y in Kn lies in the subsemigroup generated by a2 through an, then x y = f implies x = f. In contrast, the equation x a1 = f admits non-trivial solutions. He describes the solution set of this equation, shows its cardinality is 1 + |Kn-1|, and studies its algebraic structure. Moreover, he shows |K2n+1| is even, whereas |K2n| is odd.
arxiv-2604-22407: Hu and four colleagues expose a hidden failure mode in continual learning with Adam as backend. In an 8-domain continual language model, shared-routing baselines collapse close to vanilla forgetting. Only adaptive decoupled routing stays stable at 9.4, beating vanilla by about 4 units. They explain it through Adam's second-moment pathway, where projection inflates the old-direction learning rate, matching measurements within 8 percent. Their fix routes the modified gradient only to the first moment, preserving faithful second-moment statistics with overlap-aware adaptive strength.
arxiv-2604-22507: Bätz and five colleagues built RAIL-BENCH, a test suite that grades camera sight for self-driving trains on existing tracks. Railway work had no public yardstick, so the suite sets tasks, data, and scoreboards for comparison. It covers five jobs: spotting rails, finding objects, marking plants, tracking things, and judging motion from one camera. The team adds LineAP, a score for how closely a rail line matches the true shape apart from grouping.
arxiv-2604-22607: Lim and two colleagues model surfactant level from early-stage views of rising bubble shapes. Bubbles released from a needle deform with the surrounding liquid's surfactant level. Using high-speed imaging, the team examines bubbles within the first 144 ms of ascent, about 40 mm, and extracts the aspect ratio and its change. When clean, bubbles show strong shape wobbles from swapping between surface and kinetic energy. Surfactants damp these wobbles, with smaller aspect ratios and earlier peaks, and damping grows with level until near-full, where bubbles remain largely round.
arxiv-2604-23307: Southiratn and three colleagues propose CombiMOTS, a Pareto Monte Carlo tree search making molecules that hit two target proteins at once. Single-objective combinations miss trade-offs between target binding and molecular traits, and most makers ignore synthetic planning. CombiMOTS explores a buildable fragment space under vector constraints covering target affinity and drug traits. Tests on real-world data yield novel dual-target molecules with high docking scores, greater diversity, and balanced profiles, backing its promise for dual-target drug work.
arxiv-2604-23407: Li and four colleagues introduce PushupBench, 446 long-form clips averaging about 37 seconds for evaluating repetition counting in video. Vision-language models recognise what happens but fail to count how many times: the best frontier model reaches 42.1 percent exact accuracy, while open 4B models score about 6 percent, matching supervised baselines. Accuracy alone misleads, since weaker models lean on the modal count instead of reasoning over time. Fine-tuning on counting with 1,000 samples transfers to general video understanding, lifting three benchmarks, suggesting counting proxies broader temporal reasoning.
arxiv-2604-23707: El Hajji and colleagues unify definitions of the magnetisation state for low-coercive-force magnets. They propose four definitions, two from material traits and two from motor quantities. The material pair uses flux density and polarisation; the motor pair uses flux linkage and back-EMF parts. Tests on a hybrid-magnet motor across its operating plane show which metric fits material work, control, or routine checks.
arxiv-2604-23807: Suwa and Igarashi check tensor shapes at compile time without demanding proofs of type sameness. Dependent and refinement types can verify shapes but force developers to write proofs, and proof search may run long. Their staged approach extracts shape conditions early and enforces them as assertions computed at compile time, so a mismatch fails during compilation. Shape arguments stay implicit where possible, a plain surface language hides staging, and a prototype checks programs including several ocaml-torch examples.
arxiv-2604-24007: Xiao and Slock build explicit performance benchmarks for line spectral estimation, the task of recovering frequencies and complex amplitudes from signals. Fisher-based benchmarks miss threshold effects and error spillover, so the authors add an ordered Ziv-Zakai bound for frequencies and a local transfer account for plug-in amplitude error. The frequency bound matches the prior bound at low signal strength and the Cramer-Rao bound at high strength. Tests across signal levels, snapshot counts, and model orders back the benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-24407: Mishra and three colleagues present AD-Relight, a training-free method relighting Photoshop-generated ad banners in video frames. Existing ad pipelines warp banners by shape while missing scene lighting, and diffusion-based insertion and relighting models, untrained on banner data, also struggle to relight new banners. AD-Relight adapts a diffusion relighting model at test time across multiple stages, needing no banner training data. Tests show it beats relighting baselines and warping-based ad placement, and user studies show participants consistently prefer its outputs over prior approaches.
arxiv-2604-24707: Tourani and six colleagues make RGB-D visual SLAM for indoor robots passage-aware. Indoor robots need to know where they can pass from room to room. Doors and openings that robots can pass through matter for navigation, yet are little studied in modern mapping tools. Their method fuses geometric, semantic and topological cues, models doors as flat parts of walls, and infers passages from travel evidence and gaps in wall shape. In vS-Graphs, it adds passage-level structure to scene graphs and improves room links.
arxiv-2604-24907: Grover, Gupta and Křetínský introduce a new family of temporal logics for specs in motion planning. Unlike signal logic, the new logic treats paths as first-class objects, splitting geometry from logic. This yields simpler, more understandable rules and a refined satisfaction that can reflect likes over behaviours. It is more usable for human-given specs and more open to learning specs from demonstrations. They also give a learning algorithm with a prototype and discuss model checking and watching.
arxiv-2604-25207: Wang and Martin present a duet performance between two intelligent musical instruments, Sù and Agentier, and their human performers, linked by feedback. Both systems work recursively, not as predictable tools: past actions shape future behaviour. Sù works in audio space with a neural feedback synthesis system based on a RAVE model that reuses its own states. Agentier works in control space, routing Roland S-1 and QuNeo gestures into a recurrent network that feeds back into synthesis. It probes shared agency, resistance and negotiation between humans and intelligent musical systems.
arxiv-2604-25307: Roy and Bulik test how well mock Einstein Telescope data can pin down the make-up of the cosmos. The planned third-generation detector is far more keen than today's LIGO detectors and should catch star-mass mergers out to redshift 10. From a fake event list, they show a plain, fast way to read the Hubble constant or matter share from chirp mass spectra. One year of runs gives 1 percent error on the Hubble constant, and 4 percent on matter share. On its own, its sirens can bound the Hubble constant.
arxiv-2604-25407: Baron Moreno, Englert and Peters tackle dip-hunting at hadron colliders, the flip side of bump-hunting. Signal-background interference can wash out bumps and break the narrow-width guess. They flip the task: given a seen pattern, how likely is a BSM scalar source? They train parametric neural nets to learn the likelihood ratio over background and BSM factors. Testing seen data against a scan of a minimal scalar extension of the Standard Model, they give a sound check in perturbative regimes, though BSM recovery stays model-bound.
arxiv-2604-25507: Centorrino, Fève and Florens build a nonparametric way to pin down consumer tastes under nonlinear price schedules. They use shifts across several price schedules to identify both the utility function and the spread of taste types. The quantile function of unseen types solves a functional equation. Their iterative estimator lets bias shrink fast with each round while variance grows slowly, giving a near-parametric rate. Simulations and an application to a European mail carrier show the method recovers utility functions and taste spreads in finite samples.
arxiv-2604-25607: Chen and two colleagues analyse the Zc(3900) and Zcs(3985) states jointly from experiment and lattice data. The study covers electron-positron final states plus finite-volume energy levels from recent lattice QCD simulations. Open-charm loops with triangle singularities, coupled-channel interactions, and pion-kaon final-state interactions all enter. Pole contributions for both states prove indispensable. The joint description supports reading both states as SU(3) partners in one octet multiplet and as resonances. Extracted pole masses sit near 3880 MeV and 3977 MeV, with half-widths near 32 MeV and 29 MeV.
arxiv-2604-25807: D'Alessandro, Singkanipa, and Lidar prove the error scaling claimed for robust dynamical decoupling sequences with even pulse counts. Such sequences cancel pulse flaws from any parameters, with only a linear rise in pulse number. Prior work had backed them, but no full proof existed. From a fidelity-linked series expansion, the authors derive conditions for cancelling coefficients below order n. Those phases meet the conditions, grounding the design.
arxiv-2604-25907: Lin and Ie explain why supervised fine-tuning precedes reward-based training for reasoning models. They use one loss family built on the Tsallis q-logarithm. That family spans reward-only training and likelihood estimation over latent trajectories. Analysis shows the reward pole escapes cold start slowly but resists label noise. The likelihood pole escapes fast but memorizes noise. Two new estimators optimize fixed points on this continuum without annotated rationales.
arxiv-2604-26007: Thong and Vegh study a quantum mechanical system sharing the spectrum of SYK bilinear operators. The usual positivity bootstrap cannot tell apart the boundary data that pick the SYK spectrum, so it cannot determine the eigenvalues. Using fractional powers of operators instead, they obtain constraint equations that fix the spectrum without positivity. The roots converge to exact eigenvalues as truncation order grows. They call this the direct bootstrap.
arxiv-2604-26107: Ji, Kulkarni, and Zaleski simulate a two-dimensional atomizing liquid jet with volume-of-fluid methods. They test whether fractal measures capture the lacunarity of the final breakup state. Box-counting the full interface gives no single scale-free exponent. Instead two scaling ranges meet near a crossover: coarse boxes see the folded jet envelope, fine boxes sample ligaments, droplets, and smooth segments. By structure, droplets are most lacunar, with dimension below one, ligaments intermediate, and the main body highest. That hierarchy stays stable across a wide Reynolds range.
arxiv-2604-26407: Maity and three colleagues studied how a droplet on a taut wire breaks free when the wire is plucked and released. The transverse wave briefly forces the droplet base, stretching it before sheet formation and jet breakup. Maximum stretch before detachment follows the mechanical work passed through three-phase contact-line traction, balanced against viscous loss during filament extension. That balance names the contact line as the route from impulse to capillary deformation.
arxiv-2604-26607: Bhusal and three colleagues tested varied language models for automating secondary mathematics competency assessment in Nepal. A human-in-the-loop frame scored models against faculty ground truth on Grade 10 optional mathematics across four topics and four skills. Gemini-based mixture-of-experts models reached fair agreement, while the larger Orion model showed no agreement at all. The architecture-compatibility gap suggests instruction-following outweighs raw parameter scale in rubric-bound tasks. Models remain helpers, not ready for autonomous certification.
arxiv-2604-26907: Bakshi and three colleagues study how spatial exchange anisotropy reshapes the spin-1/2 kagome antiferromagnet, using Schwinger-boson mean-field theory. Strengthening exchange along one bond set versus the other two, tuned by a deviation parameter, rebuilds the low-energy spinon sector, softening the lowest spinon branch and shifting the two-spinon continuum down. At large anisotropy the spinon gap closes, signaling condensation and the onset of magnetic order. The resulting orders are anisotropic themselves, with weak moments on strong bonds and strong moments on weak sites.
arxiv-2604-27007: Kar, Lorini and Masquelier give a causal analysis of binary spiking neural networks, explaining their behavior through a binary causal model of spiking activity. From that model they compute abductive explanations with SAT and SMT solvers, using logic-based methods. They train a network on MNIST and apply both solver methods to explain classifications from pixel-level features. Compared with SHAP, a popular explainable-AI method, their approach guarantees that a found explanation holds no fully irrelevant features.
arxiv-2604-27507: Iguchi and three others show a magnetic quantum critical point inside the superconducting state of zinc-doped CeCoIn5, shown by a peak in depth at zero temperature. Using SQUID scans, they find the local transition temperature and the zero-temperature depth. By stating depth in terms of local transition value rather than zinc doping, they avoid doping doubt and extract the critical exponent. It exceeds the spin-density-wave value, showing a disorder-shaped regime, and the depth rise reflects lower stiffness.
arxiv-2604-27607: Karnjanaekarin and seven colleagues present JaiTTS-v1.0, a Thai voice-cloning speech model built by continual training on a large Thai-heavy speech corpus. Adapted from VoxCPM, a tokenizer-free autoregressive model, it handles numerals and Thai-English code-switching without explicit text normalization. It reaches a character error rate of 1.94 percent on short-duration tasks, beating the human ground truth, and matches humans on long-duration tasks. In human judgment tests, it takes 283 of 400 matchups against commercial flagships, losing only 58.
arxiv-2604-27707: Xu, Dai, and Zhang argue current agentic memory systems implement lookup, not memory. Scratchpads, vector stores, retrieval-augmented generation, and context handling retrieve by similarity to stored cases, while weight-based memory applies abstract rules to unseen inputs. Treating lookup as memory, they warn, caps generalization on novel tasks no matter how much context or retrieval quality grows, and leaves agents open to lasting memory poisoning. Drawing on Complementary Learning Systems, biology pairs fast hippocampal storage with slow neocortical consolidation, while current agents implement only the first half.
arxiv-2604-28107: Gupta and Guven propose a Bayesian Neural Kalman Filter for tracking agile drones when sensors are noisy, sparse and control inputs unknown. Coupling a Bayesian neural network, which quantifies uncertainty through weight distributions, with a Kalman correction step yields full state predictions with uncertainty carried into covariance propagation. On synthetic flight data it beats extended and unscented Kalman filters under degraded sensing, and an ensemble variant sharpens precision further at high noise.
arxiv-2605-00007:
Michael Chertkov asks whether the samples in a diffusion model could cooperate instead of working alone. Standard diffusion generation draws independent samples, each following its own drift. In his Mean-Field Path-Integral Diffusion framework, samples become interacting agents whose drift depends on the evolving population density, so the crowd helps carry probability mass toward the target.

The coupling turns distribution matching into a mean-field version of stochastic optimal transport, joining generative modeling with multi-agent control. Two regimes can be solved in closed form, and for one interaction setting he proves the guided motion is the exact straight-line interpolant between starting and target means. Applied to demand-response control of building thermal zones, the method cuts cumulative control energy clearly against independent agents while hitting the target distribution exactly.
arxiv-2605-00407:
Juhi Jang, Jiaqi Liu, and Nader Masmoudi study the one-dimensional compressible Euler equations, the basic laws of gas motion. They construct solutions that start perfectly smooth and yet break down at a vacuum boundary in finite time. Their setting is a half-line of gas touching a stationary vacuum, like the edge of an atmosphere. The solutions begin square-integrable and smooth, a tame starting point for a blowup result.

As time passes, the solutions lose smoothness near the boundary, settling to a precise fractional regularity while their gradients blow up there. The construction leans on a stability analysis of self-similar waiting-time solutions the same authors built recently. Such results matter because vacuum boundaries are where compressible flow theory is most fragile. Knowing that even regular data can force blowup at the edge disciplines theory and numerics alike.
arxiv-2605-00607:
Gaofei Shen and 4 co-authors reverse the usual direction of probing, the standard technique for asking what a language model knows inside. A decoding probe checks which features can be read out of a model's representations. That approach has two flaws: what different features add cannot be compared head-on, and links between features can distort the results. Their Encoding Probe instead rebuilds those states from readable features.

By rebuilding model states from feature sets covering sound, speech sounds, syntax, word choice, and speaker identity, the method measures how much each family contributes. They test it on text and speech transformer models. Effects tied to the speaker varied strongly with training goal and dataset, while syntax and word features each added their own share. The authors present the probe as a second lens on the model's inside, one that goes beyond asking what can merely be decoded.
arxiv-2605-00907:
Han Gong and six co-authors present TRIP-Evaluate, an open benchmark across media for large models in transportation. Models are increasingly used for regulation questions, traffic management, engineering review, and driving scene reasoning, yet transport work is rule-heavy, calculation-heavy, safety-critical, and multimodal. General benchmarks give little evidence on those demands, and existing transport benchmarks are narrow.

The benchmark holds more than eight hundred items organized by role, task, and knowledge, covering vehicle, traffic, and planning functions. Items span text, images, and point clouds with skill and level labels for fine-grained fault finding. Results show text performance improving, but clear weaknesses remain in math-heavy calculation, rule-constrained reasoning, and scene and point-cloud understanding.
arxiv-2605-01107:
Kanishka Reddy studies the geometry of feedforward neural network representations through diffusion operators. As data pass through layers, feature geometry shapes how classes separate and relate. Each feature-cloud snapshot is assigned a Gaussian-kernel Markov operator that describes one-step transport between classes, from which spectral, boundary, and local geometric information can be read.

Reddy defines an empirical class chain, states when it is an exact Markov quotient, and derives a population transition plus a simpler overlap chain based on expected class affinities. For balanced Gaussian snapshots those affinities have closed forms. Experiments on image datasets with a ResNet model find class transport grows more persistent with depth, and the diffusion chain is more stable than a nearest-neighbor counterpart under matched perturbations.
arxiv-2605-01307:
Changpeng He and five co-authors design a wireless system that mixes several base stations, smart reflecting panels, and a new kind of antenna that slides along a waveguide. Each user links to one base station, and the goal is to raise total data rate and save energy at once.

The design must set antenna spots, panel phases, beam shapes, and user links together, a tightly coupled problem with mixed choices. The team solves it with a three-stage graph neural network that learns on its own, with no labeled answers. In tests it beats standard system and learning baselines, adapts to new counts of users, panels, and stations, and answers in milliseconds. More sliding antennas raise both rate and efficiency.
arxiv-2605-01407:
Hiun Kim, Tae Kwan Lee, and Taeryun Won test how pre-training choices shape search models that rank web pages by their titles. Their model family, Expanded-SPLADE, learns sparse word weights, and its masked-language pre-training is also used at fine-tuning time, which makes the hand-off worth a close look.

The team vary the pre-training corpus and settings, then fine-tune and grade the models, with an option to prune the sparse vectors at test time. Three patterns stand out. Models pre-trained on a general corpus at a higher learning rate rank best, even though their raw language scores look worse. Under the strictest pruning, those same models cost more to run and vary more in list length. Repeating the general corpus adds little. The study maps where the language pre-training and the ranking fine-tune pull against each other.
arxiv-2605-01607:
Stefan J Hofmeister and nine co-authors chart the blur of the sharpest eye on the Solar Orbiter mission, its extreme ultraviolet imager working at a wavelength of 174 angstroms. Every telescope smears light by its own design, and knowing that point-spread pattern lets software undo much of the damage.

Part of the pattern comes from diffraction at the meshes and mounts holding the entrance filters, computed from engineering drawings: about a quarter of the light is diffracted. The softer scatter from mirror roughness is fit using a Mercury transit that partly covered the Sun in early 2023, and it spreads over two fifths of the light widely. Together, well over half the incoming light is redistributed across the detector. Correcting for it lifts bright features by up to two fifths and drains false glow from dark ones by most of their value, a marked gain in contrast.
arxiv-2605-01707:
Ahmad F Taha and Mohamad H Kazma give water distribution networks a full control-theory workup. City water systems are governed by nonlinear equations mixing flows, pressures, pumps, and valves over arbitrary layouts, and their switching parts make the math nonsmooth exactly where control gets interesting.

Three questions organize the study. When do the dynamics stay locally well-posed, and where does switching break smoothness? Can smoothing methods restore clean trajectories under changing controls? And how large are the errors when the system is linearized, with what margins of stability and controllability over a finite horizon? The smoothed models track the industry simulator EPANET closely across benchmark networks. The framework also reads energy loss through a weighted graph Laplacian, ranks pipes by sensitivity, and shows hard demand swings shrink stability margins without killing local stability or pump authority.
arxiv-2605-01807:
Ankit Kumar Panda and Rajesh Biswas evolve a magnetized relativistic fluid in the first-order BDNK frame, a modern formulation built to keep dissipative hydrodynamics causal and stable where older first-order theories failed. The arena is the boost-invariant Bjorken expansion, the standard cartoon of the fireball born in heavy-ion collisions, flattened to time-only dynamics while keeping every first-order gradient that matters.

Coupled equations carry temperature and magnetic field together, and turning the transport dials separates their two-way influence. The field answers temperature changes strongly, while its back-pressure on temperature stays secondary. Particle number density feels both gradients at once. The payoff observable is dilepton emission, pairs that escape the fireball untouched. The field reshapes their rate through the relaxation time. The coupled evolution suppresses the low-mass spectrum, mostly because positive coupling between temperature gradients and the field speeds the cooling.
arxiv-2605-01907:
Hanxiao Chen and Debarghya Mukherjee study learning across many tasks that fall into hidden clusters. Tasks in a cluster share target values, but each task also has its own nuisance parts that can be complex and high-dimensional. Past methods often assume aligned features or uniform tasks, which this setting breaks.

Their estimator joins Neyman-orthogonal losses, which reduce sensitivity to nuisance errors, with fusion penalties that pull similar tasks together. Pilot estimates from each task calibrate those penalties, and aggregation adapts to the data. The authors show the true clusters are recovered with high probability and that pooled rates scale with cluster size. They also establish normal limits for inference.
arxiv-2605-02207:
Dineth Jayakody, Pasindu Thenahandi, and Chameli Dommanige present MultiSense-Pneumo, a multimodal prototype for pneumonia screening where imaging and specialists are scarce. Pneumonia is a leading cause of illness and death worldwide, and frontline assessment already mixes symptoms, breathing patterns, spoken accounts, and chest images. Most computational tools, by contrast, use radiographs alone.

Their system joins structured symptom data, cough audio, spoken language, and chest radiographs. Parts include rule-based symptom triage, a gradient-boosted audio classifier, a domain-adversarial image model, and speech recognition with a transformer. Each input becomes a normalised concern signal, combined by an interpretable late-fusion step for triage support. The work is framed as a research prototype, not a clinical device.
arxiv-2605-02307:
Yashwanth YS and colleagues introduce SOTOPIA-TOM, a benchmark for how language model agents handle private information in multi-party interaction. Agents increasingly talk in group settings, where knowing when and to whom to disclose information matters. Past benchmarks do not measure that skill in realistic multi-party settings with asymmetric knowledge.

The environment supports both public broadcast and private direct messages. It holds 160 human-reviewed scenarios across eight industry sectors, each with three to five agents holding partitioned private knowledge and channel-dependent sharing rules. Scoring covers how well agents share useful information, seek missing details, coordinate efficiently, and protect privacy. Theory of mind, tracking what others know, sits at the centre of the test.
arxiv-2605-02407:
P Bednyakov, P Yudin, A Tagantsev, and J Hlinka show that light plus an electric field can reliably create charged domain walls in barium titanate. Charged walls act as conductive channels inside an otherwise insulating ferroelectric, which makes them attractive for reconfigurable electronics. Optical control of domain structure is a long-standing goal in that field.

The authors propose a scenario for the creation process in which the bulk photovoltaic effect plays the key role. Light-driven charge movement provides the screening charge that a charged wall needs to be stable. Phase-field simulations support that account. The results point toward devices whose conductive paths can be written and moved with light, for future electronic and opto-electronic uses.
arxiv-2605-02807:
Fabrizio Canfora, Cristóbal Corral, and Borja Diez introduce an analytic treatment of gravitational lensing when light passes through a medium full of hadrons, the particles made of quarks. The setup mirrors light in a medium with a condensate that gives the photon an effective mass, which can vary from place to place. In such a medium, photons no longer follow the usual null paths of empty space.

Hadrons are modeled by a nonlinear sigma model coupled to electromagnetism. The authors derive a corrected focusing equation with hadronic terms, and the photon paths in the short-wavelength limit. Results match plasma lensing theory, with a plus: transport traits such as the refractive index come out analytically from hadron density, with no fitted model. A worked case covers lensing by a black hole sourced by superfluid pionic vortices.
arxiv-2605-03007:
Salvatore Bottaro and three co-authors build a formalism for spotting late-time injections of energy into the cosmos, such as a dark sector phase change after recombination. Their one assumption is mild: the injection is fast compared with the horizon scale at the time. A hidden sector that stays sequestered from ordinary matter could still leave marks on the cosmic microwave background through gravity alone.

For injections after recombination, they derive how photon paths bend under scalar, vector, and tensor disturbances, and compute the microwave signal through the integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect. The signal, they show, is usually dominated by sudden injections of anisotropic stress. Applied to first-order phase transitions in a sequestered dark sector, current observations limit such energy injections to a tiny fraction of the total. Late, quiet events are not invisible.
arxiv-2605-04007:
Mingjie Jian and six co-authors present PySME version 1.0, an updated Python version of Spectroscopy Made Easy for modeling stellar spectra at survey scale. Stellar abundance analysis depends on flexible, high-performance spectral synthesis, and a central bottleneck is handling very large atomic and molecular line lists: faint lines must be preselected before formal synthesis begins.

PySME revises the line-selection framework around opacity ratio and line depth. It adds dynamic line list construction and control over the wavelength span each line affects. That shrinks what reaches the synthesis core while preserving accuracy. An updated equation-of-state treatment improves hydrogen line modeling and Balmer features, while metal lines stay close to previous results. The interface also supports parameter-dependent derived quantities updated during fitting.
arxiv-2605-04107:
Furkan Sakizli presents TSCG, a deterministic compiler that converts tool schemas for language model agents from JSON into token-efficient structured text. Production agent frameworks transmit schemas as JSON. That format was built for machine parsing rather than model interpretation. The author argues that mismatch causes most tool-use failures for small models at production catalog sizes. TSCG works at the application boundary with no model access, fine-tuning, or runtime search.

Eight composable operators and a formal compression bound of at least half on well-formed schemas make up the compiler. On an agentic benchmark of about nineteen thousand calls, TSCG was tested across twelve models and five scenarios. It raised one fourteen-billion-parameter model's accuracy from zero to over eighty percent at twenty tools. Decomposition experiments attribute the gains mainly to representation change rather than compression alone.
arxiv-2605-04207:
Jinhang Chai and three co-authors study how a seller should set prices over time when demand depends on product features and buyer traits in a partly unknown way. Part of the demand curve follows a flexible function, while the market noise follows an unknown distribution that must also be learned.

Their staged algorithm updates its estimate of the noise from data gathered while selling, rather than paying for separate random price experiments. They prove a general regret bound that works for many utility estimators. They also give rates for linear and sparse cases. These improve the best known results for this pricing setting.
arxiv-2605-04407:
Md Zakir Hossain and four co-authors test whether machine-learning systems for detecting network intrusions keep their accuracy when the network changes. Such systems often score very highly on the data set they were trained on, which can hide a failure to generalise.

Training and testing three standard models on two public data sets, they find random forests lead within each set, reaching very high accuracy. When a model trained on one set is tested on the other, accuracy collapses below forty percent. The authors connect this generalisation gap to broader work on human-centred, behaviour-aware security systems.
arxiv-2605-04507:
Zongqi Cui and Baihan Lin build a negotiation agent whose beliefs about its opponent can be inspected, rather than hidden inside a language model. A good negotiator must infer what the other side values, update those beliefs turn by turn, and act under uncertainty.

Their teacher system scores each dialogue against the six possible orderings of the opponent's priorities and updates a probability distribution over them, then chooses actions from that distribution. A smaller student model is distilled to output both its actions and its beliefs as tagged text. On a standard negotiation data set, the teacher beat prior systems and the student kept much of the belief accuracy.
arxiv-2605-04607:
Franek Stark and four co-authors present a real-time controller for a bipedal walking robot that mixes two models of different fidelity inside one prediction. A detailed whole-body model is accurate but expensive, while a simplified rigid-body model is cheap but coarse, and walking control must decide faster than the detailed model alone allows.

Their scheme uses the detailed model for the near future, where accuracy matters most, and the simplified model for later steps. A standard optimisation framework solves the resulting problem, choosing joint torques from a contact schedule and target speed without pre-planned footstep positions. The controller is validated in simulation on an eighteen-joint bipedal robot.
arxiv-2605-04707:
Samuel H. Ward and three co-authors analyse a supply problem that could slow the global rollout of nuclear fusion power: the lithium isotope lithium-6 is essential fuel for breeding tritium inside a reactor. Each plant consumes little lithium in operation, yet must hold a large enriched inventory on site.

That inventory, fifty to one hundred tonnes, combined with enrichment inefficiency, turns fuel into a major upfront capital cost, further magnified by financing. Today's enrichment technologies are also expensive, hard to scale, and environmentally risky, and highly enriched lithium-6 is a controlled substance. The authors discuss mitigations, including alternative enrichment technologies and reactor designs that ease the requirement.
arxiv-2605-04907:
Ariestotle Raj Maharjan, Jianchen Li, and Jing Liu extend Geant4, a widely used toolkit, so optical runs can be set up without writing C++ code. The plain-text geometry format now carries optical properties for bulk materials and surface interfaces through new tags. Removing code writing and repeated compiling lowers the barrier for new users.

The authors test the extension on key optical processes including Cherenkov radiation, scintillation, Rayleigh scattering, and absorption. They also show how to set up complex optical boundaries using the UNIFIED model in detail. The cases highlight the extension's value for rapid test builds and detector studies.
arxiv-2605-05007:
Zhiqing Cui and thirteen co-authors present Uno-Orchestra, a single policy for routing work inside multi-agent language model systems. Such systems usually commit to flat per-query routing or to hand-built task splitting, so depth, worker choice, and budget are never optimised together. Uno-Orchestra learns both when to split a task and where to send each piece.

The policy was trained on curated trajectories grounded in real worker interactions, choosing among allowed model and tool pairings. Against twenty-two baselines across thirteen benchmarks covering maths, code, knowledge, and tool use, it reached the best overall pass rate. It did so at roughly a tenth of the per-query cost of leading workflow systems.
arxiv-2605-05207:
Zeren Jiang and ten co-authors release Syn4D, a synthetic multiview dataset of moving three-dimensional scenes for computer vision research. Reconstructing and tracking dynamic scenes from a single video remains an open challenge, held back by scarce datasets with dense, accurate geometric labels. Syn4D supplies ground-truth camera motion, depth maps, dense tracking, and parametric human pose for its scenes.

Any pixel can be projected into three dimensions at any time and from any camera, a key feature for training and checking models. The authors evaluate the dataset across four tasks, including scene reconstruction, point tracking, camera retargeting, and pose estimation. Results highlight its potential for dynamic scene understanding and space-time modelling.
arxiv-2605-05407:
Mohamed Salim Aissi and six co-authors present PRISM, a framework for agents that must see, think, and act. A vision-language model alone often misses details that matter for the task at hand. PRISM pairs that model with a language model in a loop of questions and answers.

The language model critiques the scene description and asks goal-focused questions. The vision model answers, and the pair builds a compact, task-driven picture of the scene. On the ALFWorld and Room-to-Room benchmarks, PRISM beat leading image-based systems. The gains came from the interactive questioning, with no hand-written questions needed.
arxiv-2605-05707:
Walking controllers almost always assume a pendulum model of the body, the linear inverted pendulum, by fiat. Lingxue Lyu and Zihui Liu ask whether an optimal controller would choose that behavior on its own. They start from a small centroidal control problem that penalizes how fast angular momentum changes.

With a full-rank stance, the optimum drifts toward a pendular force pattern at a rate set by foot-span geometry, matching experiments closely. With two feet down, as in trotting, friction limits impose a floor on angular momentum rate that no tuning removes. Pendular structure, they argue, is something good control discovers.
arxiv-2605-05907:
Johannes Bertram and four co-authors critique tools used to compare neural representations in brains and deep learning models. Their study asks whether matching similarity scores mean two systems work the same way inside. It focuses on RSA and CKA, two standard measures of how alike two sets of neural activity look.

In a controlled MNIST experiment, changing the internal layout of a model left those scores almost unchanged. Yet the changed models differed in their explanations, weight patterns, and strength on new data. The authors argue that such scores cannot tell shared circuits from merely similar outputs. They propose manifold based checks, and offer a free explorer tool, as extra tests for future claims.
arxiv-2605-06007:
Hyunbae Jeon and Jinho Choi build a testing platform for spoken dialogue systems that play varied social roles. A tutor, a stubborn merchant, and a distracted worker should not all yield in the same way when a user talks over them. Yet most full duplex systems default to one rigid, always yielding policy, which breaks character for firmer roles.

PersonaKit is an open source, low latency web platform for prototyping and user testing such agents. Simple configuration files define each persona and its chances of yielding, holding, bridging, or overriding during overlap. The platform deploys comparative surveys on its own. A field evaluation with eight personas shows it can support end to end studies of these social speech behaviors.
arxiv-2605-06207:
Bowen Zheng and four co-authors rethink how visual tokenizers size their codebooks along a token sequence. Most tokenizers give every position the same codebook, and researchers scale that shared size up for better reconstruction. The authors show a hard information limit behind that habit, which they call the Entropy Cliff.

Early positions in a sequence carry high uncertainty, but the conditional entropy decays so fast that later positions become nearly fixed. On ImageNet, that point arrives within two of 256 positions at a common codebook size, turning the rest into memorization. Their Variable Codebook Size Quantization grows the codebook along the sequence instead. It cut a key generation error score nearly in half and built a coarse to fine semantic order.
arxiv-2605-06307:
Jana Gonnermann-Müller and four co-authors test whether language model students keep stable personas over time. Simulated learners promise a scalable stand in for educational research and teacher training, but the method only works if a persona holds steady across and within conversations. The team measure stability two ways, through self reported traits and through observer rated behavior, across five models and three prompt designs.

Conditions covered three ADHD related intensity levels informed by ICD-11, plus a default persona. Self reports and observer ratings held steadier at high intensity than at moderate intensity. In long unscripted dialogue, observer rated behavior drifted for high and moderate personas, even though self reports stayed stable. Scripted interactions with recurring task prompts cut that drift by up to 97 percent.
arxiv-2605-07107:
Leighton P. Barnes and Alex Dytso strengthen a classic statistical result about maximum likelihood estimation. With large samples, such estimates are known to settle into a bell-shaped distribution. The authors prove stronger forms of that behavior under added assumptions on the score function behind the estimate.

They establish tight sub-Gaussian tail bounds and convergence of all moments for the normalized error. For a smoothed version of the estimator, they prove convergence in relative entropy to the limiting Gaussian law. Under further conditions, the smoothing can be dropped entirely. Their supporting tools, including entropy-control arguments, may interest other researchers.
arxiv-2605-07207:
Nhan Trong Luu and three co-authors convert spiking neural networks from an energy-hungry training format into an efficient event-based one. Spiking networks promise low-power computing, but the direct coding used to train them wastes much of that advantage at run time. Direct-coded models still trail event-based versions badly on energy use.

The team presents the first systematic study of this transfer problem, mapping the challenges that arise when computation switches formats. They propose a set of methods to carry a pretrained direct-coded network into event-based form while preserving performance. The goal is reusing existing pretrained models without giving up the efficiency that makes spiking hardware attractive.
arxiv-2605-07307:
Yi-Chang Chen and three co-authors test whether reasoning chains need their density or their order to yield correct answers. Modern models write long sequential traces assuming every token counts and steps must be read in sequence. The team intervened on model-written chains by removing, masking, shuffling, and corrupting parts of them.

Line-level shuffling barely hurt accuracy, and even heavily reduced traces, stripped of prose and shuffled, kept most of their answers. Masking numbers destroyed accuracy, while masking prose slightly helped. Injecting false answers at triple frequency changed nothing, ruling out simple majority extraction. Answers, they conclude, rest on a sparse, order-insensitive core.
arxiv-2605-07607:
Zhixin Cheng and six co-authors work on registering images to three-dimensional point clouds, lining up a photo with a scanned scene. Viewpoint changes, the gap between camera and scanner data, and repetitive textures create scale confusion and wrong matches. Recent detection-free methods help but suffer attention drift and inconsistencies within each scale.

Inspired by how people first focus, then sweep, the team built a hierarchical focus-sweep interaction module inside a state-space framework, strengthening cross-modal links at several levels. A dynamic layer allocation strategy also chooses how many iterations each case needs, exploiting geometric constraints. On two indoor benchmarks, RGB-D Scenes V2 and 7-Scenes, the approach reached state-of-the-art registration performance.
arxiv-2605-07807:
Mallis and five colleagues address a gap in text to CAD generation, where written prompts are turned into computer aided design models. The task could substantially speed up design work, yet judging how good a generated CAD model is remains a considerable challenge. Surprisingly little work has examined text to CAD evaluation at all, despite the importance of the task.

The authors propose a new evaluation perspective based on automated testing, treating generated models as artefacts that can be put through tests. They introduce CADTestBench, a benchmark for text to CAD built on units called CADTests, and present it as the first of its kind. The test based approach makes evaluation repeatable, so rival systems can be judged on the same checks. That shared yardstick matters because generation quality had been hard to assess at all. CADTestBench is offered as the first benchmark of its kind for the task.
arxiv-2605-08107:
Bikram Keshari Behera, Rhitabrata Bhattacharyya, and Shyamal Biswas study how Drude metals reflect and absorb light. They cover the whole frequency range in one classical frame. The frame includes bound charges and currents. From it, they derive exact forms for the loss constant, the phase constant, and the reflectivity. The reflectivity matches measured data for plasmas and seawater.

For metals that conduct very well, the loss constant takes a simple form near the plasma frequency. A branch-point kink shows up there. The team calls this opto-critical behavior. They compute its exponents for the loss constant, group velocity, and dielectric response. Quantum fixes are added at the end.
arxiv-2605-08307:
Parul Raghuvanshi and Vishvendra Singh Poonia model spin chemistry inside the heliobacterial reaction center, one of the simplest photosynthetic machines. When light splits charges there, the paired radicals can recombine into triplet states, which waste energy and can damage the cell, so keeping triplets down matters for efficient photosynthesis.

Using Lindblad open-system dynamics for the spin-correlated radical pair, the authors vary hyperfine coupling strengths and recombination rates to see how triplet yield responds. Their focus is chiral-induced spin selectivity, the tendency of chiral structures to filter electron spin, acting as the regulator. The study connects a quantum spin effect to the photophysics of a living system that works without any internal magnetic field.
arxiv-2605-08507:
Otoniel Nogueira da Silva and Manoel Messias da Silva Júnior compare how singularity sameness behaves across linked families of curves. They study a one parameter unfolding of a map from the complex plane into three dimensional space, alongside four families built from its double points, where two source points share one image.

Alongside the comparison, the authors build clear counterexamples to several natural guesses about these families. They also introduce new curve families that stay topologically constant yet fail a stricter sameness test, and extend classic double point formulas to higher dimensions. Singularity theory gains sharper boundaries between notions that look alike but behave differently.
arxiv-2605-08807:
H. Khodabakhshi, Zhi-Chao Li, H. Lu, and F. Shojai link a star's core to the space just past its edge, in both ways. In the Oppenheimer-Snyder fall model, in its broad form, edge rules cut the link to plain algebra. The link ties core density to the metric just past the edge. Builders can thus rebuild still forms of space from the fall. They can also get edge motion, with no need to solve field laws one by one.

Powers in the link act as a test key. Whole powers hint at high energy fixes. Part powers mark models built to fit. The frame makes smooth black holes easier to build. It also gives one shared yardstick for claims on smooth cores and cosmic guards.
arxiv-2605-08907:
Ali Rida Khalife and Cyril Pitrou bound swirl modes of space time with fresh sky data. The data comes from ground and space scopes that map the old light of the Big Bang. Three roots in the young cosmos can seed such swirls. One is a neutrino count flaw. One is a neutrino octupole shape. One is stress that did not match in all ways, from before mass and glow drew even. First waves of space time can ride with them too.

All data sets give tight caps on the swirl share for the count flaw case. The rest allow more, still capped. One set hints at a sign that fits zero. No break from the base model stands.
arxiv-2605-09007:
Jessee Ho, Shweta Khushu, and Shaina Raza say deepfake guards aim at the wrong mark. The mark should be the trick, not the trace. Guards that call real or fake score well on stock sets. They fall hard on new growth tools. In live calls, the harm is the trick act, not a flaw in the sound or sight. The team shows five props of trace work all wear thin as tools grow. They call the false calm the Generalization Illusion.

From speech act thought, from Grice's rules of talk, and from Cialdini's sway rules, they build a mate frame. It checks the line said, the talk as a whole, and how the hearer acts. Guards gain a social layer.
arxiv-2605-09307:
Han and a colleague present a method casting inverse design in constitutive terms, for elastic networks reaching a target shape under load. From noisy stress strain readings across material, chemical, or factory setups, they build a constitutive prior, a hidden pattern learned from data. It sets out allowed material laws, letting the team blend between them in function space. The inverse task is a search over hidden factors setting how material behaviour varies across space, held to governing PDEs, with fast differentiable code respecting thermodynamic rules, including nonnegative dissipation.

The prior uses partly input-convex neural networks, and a homotopy based path slowly reshapes the target shape through middle point clouds for strength in nonconvex optimisation. Affine matching supplies a first target shape when none is given. Chamfer distance lets shapes match without mesh links, and a neural smoothness prior plus graph metric measures and controls spatial change.
arxiv-2605-09407:
Kang and two colleagues build an any-depth object detection framework letting one network span accuracy-efficiency trade-offs, with depth controlled at inference time and no retraining. Modern detectors are static, fixed-depth networks tuned for one operating point, forcing separate models. Each backbone and neck stage splits into an essential path that always runs and a skippable refinement path.

That split preserves the multi-scale feature hierarchy at every depth, unlike early exiting, which drops whole stages. Training many sub-networks of varying depth creates conflicting gradients. The team therefore distils knowledge between the two extremes, with prediction and feature alignment losses keeping each stage's outputs compatible whatever paths are taken. Built on RT-DETR and YOLOv12, full-depth versions match or beat state-of-the-art baselines with tiny extra parameters. The leanest versions run up to 1 point 82 times faster for only 2 point 0 AP less.
arxiv-2605-09507:
Tariq and two colleagues propose VASTSum, a video summarization method that treats human disagreement as information instead of noise. Summarizing a long video means picking a short set of segments that reflects what people find important. Yet annotators often disagree. The final selection step also uses discrete optimization that small score changes can overturn. Their single pass model predicts frame scores with uncertainty built in, using a variational model that learns from multiple annotators.

A training rule aligns the model with plausible human annotation modes. It does not force one consensus target. A decoder aligned penalty then steadies the knapsack selection step against small shifts in scores. On the SumMe and TVSum benchmarks the method posts consistent and competitive rank correlations across splits. It shows robustness under annotation disagreement without the cost of generative or diffusion based alternatives.
arxiv-2605-09807:
Huang and Zhao studied Ramanujan primes for Hecke-Maass cusp forms, a class of number-theoretic objects whose eigenvalues are conjectured to stay sharply bounded. For a primitive form of level N, the Ramanujan conjecture at a prime p not dividing N asserts that the absolute Hecke eigenvalue stays at most 2. The conjecture remains open for these forms, unlike the holomorphic case settled by Deligne.

The paper bounds the least prime at which the conjecture holds for two or three distinct primitive forms at once. It also gives a lower bound for the share of primes, in natural density, at which the conjecture holds for at least one form in a given set. Least-prime bounds and density bounds, the authors show, can be won together.
arxiv-2605-09907:
Zhang and five colleagues built RADAR, a framework for generating multi-agent communication structures step by step instead of fixing them or generating them in one shot. Multi-agent language-model systems beat single agents on code, math, and planning, but their power hinges on communication topology, the pattern of who talks to whom. Fixed or one-shot topologies waste tokens on simple tasks and cap capability on hard ones.

RADAR is redundancy-aware and query-adaptive: it generates topology gradually, guided by the effective size of the graph, cutting needless communication. Motivated by conditional discrete graph diffusion models, the framework treats topology design as a sequential generation process. Across six benchmarks, RADAR beat recent baselines with higher accuracy, lower token use, and greater robustness, and its code and data are public.
arxiv-2605-10007:
Grieskamp, Zhang, Kashyap and Silverman extend the Move Prover to imperative first-class functions. This recent Aptos addition lets functions be passed around, stored in structs and held in persistent storage, allowing dynamic dispatch. The paper describes how function values are represented in Move's specification language and implemented in the prover. Behavioural predicates capture each function by single-state or two-state conditions on aborts and pre- and post-conditions.

State labels name intermediate memory states so predicates can compose across sequences of transitions. At the solver level, function values are encoded by sorting among the functions able to reach a call site. Known functions are handled directly, unknown ones through their predicates. The approach goes beyond Dafny by supporting state-changing functions with Rust-style references and globals, and it yields leaner solver encodings than separation logic thanks to Move's static memory separation.
arxiv-2605-10507:
Noé Blassel and nine colleagues review number methods for computing transport coefficients in molecular dynamics. Transport coefficients quantify how physical properties of a moving system behave under pushes, with uses from life science to materials science. Obtaining exact values, either from lab work or by models, has always been a challenge. Their 2026 paper reviews many number approaches, grouped into three kinds.

First, off-balance methods apply an outside driving field, measure the average response, and find the related linear response coefficient. Second, approaches putting the value through a time correlation function for steady motion, mostly Green-Kubo and Einstein formulas. Third, short-term techniques compute the value by watching a pushed motion return to balance. For all three kinds, the authors provide elements of number analysis for estimating number errors, and briefly present spread-cutting approaches such as control variates, importance sampling, and coupling methods.
arxiv-2605-11107:
Youssef Zaazou and Mark Thomas build background-proof representations for vision-language models by exploiting linear structure in embedding spaces. Vision encoders like CLIP and SigLIP 2 inherit spurious foreground-background links that undermine robustness, a salient failure on benchmarks like Waterbirds.

Revisiting the high linear additivity of VLM embeddings, the pair splits scene representations into foreground and background parts and pretrains with synthetic data to construct background-proof features. The method achieves the first worst-group accuracy above 90 percent on Waterbirds under perfect spurious correlation, with no minority-group training examples, plus strong sim-to-real transfer without real debiased data. Vision teams get robustness that does not demand curated debiased data sets.
arxiv-2605-11307:
Ajay Vikram Periasami, Junlin Wang, and Bhuwan Dhingra introduce Vision2Code, a multi-domain benchmark for evaluating image-to-code generation. Image-to-code generation asks whether a vision-language model can recover an image's structure as executable code.

Existing benchmarks focus on narrow domains, depend on paired reference code, or rely on generic rubrics missing domain errors. Vision2Code is a reference-free multi-domain image-to-code benchmark. It holds test examples spanning charts, geometry, graphs, scientific imagery, documents, and 3D scenes. Models generate programs, rendered and scored against the source image by a VLM judge using dataset-specific rubrics and guardrails for severe failures. Diagnostics separate execution failures from reconstruction quality. Human checks show this protocol beats a generic visual rubric and embedding-similarity baselines. Across nine models, performance is domain-dependent: leading models do well on regular charts and graphs but stay weak elsewhere.
arxiv-2605-11407: Tian Bai, Yixin Cao and Mingyu Xiao give a complete complexity classification for feedback set problems on bounded-degree digraphs, including the planar case. Both vertex and edge versions are NP-complete on digraphs of maximum degree three. On planar digraphs, feedback vertex set is polynomial-time solvable when every vertex has in-degree at most one, or out-degree at most one, and NP-complete otherwise. They also give tight degree bounds for connected feedback vertex set on undirected graphs, planar and non-planar.
arxiv-2605-11507: Marsden, Rousset and Schratz prove convergence of a filtered Lie-splitting method for wave maps with rough starting data in dimension 3. The analysis runs in discrete Bourgain spaces, fruitful for low regularity analysis. A key difficulty is preserving the null structure at the discrete level, since low regularity analysis of wave maps depends on it. Since time derivatives enter the null structure, the scheme needs careful design, and those derivatives drive the largest numerical error. Even so, convergence holds for all subcritical initial data.
arxiv-2605-11607: Hu and Wang develop exact Stiefel tuning for chance partial least squares with tuned doubt. Chance PLS models two-view learning with readable factors and tuned doubt, yet old pipes face noise-signal coupling and right angles. Their tool mixes noise guessing, odds tuning and future tuning. Noise is guessed from the low-eigen subspace via exact Stiefel-surface tuning, hitting a finite-sample rate matching a minimax lower bound. Across fake settings and two multi-omics benchmarks it hits near-nominal cover.
arxiv-2605-11907: Igor Strozzi's 2026 study measures how procedural-skill fine-tuning contributes across three Qwen3.5 model sizes on a 200-task holdout. The fine-tuning lift proves roughly uniform across sizes, while differences in post-tuning scores trace a W-shaped baseline trajectory: the five-step procedure hurts the smallest and largest models but helps the middle one. He also exposes a bench artifact in which a deterministic answer extractor under-counted free-form conclusions, biasing earlier comparisons against the curated condition.
arxiv-2605-12207: Arijit Sehanobish and Charles Lovering ask whether trained parameters matter in low-rank adaptation. With supervised tuning, random and informed subsets perform comparably. With GRPO, random picks fail to beat the untrained model, while gradient-guided picks recover accuracy. Gradient structure explains the split: supervised gradients are low-rank and stable, so any subset gathers updates, while GRPO gradients spread wide and point near-orthogonally, so only elements keep the signal. Their scoring method finds the parameters in under 10 seconds at under 0.5 percent of cost, on residual-stream projections.
arxiv-2605-12407: Madison reviews two machine-learning attacks on the toughest errors in future Z-pole luminosity measurement. Small-angle Bhabha scattering stays the standard channel, while photon-pair events offer a second route, and both suffer from background and beam effects. A boosted decision tree sorts events by particle type, and only an upgraded luminosity calorimeter rejects the scattering background at the required precision. For beam deflection bias, a new symbolic regression method beats the boosted tree and cuts that uncertainty to a few parts per million.
arxiv-2605-12607: Cordwell and Rafikov map how planets damp the density waves they excite in planet-forming discs. Those waves carry push across the disc, so reading seen patterns requires knowing where wave push is dropped. The team runs many fluid runs varying stickiness, cooling time and planet mass, pulling radial curves of push drop. They measure damping rate as a joint function of those three factors, finding sharp wave growth toward shock making often rules. That factor and cooling shape the outcome in distinct regimes.
arxiv-2605-12807: Phan, Flamich, Khisti and Asoodeh address a practical problem in Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling: judging when several chains have settled. They couple multiple Metropolis-Hastings chains using multi-marginal coupling, then build a shared-randomness Poisson Monte Carlo construction with an adaptive update rule that avoids a dimension-linked slowdown. In tests their approach joins chains sooner, cutting meeting times by up to half.
arxiv-2605-12907: Kong, Zhu and Xie offer a full, self-contained primer on Grassmann tensor networks, tools for strongly correlated fermionic systems. These tools wed tensor networks to Grassmann algebra in the coherent-state path-integral picture, yet see too little use in real runs. The authors move from basic Grassmann tensor moves to the Grassmann form of standard routines, then test the tools on models from particle physics and condensed-matter physics.
arxiv-2605-13007: Araya and Harada complete the classification of ternary maximal self-orthogonal codes of length 25, a family of error-correcting codes over a three-symbol alphabet. Such codes had been classified only up to length 24. The short note provides the full classification for the length-25 case, closing the next open case in the sequence and extending the known catalogue by one length.
arxiv-2605-13107: Smirnov and Vershynin ask how a balanced random walk can stay inside a convex shape without ever stepping out. Their online method drops chosen moves as the walk goes, and the expected number dropped stays tied to a Fisher-style measure of the shape. For a cube, the guarantee does not weaken as dimensions grow: unit-length moves in ordinary distance remain within set bounds along every axis. On average, only a small fixed share of moves gets thrown away.
