Heyi Zhang and colleagues image a young binary star system at fine resolution in this 2026 arXiv paper. The HH 46/47 system is a classic laboratory of star formation, pairing a newborn binary with a striking molecular outflow. Using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, the team observed the outflow and its envelope-disk system. The millimeter continuum reveals a compact central source surrounded by a disk around both stars, with substructures.

The companion star is not detected in the millimeter continuum. It coincides with a local intensity minimum, a dip in the disk's emission. Two spur-like features extend from the primary source toward the companion, likely induced by its gravity. Different molecules trace different layers. One carbon monoxide variant maps the extended envelope, while sulfur monoxide probes the inner envelope. The images let teams watch a companion sculpt the disk from which planets may form in time.
arxiv-2606-08807:
Heickal and Lan test whether the form of AI feedback changes how programming students learn, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In a Python course, students who submitted wrong code were randomly assigned one of three kinds of help. The options were natural language hints from a language model, AI-generated failing test cases, or no AI feedback. The recordings became the ProgFeed dataset. It holds 6,693 submissions from 215 students across 17 labs.

Natural language feedback was linked to higher completion rates and faster arrival at correct solutions. Test case feedback was uneven, and its effect hinged on validity: only sixty-six percent of generated test cases were correct. Even valid test cases did not reduce the submissions students needed, suggesting beginners cannot yet exploit counterexamples. Quality checks found the natural language feedback helpful in ninety-two and a half percent of cases.
arxiv-2606-09107:
Inoue and Itaba generalize a cohomology theory from groups to braided quantum-algebraic worlds, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cohomology measures obstructions in algebra. Symmetric cohomology, Staic's theory for groups, extended to Hopf algebras, uses symmetric-group actions on a cochain complex. Many modern objects, quasi-triangular bialgebras among them, live in braided monoidal categories, where swapping factors twists rather than exchanges.

The authors define the braided cochain complex and cohomology for braided coalgebras in linear monoidal settings, with braidings defined on one object. To compare across settings, they describe relative maps, letting one setting's theory speak to another's. Main theorem: the braided cochain complex of quasi-triangular bialgebras does not change under Morita equivalence, under a condition on the setting. This is automatic in finite dimensions, the usual case. Quantum algebra gains a theory respecting its objects' braided nature, not flattening it into symmetry.
arxiv-2606-09307:
Arashi builds a Bayesian regression framework for data with many outcomes and predictors, where errors break the Gaussian bell curve, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard estimators assume Gaussian errors and treat coefficient sparsity separately from dependence sparsity. Macroeconomic series, asset returns, and gene expression show heavy tails, skewness, and outliers biasing both. The framework swaps in flexible error mixtures: multivariate t, skew-normal, and skew-t.

A horseshoe+ prior, a global-local shrinkage prior pulling noise toward zero while sparing real signals, sits on both at once. It covers coefficients and the error precision matrix, coupling the two sparsity patterns. Theory delivers joint posterior contraction, selection consistency, and a guarantee that one huge outlier's influence vanishes under t errors. Simulations show it matches Gaussian methods when errors are Gaussian and wins, often widely, under heavy tails. FRED-MD macro data and S&P 500 returns yield sparse, readable maps.
arxiv-2606-09607:
Yongzhong Xu asks whether cheap clues can prove that a group of attention heads forms a true circuit in a language model in this 2026 arXiv paper. Interpretability work now treats groups of parts, not lone units, as the key objects. A common shortcut groups heads that fire together and calls the group a circuit.

His test is a closure check. He removes the grouped heads and weighs the harm against matched random groups. On two dense models of about a billion parameters, the grouped heads passed: harm clearly topped the random case. In a mixture-of-experts model, one grouped set looked real by the numbers yet failed the check. Cutting it helped the model instead. Two other cheap clues, sharp attention and spread of use, also split from true function. Xu's moral: such clues propose circuits, but only removal tests confirm them.
arxiv-2606-09707:
Gianluca Barmina, Annemette Broch Pirchert, and Andrea Blasi Núñez present a tool for editing trained model weights in a checked, repeatable way in this 2026 arXiv paper. Big checkpoints are hard to inspect and reshape. Teams often patch them with ad-hoc scripts, which break in quiet ways. BrainSurgery swaps scripts for plans.

Each plan is a declarative YAML file that names the edits to run. Regex and structure rules pick out tensors by name or place. Built-in assertions check shapes, data types, and values, so faults surface at once. The tool hides storage formats and memory handling from the user. A demo walks through four examples and three case studies, from model upcycling to LoRA extraction. One check applied a chain of edits and then reversed it. Across fifty prompts, the restored model matched the first one's output, with top pick agreement of one hundred percent.
arxiv-2606-09807:
Thomas Ransford tours function spaces with a freak trait, and ties them to a basic series puzzle that no one has cracked in this 2026 arXiv paper. The spaces hold holomorphic functions on the unit disk, gauged by a norm. Each holds one odd function: sums of polynomials can close in on it in norm, yet its own Taylor partial sums cannot. No blend of those sums works either.

That freak trait sorts spaces into grades. In the best grade, plain partial sums converge for every member. A middle grade needs a summability method, a weighted blend that tames the sums. The worst grade keeps polynomials from filling the space at all. Named spaces land in each grade, from Hardy and Bergman spaces to the Bloch space. The hunt for concrete freak spaces boils down to a plain-looking question about convergent series. That question, Ransford shows, is still open.
arxiv-2606-09907:
Rahman and colleagues tackle two linked problems in learning from patient records over time, in a 2026 arXiv paper on medical AI. Clinical data mixes imaging, text, and records, but at any visit some sources are often missing. A measurement's meaning also depends on the patient's disease trajectory, the path their condition follows across visits. Earlier methods handled missing data or time patterns, rarely both.

Their framework, LongMoE, fills missing modalities with a context-aware imputation module, meaning it estimates absent inputs from what is present. A trajectory-aware encoder models disease progression across irregular visit gaps, and a sparse mixture-of-experts design routes each patient to specialized sub-networks. On the ADNI and OASIS-3 brain study datasets and the MIMIC-IV hospital records, LongMoE stayed robust when current modalities were missing or weak. It also remained competitive when all data was available, supporting longitudinally aware clinical learning.
arxiv-2606-10107:
Stillwagon and his team propose a fairer score for cell segmentation models, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computer vision evaluation. Widely used metrics in biological imaging have mathematical weaknesses. Hard overlap thresholds make scores jump discontinuously, and per-object scaling distorts results when object sizes vary. Greedy matching also pairs predictions with truth in an order-dependent way.

Their metric, Maximum Matching Accuracy, is threshold-free and continuous. It finds a globally optimal one-to-one matching between predicted and ground-truth objects and aggregates total overlap with per-pixel scaling. Across synthetic failure cases, progressive corruption tests, and a model ranking comparison, it produced scores that were more stable, more sensitive, and more interpretable. The beaten rivals included AP at fifty percent overlap, Panoptic Quality, SEG, and AJI. The authors offer it as a principled foundation for benchmarking cell segmentation.
arxiv-2606-10307:
Keramati and his team find that a debating model's opening tokens reveal the quality of reasoning to come, in a 2026 arXiv paper on language model testing. They ask whether built-in confidence signals, the token-level log-probabilities produced during writing, predict reasoning quality as scored by a language-model judge. Using a debate-based essay scoring setup, they compare confidence proxies against rubric-based judge scores across two ASAP essay sets.

Early-token confidence, above all within the first few generated tokens, is steadily the strongest predictor of reasoning quality, beating full-sequence stats. A clear asymmetry appears between agent roles, with confidence aligning more strongly with quality for supportive reasoning than for adversarial critique. The results suggest early decoding dynamics provide a light, strong signal for gauging reasoning trust in multi-agent systems without costly judging passes.
arxiv-2606-10407:
Simen Hexeberg and his team teach object detection models to pinpoint bird calls inside noisy tropical soundscapes, in a 2026 arXiv paper on bioacoustics. Passive acoustic monitoring observes wildlife at scale, but most models only predict species presence within a time window without pinpointing calls exactly in time or frequency, limiting later analysis. They frame call detection as object detection on spectrograms, the time-frequency pictures of sound, and train YOLO11 models to draw boxes around calls in dense Singapore soundscapes.

A scoring metric they propose, Intersection over Minimum, handles fuzzy acoustic edges better than the standard overlap measure. Their best model nearly doubles the baseline's detection score on in-sample Singapore recordings in the reported comparison. The results suggest object detection methods are a promising route to time-frequency spotting of animal calls in complex settings, supporting finer field analysis than presence-only watching.
arxiv-2606-10507:
Diao and colleagues tackle long-horizon tasks for language-model agents in this 2026 arXiv paper, where performance fades as multi-turn jobs stretch out. One cause is long-context interference: the growing history buries the global task state, weakening later decisions. Their method, HIPIF, trains an agent to plan around explicit subgoals and to fold, meaning summarise and shelve, each finished subgoal's history. Reflection checks progress, and subgoal-tied process rewards guide the rest.

The training is end-to-end and needs neither costly helper models nor expert demonstrations written for each task. Across three public agentic benchmarks, HIPIF consistently outperforms competing methods while also improving efficiency. The design mirrors human practice, breaking big jobs into subgoals and compressing finished work, a promising direction for agents that must stay coherent over long tasks.
arxiv-2606-10607:
Li and a large team of co-authors combine rival causal discovery algorithms in this 2026 arXiv paper. Causal discovery tries to recover the cause-and-effect graph among variables from observational data. The trouble is that different algorithms return conflicting graphs, each ignoring what the variables mean. The Causal Ensemble Agent pools the statistical experts' opinions across graph levels, then calls a language model in as referee only when pooled confidence sits near a decision boundary.

The referee reweights experts case by case, using feature descriptions the statistics never saw, and the ensemble composes a fuller graph than any member produced. On synthetic and real-world datasets the framework achieves the strongest overall performance across a wide range of discovery methods. Language models, the authors argue, belong in causal analysis as meta-analysts over evidence, not as oracles.
arxiv-2606-10907:
Iannelli and Ai measure how AI brand mentions steer web behavior in this 2026 arXiv paper. When a chatbot names a brand to a user with no recent engagement, no web log credits the assistant. Joining opt-in clickstream data to the same users' chats with ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, the authors separate genuine recommendations from incidental name-drops of brands the user already knows.

For true recommendations, same-name Google searches rise by 4.3 percentage points over matched placebos. Visits to the brand's own site rise by roughly two points, and retailer-page visits by about one point. Incidental mentions move behavior far less, and last-click analytics miss the effect entirely.
arxiv-2606-11307:
Cowie and Fender revisit how astronomers estimate the energy of synchrotron sources in a 2026 arXiv paper. Synchrotron self-absorption, SSA, appears across many sources, and its spectral peak is a powerful tool for estimating the emitting region's conditions and minimum energy. Traditional estimates assume the region is quasi-spherical and homogeneous. Many observed spectra, though, show flatter slopes below the peak than that picture predicts.

The authors first re-derive the standard estimates carefully, obtaining the most accurate standard minimum-energy equations. They argue an uneven emitting region best explains the flattened spectra. Using power-law slab and sphere models, they find inhomogeneity can make traditional methods underestimate minimum energy and region size by over an order of magnitude. They derive correction factors depending on the flattened spectral index and its frequency range, plus factors for non-spherical homogeneous regions, and explore polarization and light-curve effects.
arxiv-2606-11407:
Reif, Sahi, Serganova, and Sherman prove a Harish-Chandra isomorphism for supersymmetric spaces in a 2026 arXiv paper. The classical theorem describes the center of the enveloping algebra by Weyl-group-symmetric polynomials on a Cartan subalgebra. Extending it to Lie superalgebras required new invariance conditions, debated since Sergeev and Gorelik-Kac.

They describe the eigenvalue polynomials of invariant operators on such spaces. These satisfy novel conditions the authors call odd. They also prove it for ghost distributions, which obey a square root of those rules. All proofs use algebra alone, via a rank-one reduction and the Chevalley restriction theorem. The work extends the theory from algebras to the spaces built on them, including special linear and orthosymplectic examples.
arxiv-2606-11807:
Balázs Németh, Mohamed Warda and Ronojoy Adhikari develop a geometric theory of active filaments in this 2026 arXiv paper. Slender elastic bodies, from sperm tails to soft robotic arms, often sit in viscous fluid and power themselves. Their internal forces can be nonreciprocal, violating the rule that action and reaction match, so strain produces a net response.

Assuming the physics is unchanged by rotations and translations, the authors derive a shape-space formulation: equations that separate the body's intrinsic deformation from its rigid motion. The result is a reaction-advection-diffusion system, a geometric flow where activity-driven instabilities create patterns. Depending on parameters, it settles into steady shapes, oscillates, or moves chaotically. These regimes appear as rigid, swimming and chaotic motion. The framework unifies recent observations in slender active structures under one theory.
arxiv-2606-12007:
A V Druzhinin and C Cancellieri model how thin films relieve their internal stress in this 2026 arXiv paper. Films deposited far from equilibrium carry residual stress, and its relaxation can damage devices. The mechanism here is plastic: screw dislocations, line defects in the crystal, pile up against the impenetrable interface between film and substrate.

Starting from the initial shear stress, the authors link plastic strain to dislocation density and derive an equation connecting residual stress to that density. Applying force balance gives the dislocation distribution for any non-uniform starting stress profile. They solve it numerically by collocation for constant, linear, parabolic and exponential initial profiles. The relaxed stress depends strongly on the film segment's thickness-to-width ratio. In every case equilibrium demands a pile-up mixing dislocations of both signs of Burgers vector, the measure of a dislocation's strength.
arxiv-2606-12107:
Martin Hasenburger and five colleagues watch an aluminium alloy melt at the nanoscale in this 2026 arXiv paper. Melting of eutectic alloys, mixtures that liquefy at one sharp temperature, is classical metallurgy. The tiny-scale mechanisms were out of reach in experiments until in-situ electron microscopy with micro-heating chips matured.

The team tracked a nanocrystalline aluminium-copper alloy poor in copper in a transmission electron microscope, tracking chemistry and resistance. Melting began in the hotter centre and spread outward, with grain boundaries the main sites for liquid formation through copper enrichment. The compound phase melted before the matrix around it finished melting. Most strikingly, liquid copper travelled over two hundred fifty micrometres, far beyond solid-state diffusion limits, leaving pale rims at the chip's outer edge. The authors promote the method as a platform for studying phase changes in many such materials.
arxiv-2606-12207:
Lai and co-authors survey how test sets for embodied AI, robots and agents acting in physical worlds, get built, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Unlike static datasets, an embodied benchmark bundles tasks, environments, robot data, demonstrations, and scoring rules into one system. The survey follows a five-stage pipeline from task design and data collection through annotation, metric building, and evaluation with diagnostic feedback. Each stage is traced from hand craft through automation to foundation-model help and agentic loops.

The finding: automation rarely deletes cost; it moves it. Savings in human authoring reappear as spending on validation, audit trails, version control, and long-term governance. Agentic closed-loop building promises fresh benchmarks but demands strong audit and rollback discipline. Manual judgment stays necessary where safety and social values are involved. Progress now depends less on bigger suites than on pipelines that stay diagnosable, auditable, and refreshable.
arxiv-2606-12307:
Sougata Bhattacharyya and co-authors find that concentrating entanglement into one strong link backfires under the commonest noise, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A W state spreads one excitation evenly across three qubits, entangling all pairs equally. An asymmetric cousin reshapes the network: two strong vertex-base links and one weak base-base link. The authors track concurrence, an entanglement measure, under several noise types.

Under phase damping the strength hierarchy survives at all noise levels, with no sudden death of entanglement. Under amplitude damping, energy loss, the order flips. The symmetric W state becomes most robust, while the weak base-base concurrence vanishes at a noise threshold. The strong link's structure makes it fragile, an effect the authors name super-link fragility. Under depolarizing noise the asymmetry advantage is erased. Robustness, they conclude, depends jointly on network geometry, excitation sector, and noise symmetry, never on starting entanglement alone.
arxiv-2606-12507:
Rezaei and co-authors fire the judge and let the rubric teach directly, in this 2026 arXiv paper. For open-ended tasks like medical advice, no single right answer exists, so trainers grade model outputs against rubrics, scoring criteria. Standard methods pay an AI judge to score every attempt, which is costly, biased toward the judge's quirks, and yields one sparse score per answer. Their RGSD instead makes the rubric privileged context: the base model, shown the rubric, acts as a teacher.

The student, which never sees the rubric, samples one answer per prompt. Training then matches the student's next-token probabilities to the teacher's, a dense signal replacing the end score. No judge calls occur during training. Across Qwen models from three to eight billion parameters, in medical and science domains, RGSD matches judge-based GRPO on rubric satisfaction. Rubrics enrich the teacher more than self-written reference answers do.
arxiv-2606-13607:
Zach Studdiford and Lupyan compare human and machine reasoning failures in this 2026 arXiv paper, and find them surprisingly alike. When language models generalise poorly or err haphazardly, critics often conclude the models are merely pattern matching, unlike humans who supposedly reason from world models. The authors evaluate human participants and twenty-five language models on common-sense reasoning. Both groups show similar patterns of errors. The team then identifies the attention heads, the internal components routing information, that drive the model responses, and finds they implement a form of pattern matching.

Strikingly, those same heads predict reasoning errors in people, errors triggered by seemingly irrelevant prompt details. The shared mechanism suggests human everyday reasoning also leans heavily on pattern matching, not just abstract principle. The paper reframes the debate: the question is not whether models pattern-match, but whether human cognition differs in kind or only in degree.
arxiv-2606-13707:
Fan Zhang and colleagues present Orchestra-o1 in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework for agent teams that work across every modality. Agent swarms have shifted language model systems from single agents to teams, making orchestration, the splitting and coordination of tasks, the key layer. Existing frameworks handle only a narrow set of modes and generalise poorly when text, image, audio, and video coexist. Omnimodal cases, such as analysing a recorded meeting or producing multimedia content, expose exactly that weakness.

Orchestra-o1 introduces a mechanism enabling modality-aware teamwork across mixed inputs. Agents specialised by modality can be assigned, sequenced, and combined under one coordination scheme rather than stitched together ad hoc. The authors position the framework for tasks whose inputs arrive in every format at once. As agents move from text-only benchmarks into real media workflows, orchestration that treats modality as a first-class dimension becomes essential.
arxiv-2606-13807:
Rosemeier and Klein design a faster way to compute solutions of equations whose answers wiggle very rapidly. Such oscillatory systems appear in fluid dynamics, mechanics, and plasma physics. Standard solvers must take tiny time steps to follow each wiggle, making long runs expensive. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds a time-stepping scheme linked to the WKB method, a classic tool for wave-like behavior, using a change of variables derived in the paper.

In the transformed variables, the leading rapid oscillations vanish or appear only at higher order, so larger steps stay accurate. The authors test the scheme on several equations, including the van der Pol oscillator, a circuit-like system with self-sustained pulses. They vary the small parameter that sets the scale gap and show how settings must adapt as it shrinks. Across the tests, cost stays bounded even as oscillations grow faster.
arxiv-2606-13907:
Berkesch, Erman, and Favero repair a broken dictionary between geometry and algebra for spaces called toric varieties. For the simpler simplicial kind, Cox's theory links subvarieties to graded ideals in a special ring. For nonsimplicial varieties that link simply fails: distinct ideals can describe the same subvariety. Their 2026 arXiv paper replaces the Cox ring with a variant built only from Q-Cartier divisors, divisors some multiple of which behave well.

With that change, the ideal-variety correspondence is restored in the nonsimplicial case. Subschemes and sheaves gain an explicit classification through multigraded modules. The construction also yields a toric Deligne-Mumford stack, a refined object remembering extra symmetry data. Finally, the authors extend GKZ and Mori theory, the standard combinatorics of toric birational geometry, into this stacky setting. The package removes deficiencies that had confined Cox-style methods to the simplicial world.
arxiv-2606-14007:
Fatunmbi, Gandhi, and Logan move blockchain plot creation onto graphics cards. Proof-of-Space consensus replaces energy-hungry repeated hashing with precomputed storage plots. Making those plots is itself slow because hashing dominates. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents VaultxGPU, extending the VaultX plotter by offloading its Blake3 hashing to the GPU with custom kernels for NVIDIA CUDA and the portable SYCL framework.

The design keeps lookup tables in graphics memory and fuses sorting and matching into one kernel. Across plot sizes K twenty-seven through thirty-one, the SYCL version ran fifty-nine point two times faster than a single-thread CPU. A K thirty-one plot took forty-five point four seconds instead of two thousand six hundred eighty-eight. It beat the best three hundred eighty-four-thread CPU setup too. The remaining bottleneck is disk writing, at fifty-nine to eighty-two percent of pipeline time.
arxiv-2606-14307:
Barberteguy and colleagues teach a 3D reconstruction network to also label what it rebuilds, in one unified model. The input is ordinary photos, with no camera data at all. Feedforward networks now produce dense 3D point clouds from unposed photos, but lack semantic understanding. Earlier add-ons froze the backbone or needed heuristic clustering at inference. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents Pano3D. A set-based mask decoder with learned queries is appended to the backbone. The system is finetuned jointly with geometric and semantic losses, no external models or postprocessing.

The bet: object recognition is already latent in reconstruction features encoding boundaries and 3D coherence. Joint training proved mutually beneficial. Pano3D reached state-of-the-art 3D panoptic results on ScanNet, ScanNet200, and ScanNet++, across online and all-to-all attention backbones.
arxiv-2606-14907:
Ellison Murray trims the cost of correcting satellite power amplifiers in a 2026 arXiv paper. Power amplifiers distort signals, blurring their spectral purity. Digital pre-distortion fixes this by pre-warping the signal to cancel the amplifier's flaws. Full-complexity fixes are too heavy for satellites. Size, weight, and power budgets there are strict.

Murray proposes Least Squares Thresholding for picking a sparse set of correction terms. It is compared with two standard sparse solvers, Orthogonal Matching Pursuit and plain Matching Pursuit. Thresholding matched the stronger method's linearization quality almost exactly. But it cut complexity by a factor of about two point eight. That near-free saving matters on orbit, where every watt and gram counts. The work frames sparse correction as a trade-off to tune, not a fixed recipe. It targets satellite communication systems first.
arxiv-2606-15007:
NVIDIA introduces Nemotron 3 Ultra, an open language model built for long-running agent work, in a 2026 report. The model mixes experts with a hybrid Mamba-attention design to raise speed without losing accuracy. It holds five hundred fifty billion parameters, with fifty-five billion active per token. Context extends to one million tokens for extended tasks.

Pretraining consumed twenty trillion text tokens in low-precision NVFP4 format, in two phases of broad then high-quality data. Post-training adds supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and distillation from many teacher models. Features such as LatentMoE and multi-token prediction push inference throughput higher. The report claims roughly five to six times the throughput of rival open models at matched accuracy on agentic benchmarks. NVIDIA releases the base, post-trained, and quantized checkpoints on HuggingFace. Training data and the full recipe are released as well.
arxiv-2606-15107:
Chen and coauthors benchmark language models on irregular time series question answering in a 2026 study. Real time series arrive irregularly: sensors log at uneven times and missing values carry meaning. Existing question answering benchmarks assume tidy, regular sampling instead. Random dropout creates fake irregularity that ignores why data went missing.

Their benchmark, IRTS-ToolBench, holds seventeen hundred questions across ten task types and thirteen domains. A language-model-guided pipeline converts regular series into irregular ones in semantically grounded ways. Irregularity follows cause-driven patterns, such as trigger-based or artifact-based sampling gaps. A library of thirty tools supports agent-style solving, with golden tool sets for scoring. Evaluation covers both answer correctness and tool-use behavior. Current models show real reasoning ability on irregular data, especially with context and tools available. Higher-level temporal reasoning still fails often, and agents need strong scaffolding to use tools reliably.
arxiv-2606-15307:
Kmainasi and coauthors train multimodal models to flag hateful and propagandistic memes with explanations, in a 2026 content moderation paper. Memes hide harmful intent in the interplay of image and caption, which neither reveals alone. The team benchmarks off-the-shelf reasoning models on English and Arabic meme datasets. They then extend those datasets with distilled rationales and detailed propaganda labels. Their training recipe applies reinforcement learning with rewards for accuracy and explanation quality. A length penalty keeps the model's reasoning from shrinking away.

On the English Hateful Memes benchmark, accuracy rose by about two points over prior work. On the Arabic ArMeme benchmark, macro-F1 jumped by over seven points. The trained model also produces written explanations for its verdicts. Sequence-classification baselines still win on Arabic accuracy alone. The model balances per-class performance better while explaining itself. Self-supervised training on unlabeled memes added signal.
arxiv-2606-15507:
Dasdan and colleagues audit the moral reasoning of LLaMA 3.1-8B-Instruct in 2026 from the inside, using mechanistic interpretability tools rather than judging only its answers. They run fifty-four moral prompts in four batteries: dilemmas, policy questions, role-play scenarios, and controlled trolley contrasts. Cluster-level and neuron-level metrics track which internal features dominate.

Both families converge on a Situational Anchor Effect: domain-specific representations top the activation list in every battery, whatever the moral content. Ethics-labelled capacity stays near five percent throughout, but its salience swings with prompt framing. In trolley variants, ethics features rise in rank without growing in capacity, and the model attends to whichever surface feature the prompt varies. One candidate ethics neuron stays stable across temperatures. The authors argue that fine-tuning reorders surface text but leaves domain-first frames intact, so output checks alone cannot certify moral reasoning.
arxiv-2606-15707:
Karmakar and colleagues demonstrate a tunable way to transform optical skyrmions in 2026, using the chirality of the medium the light passes through. Optical skyrmions are topologically protected swirls of light polarization, promising for communication, storage, and particle manipulation. Reshaping them on demand, between Bloch-type, Néel-type, and intermediate textures, has been awkward with conventional optics.

The team sends vector vortex beams through an active mixture whose enantiomeric excess, the imbalance between mirror-image molecules, they control. Tuning that excess converts skyrmions reversibly between Bloch, Néel, and intermediate states, and the same trick transforms bimerons once a birefringent plate is added. The skyrmion number stays conserved, even for higher-order textures, showing the transformations are robust. The common-path setup is stable and cheap, needing fewer wave plates than rival schemes. Chemical tuning of light's topology offers a flexible platform for information processing with structured light.
arxiv-2606-15907:
Izmestiev and colleagues revisit the flexibility of discrete conjugate nets in 2026, polyhedral surfaces of quadrilateral faces arranged like a square grid. A generic such net is rigid: it admits no deformation beyond rigid motion. A published claim held that a non-degenerate net whose 3-by-3 subnets are all flexible must itself be flexible.

The claim, it turns out, is false as stated: the authors construct counterexamples. They then prove a corrected version under stronger side conditions, restoring the local-to-global implication where it belongs. Their global theorems extend to all simply connected nets, while nets with holes need different methods, illustrated through flexible tubes. The work has a mechanical echo: the nets correspond to parallel manipulators, where the same distinctions separate flexing mechanisms from first-order rigid ones.
arxiv-2606-16107:
Xu, Huang, and Wu tackle variable-rate image compression in 2026, where one model must serve many quality levels. Deep compression now beats traditional standards on quality, but changing the rate usually needs several networks or one complex model. Both options cost storage or computation. The authors borrow a fine-tuning trick from language models instead.

Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, tunes a model through small added matrices that later merge back into the weights. Their LoRA Rate-Adaptive Module, LoRAM, applies this idea progressively so one model can switch rates. Because the pieces merge back, they add no extra computation at use time in the design described. Variable-rate compression uses only 0.1 percent added parameters in the reported system. Tests verify LoRA-based adaptation works well for this task. One compact codec spanning rates could simplify streaming and medical imaging alike.
arxiv-2606-16207:
Abhishek and Mummidi build a neutrino model in 2026 where one symmetry pattern fixes the whole lepton flavor structure. Neutrinos have tiny masses and mix at large angles, facts the Standard Model alone cannot explain. Radiative models generate those masses through loops instead of a direct term. The scotogenic model is one such loop scheme, with dark sector particles in the loop.

Here the finite modular group S4 controls the flavor symmetry. All Yukawa couplings, the numbers setting masses and mixing, come from modular forms: functions of a single complex parameter, the modulus. One parameter thus replaces the usual flavon fields and their vacuum values. The scotogenic loop mechanism sits inside this modular frame. The combined model addresses neutrino masses, leptonic mixing, and the cosmic baryon asymmetry together, the last through flavored resonant leptogenesis. A scan over the modulus maps the viable space: fewer free inputs, sharper predictions.
arxiv-2606-16407:
Trinley and co-authors open the hood of language models in 2026 to find why they mishandle pronouns when several referents carry different ones. Behavioral tests alone cannot show which internal mechanism fails. The authors test three candidate mechanisms: group entity binding, which ties a pronoun to its referent group; recency bias, which favors the latest mention; and stereotypical bias, which follows social expectations. Using Boundless Distributed Alignment Search, they hunt for each mechanism inside the network.

All three turn up as separable causal subspaces spread across the network's depth. Together they account for 91 to 99.5 percent of model behavior on the task, per the report. Most models lean mainly on recency and stereotype, while group binding contributes little and sometimes adds noise. Attention analysis reveals two competing copying routes: a localized concept-level route shared by binding and stereotype, and a distributed token-level route used by recency.
arxiv-2606-16507:
Spindler and co-authors release in 2026 segmentation maps tracing the spiral arms and bars of 639,636 galaxies, drawn by a neural network taught by citizen scientists. The maps come from the DESI Legacy Survey imaging. A U-net-style network, dubbed ZooBot:3D, trains on pixel masks from the Galaxy Zoo: 3D project, where volunteers outlined galactic structures by hand. Its outputs are soft maps: each pixel carries the model's confidence that it lies in a spiral arm or a bar.

Within the catalogue, 512,216 galaxies show a high likelihood of spiral arms, and 230,511 a strong or weak bar, per the survey classifications. The model also shows an emergent knack for finding rings, although ring galaxies were scarce in its training data. Cross-matched subsamples tie the maps to the MaNGA and SAMI spectroscopic surveys, with about 29,000 and 5,000 objects respectively. The full dataset is public.
arxiv-2606-16707:
Li argues in a 2026 paper that a personal AI agent should store its memory of the user as running code. Today's agents keep memory as loose text, a graph, or a flat list of facts, then fetch whichever entries look similar to a new request. That style recalls single facts well, but handles contradictions, totals and hard rules poorly.

The proposal, User as Code, models the user as a living software project. Typed Python objects hold the user's state, and ordinary functions encode the rules that govern it, so storage and reasoning share one runnable medium. A two-phase pipeline first logs every fact without discarding anything, then periodically checkpoints the log into clean structured code. On a standard long-conversation benchmark, recall matches the best prior systems. On aggregate questions, like counting last year's trips, retrieval memory collapses while code-based memory holds up.
arxiv-2606-16807:
Pirlogeanu and colleagues link spoken words to written words through images in a 2026 speech technology paper. Many languages lack transcripts, so training speech systems the usual way is impossible or costly. Pictures with spoken descriptions can be gathered anywhere, though, even where literacy is low.

Their method starts from image captions written by captioning systems, giving a vocabulary of visible concepts. For each written word, they gather utterances whose pictures were captioned with that word. An unsupervised word discovery step then aligns those utterances to locate the spoken segment matching the word. No text supervision is used at any point. In retrieval and keyword spotting tests, the approach beats a strong neural baseline while staying easier to interpret. A continuous-feature version scores best overall, while a discrete version runs more cheaply. The English proof of concept motivates work on low-resource languages without written records.
arxiv-2606-16907:
Yanda Tao and colleagues present Tangram in a 2026 systems paper on training large language models over mixed GPU clusters. Real clusters grow over time, so they mix graphics processor types with different speeds, memory and links. Automatic parallelizers that split models across devices face an exploding search space on such mixed hardware, and they often drop useful parallelism modes to cope.

Tangram hides the mixture from the planner. Profiling finds homogeneous islands, groups of similar devices bought together. The model is cut into slices, each slice is planned by an existing homogeneous parallelizer on one island, and the slices are composed into balanced pipelines. A narrow interface connects Tangram to existing tools, and heterogeneity-guided pruning speeds the search by about an order of magnitude. Measured training throughput beats current heterogeneous parallelizers by more than a factor of two at best, while matching homogeneous tools on uniform clusters.
arxiv-2606-17107:
Li reframes a language model's key-value cache as a notebook in a 2026 inference paper. Prefix caching reuses computation only for an exact shared prefix; changing one field invalidates everything after it. Patching the field's cached vectors fails: the model keeps acting on the old value.

Experiments across four model families show why: during prefill, the model writes conclusions conditioned on that field onto downstream tokens, its notes. The field's own vectors drive under one percent of the decision. Two capabilities follow. The cache is editable: append a salient erratum and the notes amend themselves, at a tiny fraction of recompute cost. It is also composable: notes are portable, so a precompiled skill can be spliced into a new context, matching full recomputation. In an online serving benchmark, the trick keeps cache hit rates high and slashes time to first token.
arxiv-2606-17207:
Antoci and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on a puzzling class of pulsating stars. They call them wildly oscillating stars, or WOS for short. Space telescopes show dense, ridge-like clusters of frequencies in some A and F type stars. The clusters sit below the fundamental radial mode, where classical theory expects none.

The team analysed Kepler and TESS photometry and built frequency diagrams. Rotation, binarity, and standard excitation models were all tested as explanations. The effect appears only where two known instability strips overlap on the diagram. In at least two stars, many peaks are nonlinear combination frequencies of other modes. Yet the parent modes must sit inside the cluster itself, so current models still miss the cause.
arxiv-2606-17407:
Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on light-like waves in a honeycomb array of microcavity pillars holding exciton-polariton condensates, part light and part matter. Dirac cones in such lattices normally come in pairs, and breaking symmetries opens both to create a topological gap. Here, breaking inversion symmetry by splitting one sublattice's pillars, plus time-reversal breaking from a magnetic field and spin-orbit coupling, leaves the cones unpaired in the spectrum of the device.

Even without a full spectral gap, one-way edge states still emerge and can turn corners of the array. Resonant pumping brings bistability, letting operators excite chosen edge states selectively with light. The team obtains a stable, localised edge soliton that circulates around the rim of the structure indefinitely without radiating away. The platform points to new devices for nonlinear topological photonics in practice.
arxiv-2606-17507:
Xu and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on using language models to mark student answers for high-stakes exam preparation, with the marking grounded in official curriculum documents. Prompt tricks alone are not enough at that level of stakes, the authors argue. Their pipeline, built with an industry partner, first pins down a question's topics, subtopics, and cognitive demand, then assembles official context from syllabus artefacts and marking guidelines issued by education authorities.

Syllabus intent enters through concrete items: prescribed verbs, stated outcomes, performance band descriptors, glossary definitions, and marking principles. A staged workflow drafts question-specific rubrics, then derives the marking criteria used to score each response. Early evaluation shows marking close to human tutors, with justifications that trace more clearly to official sources. The pipeline already runs inside an online study platform, where override data are being collected.
arxiv-2606-17707:
Yang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper asking whether generative recommenders trap users in information cocoons more or less than the classic kind. Recommenders feed on their own past suggestions, narrowing what users see until tastes harden into bubbles. Generative systems differ fundamentally: they emit items as code sequences rather than scoring fixed catalogue entries, which might change how cocoons form. The team built RecLoop, a closed-loop simulation where language-model user agents interact with recommenders over many feedback cycles with periodic retraining switched on.

Thousands of agents shopped two product data sets across fifteen cycles in the simulation. Generative recommenders preserved broader exposure and slowed the drift toward sameness across users compared with sequential baselines. Yet concentration still grew inside the generated code space itself, a model-level cocoon the authors measure separately. Token choice and model scale strongly shaped how severe the effect became.
arxiv-2606-17807:
Olleik and colleagues study how Lebanese households cope when the public electricity grid fails for long stretches. Lebanon has near-universal electrification on paper, yet chronic shortages shape daily energy use. Drawing on an original survey of one thousand households, the 2026 paper examines both backup supply choices and changes in how people use power.

Households rely mainly on diesel generators, solar panels paired with batteries, or hybrid mixes of the two. Wealth strongly shapes who can afford backup and how much of their demand gets met, and a shift toward solar and batteries is clear among better-off families. The authors also document wasted solar output, load shifting, and suppressed demand, arguing that backup access and unmet demand must be distinguished in energy policy.
arxiv-2606-18607:
Ni and Lai propose a method for finding unknown energy potentials inside phase field models from observed data, in a 2026 paper on inverse problems for materials modeling. Phase field simulations track how microstructures evolve using equations such as Allen-Cahn and Cahn-Hilliard, but the nonlinear potentials driving them are hard to measure, which limits how predictive the models can be.

Their Dual Time Phase Field Inversion framework turns recovery into a fitting problem matching model output to the measured final field. They prove the measured field is differentiable in the unknown potential and that the regularized objective is locally convex, so a local optimum exists. Automatic differentiation supplies the gradients cheaply. In tests the method accurately rebuilt both polynomial and logarithmic potentials and stayed robust under measurement noise. It extends to field-dependent mobility and joint parameter identification in coupled systems.
arxiv-2606-18807:
Belova, Dementiev, and Sagunov ask whether machine-learned predictions can speed up the exact exponential-time algorithms used for NP-hard problems, in a 2026 theoretical computer science paper. Learning-augmented algorithms had shown them beating worst-case guarantees for polynomial-time problems. But exact algorithms for problems such as feedback vertex set, hitting set, and weighted satisfiability live under exponential running times and conjectured barriers.

The authors answer yes, with a general approach that adds to a family of exact algorithms for subset selection problems. A noisy predictor only just better than random guessing already suffices to provably shrink the search space. The runtime speedup scales smoothly with prediction quality. That is an information leverage effect, in which a linear amount of signal tames an exponential search. The assumptions are weak: pairwise independence of prediction errors suffices. One variant does not need to know the predictor's accuracy.
arxiv-2606-19207:
Xie studies extrema of Gaussian fields with a microscopic slowdown in a 2026 probability paper. The family of fields has a covariance structure that slows down unevenly at small scales. A tuning parameter moves the field between a log profile at one end and a log-log profile at the other. In one dimension the objects act like branching Brownian motion in a cooling environment.

The correct centering of the maximum at large times is found. It then proves tightness of the recentered maximum. The leading growth of the maximum varies linearly with the tuning parameter. The second-order correction behaves differently. It shows a phase transition at a threshold value of the parameter, where the correction changes form. Extrema of log-correlated fields link to branching processes and to multiplicative chaos, so sharp centering results feed several active areas of probability at once.
arxiv-2606-19507:
Meredith Shea studies a split Aztec diamond tiling model in 2026. An Aztec diamond is a diamond-shaped region tiled by dominoes, a classic model in statistical mechanics. Shea splits the region into two unequal parts whose sizes stay fixed in ratio as the diamond grows.

Each part carries its own two-periodic weighting, a repeating pattern of tile weights. The larger part is the dominant side, the smaller the non-dominant side, and their border is the interface. Shea derives an integral formula for the model's correlation kernel. From it comes a partial account of the scaling limit, plus a conjecture for the rest. The dominant side's limit shape matches the standard two-periodic diamond and ignores the other side. The smaller side's shape is new, depending on both weightings and the interface position. A full limit shape follows when the dominant weighting parameter tends to zero.
arxiv-2606-19707:
Douglas Bridges builds an axiomatic theory of justification inside constructive set theory in 2026. Constructive Morse Set Theory treats every term as also a formula, and vice versa. That feature suits a formal account of what it means for one statement to justify another.

Bridges introduces a new notion, written jst P p, for the claim that P proves or justifies p. The reading follows the BHK interpretation of intuitionistic logic, where proofs are constructions. Axioms for the notion come first, stated inside set theory itself. Many consequences then follow by derivation. Under stated restrictions, the axioms align with the intended BHK readings of the intuitionistic logic axioms. Justification logic usually lives in modal systems apart from set theory. Bridges instead grounds proof talk in the same universe as the mathematics it describes.
arxiv-2606-19907:
Jan Kelleter and six colleagues fight seismic gravity noise at the future Einstein Telescope with neural networks in 2026. Seismic waves tug test masses through their own gravity, a Newtonian noise floor for low-frequency listening. Seismometer arrays can predict that noise so it can be subtracted.

A simulation breeds density fluctuations from random plane waves and Gaussian wave packets. It computes both the ground displacement field and the resulting Newtonian noise. Neural networks and the classic Wiener filter compete at prediction. On near-stationary wave fields the two approaches tie, with networks slightly ahead. Single dominating events, long or short, change the picture sharply. Convolutional and graph networks beat the Wiener filter by factors of fifteen to eighty there. Noise amplitude spectra fall by factors of ten to thirty in those event cases.
arxiv-2606-20207:
Ruilin Hu and five colleagues prove that the 3D Navier-Stokes equations for fluids of varying density have strong solutions. The solutions start from unusually rough initial data. Their 2026 paper studies the inhomogeneous incompressible system, where density is transported by the flow. The velocity must start in a space called VMO-inverse, rougher than the classical energy class, and the density is smooth with a positive lower bound.

Local existence of strong solutions is established for such data. If the density is slightly smoother and the initial perturbation and velocity are small in the right norms, the solution exists globally. The proof uses transport estimates for density regularity and a new freezing coefficient method for the momentum equation. Knowing exactly which starting roughness still yields a well-behaved solution defines the theory's reach.
arxiv-2606-20307:
Huai-Dong Cao, Xiaofeng Sun, and Yingying Zhang give a dynamical construction of Hermitian-Einstein metrics on stable holomorphic vector bundles. Their 2026 paper builds on recent results for the prescribed Hermitian-Yang-Mills tensor and its twisted variants. A Hermitian-Einstein metric is a canonical geometry for a bundle: its curvature, contracted against the Kähler form, is a constant multiple of the identity. Stability, a slope condition on subsheaves, is the property expected to guarantee such a metric exists.

The authors' iteration produces the metric dynamically, and the construction extends to Higgs bundles. In an appendix, the heat flow method yields a new proof that solutions of the twisted tensor equation exist and are unique, plus its Higgs generalization. The results sit inside the Donaldson-Uhlenbeck-Yau circle linking stability to canonical metrics. A dynamical route matters because it suggests algorithms, not just existence theorems.
arxiv-2606-20707:
Christian Internò and many colleagues introduce GeoPhys in 2026, a fast way to judge whether a video event is physically plausible. Humans spot impossible events in milliseconds. Machine methods are often slow and costly. They may rely on large multimodal judges or special training changes. GeoPhys argues that plausibility signals already sit in the frame embeddings of frozen image encoders, as five geometric properties.

Those signals correlate with human brain responses to object permanence violations. GeoPhys also separates implausible from realistic videos with high scores: 98.3 percent on LikePhys and 93.3 percent on IntPhys2. Several large video models perform near chance on the same tests. Used as a verifier during generation, GeoPhys lifts one large video model from 50.01 to 64.50 percent on PhysicsIQ, at lower cost. A cheap geometry check could help filter unrealistic generated video before costly human review.
arxiv-2606-21007:
Hajar Aziz and ten colleagues investigate a distant galaxy nicknamed lil gal in 2026, found by chance in Webb telescope images of a nearby galaxy. In two mid-infrared bands it looks like a spiral galaxy with a central bulge. In a third band, a second peak appears offset from the bulge. That raises three candidate explanations: a clumpy disk, an unrelated background galaxy, or a merger.

Multi-band analysis across Webb and Hubble images gives a photometric redshift near one. Spectroscopy from Keck reveals two sets of emission lines. They correspond to the two sources, at nearly the same redshift. The pair is therefore a merging galaxy system. Projected separation is about five kiloparsecs. A serendipitous find becomes a case study of galaxy assembly at cosmic noon, when mergers helped build the galaxies seen today.
arxiv-2606-21107:
Minwoo Kim, Junyong Park, and Sungkyu Jung propose an empirical Bayes method in 2026 to improve the utility of differentially private statistics without weakening privacy. Differential privacy protects individuals by adding noise. The Gaussian mechanism is simple and widely used. Its output is noisy by design, and many enhanced methods are complex or costly. Their idea is to denoise the output after the fact.

Empirical Bayes estimation takes the Gaussian mechanism output as its only input. It shrinks noise using structure learned from the output itself. Mean-squared error falls while the privacy level stays the same. Numerical studies cover histogram release, principal component analysis, and linear regression. The approach often beats existing private algorithms. A simple post-step that helps many tasks at once is valuable, because privacy budgets are precious and complex private pipelines are hard to deploy correctly.
arxiv-2606-21307:
Jiacheng Wang and seven colleagues propose TASER in 2026, a continual learning framework for models that must absorb very different tasks in sequence, from math reasoning to legal summaries. Most continual learning assumes tasks resemble each other, so fixed capacity either forgets old skills or wastes room. TASER instead grows a library of small atomic skills, deciding for each new task how many fresh skills to add, based on task divergence and model uncertainty.

Orthogonality checks keep the skills distinct and reusable, and a light gating mechanism routes each task to the skills it needs. The team also releases HeteroCLBench, nineteen tasks across nine cognitive dimensions under one sequential protocol. On that benchmark TASER beats strong baselines, learning new tasks while forgetting less, a step toward models that keep pace with shifting real workloads.
arxiv-2606-21607:
Di Yang and four colleagues present T-MOR in 2026, a framework that learns human action representations from skeleton data while borrowing supervision from video and language. Vision-language models read appearance well but barely model motion, even though actions are defined by how bodies move over time. T-MOR aligns skeleton sequences with matching video and text through multi-modal contrastive learning, then runs at test time on lightweight skeleton input alone.

Training uses PoseCap-1M, a new dataset of over one million synchronized video, skeleton, and text triplets spanning diverse activities. Across benchmarks including Toyota Smarthome, UAV-Human, Penn Action, and Charades, T-MOR improves action classification and frame-wise detection over prior methods. It also generalizes strongly in few-shot and zero-shot tests, evidence that motion-centered representations transfer well between tasks.
arxiv-2606-21707:
Favaro and Fortini work on a classic statistics problem in 2026: estimating sums that mix observed values with hidden ones. Empirical Bayes methods handle such sums under mixture models, but older versions lean on narrow assumptions or cover only a few target functions. Their paper develops a more flexible alternative called quasi-Bayes empirical Bayes, designed to stay broad and cheap to compute.

The method builds the mixing distribution step by step using Newton's algorithm, then plugs that estimate into the target sum. Error bars come from large-sample theory, which describes the estimate's long-run spread with a Gaussian limit law. The authors prove the quasi-Bayes and true Bayes estimates merge as samples grow, and that the method stays consistent when the model is right. Tests on synthetic and real data matched or beat older empirical Bayes methods in accuracy and stability.
arxiv-2606-21907:
Vashistha, Sarkar, and Farahi tackle deconvolution in 2026, the problem of recovering a hidden signal's distribution after measurement noise has blurred it. Instruments rarely record the quantity itself, and for flexible generative models the formula needed by classic methods is often impossible to write down. Their answer is a likelihood-free method built on simulation based inference.

The method fits a latent generative model so its noise-blurred distribution matches the observed data distribution, using a convolutional maximum mean discrepancy loss as the yardstick. The learned density then acts as an empirical prior for denoising single measurements. The framework handles noise of varying size across observations and works with rich model families such as Gaussian mixtures and normalizing flows. The authors prove finite-sample error bounds and convergence rates that match classical theory: polynomial rates for ordinary-smooth noise and logarithmic rates for super-smooth noise.
arxiv-2606-22007:
Price reviews, in 2026, the state of Monte Carlo event generators for future lepton colliders, software that simulates particle collisions event by event so theory can be compared with detector data. Future lepton collider programmes will demand far more from these tools than current machines do. The review, an invited workshop contribution, selects the challenges Price judges most pressing rather than attempting complete coverage.

The topics include electroweak corrections, beam radiation, and beam dynamics, all of which distort the clean collisions lepton machines are famous for. Quantum chromodynamics calculations and the modelling of how quarks settle into ordinary particles also need sharper treatment. Price frames these tools as the link between theory and measurement: without fully exclusive simulated events, the goals cannot be checked against reality. The discussion aims to guide where effort should concentrate before the new colliders arrive.
arxiv-2606-22107:
Oke and Dossa build, in 2026, a rigorous framework for supersymmetric quantum systems whose momentum operator is deformed by geometry. Earlier work ensured it behaved correctly only through boundary conditions. Their construction makes it strictly self-adjoint by design, for both linear and quadratic deformation shapes, inside one scheme.

The scheme yields exact energy spectra and reveals a hidden su(1,1) symmetry in the systems. The authors also give the first full heat treatment, computing the partition function by the Euler-Maclaurin method. Deformation reshapes the density of states in distinct ways. The linear shape produces a divergent peak in heat capacity, from states piling up near a top energy. The quadratic shape instead saturates the heat capacity below the Dulong-Petit limit.
arxiv-2606-22207:
Vera introduces Lexical Consensus in 2026, a test framework for studying whether software agents can learn grounded word meanings from experience. Agents see frozen DINOv2 visual features and must acquire Carroll-style invented words for visual concepts. A family of simple learners, from centroid prototypes to exemplar nearest neighbours, is tested across controlled settings.

The central finding is a robust perceptual-coherence gradient. Native categories are learned most easily, coherent overreach remains learnable, disjunctive concepts degrade, and far-disjunctive ones approach chance. A pre-registered experiment over CIFAR-100 confirms perceptual distance, not semantic closeness, governs the gradient: the perceptual predictor explains a substantial share of variance while the semantic one adds almost none. Exemplar models beat centroid prototypes at label-to-image retrieval for multi-peaked concepts. Frozen perceptual geometry thus both enables grounding and bounds what can be learned.
arxiv-2606-22307:
Dang and colleagues propose Manifold Restore Mixing in 2026, a data augmentation method for protein representation learning that repairs the structural damage such methods usually cause. Standard methods add useful variation but risk disrupting protein structure and function. Homology modelling tools preserve structure but reduce diversity. The authors first document these structure defects and the performance loss they cause in existing methods.

Their method mixes the hidden states of original and augmented protein data, inspired by manifold mixup. The mixed samples restore structural information lost in augmentation while keeping diverse variation. A sample difficulty scheduler adjusts the mixup spread during training, feeding the model ever harder mixed samples. Experiments across several backbones and downstream tasks show the method works well and transfers. Code and weights are released openly.
arxiv-2606-22507:
Yoshihito Kuno and Takahiro Orito study what noise does to a topological quantum state in this 2026 physics paper. Their starting point is an extended cluster state, a symmetry protected topological phase guarded by many subsystem symmetries. Decoherence, the leakage of quantum information into the environment, is usually treated as purely destructive.

Applying decoherence to one subsystem at a time induces local charge fluctuations there, while the untouched subsystems settle into a mixed symmetry protected state. Step by step, a hierarchy of such mixed-state phases emerges, each still guarded by the surviving strong symmetries. The phases can be told apart by Rényi-2 string order parameters. The hierarchy ends when the last subsystem falls into a strong-to-weak symmetry breaking state with glassy GHZ-type long-range entanglement. The work shows decoherence can organize a whole family of nontrivial mixed states, not just destroy order.
arxiv-2606-22607:
Alexandru Enciu and eleven colleagues report detector electronics for a nuclear physics experiment in this 2026 paper. The HYDRA time projection chamber is a dedicated pion tracker built to study hypernuclei, exotic nuclei containing a strange quark, within the R3B experiment at GSI/FAIR in Germany. Its readout uses the VMM3a chip inside the Scalable Readout System, offering high rates with precise charge and timing measurement.

The team adapted that readout architecture to the chamber's pad plane. The work covers custom adapter boards, power distribution, and synchronization with the wider R3B data acquisition system. A series of laboratory and integration tests then evaluated the full readout chain. Results demonstrate reliable operation and precise timing performance. The chain proved compatible with the R3B acquisition framework, establishing the system as a suitable readout solution for the chamber. The paper is an instrumentation report rather than a physics result.
arxiv-2606-22707:
Peter Renkel offers a test of a quantum collapse theory in this 2026 paper. Continuous Spontaneous Localization says quantum superpositions collapse on their own at a rate growing with mass, an idea needing sensitive experiments to confirm or exclude. His design uses a trapped nanoparticle as a reversible pointer, rather than preparing the particle itself in superposition.

A microscopic two-branch system applies opposite weak forces, briefly amplifying which-branch information into separated pointer positions. After one trap period the positions and momenta recombine. Ordinary quantum mechanics then predicts the microscopic coherence is recovered. The collapse theory instead predicts an irreversible visibility loss accumulated while the pointer's mass was separated. For a nanoparticle of 10^-18 kilograms driven by a force of 10^-21 newtons at 0.4 kelvin, the sensitivity reaches collapse rates near 10^-11 per second in the aggressive setup. That would improve direct matter-wave bounds by up to five orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2606-23007:
Xun Chen and colleagues probe a frustrated magnet called GdZnPO in a 2026 condensed matter paper. In frustrated magnets, competing interactions stop spins from settling into a simple pattern. The result can be a spin liquid, a state with restless spins and no fixed order. GdZnPO arranges its large spins on a honeycomb lattice. Theory had suggested its many spiral states could cooperate into a spiral spin liquid. The team tests that idea with nuclear magnetic resonance, which reads local magnetism through atomic nuclei.

Chen and colleagues find uniform magnetization and lively low-energy spin motion at middle field strengths, persisting to very low temperature with no sign of broken symmetry. That behavior supports a spin liquid state. At weaker fields, a faint stripe order appears at low temperature, yet strong fluctuations remain. The spin size only weakly lifts the spiral degeneracy, leaving order subtle and dynamics robust.
arxiv-2606-23307:
Chang Han and colleagues propose a new route to primordial black holes in a 2026 cosmology paper. Primordial black holes form when huge early density ripples collapse. Making enough of them needs a strong boost to curvature ripples on small scales. The authors place that boost after inflation, during a stiff epoch when the universe's expansion behaves unusually. Primordial magnetic fields carry an electromagnetic stress with a vector part. That vector part sources metric vector ripples, which stay nearly constant through the stiff epoch and persistently feed second-order scalar ripples.

Han and colleagues show the induced curvature ripples grow toward the low-frequency edge of the stiff band with a steep characteristic slope. For magnetic fields from a standard Ratra-type generation scenario, the ripples can produce black holes in abundance. The yield could make up a substantial fraction of the dark matter.
arxiv-2606-23507:
Namitha Pradeep and Ben Zwickl audit quantum textbooks and courses for room to teach quantum sensing in a 2026 education paper. The second quantum revolution advances computing, communication, and sensing together. Education has raced ahead on computing while sensing stays largely overlooked. To find entry points, the authors analyze six widely used textbooks spanning modern physics, quantum mechanics, and quantum computing. They tag every excerpt mentioning sensing-related keywords and record the context of each appearance. Network maps then show which keywords appear in which contexts, and how often.

Pradeep and Zwickl score the tagged excerpts with a rubric for conceptual and mathematical depth. Coverage varies widely across subjects in both content and depth. Spin-first and position-first textbooks differ notably in how they treat core concepts like superposition and entanglement. The authors also mine a database of over eight thousand quantum course descriptions for sensing mentions.
arxiv-2606-23607:
Li and Shen scale up a method for merging separately trained neural networks into one, in a 2026 paper on deep learning. Linear mode connectivity means two models can be joined by a straight line in weight space without the loss spiking midway. When that holds, merging is as simple as averaging weights. In practice, trained models sit in mismatched arrangements, since many weight patterns compute the same function, and naive averaging hits a loss barrier.

Their framework applies function preserving transformations to align the two models. A dual learning procedure then trains both transformations at once, each moving toward a shared straight path. On WikiText tasks the method reaches near zero loss barriers at medium scale. A large vision transformer keeps accuracy above sixty nine percent along the path, and billion parameter models show only small barriers.
arxiv-2606-23707:
Liu, Zhou, Yang, and Yao rebuild missing brain signal channels by learning a continuous field over the scalp, in a 2026 paper on neural engineering. Electroencephalography uses electrodes on the scalp to record brain activity. Real recordings lose channels randomly to bad contacts and device differences, and high density setups are costly and cumbersome. Spatial super resolution aims to recover the full signal set from sparse measurements, but most methods learn one fixed mapping between set layouts and break when the missing pattern changes.

The authors recast the task as learning a shared scalp field from whichever channels are observed. An encoder compresses the available channels, together with their coordinates, into one latent condition. A decoder then answers queries at any electrode coordinate, even locations never seen in training. On several datasets the method cuts error sharply for unseen electrodes.
arxiv-2606-23907:
Capasso, Lancellotti, and Shumyatsky extend a classical theorem linking how central a group is to how small its commutator structure must be, in a 2026 paper on group theory. Baer's theorem says that if the s-th term of a group's upper central series sits at finite index, then the next lower central term is finite. Later generalizations replaced finiteness with finite rank. The authors work with generalized soluble groups and a quotient mixing both series at levels s and t.

If that mixed quotient has finite rank r, then the lower central term at level s plus t has finite rank bounded by a function of r, s, and t alone. A parallel result uses Chernikov groups of bounded size instead. The theorems push rank analogues of Baer's result from finite p groups to a broad class.
arxiv-2606-24107:
Zhou and colleagues generate short dramas from written plots, with proper camera craft. Short dramas are the fast-cut vertical serials popular on phones. Generic video tools handle single prompts well but stumble over fast shot rhythms, dialogue-driven focus shifts, and steady camera work. Their 2026 framework, DramaDirector, gives the planner real geometry to copy: a gallery of genuine short-drama shots, sorted by depth and pose.

Each shot is split into static visual conditions and dynamic narrative conditions, which keeps look and story apart. Training mixes supervised fine-tuning under a strict schema with reinforcement learning guided by a learned text-visual reward. Retrieved depth-and-pose references then steer first-frame generation and image-to-video synthesis. The team also releases DramaBoard, a benchmark from dozens of live dramas and tens of thousands of shots. Tests put DramaDirector ahead of rival systems on faithfulness and consistency.
arxiv-2606-24207:
Ouyang, Pan, and He bring quasi-Monte Carlo sampling to the simulation of stochastic differential equations. They sit behind finance and physics models. Quasi-Monte Carlo replaces random sampling points with carefully even low-discrepancy sequences. Their 2026 analysis first proves rigorous error bounds for the method paired with the Euler-Maruyama scheme, the standard stepping method. Sampling error decays faster than under classical Monte Carlo.

The catch is dimension. Euler-Maruyama's slow error decay demands many time steps, inflating the integration dimension quasi-Monte Carlo must handle. A Multilevel Stochastic Time Grid method, built on exact simulation techniques, answers that problem. The authors prove it keeps the fast sampling convergence under randomised quasi-Monte Carlo. Its truncation error decays extremely fast, so a target accuracy needs far fewer steps. Ouyang's team concludes the pairing delivers accuracy at a drastically reduced effective dimension.
arxiv-2606-24507:
Kiermeyer and colleagues train one neural network to design quantum control pulses for a whole family of situations. Adaptive quantum control needs robust, high fidelity pulses generated in real time, across constantly varying conditions. Gradient ascent pulse engineering, the standard optimiser, solves each instance independently, discarding everything learned between runs and paying full restart costs whenever parameters shift.

Model-based reinforcement learning replaces per instance work. A single network, with the system's Hamiltonian embedded in its training pipeline, generates robust gates across gate setups, with no precomputed training data. Demonstrated on a single spin, the trained networks produce pulses for any rotation angle, across durations, detunings, and uneven fields, within milliseconds. Scores match multi seed runs of the standard optimiser. Any setting entering the Hamiltonian can become a network input, extending the approach across systems. Kiermeyer's 2026 framework also reads the trained network for latent structure inside good pulse sequences.
arxiv-2606-24707:
Júlio Araújo and four colleagues work on convexity in oriented graphs. A convexity space pairs a set with a family of subsets called convex, closed under intersections and nested unions. A convexity is geometric when every convex set is the hull of its extreme points. The authors study two convexities built from directed paths on three vertices. In one, a set is convex if no outside vertex centres a directed path with endpoints inside. A starred variant adds a condition on arcs.

Araújo and colleagues give exact conditions on the graph for each convexity to be geometric. For the first convexity, the conditions yield a polynomial time test for geometricity. For the starred one, they prove the same decision problem is coNP hard in general. They then define a family called acyclic indifference oriented graphs. On that family, the starred decision problem becomes polynomial time again.
arxiv-2606-24807:
V. Ashley Villar, Sebastian Gomez, Edo Berger, and Alex Gagliano test whether a supernova's host galaxy helps classify the explosion from light alone. The Vera Rubin Observatory will discover supernovae far faster than spectrographs can follow them up. Photometric classifiers must therefore sort events in real time and for archives. Most use light curves, sometimes with redshift. This study asks what observable host galaxy traits add. Hierarchical class labels, respecting the family tree of supernova types, structure the task.

Host galaxy information alone isolates fairly pure samples of Type Ia supernovae, above ninety percent purity, with or without redshift. With redshift, samples of Type II and superluminous supernovae pass seventy percent purity. When full light curves are present, host traits add little accuracy if redshift is known. Without redshift, they raise classification accuracy significantly. The team also introduces a weighted hierarchical cross entropy loss for the task.
arxiv-2606-25107:
Phone based health programs can send prompts at just the right moment, adapting to a person's changing state. Jack Wolf, Nandita Mitra, and Ashkan Ertefaie address a hard statistics problem behind such programs in 2026. The goal is learning the best prompting policy when success is judged by a final, end of study outcome. Dozens of decision points per person make older estimators unstable and biased. Their answer is an estimator that makes no rigid shape assumptions about the data.

Wolf and his co-authors build a curve that shows the expected final outcome under a whole family of random prompting policies. A data driven tilting step steadies the estimates when decision points pile up. They prove the curve settles into a predictable pattern, which allows confidence bands and honest inference about which policy is best.
arxiv-2606-26107:
Jatin Bhusal and Salma Tamang present a pilot system that turns spoken Nepali words into emotional sign language avatars. Sign systems rarely carry emotional expression, and low-resource languages get the least attention. Their framework, NEST-V1, targets Nepali Sign Language. Four common words anchor the pilot: thank you, hello, house, and me. Each appears in happy, neutral, and sad forms.

One shared acoustic encoder does double duty. It recognizes the spoken word and classifies its emotion at the same time. Six hundred labelled clips from fifty speakers form the dataset. Speech recognition accuracy lands near eighty-one percent. Emotion recognition lands near seventy-nine percent. The shared design uses about a third fewer parameters than separate models would. The whole system holds just over twenty-two million parameters, light enough for edge devices. The pilot stakes out a path toward real-time, emotionally expressive signing tools for deaf communities.
arxiv-2606-26707:
Christian Scano and seven colleagues present DroidBreaker, an attack framework against machine-learning Android malware detectors. Attackers modify malicious apps to evade detectors while keeping them working. The authors first show existing attacks are largely impractical. Transplanting whole benign modules bloats apps and breaks builds. Fine-grained tricks are weak, and obfuscation often leaves apps unusable despite passing shallow smoke tests.

DroidBreaker manipulates only the app components the target model weighs most. Attacks work in white-box and black-box settings and use few queries. The manipulations are fine-grained and build-safe by design. The framework checks that modified apps preserve their intended behaviour, not just that they install. The authors argue evaluation must demand working malware, otherwise attack success rates are inflated.
arxiv-2606-26907:
