Population growth and ageing drove much of that rise. Goals for 2020 look out of reach without new approaches. Policy makers get a stark global picture.
europmc-pmc5981007:
Ong and co-authors review inflammation after acute myocardial infarction and its treatment promise. Their review appeared in Pharmacology & Therapeutics. Heart attack and later heart failure kill and disable many people worldwide. The inflammatory response helps set the final infarct size. A response that drags on can harm heart reshaping afterwards. That makes inflammation a key target for new therapies.

The review maps the many players in this response. Their roles shift as healing proceeds day by day. The authors highlight fresh chances to aim drugs at inflammation. Goals include smaller infarcts and less adverse reshaping. Better outcomes for heart attack patients frame the survey.
europmc-pmc6030107:
Wang and co-authors report a new colistin resistance gene. Their research article appeared in Emerging Microbes and Infections. Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic for tough infections. Mobile resistance genes can spread that trait between bacteria. Seven such genes were known before this work.

The new gene, mcr-8, sits on a transferable plasmid. It was found in Klebsiella pneumoniae from livestock. Adding the gene alone raised colistin resistance sharply. Tests covered both E. coli and Klebsiella hosts. Some isolates also carried a carbapenem resistance gene. A matching gene appeared in a hospital patient isolate. The authors warn the gene has already spread widely. Readers get an alert on a growing public health threat.
europmc-pmc6031707:
Caruso and Poon review vesicles released by dying cells. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Cells release tiny packages called extracellular vesicles. Healthy cell vesicles are already well studied. Vesicles from apoptotic cells got far less attention.

Growing evidence gives these vesicles immune roles. They can carry signals that attract cleanup cells. They also carry antigens from the dying cell. Some loads promote inflammation, others calm it. Viruses can even hijack them to spread infection. The review covers how such vesicles form. It links them to autoimmunity, cancer, and infection. Readers get an entry point to an emerging field. Dying cells, it shows, still shape immune responses.
europmc-pmc6032107:
Atri and co-authors review macrophage polarization in human infection. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Macrophages shift between states as conditions change. One state drives inflammation and attacks microbes. Another calms inflammation and heals tissue.

Animal models suggest two clean, opposed states. Human disease looks messier in practice. Patients often show mixed or shifting profiles. Signals like interleukins and tumor necrosis factor mark each pole. The review covers basic polarization biology first. It then examines infectious and neglected diseases. Leishmaniasis gets special attention as a case study. The authors discuss steering macrophage states as therapy. Readers get a nuanced guide beyond the simple M1 and M2 split.
europmc-pmc6052107:
Yang and co-authors trace crosstalk between liver tumor cells and macrophages. Their research article appeared in Cell Death and Disease. Macrophages inside tumors often help cancer progress. Wnt signals are known to shape liver tumors. Whether tumor Wnt signals reprogram macrophages was unclear.

The team show Wnt signals switch on in maturing macrophages. Blocking a key pathway protein made macrophages fight tumors better. Tumor cells release Wnt signals into their surroundings. Those signals push macrophages toward a tumor-friendly state. The effect runs through a growth gene called c-Myc. Silencing Wnt release in tumor cells slowed growth in mice. Human liver tumor samples matched the pattern. Readers get a target pair for future liver cancer therapy.
europmc-pmc6060507:
Liu and co-authors review FOXO3a, a transcription factor tied to cancer growth. Their review appeared in Molecular Cancer. FOXO3a controls cell death, division, and cycle timing. It also answers stresses like ultraviolet light and oxidation. A web of signals switches it on or off.

Many cancers switch FOXO3a off instead. Mutations or protein trapping in the cytoplasm do the job. Raising its activity in lab studies slows tumor growth and spread. Silencing it removes protection against tumors. The review weighs its roles across breast, liver, colon, and other cancers. Readers get a map of a suppressor that therapy might one day reactivate.
europmc-pmc6082907:
Liu and co-authors map placental cell types at single-cell resolution. Their study appeared in Cell Research. The placenta anchors the fetus and feeds it. How its cell types divide and develop stayed unclear. The team sequenced sorted cells from early human placentas.

New subtypes emerged across known cell groups. Each carried its own gene signature. The study found 102 hormone genes active across subtypes. That points to broad hormone control of fetal growth. It also maps how the mother's body adapts to pregnancy. Differentiation paths now read at single-cell detail. Readers get a baseline for studying miscarriage and preeclampsia.
europmc-pmc6087007:
Liang and co-authors identify a long non-coding RNA that drives ovarian cancer spread. Their research article appeared in Molecular Cancer. The RNA, named PTAR, runs high in the mesenchymal tumor subtype. That subtype spreads through the abdomen. PTAR levels tracked the spread driver ZEB1.

PTAR works by soaking up a microRNA called miR-101. With miR-101 bound, ZEB1 stays switched on. Cells then shift shape and migrate more. Silencing PTAR blunted that shift. It also cut tumor growth and spread in mice. Forcing PTAR up had the mirror effect. Readers get a new three-part axis for blocking metastasis.
europmc-pmc6102907:
Bobb and co-authors release software for studying health effects of exposure mixtures. Their article appeared in Environmental Health. People face many pollutants at once. Their joint effects can bend and interact. A method called Bayesian kernel machine regression handles that tangle.

Use of the method had stalled for lack of tools. The new bkmr package runs in R. It adds plots for high-dimensional response surfaces. A probit version handles yes-no outcomes. A faster approximation cuts runtime sharply. Worked examples come with full code. The method also picks which exposures matter most. Readers get a usable kit for mixture epidemiology.
europmc-pmc6109107:
Cortese and co-authors offer a systematic review and network meta-analysis in The Lancet Psychiatry on drugs for ADHD. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder affects children, teens, and adults. Which drug should come first is still debated. Guidelines do not agree across age groups.

The team gathered double-blind trials that compared seven drugs with each other or with placebo. The drugs include methylphenidate, amphetamines, atomoxetine, and guanfacine. They ranked the drugs by how well they ease symptoms and how well people tolerate them. The rankings are given separately for each age group. The work gives clinicians a head-to-head map where direct trials are scarce.
europmc-pmc6167407:
India State-Level Disease Burden Initiative Cancer Collaborators report a study in The Lancet Oncology on cancer across the states of India. Earlier estimates came from registries and national surveys, but no single systematic picture covered every state. The study forms part of the Global Burden of Disease project.

The team used 42 population-based cancer registries and the nationwide Sample Registration System. They estimated cases, deaths, and disability for 28 cancer types in each state from 1990 to 2016. Lip and oral cavity cancer was the most common cancer in Indian men in 2016. Rates varied several-fold between states. The work gives each state its own cancer profile for planning.
europmc-pmc6180207:
Moulton wrote a review in Frontiers in Immunology on sex hormones in acquired immunity and autoimmune disease. Women mount stronger immune responses to infections and vaccines than men. The price is a far higher rate of autoimmune disease. Why both patterns occur is not clear.

Both the innate and adaptive immune systems carry receptors for sex hormones and answer their cues. The review focuses on estrogen and the adaptive response. Systemic lupus erythematosus, a disease that mostly strikes women, gets special emphasis. Hormone-based treatments, such as the steroid DHEA, are discussed as options. Readers get a compact account of how hormones help explain sex gaps in immunity.
europmc-pmc6194107:
Barra and Fachinetti wrote a review in Nature Communications on the dark side of centromeres. Centromeres are the chromosome regions that ensure the genome is shared faithfully at cell division. They direct the machinery that separates chromosomes and so prevent wrong chromosome numbers. Their structure, though, is a liability.

Centromeric DNA is complex and prone to rearrangement. The review sets out the types of structural abnormalities found there. It explains their causes and their consequences for genome stability. Such aberrations are linked to human diseases, including cancer. Keeping centromeres intact is a hard but vital task for the cell. The authors show how a guardian of order can also seed disorder.
europmc-pmc6202307:
Foroozandeh and Aziz wrote a review on how cells take in tiny particles. Such particles are used to carry drugs and genes. They can also harm cells if they enter the wrong way. The review appeared in Nanoscale Research Letters. It covers work on uptake paths and cell routes.

The review sets out the main entry paths cells use. It then tracks where particles travel once inside. Size, shape, charge, and surface traits shape which path is used. Those traits also shape later fate and harm. The authors argue that this knowledge helps design safer particles. Good design can send a drug to the right cell part with less harm.
europmc-pmc6237607:
Huang reviews a three-part RNA control axis in heart disease. Long noncoding RNAs do not code for proteins. MicroRNAs are short RNAs that block protein messages. Their interplay shapes many body processes. The review appeared in the Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine.

Both RNA types link closely to heart and vessel disease. Links include heart remodelling, heart failure, and rhythm faults. They can serve as markers or drug targets. New evidence shows the three RNA types talk to each other. Long RNAs can sponge up microRNAs. That frees the messages those microRNAs would block. The author sums up this crosstalk in disease. The axis may explain how stress triggers heart pathology.
europmc-pmc6305407:
Bachiller and co-authors review how microglia respond in brain diseases. The review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. Microglia are the brain's resident immune sentinels. They shape synapses, clear debris, and support neurons. Their response changes with each disease setting. Age, region, and cell neighbors all shape that response.

The authors trace microglial behavior across disorders. Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases feature in the survey. Frontotemporal dementia is covered too. Inflammation can protect the brain or harm it. Which path dominates depends on context. The review offers a road map of these shifts. It aims to guide disease-specific treatment ideas.
europmc-pmc6321407:
Antimisiaris and co-authors review exosomes and copycat vesicles for drug delivery. The review appeared in Pharmaceutics. Natural exosomes home to certain organs with striking precision. That trait inspires engineers who design drug carriers. Some teams load real exosomes with drugs. Others build liposome mimics with like traits.

The authors survey the approaches tried so far. Each route has clear shortcomings. Loading, targeting, and scale-up all pose problems. Cell-derived vesicles vary from batch to batch. Man-made versions may lack key cell signals. The review closes with the field's main challenges. It serves readers who design new drug carriers.
europmc-pmc6381007:
Sorokowski and co-authors present a meta-analysis in Frontiers in Psychology on sex differences in smell. Many people assume women smell better than men. Some large studies, though, found the two sexes about equal.

Pooling past studies, the team tested three skills: threshold, discrimination, and naming smells. Samples ran into the thousands for each skill. Women scored slightly higher on most tests, but the gaps were small. The authors weigh test type and age as parts of the story. Their result tempers a common belief with measured effect sizes.
europmc-pmc6384907:
Warren and co-authors review the BCL-2 protein family in Cell Death and Disease. These proteins control apoptosis, the orderly death of cells. First found through a blood cancer in the 1980s, the family now has many members.

Members fall into three groups: those that block death, and two groups that drive it. Short forms of the same protein can act in opposed ways. Their settings shift by cell type and stress type. The review sorts these isoforms and their cancer links. That detail matters because many cancer drugs aim at this family.
europmc-pmc6396507:
Zou and co-authors report a mouse study in Translational Neurodegeneration on Parkinson's disease. Clumps of alpha-synuclein protein build up in the Parkinson's brain. Brain drainage systems, including vessels in the meninges, help clear such proteins.

The team blocked drainage at neck lymph nodes in mice that overproduce a mutant form of the protein. Blocked mice cleared fluid tracers more slowly. Protein clumps and Parkinson-like signs grew worse over six weeks. The work suggests that keeping brain drainage open matters in this disease. It frames drainage as a possible treatment target.
europmc-pmc6412907:
Lisio and co-authors review high-grade serous ovarian cancer in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Ovarian cancer is the most often fatal cancer of the female reproductive tract. Death rates for it have barely moved since about 1980.

This subtype accounts for a large share of those deaths. It is one of many distinct ovarian cancers sharing one site, they stress. The review covers its basic biology and how that biology shapes behavior in patients. It then surveys current treatment standpoints. Better grasp of the disease's roots is where progress must start, they argue.
europmc-pmc6422907:
Fogaca and Duman review GABA dysfunction in stress and depression, in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. Major depression alters brain circuits in the prefrontal cortex, often after chronic stress. The old account blamed low monoamine signals, but proof has shifted.

Patients and stressed animals show low GABA, the brain's main calming signal. Markers of the interneurons that release it also fall. That leaves excitatory cells under-checked, the authors argue. The review covers receptor changes and genetic models that back this view. It points to restoring inhibition as a treatment direction beyond older drugs.
europmc-pmc6427007:
Scorrano and co-authors, writing as a panel of specialists, set out shared definitions for membrane contact sites, the close meeting points where organelles exchange materials inside cells. Researchers had described such contacts for decades, but the young field used conflicting terms and measures. A common vocabulary was needed before results could be compared cleanly.

Working rules cover how to define a contact site, how to measure the gap between membranes, and how to judge experiments that claim one. Method notes weigh tools from electron microscopy to FRET-based reporters, each with strengths and traps. For cell biologists, the statement offers a reference point that should make future contact-site claims easier to test and dispute.
europmc-pmc6562607:
Doss and Sachinidis take stock of induced pluripotent stem cells a decade into the field, writing in Cells. Reprogrammed from a patient's own skin or blood cells, iPSCs can become almost any cell type. They have exposed the cellular mechanics of many single-gene diseases, powered drug screens and safety tests, and grown into organoids and organs-on-chips. The first trials of iPSC-derived cell products are under way.

Yet the review's stress falls on what still blocks the clinic. Turning lab promise into safe, standard, reproducible therapy runs into stubborn problems of cell quality, consistency and risk that the field has not solved. The authors map those challenges and what must change before regenerative medicine can rely on these cells at scale.
europmc-pmc6602507:
Zhou and co-authors present NetworkAnalyst 3.0, a web platform for gene expression data. Their article appears in Nucleic Acids Research. The platform reads expression data through the lens of interaction networks. It first appeared in 2014 and has grown with user feedback. The public server runs over 220,000 jobs per year.

Version 3.0 supports gene expression profiling for 17 species. Users can build tissue-specific protein networks and gene regulatory networks. Co-expression networks serve toxicology and drug studies. Networks can be explored in 2D, 3D, or virtual reality. Meta-analysis views include heatmaps, Venn diagrams, and chord diagrams. Users can save projects and resume them later. The platform stays free online.
europmc-pmc6653007:
Xu and co-authors review the molecular mechanisms of ferroptosis and its promise for cancer therapy. Their review appears in the Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine. Ferroptosis is a form of programmed cell death. It is driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxides. The term dates to 2012 and the Stockwell laboratory. Small molecules like erastin and RSL3 can trigger it. Cysteine supply sits at the pathway's heart. Blocking cystine import drains glutathione from cells. That disables the protective enzyme GPx4.

Lipid damage then runs unchecked until death. Cancers differ widely in ferroptosis sensitivity. The review maps inducers, pathways, and organelle roles. It also weighs ferroptosis against drug resistance. Open questions close the survey.
europmc-pmc6685307:
Seyedian, Nokhostin, and Malamir review the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of inflammatory bowel disease. Their review appears in the Journal of Medicine and Life. The disease splits into ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. Both cause chronic digestive inflammation. Their causes remain incompletely understood. Genetics, diet, geography, and immune responses all contribute. Symptoms overlap heavily between the two forms. Crohn's can strike anywhere along the gut. It affects all layers of the bowel wall. Colitis stays within the colon's mucosal layer.

Diagnosis combines clinical, endoscopic, histologic, and radiological tests. About a tenth of cases defy clear classification. Treatment aims at control rather than cure. The review surveys newer methods for patients.
europmc-pmc6835707:
Giordano and Tommonaro review curcumin and cancer in the journal Nutrients. Curcumin is the yellow polyphenol in turmeric, first extracted from the plant Curcuma longa in 1815. It draws interest for many effects, from calming inflammation to fighting microbes. Its promise against cancer is the most studied claim of all.

The review traces the cell pathways curcumin touches. It can adjust growth factors, enzymes, and the proteins that decide whether a cell lives or dies. In lab work it slows cancer cell growth through several of these routes at once. Poor absorption in the body remains a problem. The authors discuss analogues and combinations meant to fix that weakness.
europmc-pmc6899507:
The GBD 2017 Diet Collaborators measure the health cost of poor diet in The Lancet. Diet is a preventable driver of non-communicable disease, yet its total burden had never been systematically tallied. The team estimated what adults aged 25 years and older actually ate in 195 countries. They then linked shortfalls and excesses to deaths and disability from 1990 to 2017.

Low intake of nuts and seeds ranked first among dietary risks for deaths in most large countries. Whole grains and fruits also fell far short of the levels tied to lowest risk. High red meat, processed meat, and sugary drinks sat near the bottom of the risk ranking. Rates were worst in lower-middle income countries.
europmc-pmc6913007:
Ou and co-authors benchmark tools that annotate jumping genes, in Genome Biology. Transposable elements are DNA stretches that copy or move themselves around genomes. In large, repetitive genomes they are everywhere, and modern assemblies finally span them. Dozens of annotation programs exist, each aimed at one element class, but they had never been compared head to head.

The team tested the field against a hand-curated library of rice elements. The best tools kept sensitivity near 95 percent, with accuracy reaching 86 percent after filtering. Combining the winners, their pipeline annotated 7.3 percent of the rice genome as such elements. The library alone had covered only 3.6 percent. The pipeline is offered for species lacking such a resource.
europmc-pmc6918207:
Paranjape and co-authors argue that medical training must teach artificial intelligence. Their article appeared in JMIR Medical Education. Care is changing fast as data tools enter daily practice. Doctors will need to work well alongside machines. They must know what these tools do well, and where they fall short.

Shortfalls include unclear reasoning and questions of liability. Gains could include lower cost, better quality, and wider access to care. The authors propose weaving AI across the whole curriculum, not adding it as one side course. They set out a framework for that change. Training, they argue, should continue after graduation, for students and senior doctors alike.
europmc-pmc7007907:
Ramón y Cajal and co-authors review the mixed cell populations inside single tumours and what they mean for treatment. Their review appeared in the Journal of Molecular Medicine. No tumour is uniform. Cells within one specimen differ in genes, chemical marks, proteins, and behaviour.

That variety arises as mutations and other changes are selected under pressure from the surroundings, including low oxygen and chemotherapy itself. Clones cooperate, compete, and sometimes slip through treatment that kills their neighbours. The result is a Darwinian contest between tumour cell populations and their environment. Understanding this mix is hard, but it may explain why therapies fail when resistant cells survive. The authors survey the drivers and consequences of the diversity. Liquid biopsies and machine intelligence appear among the tools they discuss for tracking it and designing smarter attacks.
europmc-pmc7010707:
Yim and Mizushima review how lysosomes behave during autophagy, the cell's self-eating system. Their review appeared in Cell Discovery. Autophagy delivers worn cell material to lysosomes, acidic bags of enzymes that digest it. The best-known form wraps cargo in a double membrane first; two other forms act right at the lysosome surface.

Lysosomes do more than digest. They help switch autophagy on and off, and damaged lysosomes become cargo themselves. During autophagy they grow more acidic, boost their enzymes, and cluster near the nucleus. New lysosomes bud off spent ones through tubules and regain strength. The starvation sensor mTORC1 sits on the lysosome when food is plentiful and leaves to trigger recycling when it is not. Many details of this organelle's own regulation remain scarce. The review maps what is known and names the open questions worth chasing.
europmc-pmc7018807:
Chen and co-authors present a chemistry study in Scientific Reports. They examine 18 common phenolic acids, plant compounds known as antioxidants. Their question is structural. Which parts of each molecule, such as methoxy, hydroxyl, and acid groups, make the antioxidant effect stronger or weaker?

The team measured activity with two standard lab tests, DPPH and FRAP. They also ran density functional theory calculations for five energy values. Those values map onto three ways a molecule can neutralise free radicals. The authors report that certain acid side chains and added methoxy or hydroxyl groups raise activity. They argue that one reaction route, SPLET, best explains the results in water. The findings link molecular shape to measured antioxidant strength.
europmc-pmc7054407:
Hu and co-authors study the lymphatic vessels of the meninges in brain tumours for Cell Research. Meningeal lymphatic vessels drain fluid and carry immune cells from the central nervous system to cervical lymph nodes. Their part in brain tumour drainage and immunity was unexplored. The team examined these vessels in mice bearing gliomas or metastatic melanomas inside the skull.

The dorsal vessels remodelled extensively as tumours grew. Gene activity in their lining cells shifted toward drainage, inflammation, and immune functions. Disrupting the dorsal vessels impaired fluid drainage from tumours and reduced both cancer cell spread and dendritic cell traffic to deep cervical lymph nodes. Boosting vessel growth had the opposite effect. Most strikingly, broken dorsal vessels cut the benefit of combined anti-PD-1 and CTLA-4 checkpoint therapy, while tumours overproducing VEGF-C, a vessel growth factor, responded better. Drainage routes, it seems, help immunotherapy reach brain tumours.
europmc-pmc7059907:
Reynolds, Akerman, and Mann review dietary fibre and whole grains in diabetes care in PLOS Medicine. Fibre is promoted in healthy diets and in diabetes management, but its effect on death rates and blood sugar control needed a fresh accounting. The team systematically gathered prospective studies and controlled trials in adults with prediabetes or diabetes, changing fibre intake without other lifestyle changes.

Two multicountry cohorts following 8,300 adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes for an average of 8.8 years linked higher fibre diets to fewer deaths: an absolute reduction of 14 deaths per 1,000 participants. Forty-two trials with 1,789 adults showed that raising fibre improved blood sugar control and several heart and metabolic risk factors. Dose-response analysis and evidence grading supported the conclusions. The authors argue fibre deserves a firmer place in diabetes guidance.
europmc-pmc7080807:
Tang and co-authors sequence full-length transcripts in leukaemia in Nature Communications. Mutations in the splicing factor SF3B1 are a known feature of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and change how genes are spliced. Short-read sequencing sees splicing events one at a time; it cannot tell which changes travel together in one message. Nanopore sequencing reads whole transcripts end to end.

The team sequenced full-length cDNA from leukaemia samples with and without the SF3B1 mutation, plus normal B cells, gathering 149 million pass reads. Their workflow, FLAIR, identifies high-confidence transcripts and runs splicing and isoform analyses. Results confirmed the known shift in 3 prime splice site use tied to the mutation, and revealed a strong downregulation of retained introns. Linking events within single molecules let the authors weigh productive against unproductive isoforms. The study backs long-read sequencing for cancer and splicing research.
europmc-pmc7085407:
Rius-Pérez and co-authors review PGC-1α, a protein that links energy use, oxidative stress, and inflammation, in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. PGC-1α helps build mitochondria, the cell's power stations, and is strongest in tissues with high energy needs. Its failure is tied to metabolic syndrome and its complications.

The protein turns on antioxidant genes that keep reactive oxygen in check. When its levels fall during inflammation, oxidative stress rises and inflammatory signalling grows stronger. In metabolic syndrome, the same failure distorts how tissues handle energy. The authors present PGC-1α as a meeting point of these systems and a possible target for treating metabolic diseases.
europmc-pmc7105007:
Thompson and co-authors present a better way to estimate how fast an outbreak spreads while it is still unfolding, in Epidemics. The reproduction number, the average count of new cases each case causes, guides control decisions. Their framework uses up-to-date serial interval data and accounts for cases imported from elsewhere.

The method is demonstrated on past outbreaks of influenza, Ebola, and MERS. It is released as the R package EpiEstim and an online app, so response teams can use it directly. Poor estimates can mislead policy, the authors argue, and timing gaps between linked cases are often recorded badly. Their approach aims to give decision-makers numbers they can trust in real time.
europmc-pmc7156507:
Goldsack and co-authors propose a shared framework for judging digital health sensors, called V3, in NPJ Digital Medicine. Wearables and phone sensors now measure bodies in drug trials, but terms and standards differ between engineers, doctors, and regulators. Their framework splits the judging into three steps.

Verification asks whether the sensor reads its raw signal correctly. Analytical validation asks whether its software turns that signal into accurate values, checked against trusted standards. Clinical validation asks whether the measure means something real for patients. The authors aim to give the whole field one shared language, so evidence for these tools can be compared and trusted across studies and settings.
europmc-pmc7166207:
Borgström and co-authors report the burden and management of fragility fractures across six European countries for the International Osteoporosis Foundation, in Archives of Osteoporosis. Fragility fractures, breaks from minor falls in weakened bone, are the main harm of osteoporosis. The report covers the five largest EU countries plus Sweden.

In 2017 the six countries saw an estimated 2.7 million new fragility fractures, costing 37.5 billion euros and losing 1.0 million quality-adjusted life years. Fractures are projected to rise 23% by 2030, to 3.3 million, with costs up 27%. Disability burden per head exceeded that of stroke or chronic lung disease. A wide treatment gap, patients left without bone protection after a first break, is flagged as the clearest opportunity.
europmc-pmc7199907:
Lamers and co-authors show that SARS-CoV-2 can infect human gut cells and multiply there. Their study appeared in Science. COVID-19 was seen mainly as a lung disease spread through the air. Yet patients often had gut symptoms too. The virus's entry protein, ACE2, is abundant on intestinal cells.

The team grew mini-guts called organoids from human small intestine. Enterocytes in these organoids were readily infected by both SARS viruses. Microscopy confirmed the virus inside the cells. Large amounts of new infectious virus were released. The findings make the intestine a second target organ. They also raise questions about fecal spread and gut symptoms. Gut models may help test future treatments.
europmc-pmc7205607:
Chen and co-authors test erianin, a natural compound from an orchid extract, against lung cancer cells. Their study appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Erianin comes from Dendrobium chrysotoxum, a plant used in traditional remedies. Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death, is a promising cancer target. The team asked whether erianin could trigger it.

Erianin killed lung cancer cells and slowed their migration in lab tests. The death took the ferroptosis route, driven by iron and fat oxidation. Calcium signaling through calmodulin proved essential to the process. Blocking that signal weakened the compound's effect. Iron and reactive oxygen built up inside the cells. The study names a new candidate for ferroptosis-based therapy. It also maps how the compound forces cancer cells to die.
europmc-pmc7222307:
Martínez-Sáez and co-authors map how often PIK3CA mutations occur in breast cancer and what forms they take. Their study appeared in Breast Cancer Research. A mutation test and a matching drug, alpelisib, are approved for advanced cases. Clinicians rely on the test to pick patients for the drug. How many mutations the test misses was unknown.

The team pooled data from 6,338 patients across 10 public studies. They charted the full spread of PIK3CA mutations found. Some tumors carried two or more mutations. The approved test detects only a defined set of them. Computer analysis estimated what share of real mutations fall outside that set. The results matter for patients told their tumor is mutation-free. A negative result may sometimes be a test limit, not biology.
europmc-pmc7228407:
Guo and co-authors test whether diabetes worsens the course of COVID-19. Their study appeared in Diabetes/Metabolism Research and Reviews. They studied 174 consecutive confirmed patients. Of these, 24 had diabetes but no other major illnesses. That clean comparison isolates diabetes itself as a factor.

Patients with diabetes faced higher risk of severe pneumonia. Their blood showed more tissue injury enzymes and stronger inflammation. Clotting ran high, tied to disturbed sugar control. Lymphocyte counts and hemoglobin ran lower than in other patients. The authors conclude diabetes contributes to poorer outcomes. They argue such patients need closer monitoring from admission. The study was among the early ones to separate diabetes from general frailty.
europmc-pmc7251107:
Hong and co-authors report a first-in-human phase 1 trial of MRX34, a fat-particle copy of a natural microRNA, in patients with advanced solid tumors. Their study appeared in the British Journal of Cancer. MicroRNA-34a normally helps control gene activity, and its loss is linked to cancer. Patients had tumors that no longer responded to standard treatment.

Eighty-five patients joined dose-escalation and expansion groups. Common side effects included fever, chills, fatigue, and nausea. Blood tests showed the drug reached tumors and changed target gene activity in a dose-dependent way. Three patients had partial responses and 16 had stable disease for at least 4 cycles. The trial closed early after serious immune-related side effects caused four patient deaths, though the authors saw proof that microRNA therapy can work.
europmc-pmc7280307:
Zheng, Liwinski and Elinav review how inflammasomes are switched on, kept in check, and turned into drug targets. Their review appeared in Cell Discovery. Inflammasomes are protein complexes inside cells that sense danger, from invading microbes to the body's own damage signals. Once assembled, they release inflammatory messengers and can kill the cell.

Proper activation defends against infection and injury. Runaway activation feeds diseases ranging from autoinflammatory disorders to heart and metabolic disease, cancer, and brain degeneration. Cells therefore regulate assembly tightly at many steps. The authors summarize recent work on how these complexes are ordered, how stimuli trigger them, and where regulation fails. They also judge efforts to turn that knowledge into medicines.
europmc-pmc7296907:
Pons and co-authors argue that damage to the vascular endothelium is the cornerstone of organ failure in severe COVID-19. Their review appeared in Critical Care. Tissue studies found the virus infecting endothelial cells directly, with widespread inflammation of vessel linings and clots in both veins and arteries.

Blood clotting events, especially lung embolism, are common in these patients, alongside raised D-dimer and activated coagulation. The cytokine storm, with high interleukin-6 and related signals, likely adds to vessel dysfunction and draws immune cells into small vessels. The authors review trials aimed at this damage, from blocking viral entry and clotting to calming the immune response, and call for more studies focused on the endothelium.
europmc-pmc7310007:
Jiang and co-authors review the cGAS-STING pathway, a DNA-sensing alarm inside cells, as a tool for cancer immunotherapy. Their review appeared in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. When stray DNA appears in a cell's fluid, this pathway fires, producing interferons and priming T cells to attack. Drugs that activate STING have shown strong results in preclinical cancer work.

Combinations look most promising: STING activators given with cancer vaccines, checkpoint inhibitor antibodies, or transferred T cells could treat medium and advanced cancers that resist single therapies. Obstacles remain, from dosing to delivery and side effects. The authors examine the pathway's biology, current applications, and what must be solved before STING-based treatment becomes routine in the clinic.
europmc-pmc7331607:
Chou and co-authors study osteoarthritis in Scientific Reports by listening in on joint tissue cross-talk. They used single-cell RNA sequencing, which reads gene activity cell by cell, on matched cartilage and synovium samples. The method profiled 10,640 synovial cells and 26,192 cartilage cells.

They sort the cells into 12 synovial types and 7 cartilage cell types. Healthy cartilage held more steady-state and growth-plate-like cells, while damaged cartilage held more repair and fiber-forming types. Dozens of signal proteins from synovial cells appear to steer the cartilage cells, and the signals show up in joint fluid. Inflammatory macrophages emerge as a key source of IL-1beta, a known driver of the disease.
europmc-pmc7350507:
Zhang and co-authors sort COVID-19 patients by immune pattern in Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences, using records from one center in Wuhan. They studied 222 patients and tracked antibody IgG levels alongside the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, a simple blood count balance. The question was whether a strong antibody response signals worse disease.

IgG appeared from day 4 of illness and peaked in the fourth week. Combining the two measures gave four patient types. Those high on both were severe in 72.3 percent of cases and recovered slowest, while those low on both were severe only 15.6 percent of the time. All deaths fell in the high-ratio groups. A strong late antibody response, they conclude, tracks deterioration rather than protection.
europmc-pmc7616807:
Romanello and co-authors also authored the 2021 Countdown report, subtitled code red for a healthy future. It landed in the year of the COP26 climate talks. Nations faced pressure to honor the Paris Agreement goals.

This edition rests on 44 indicators of climate and health. Consensus came from 43 academic bodies and UN agencies. Heat exposure hit new highs in the 2020 data. Older adults saw 3.1 billion more heatwave person-days. Infants saw 626 million more such days that year. The baseline was the 1986–2005 annual average. Record heat struck the Pacific Northwest in June that year. Hundreds died early from that heat event. The report urges faster action to protect health worldwide.
europmc-pmc7674007:
Volz and co-authors test whether a spike change helps SARS-CoV-2 spread. The change, called D614G, rose fast around the world. That rise could mean the variant spreads better, or it could be chance from early seeding. The team focused on the United Kingdom.

They used more than 25,000 viral genomes from the UK. Gene-based tests fit a true edge for the G form over the D form. Patients with the G form carried more virus and tended to be younger. Yet they were no more likely to die or to be gravely ill. Growth of G clusters still varied, so the authors urge ongoing study.
europmc-pmc7704107:
Buccino and co-authors build a shared frame for sorting brain spike data. Spike sorting picks out the firing of single neurons from electrode traces. Many software tools exist for this task, but they clash with each other. That makes fair tests and repeat results hard to get.

The Python framework, SpikeInterface, wraps most modern sorters in one codebase. With a few lines of code, users can run and compare sorters side by side. They can also clean data, view results, check quality, and export the output. Tests on real and fake data show how it cuts hand curation. The authors aim to make spike sorting more open and sound.
europmc-pmc7723407:
Weisblum and co-authors test how easily SARS-CoV-2 can escape neutralizing antibodies. Antibodies from infection or vaccines are a key defense. Given ones are also a leading therapy. The team used a hybrid reporter virus that carries the SARS-CoV-2 spike. They grew it under antibody pressure to see what changes arise.

Variants with spike changes that resist single antibodies or patient plasma arose with ease. Some changes sat in the receptor-binding domain, others in the front domain. Such resistant variants already drift at low levels in virus now in circulation. The authors show that antibody mixes aimed at distinct sites can block this escape route and keep therapy useful.
europmc-pmc7779007:
Tweedie and co-authors describe the gene naming resources at genenames.org in 2021. The HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee, or HGNC, assigns unique symbols and names to human genes. Its partner group, the VGNC, does the same for other vertebrates that lack their own committee.

The HGNC database holds over 42,000 approved gene symbols. Over 19 000 of these mark protein-coding genes. More than 2,000 symbols for disease-linked genes are now marked as stable. The VGNC core species grew beyond chimpanzee, cow, horse, and dog. Cat, macaque, and pig are now included. Gene groups now cover olfactory receptors and cytochrome P450s. Both resources publish all data freely on their websites.
europmc-pmc7884707:
Zhou and co-authors present a review of cancer stem cells and resistance to therapy. Cancer stem cells can renew themselves and seed new tumour growth. Those traits help tumours survive treatment and come back. The review gathers what is known about how the resistance works.

The authors cover how these cells are identified in different tumours. They explain resistance that is built into the cells and resistance that comes from their surroundings. Key signalling pathways that let the cells ride out treatment are set out in turn. The review then surveys drugs and other agents aimed at these cells, from a clinical angle. It aims to guide new drug searches and better treatment plans. Readers see both the biology and the practical options.
europmc-pmc7967607:
Jones and co-authors present a systematic review of the COVID-19 pandemic's effect on adolescent mental health. Hard data on this group were scarce early in the crisis. The review follows standard guidelines for such work. It gathers quantitative studies run during the first two years of the pandemic, from schools and clinics across many countries and backgrounds.

The review covers 16 studies with 40,076 participants. Teens showed higher rates of anxiety, depression, and stress than before the pandemic. Use of alcohol and cannabis also rose in this group. Some factors softened the blow. Social support, sound coping skills, and talks between parents and children all helped. Home quarantine itself showed some protective sides. The authors urge schools and services to use every resource on hand. The harm is real, but so are the buffers.
europmc-pmc8012207:
Eze and co-authors build a single-cell atlas of the early human brain. The human cortex grows from a uniform sheet of neuroepithelial cells. Those cells give rise to radial glia, the cortex's stem cells. The team sequenced single-cell RNA across five brain regions: telencephalon, diencephalon, midbrain, hindbrain, and cerebellum. The goal was to catch the first cell types as they emerge.

The authors identify nine progenitor populations near the telencephalon. That is more variety than earlier work described. One common mesenchymal-like population vanishes once neuron production begins. Two progenitor clusters look enriched in early human development compared with mouse. Brain organoids matched the real tissue poorly at these stages. Fidelity improved as neurogenesis advanced.
europmc-pmc8078907:
Monin and co-authors test how well one or two vaccine doses protect patients with cancer. The Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine's record in such patients was unknown. The team recruited from three London hospitals starting in December 2020. The cohort held 151 patients with cancer and 54 healthy controls. Blood was drawn before dosing and at set weeks after.

Three weeks after one dose, 94% of healthy controls had anti-spike antibodies. Only 38% of patients with solid cancers reached that mark. Patients with blood cancers fared worst, at 18% after the single dose. A second dose at day 21 lifted responses in those who got it. Safety signals stayed in line with the general population. The interim results argue against long dose delays for cancer patients. Their weak first response needs the prompt boost.
europmc-pmc8185607:
Kompaniyets and co-authors ask which health conditions track with severe COVID-19 in children. Their cross-sectional study held 43,465 patients aged 18 years or younger. More than one quarter had at least one underlying condition.

Asthma, obesity, and neurodevelopmental disorders were among the most common conditions. Certain mental health conditions also appeared often. Some conditions, and medical complexity in general, tied to higher risk of severe illness. The findings widen what clinicians know about risk in young patients. They can guide prevention work and care planning for children. Their findings expand knowledge of COVID-19 in children.
europmc-pmc8189907:
Warnat-Herresthal and co-authors introduce Swarm Learning for private clinical machine learning. Machine learning can spot severe disease in blood data. Privacy law, though, blocks pooling patient data in one place.

Swarm Learning trains models where the data sit, with no central coordinator. It links owners through a blockchain-based peer network. Only model updates move, not patient records. The team shows the method at work on clinical tasks such as leukaemia detection. It goes beyond federated learning by dropping the central server. Hospitals worldwide could join one model while keeping data at home.
europmc-pmc8385107:
Liu and co-authors show how faulty cholesterol balance helps cancer cells resist a form of cell death. High cholesterol and lipid disorders link to higher cancer risk and worse outcomes. The team focused on 27-hydroxycholesterol, a common cholesterol breakdown product in blood.

Long exposure to this compound selected for cells that take up and make more lipids. Those cells grew tumors more readily and spread more. The stored lipids forced the cells to keep GPX4 active, a protein that blocks ferroptotic death. Cutting GPX4 weakened their growth and spread. The authors frame ferroptosis resistance as a trait that helps metastatic cells survive.
europmc-pmc8386807:
Patel and co-authors report a multicenter study of mucormycosis linked to COVID-19 in India. This fungal infection rose during the pandemic. The retrospective study ran from September to December 2020 and compared cases with and without COVID-19.

Among 287 mucormycosis patients, 187 had COVID-19-associated disease. Case counts rose sharply compared with the same months in 2019. Uncontrolled diabetes was the most common underlying disease in both groups. In about a third of the COVID-19 cases, COVID-19 was the only underlying disease. Low oxygen from COVID-19 and poor use of glucocorticoid drugs each linked to the infection on their own. Older age, brain involvement, and intensive care raised death risk, while stepwise antifungal treatment improved survival.
europmc-pmc8409907:
Antonelli and co-authors study infections that occur after COVID-19 vaccination in the United Kingdom. Vaccines work well in trials and in real-world data, yet some users still catch the virus. The team used the COVID Symptom Study app to find who stays at risk.

This nested case-control study drew on self-reported data from adult app users. Cases had a positive test at set times after their first or second dose. Controls had negative tests and no prior infection. The authors compared health traits, place, and vaccine timing between groups. They also described how post-vaccination illness looks, to guide care for those still exposed.
europmc-pmc9259607:
Qin and co-authors categorize signaling pathways in ischemic stroke and the therapies that target them. Stroke from blocked blood flow is a leading cause of death and disability. Its biology spans excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, cell death, and inflammation. Many pathways, harmful or protective, weave into one complex network.

The review groups pathways by the process each one joins. For each group, it discusses drugs aimed at that biology. Clinical trials tied to those pathways are summarized in detail. Some target clot removal, while others aim to shield neurons. The authors stress that knowing the network can guide new treatments. Readers get a structured map from molecular events to trial-stage care.
europmc-pmc9261907:
Luo and co-authors systematically review hypoxia signaling in human health and disease. Hypoxia means low oxygen inside cells. Hypoxia-inducible factors sense that drop and switch on many downstream genes. Those genes govern metabolism, growth, immunity, infection response, and tumor spread.

The review covers how the pathway turns on and how it is controlled. It details cross-talk with other major pathways, including PI3K-mTOR and NF-kappaB. Roles in cardiovascular, metabolic, and inflammatory diseases are summed up. Therapeutic targets within the pathway are highlighted in a dedicated section. Such targets may yield drugs that restore balance in low-oxygen states. Readers get a full account of a central oxygen-sensing system.
europmc-pmc9262707:
Sereika and co-authors show that Oxford Nanopore R10.4 long reads can yield near-finished bacterial genomes on their own. Long reads recover highly continuous genomes from cultures and metagenomes. Until now, short-read polishing was needed to fix insertion and deletion errors. Those errors cluster in homopolymer runs.

Tests on a standard mock community told a clear story. Adding short-read polishing did not improve R10.4 assemblies in any real way. Near-finished genomes came from R10.4 data alone at about 40-fold coverage. Better homopolymer calling explains most of the gain over the older R9.4.1 chemistry. The result cuts cost and complexity for microbial genome work. Reference polishing is no longer a required step.
europmc-pmc9337707:
Zou and co-authors extend a genetic fine-mapping model to work from summary data alone. Fine-mapping narrows a disease-linked DNA region to a few likely causal variants. The SuSiE model did this well but needed raw data from each person. Such data are often blocked by consent and privacy limits.

The new variant, SuSiE-RSS, runs on per-variant scores plus correlation values from a reference panel. The team shows rival tools secretly use the same swap of likelihoods. They add checks that flag clashes between the scores and the reference. A refinement step improves fit on some data sets. In simulations the method matched the best rivals in speed and accuracy. That opens fine-mapping to far more studies.
europmc-pmc9674007:
Inoue and co-authors show that a maternal histone mark controls imprinting without DNA methylation in mouse embryos. Sperm and egg carry unlike epigenetic landscapes into the zygote. After fertilization, most marks even out between the parents. Imprinting control regions are the known spots that escape.

The team mapped open chromatin spots by parent in zygotes and morula embryos. They found 76 genes with open spots on the father's copy only. Those spots held no DNA methylation at all. The mother's copy instead wore the mark H3K27me3. The genes were read from the father's copy in early embryos. Stripping the mark away woke the mother's copy up. Most of this imprinting faded in the embryo line proper. At least 5 genes kept it in the outer support lineage. Those genes cover all known methylation-free imprinted cases.
europmc-pmc9885707:
Maalej and co-authors assess CAR cell therapy for solid tumors, a field still facing hard limits. Engineered CAR-T cells work well in blood cancers such as leukemias and lymphomas. Solid tumors resist them through poor trafficking, weak infiltration, and a suppressive tumor setting. Side effects add further risk.

The review sets out two newer options, CAR-NK cells and CAR-macrophages. CAR-NK cells need no HLA match and show limited toxicity. They can also be made at scale as off-the-shelf products. CAR-M cells add phagocytosis, antigen presentation, and broad tumor infiltration. The authors compare gains and drawbacks for each type. They suggest combined treatments to raise the effect of CAR cell therapy.
fbi-vault-special-counsel-mueller-invest: The records freed from the Special Counsel Mueller investigation include this withholding log, release 7, held by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The deleted-page sheet covers Bates pages 2964 to 3263 of the court-ordered release. It counts 89 pages withheld in full. Page after page is marked Referral or Consult: the sheet was sent to another agency for its call. Later pages carry the coded grounds b6 and the b7 family. The part holds no report text. It is the map of what, in this release, a reader may not see.
ferrero-greatness-decline-rome-vol-1-190:
Guglielmo Ferrero's The Greatness and Decline of Rome, Volume 1, appears in Henry J. Zimmern's translation of 1907. Subtitled The Empire-Builders, the volume covers Rome from the Gracchi to Caesar. Ferrero, an Italian historian, reads Caesar's age as modern politics in ancient dress. Parties, finance, and empire drive his story.

He treats the conquests of Gaul and the civil wars with brisk narrative skill. The book was the great popular Roman history of the early 1900s. Scholars faulted some bold guesses, yet readers loved its pace. Ferrero wrote for the educated public across Europe and America. Volume 1 of five opens his lively, disputed epic.
flammarion-mysterious-psychic-forces-190:
Camille Flammarion brought a star man's fame to the dark room in Mysterious Psychic Forces, his book of 1907. Flammarion was the most loved voice on the stars in France. Late in life he turned his keen eye to seers. He sat with Eusapia Palladino, the famed name from Italy, and weighed her feats through long, strict tests in his own rooms.

He grants strange force, yet keeps his doubts in plain view. His rank made the book a mark on the main land. It shows a great mind torn twixt awe and care. Its fame still stands.
ford-privy-seal-1907:
Privy Seal, published in 1907, is the middle volume of Ford's Katharine Howard trilogy, his historical sequence on the fifth wife of Henry VIII. The first volume brought Katharine to court; this one charts the machinery around the throne.

Thomas Cromwell, the king's great minister, falls as factions shift, and Katharine rises toward the crown through a court of spies and suitors. Ford tells Tudor politics as atmosphere and impression rather than pageant. The trilogy was his bid for serious standing as a novelist. Read together, the three books build one of the finest historical sequences in English.
forster-longest-journey-1907:
E. M. Forster published The Longest Journey in 1907, his second novel. Forster later said it was the book of his that he felt closest to. It draws on his Cambridge years and his unease with respectable English life.

Rickie Elliot, a lame and sensitive Cambridge graduate, writes stories and searches for honest connection. He marries into a dull, controlling family and betrays his own gifts. Then a rough half-brother appears, and Rickie must decide what loyalty really means. The story turns tragic as Rickie tries to rescue the brother he first denied. It is Forster's most personal and painful novel.
francke-history-western-tibet-1907:
August Hermann Francke was a Moravian missionary and scholar who lived for years in Ladakh, on India's border with Tibet. His History of Western Tibet, published in 1907, is the pioneering history of that high Himalayan land. Francke read its chronicles, inscriptions, and folk songs at first hand.

He traces the kings of Ladakh from the old Tibetan empire through Buddhist rule to the Dogra conquest of the 1840s. Rock carvings and royal songs fill gaps where written records run thin. The book remains a base source for the history of Ladakh and of Tibetan Buddhism on India's frontier.
freeman-light-of-soul-1907:
Harper published By the Light of the Soul in January 1907, with pictures by Harold Brett. Freeman dedicated the novel to Harriet and Carolyn Alden. Chapter one places young Maria Edgham in a church vestry during the weekly prayer meeting.

A young man reads aloud that God chastens those he loves, and a soft sob answers behind Maria. Mrs. Jasper Cone, who lost her baby the week before, is weeping there. Maria feels spite at the sound, which opens her long inner struggle. The drama stays inward, as conscience, desire, and the claims of others pull a dutiful woman toward a fuller life.
frus-1861-d107:
Gideon Welles, the Secretary of the Navy, received a letter from William H. Seward on 19 October 1861. The letter is document 107 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Most papers in the volume cross the ocean, but this one crosses the cabinet room. The Navy ran the blockade that Britain watched so closely. Seward and Welles had to keep their stories straight, since each naval act could become a diplomatic crisis by the next mail. Welles, a former newsman, kept a famed diary that still ranks beside this record. A famed diary beside a full record gives the Navy's war a double witness.
frus-1861-d207:
On 11 July 1861, Mr. Wood wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 207 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d307:
A letter from Mr. Varas reached Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 August 1861. It stands as Document 307 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Inbound mail like this one showed Washington how the war looked from outside its own posts. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d107:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 18 July 1862. It stands as Document 107 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d207:
Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed Lord Lyons on 6 February 1862 in a note printed as Document 207 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons was the British minister in Washington, the man Seward saw most among foreign envoys.

February brought the Union a bright win with the fall of Fort Henry in Tennessee, news that colored foreign readings of the war. Britain and France both measured their steps by such results. A brief Seward note in this month belongs to the constant traffic between the two offices. Through it Washington argued that the Union would win and should be left to do it.
frus-1862-d307:
The third Seward dispatch of 23 August 1862 stands as Document 307 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Like its mates, it went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris.

Read alone, a third same-day letter looks like a fragment. Read with Documents 305 and 306, it completes the Department's Paris brief for that mail. The habit of judging these papers in clusters, not singly. Is the first skill the Foreign Relations volumes teach, and the August cluster teaches it well. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d407:
Dated 5 August 1862, this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to Horace J. Perry at the legation in Madrid. It stands as Document 407 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official diplomatic record.

Three days after his last order to the same desk, Seward was writing again, a sign of how fast the Spanish questions moved that summer. Confederate agents sought ships, coal, and sympathy in Spanish ports. Union agents worked to shut those doors. The dispatch belongs to that contest, and it shows the steady, almost daily hand Washington kept on its smallest European posts during the Civil War.
frus-1862-d507:
James Shepherd Pike sent this report from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 June 1862. It is Document 507 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Pike wrote on the day the Seven Days battles began in Virginia, though weeks would pass before he knew it. His letter dealt with the Netherlands as he found it that week. He found a careful ministry and a busy press. He also found merchants counting the cost of the war. Reports of this kind look routine, but they were the only eyes Washington had in The Hague. Read in sequence, Pike's dispatches show Dutch opinion holding roughly steady for the Union through the shocks of that summer.
frus-1862-d607:
Thomas Corwin reported from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 August 1862. The dispatch is Document 607 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Corwin wrote from a capital whose government was fighting a French invasion with scant money and men. His late-summer report described the republic's endurance and the French advance as they appeared from Mexico City. Washington, then losing battles of its own, could offer Mexico sympathy and a clear record of protest. Corwin's letters supplied the facts that record required. The dispatch keeps the Mexican file's grave, steady tone through the war's darkest month for both republics.
frus-1862-d707:
James R. Partridge wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 August 1862. Partridge was an American envoy in Central America, a Maryland lawyer sent out by the Lincoln government. The letter is document 707 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Envoys in the small republics reported on local politics, trade, and the transit routes that linked the Atlantic and Pacific. Partridge's letter belongs to that watch. Washington's stake there was out of scale with the posts' size, since a future canal made every mile of the isthmus count. This dispatch is one page of the record that stake produced.
frus-1863p1-d107:
On 2 March 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams, the eleventh of twelve dated that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 107 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The next-to-last sheet of a batch often mops up: a late fact, a small claim, a word of tone. Seward's eleventh letter of 2 March sits in that place in the row. The batch it belongs to is the marvel. It re-laid a whole brief in a day, for the post that could most help or harm the Union. This letter is one of its last strokes.
frus-1863p1-d207:
From Washington on 23 May 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 207 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Instructions like this one show how the Lincoln government ran a war abroad while fighting one at home. The paper trail is the diplomacy itself, order by order. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d307:
Washington's orders to London on 9 October 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 307 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. By then the British government had moved to hold the Confederate rams, and the sharpest crisis of the year was cooling. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d407:
In Washington on 3 March 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 407 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

The two men met and wrote constantly, and both knew a quarrel between their countries could hand the South its independence. That shared fear kept the tone correct even when the words were sharp. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d507:
Secretary of State William H. Seward took up his pen on 12 May 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d607:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington wrote this official letter to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 August 1863. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1917-72PubDipv07:
Public diplomacy under Johnson fills this retrospective volume. It spans 1964 through 1968 in yearly blocks. Documents count up year by year to 1968. Three appendices close the book. They treat Little Rock's long shadow, the President and the press, and an exhibit called U.S.A. 1967. The files track how America argued its case abroad.

A mid-volume speech states the case in Asia. Johnson insists Communists there still believe in force. Enduring peace in Asia, he says, would benefit all mankind. Failure there would secure nothing anywhere. A Soviet poet's visit earns a footnote nearby. Yevtushenko's tour belonged to the same contest of images. The volume shows persuasion as policy. Speeches, exhibits, and polls serve one campaign.
frus-1919Parisv07:
Volume VII hands the conference to the heads of delegations. Their minutes run from July 1 to August 28, 1919. The Four have gone; the machinery grinds on. Daily meetings settle what the treaty left open. A mid-volume paper argues Finland's Swedish question. Swedes number 340,000 of 3.3 million Finns, it says. They crowd the coasts, heirs of old conquest and settlement. Their status belongs to the peace's unfinished business.

Such petitions reached the council all summer. Every border hid a minority question. The volume's minutes run at a steady afternoon hour. Routine replaces drama after June. Yet the map still shifts in these pages. Delegations inherit the Four's leavings.
frus-1941v07:
Colombia leads the 1941 seventh volume on defense. Military teamwork and Lend-Lease terms fill its front. Air and naval missions are extended by pacts. All Colombia's platinum is sought for America alone. Its foreign debt restarts with Washington's good offices. Export-Import credit rides beside that file. Costa Rica fears Axis ships at Puntarenas. Two burn; their crews are deported in files. A military mission and rubber studies follow. Cuba bargains defense steps with Washington next. Its Lend-Lease pact signs in November. Money aid and a trade top-up follow.

Haiti signs a money accord at mid-volume's place. Sparks cables the February signing from Port-au-Prince. The volume is the Caribbean arming. Small states trade bases for credit. Each file prices the exchange.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d107: On November 9, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, as both men counted down to their journeys. His message is Document 107 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The prime minister would travel by warship and aircraft through the Mediterranean, as the president would by sea. The record gives the date and the two names and no subject. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series among the departure papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d207:
Robert Kelley, the American chargé in Ankara, sent a long most-secret telegram to Washington late on 10 November 1943. It follows his report of 8 November and gives the British ambassador's own summary, shared that afternoon on his return from Cairo, of the Eden and Numan talks.

Numan had flatly refused Allied air bases, citing German power to bomb Turkish cities and a public not ready for war. On joining the war, he said Turkey would want to help in earnest, not stand aside making faces at the Germans. Above all he feared Soviet entry into the Balkans, and wanted pledges that Moscow sought no land or bases there. He agreed to take the questions back to Turkey's leaders.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d307:
An American draft of the Cairo communiqué, dated 25 November 1943, carries handwritten amendments by Harry Hopkins. The draft itself was dictated by Hopkins the day before and put before Roosevelt; this version adds three closing paragraphs naming those who attended the conference.

Its text says the three leaders and their military missions have agreed on future operations against Japan from China and Southeast Asia, and promises unrelenting pressure by sea, land, and air. Japan's Pacific islands will be taken from her forever, the land stolen from China, such as Manchuria and Formosa, returned, and Korea made free and independent after Japan falls. The three nations pledge to fight on together until Japan surrenders unconditionally. Hopkins' margin notes add phrases about conquests taken by violence and greed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d407: Harry Hopkins passed President Roosevelt a short handwritten note at Tehran on 1 December 1943, during the political meeting of the three leaders. The whole note takes three lines. It opens with the time, ten past eight in the evening. Hopkins then asks whether Roosevelt wishes, at dinner, to introduce the method of the Allied occupation of Germany after her collapse. Nothing in the entry records the President's answer.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d507:
Prime Minister Churchill handed this composite memorandum to Harry Hopkins on December 7, 1943, the day after the Second Cairo Conference closed. A composite paper gathered several points into one document for the President's side. The State Department printed it in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Churchill was a tireless writer of minutes and memoranda, and handing one to Hopkins was his way of placing British views directly before Roosevelt. The paper belongs to the argument that continued even as the delegations packed to leave Cairo. For readers, it shows the Prime Minister still pressing his case on paper after the formal sessions had ended.
frus-1944-quebec-d107:
State Department staff prepared a briefing paper dated September 5, 1944. Briefing papers state a question, the facts, and a recommended position. The department printed this one in the Quebec 1944 volume. It was ready one week before the conference.

Good briefing papers let a leader master a topic fast. Department experts distilled files into a few clear pages. The Quebec agenda gave them plenty to distill that September. Germany's treatment, allied aid, and Pacific strategy all needed decisions. For readers, the paper shows expertise being packaged for power. It is the staff system working exactly as designed.
frus-1944-quebec-d207:
The Joint Chiefs met on September 16, 1944, to turn the Roosevelt-Churchill zones agreement into a formal paper. Leahy presented his memorandum outlining the British and American areas, with access to northwestern seaports and passage through the British area. Marshall and King wanted one port specified under complete American control, able to handle some 10,000 tons of supplies daily.

King proposed Bremen, and Marshall drafted the paragraph vesting control of Bremen and its staging areas in the American zone commander. The amended memorandum was approved for the Combined Chiefs, later circulated as C.C.S. 320/26. The meeting also heard Stilwell's grim report from China and approved Marshall's draft message from the president to Chiang Kai-shek.
frus-1944v07:
Latin America fills Volume VII of the 1944 Diplomatic Papers, opening with the Montevideo defense committee and plans for the Mexico City war and peace meeting. Arms supply, staff talks, and coffee trade set the regional frame. Country chapters then run across the hemisphere.

Argentina dominates, as Washington withheld recognition from the Farrell regime and pressed neighbors to stand firm. Bolivia's junta, its tin, and its trade follow. Brazil's air pact and its force sent to the Mediterranean also appear. The papers show wartime partnership mixed with open pressure on states that held back.
frus-1945-50-intel-d107:
Acting Secretary of War Howard Petersen wrote to Quinn, the new director of the Strategic Services Unit, on 3 April 1946. The SSU was on its third chief in a year. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Petersen's letter belongs to the unit's last season, when its absorption into the Central Intelligence Group was being arranged in detail. A department's acting secretary writing to a shrinking unit's chief shows the end being managed from the top, not left to drift. Readers can follow the SSU thread to its close in these spring papers. Each one moves men, money, or duties from the old remnant to the new group, until the remnant's name fades from the file.
frus-1945-50-intel-d207:
The Deputy Director of Central Intelligence (Wright) addressed a memorandum to the President’s Special Counsel (Clifford) on 28 January 1947. It is document 207 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d307: The title "Memorandum for the File" heads a text dated 16 November 1948. It stands as document 307 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The first Dulles Report season had begun: an outside team judged the CIA while the agency and its partners answered back. The form is brief by design: one event, one date, and the names that make the entry checkable.
frus-1945-50-intel-d407:
Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter wrote once more to Sidney Souers of the National Security Council on 27 December 1949. The memo is document 407 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Souers, the Council's executive secretary, had led the CIA before Hillenkoetter and knew its weak points well. Notes between the two men linked the agency to the White House staff. This late December memo closes a year of steady paper between the CIA and the Council. The year end date gives the memo a stock taking tone, closing one year of the young system.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d107:
Germany's surrender terms were drafted long before the war ended. The European Advisory Commission worked in London under terms set at the Moscow Conference. It sent the three allied governments this report, with a draft instrument titled “Unconditional Surrender of Germany.” The report is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The commission calls its draft mainly a military instrument in three parts. The preamble has Germany admit the complete defeat of her armed forces on land, at sea, and in the air. Short military articles then order all German forces to stop fighting. Later parts let the allied representatives take the first steps of control. The text became one of the basic papers of the occupation.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d207:
De Gaulle asked Roosevelt to hurry arms for eight French divisions, and Ambassador Caffery cabled the letter's text from Paris on 2 January 1945. The cable is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The French leader writes as an ally straining to field more men.

Germany will not be beaten completely, de Gaulle argues, without new forces thrown in. France, despite three million men lost or absent, can raise her strength powerfully and fast, and burns to do so. Her arms factories are restarting, but machine tools are battered and raw materials short. America armed eight divisions in North Africa, an effort not lost, and has lately agreed to equip eight more. He thanks the President, and begs speed: the French army can use all of it in battle within three months.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d307:
