In place of a missing meeting record, the editors of this FRUS volume supply a short note on what can still be known. No account of the session's substance survives in the files, they explain. What remains comes from Secretary Stettinius's own later book and from a cable he sent that day.

From those scraps, the note reports a decision. The American and British chiefs of staff backed approval of the zones of occupation in Germany. Stettinius then wired Ambassador Winant in London so the plan could move ahead. The note is a small lesson in how editors rebuild a record from fragments.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d407: Stettinius wrote this brief message by hand at Yalta on February 9, 1945, and Hiss carried it to Gladwyn Jebb during the foreign ministers' meeting. Its point was care about blame. The delegations must be sure that no duty rested on them in relation to states such as Iceland, Turkey, or Egypt joining the world body. Hiss's notation dates the errand to 12:30 that afternoon. He also recorded that he inserted the word Egypt himself. The slip survives in the Hiss collection.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d507:
Shipping waits for Washington in this memorandum from James Byrnes to the President, dated March 8, 1945. At Yalta, Byrnes recalls, Churchill had wished to discuss shipping and the British import program. Hopkins and Byrnes advised Lord Leathers that the problem was too complicated to settle so far from the basic data. It would have to be resolved in Washington.

Leathers accepted that view, Byrnes reports. He said several times that he would come to the United States at an early date to discuss the shipping situation. The excerpt, from the Roosevelt Papers, shows a Yalta side issue being deliberately postponed — and the postponement holding.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d107:
The U.S. Chiefs of Staff set out their view on staff size for Terminal in a memorandum dated June 28, 1945. The paper, C.C.S. 880/3, is document 107 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It answers a British memorandum of June 25 on how the two military staffs should be manned at the Berlin meeting.

Large military staffs should not be taken, the American chiefs hold, and detailed talks needing a big staff, on the scale of earlier conferences, should not be held there. They plan to bring only very small staffs, and they expect the agenda to be handled quickly. Subjects needing deep study belong in the normal Combined Chiefs of Staff machinery. If the British see the agenda differently, the Americans ask to be told.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d207:
Edward Page recorded Molotov probing the Italy item in a memorandum extract dated July 11, 1945. The extract is document 207 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Ambassador Harriman had called on Molotov to ask whether he had questions on the American agenda sent over on July 7.

Molotov asked whether it was proposed to study the peace treaty for Italy. Harriman replied that his letter spoke only of policy toward Italy, and he did not know whether the President would propose studying the treaty at Berlin, or whether such study was timely. He asked whether the Soviet government had studied the matter. Molotov did not answer that question. He said, however, that he was anxious to know whether anything was being prepared on a draft treaty. The fencing shows both sides testing each other's intentions before the leaders met.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d307:
Barnes warned from Sofia on July 9, 1945, that American silence was costing ground in Bulgaria. His subject was Russia's threat of force against Turkey over the Straits. Washington had made no public response while the United Nations charter was being signed. Local Communists, he wrote, drew their own lesson from that.

To them, silence proved American weakness beside Soviet strength. The claim strengthened Communist hands and weakened the Bulgarians still fighting for a free course at home and abroad. Barnes argued that quiet diplomacy, with only private words in Moscow, could never better matters in the region. His cable pressed for a firmer public stand.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d407:
A fight over one sentence fills Winant's extracts from London of July 7, 1945. On July 6 the European Advisory Commission agreed the preamble to the French zone agreement, and approved the report that would accompany it, except for its final sentence. That sentence recommended the four governments order their commanders in Germany to fix, jointly, the Berlin area France would occupy.

The American, British, and French delegations approved the sentence. The Soviet representative, Gousev, pressed for its omission. He insisted that since the Crimea decision formed the French zone from the American and British zones, the French area in Berlin must also come from those two zones alone. The sentence stayed in dispute.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d507:
Warsaw travel and Polish troops in Britain fill Winant's cable from London of July 9, 1945. Hankey has postponed his departure for Warsaw until July 12, the Foreign Office official said, and may not leave until July 15. Britain is negotiating in Moscow for a direct air service to Warsaw, but he may have to fly by British plane to Berlin, then by Russian plane on to Warsaw.

On Polish troops, the War Office has issued a circular to all British commanders of Polish detachments. They are to assure the Poles under their command that no Pole will be returned to Poland against his will. Britain also hopes to abolish the Polish Ministry of Defence in the immediate future.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d607:
An extract from a briefing paper on Japan's surrender, dated June 29, 1945, sets goals on the Cairo Declaration. It is document 607 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The paper is the same briefing text that appears in extract in two other documents of the volume.

The minimum goal is twofold. The Soviet government should adhere to the Cairo Declaration. The three powers should also agree to consult each other and China before acting on its land terms. That would back the return of Manchuria and Formosa to China and a free Korea. It would also stop any one power from setting up a friendly regime on its own. The maximum goal goes further. The powers, with China's help, would jointly back the growth of a strong, democratic, independent Korea.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d707:
Turkey's foreign minister Saka called on Ambassador Winant in London on July 13, 1945, to state his country's case. Winant's secret summary is document 707 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Saka came with the Turkish ambassador at his side.

Saka said Turkey had been willing to admit that its friendship treaty with Russia needed revision. Ankara had asked Moscow what it proposed as the basis for a new treaty. No answer came until Molotov returned from San Francisco. Then, to Turkish surprise, he set preconditions for even considering a revised treaty. Russia would expect the cession of Kars and Ardahan in the east. It would expect Soviet bases on the Straits as well. An understanding on revising the Montreux Convention was the third demand. Despite supposed Yalta assurances, Saka said, Turkey now had grave fears of Soviet intent.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1007:
Soviet delegates presented this proposal on the German navy and merchant marine to the foreign ministers on July 19, 1945. It claims a one-third share for the Soviet Union across the board. The share covers the whole German navy, even ships still building or under repair when Germany surrendered.

A third of naval reserve weapons, ammunition, and supplies would also pass to the USSR, matched by ship class. So would a third of the German merchant marine. Transfers would start on August 1 and end by November 1, 1945. An expert commission, named by the three Allied naval commands, would handle the handover of ships in ports at home and abroad.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1107:
Charles Yost, executive secretary of the Central Secretariat serving the American team, wrote this memorandum on 9 August 1945. That date fell a week after the Potsdam Conference ended. The secretariat was the summit's paperwork hub, the office that handled schedules, papers, and the flow of records.

A wrap-up note like this one belongs to the work of closing out a summit. Files had to be sorted, copies made, and the record put in order for the trip home. The text shows the plain, needed labor that turns weeks of talk into a usable archive. Big events run on small tasks, and this is one of them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1207:
Prime Minister Tito and Foreign Minister Subasic of Yugoslavia wrote jointly to President Truman on 25 July 1945. Tito, the partisan chief turned ruler, led a government the West did not fully trust. Subasic spoke for the royalist strand joined into that government.

A joint appeal from the pair sought American goodwill for the new Yugoslav state. Belgrade wanted standing, aid, and a hearing while the summit weighed Balkan questions. The letter shows Yugoslavia courting Washington while keeping Moscow close. It is a bid from a small state caught between giants, made in the most formal way open to it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1307:
Harrison wrote to Stimson on 21 July 1945, keeping the Interim Committee channel warm. The committee's acting chairman reported to the war secretary as the summit's first week closed. Their subject was the atomic file: the test's meaning, the choices ahead, and the words to use about both.

By then the full test report had reached Potsdam and the president had been briefed. The choices about the bomb's use were narrowing. Harrison's notes helped Stimson carry them. This message is one more link in a quiet chain. That chain ran from a New Mexico desert to a German palace, by way of two men's pens.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1407:
A second Caffery cable to Secretary Byrnes is dated 6 August 1945. Caffery's Paris embassy was reporting on several French questions at once that week. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Secretaries of state read only a slice of the paper their departments produce. So cables sent to Byrnes by name mark the files Caffery most wanted decided. Two in one day to the secretary is a strong signal from an ambassador. Read with the cables to the acting secretary from the same dates, this one shows sorting by rank. Routine matters went down one channel. The pressing ones went up the other.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-107:
A second delegation memorandum dated July 25, 1945 joins the American staff papers in the Potsdam record. The volume holds several such memos from the same day, a sign of the workload. Each carried a piece of business between offices or up to senior men. This one was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official Foreign Relations series.

Staff memoranda rarely make dramatic reading, and that is their strength. They record what officials thought they knew on a given day. Historians use them to date ideas and trace who pushed them. The memo adds one firm point to the map of the conference's middle days.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d807:
Kirk reported from Rome on July 23, 1945, in document 807. The ambassador in Italy wrote to the Acting Secretary as Potsdam passed its midpoint. Italy's peace terms were among the questions shadowing the talks. His report joined the Italy thread in the second Potsdam volume.

A midpoint report from Rome shows a capital recalculating. Early summit news had reached Italy; hopes rose or fell with it. Kirk filtered that mood for Washington. Readers see an envoy managing both facts and feelings. The document adds the view from a beaten country's capital at the hour its fate was being weighed elsewhere.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d907:
American drafters wrote this working paper on restitution at Babelsberg on July 22, 1945. A file note names Collado as its author. The paper lists the kinds of looted property that could be claimed back, wherever they were found.

The list covers heavy farm and factory equipment, machine tools, and unique machinery. It also covers rolling stock and other transport gear. A fourth class holds art, religious and cultural objects, libraries, and lab gear. Lost items in that class could be replaced with similar enemy property. Claims would be handled by the owner's own state.
frus-1945v07:
China in the year Japan fell fills Volume VII of the 1945 Diplomatic Papers. War ties and aid lead, then Ambassador Hurley's bid to end the Nationalist-Communist clash. After the surrender, civil strife spread and American troops helped move Japanese forces out.

Hurley's resignation and the start of the Marshall Mission close the political story. Other blocks cover the Sino-Soviet treaty, revolts in Sinkiang, and Soviet acts in Manchuria. Gold shipments and inflation fill the finance papers. Few volumes catch a country at such a turning point. Trade and firm rights fill the closing papers.
frus-1946v07:
Volume VII for 1946 covers the Near East and Africa, with oil at the top of the regional agenda. Greece follows, with watched elections and a growing aid program. Frontier claims against its northern neighbors fill many cables.

Iran takes the longest run, as Washington pressed Soviet troops to leave and backed Tehran at the United Nations. Palestine's future and Jewish entry fill the next block. Syria, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey close the volume. The papers catch the region at the start of a long contest. Air accords and surplus sales fill the smaller country sections.
frus-1947v07:
China alone fills Volume VII for 1947, and the story is civil war. Month-by-month sections track Communist offensives in Manchuria and the strain on Nationalist forces. Liaison teams were expelled, and talks stayed dead.

Reports from Formosa record anger at mainland rule. The Wedemeyer mission appraised the whole scene that summer. Arms aid, the lifted embargo, and naval transfers fill the later papers. Dairen, Sinkiang, and Tibet each get sections. The cables show a government losing ground while its main backer weighed how much more to give. Consular staff safety drew attention as cities changed hands.
frus-1948v07:
China's collapse is the story of Volume VII for 1948, told month by month. Early sections note a lull, Assembly votes, and student unrest. Manchuria then slips away, city by city, in embassy and consular cables.

Ambassador Stuart's advice and Washington's replies mark the policy debate. Tsinan, Changchun, and Mukden fall in the autumn run. Talks of Chiang's retirement close the year. Tibet, Sinkiang, and the stranded Dairen consulate fill side sections. The volume reads as a front-row record of a regime's last full year. Embassy move plans show how near the end seemed.
frus-1955-57v07:
Central and South America fill Volume VII of the 1955–1957 set, country by country. Guatemala leads the Central American run, in the wake of the 1954 coup. Panama follows, with canal ties and the Suez crisis's local shock.

Argentina, Bolivia, and Brazil take the longest South American runs. Chile, Colombia, Peru, and Venezuela fill the rest. Each file mixes politics, trade, and arms. Embassy reports show Washington dealing with juntas, elected leaders, and strongmen in turn. The common thread is aid sought, granted, or withheld as ties rose and fell. The closing files weigh each ally's share of the common defense burden.
frus-1964-68v07:
Volume VII of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964-1968, covers Vietnam from September 1968 to January 1969. Its chapters follow the Paris peace talks month by month. They trace efforts to move the talks forward, the October breakthrough, and the talks on terms for a bombing halt. Later chapters cover the halt itself and South Vietnam's slow path to the table.

The documents are cables, memos, and records of talks from the last months of the Johnson White House. They show U.S. envoys weighing Saigon's refusal to join the talks. They also record the Anna Chennault affair and its effect on the talks. The volume ends as the expanded talks open in Paris.
frus-1969-76v07:
Volume VII of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1969-1976, follows Vietnam from July 1970 to January 1972. The first chapter covers the fallout from the Cambodia incursion. The next covers planning for new operations in Cambodia and Laos. Operation Lam Son 719, the South Vietnamese thrust into Laos, gets its own chapter. The volume closes with months of stalemate on both the battlefield and the talks.

Memos and meeting records show debate over how far to back Saigon's cross-border moves. After Lam Son 719, the papers weigh what went wrong. The search for a settlement runs on, without result. The volume ends with both sides dug in.
frus-1969-76ve07:
South Asia from 1969 to 1972 fills Volume E-7 of the 1969-1976 series. The first section covers India and Pakistan before the crisis, to February 1971. The second covers the crisis and war of 1971. A third follows ties with both states in 1972. Closing sections treat Afghanistan and the new state of Bangladesh. The Bangladesh section runs from December 1971 to December 1972.

The papers overlap the South Asia crisis volume but add depth on aid and ties. Refugee relief and food aid fill many pages. Recognition of Bangladesh is debated in the final section. The volume rounds out the E-series record of the subcontinent.
fuller-star-in-the-west-1907:
An army officer took Crowley in earnest as a poet when few would, in 1907. The Star in the West, by John Fuller, is a critical essay on Crowley's works. Fuller would later win fame as a theorist of war and the tank.

He reads the young Crowley's verse and prose as the work of a major, strange gift. The essay sorts the books, weighs their worth, and defends their fire against a cold press. It is the first serious study of Crowley as a man of letters. The book catches him before the legend swallowed the writer.
gao-gaoreports-b-296307:
Delta Dental of California protested a Defense Department award for dental cover in GAO decision B-296307, dated July 28, 2005. The winner was United Concordia Companies. The plan was the TRICARE dental plan. Members join by choice. The firm said its marks were unfair and off the stated tests. It also hit the price check.

GAO denied the protest. The record showed marks were sound for both bids. The stated tests were used in a fair and even way. A long review of a large buy found no flaw that would change the pick. The ruling is a broad guide on even-handed scoring.
gao-gaoreports-b-297207:
Marine Industries protested the rejection of its bid for ship repair work in GAO decision B-297207, dated December 2, 2005. The buyer was the Navy at Puget Sound. Three rival firms won deals. The call asked for a brief plan for quality checks on done work. The firm's plan was ruled too thin.

GAO denied the protest. The firm said its plan was in the works. It did not say the plan would be set by award. It also named no old plan it would swap out. That gap left the bid short of the call. A plan in the works, with no pledge to be set in time, does not meet a plan term.
gao-gaoreports-b-297807:
Al Long Ford protested the rejection of its bid for trucks in GAO decision B-297807, dated April 12, 2006. The winner was American Equipment Company. The buyer was the Army tank and auto command. The goods were light utility trucks, plus parts and books. Counts ran from 500 trucks to 6,000 trucks. Ship speed was the firm's edge.

GAO sustained the protest. Fears on the firm's ship plan came to light after talks had closed. Those fears should have been clear before talks closed. Talks should have been reopened to air them. Ship speed had to be met for the firm to have a shot at the deal. Shut talks on a key point broke fair play.
gao-gaoreports-b-299407:
International Filter Manufacturing protested a Defense Logistics Agency plan to run a part kits buy with no set-aside. The buy ran through a request for quotations. The firm is a HUBZone small business that makes filters. GAO ruled in B-299407 on April 10, 2007.

One point ended the HUBZone claim at the start. The buy fell below the simplified acquisition threshold. At that size, no HUBZone set-aside was required. The firm's wider claim also failed. The agency's market probe showed no fair hope of two or more bids from that class. Past deals did not change the count. An open buy could stand. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-316107:
New vote gear bought to swap old gear is cleared in this GAO decision, B-316107, dated March 19, 2008. The Help America Vote Act of 2002 funds vote upgrades in the states. One clause lets the Election Assistance Commission pay states for kit that meets the act. States pick the type of kit they use. A state asked if funds could swap one fit type for a new fit type.

GAO held the swap sits in the shop's fair room to judge. The act leaves type picks to the states. A swap of fit kit for fit kit fits the grant aim. The shop's plan to bless such swaps was upheld.
gao-gaoreports-b-400107:
Exec Plaza, LLC lost its protest (GAO decision B-400107, dated August 1, 2008). The case deals with a call for lease of office space. Some terms of the call hit the past landlord alone. That firm is the one that brings this fight. It said the split terms warp the race in favor of new hands. The terms dealt with the costs and facts of the held site.

GAO denied the protest. The agency showed the terms rest on fair needs. A past landlord holds facts a new hand lacks. Terms can weigh that edge in a fair way. A split load is not a flaw when the need is real and shown.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-407:
Financial Audit, GAO-05-407 of May 4, 2005, digs back into why the nation's own books still earn no clean grade. For 8 years, flaws in checks and in how sums are built have kept GAO from a firm view on the joint U.S. books. In December 2004, GAO told of flaws found in the fiscal year 2004 audit. The Treasury's own build steps held a share of them.

The text here gives those flaws in full. It sets the fixes GAO urges for them. It tells the state of 142 past tips that still stand open. Till the build path firms, the top books stay in doubt.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1007:
Backup funding for the Treasury is designed in GAO-06-1007, a report dated September 26, 2006. The 2001 attacks shook the markets Treasury relies on to borrow. GAO asked what steps Treasury and others took that week to pay on time. It asked what has been done since to harden the auction process. And it gathered views on how any backup funding tool should be built.

Headings trace the story. Treasury canceled an auction that week and used cash balances to meet its duties. The Federal Reserve supplied liquidity by several methods. Since then, both have added backup sites and system capacity. Dealers have acted too, with more steps suggested. Even so, GAO found it fitting to explore funding paths outside the auction process. A tiered approach to backup options has emerged from the talks, it reported.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-607:
Dated May 31, 2006, GAO-06-607 is a GAO report on how federal agencies release statistics to the public. It grew out of a 2003 change by the Census Bureau in the day and place it released its income and poverty data. Some data users saw the change as a move to bury bad news. They questioned whether the Bureau played fair with its releases.

GAO found the Bureau mostly followed its own release rules for the 2003 through 2005 data. GAO noted one break with tradition in the day and place of release. GAO also checked the Bureau and 13 other statistical agencies against practices urged by the National Research Council. Wider use of those practices, GAO said, would better guard trust in federal data.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-807:
Child care access for families with limited English is studied in GAO-06-807, the GAO report of August 17, 2006. Quality early care can greatly improve a young child's readiness for school. Parents who speak little English may face extra hurdles in finding and using child care aid. GAO gathered facts on participation in subsidized programs. GAO also asked what selected agencies do to help such parents.

GAO found that children of parents with limited English were less likely to join subsidized programs. Their parents faced multiple challenges, from language barriers to complex paperwork. Some agencies had taken steps to assist, such as translated materials and outreach. GAO said more information sharing and program review by the health department could enhance access. The report shows how language can quietly gate a public benefit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1007:
Fast growth at Army bases, and the roads and services to match, are the risk in GAO report GAO-07-1007, dated September 13, 2007. Base closures, troops coming home from abroad, and unit reshaping will swell 18 home bases through 2011. Some will grow by more than 50 percent.

New troops drive over $17 billion in expected build costs. Nearby towns face their own costs for roads, schools, and pipes. GAO, acting on its own, visited nine large gaining bases and their towns. It weighed the Army's hurdles in giving timely support. It also tracked how towns plan and pay for growth of their own.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-307:
Some doctors order more care than peers treating like patients, and Medicare pays. GAO studied how to spot them in GAO-07-307, a report dated April 30, 2007. A 2003 law told GAO to examine doctor pay in fee-for-service Medicare. GAO built a method using 2003 claims from 12 metro areas. It grouped patients into 31 health classes. It flagged the costliest fifth in each class. It also studied 10 buyers that grade doctors.

Every area had generalists with outsized shares of costly patients, GAO found. Their patients were 15 percent more likely to enter a hospital. They were 57 percent more likely to be hospitalized repeatedly. All 10 buyers profile doctors for efficiency. They steer patients or drop doctors based on the grades. The Medicare agency holds claims data to do likewise. But it may lack power to tie results to pay. GAO called profiling a promising path.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-407:
The Architect of the Capitol (AOC) runs the Capitol Hill complex, and GAO-07-407, released February 28, 2007, grades its reform drive. AOC cares for the Capitol, the Library of Congress, and the House and Senate office buildings. In 2003, GAO urged AOC to plan better and answer more clearly for its work. Congress then told GAO to track the follow-through.

This fourth status report weighs gains made and steps still owed. GAO read agency papers, spoke with officials, and drew on reviews of the Capitol Visitor Center. AOC mostly agreed with the grade. It said two more fixes, on money handling and worker safety data, were done. GAO held that more work was needed on both. Steady leadership, GAO said, was the key need.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-707:
The spot cheddar cheese market in Chicago is examined in GAO-07-707, dated June 21, 2007. Trades on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange shape prices for most U.S. cheese. They also feed into farm milk prices and milk futures. Fears of price rigging have long dogged it. GAO compared the old Wisconsin exchange with the Chicago one and read trade data. It also weighed how the market feeds federal milk pricing.

Few trades occur each day, and a small set of large firms makes most of them. That thin trade leaves room for a few players to sway prices. Prices set there still anchor long-term dairy deals. Oversight by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission had grown since the old exchange days. GAO urged the Agriculture Department to weigh plans to drop a cheese price survey from the milk price formula. If the survey stays, GAO said, it should audit the data.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-807:
Supply support for joint military operations is examined in GAO-07-807, dated June 29, 2007. During the Iraq war, Army and Marine units faced problems getting supplies. Those problems echo long-standing flaws in Defense Department supply chains. The department named joint theater logistics as its fix. That idea means services share supply work in a war zone. GAO judged the plan against sound management principles. It tracked how far the shared approach has spread.

No coordinated plan guides the effort across the department, GAO found. Goals and strategies stay vague, and no one answers for results. Measures track activity, not outcomes on the ground. Each service still funds and runs its own logistics systems. That split makes joint work hard to build. GAO urged one managed approach for the whole effort. It also urged the Defense Logistics Agency to merge storage and shipping where it can. The department agreed with both calls.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-907:
Job rights claims by returning troops are checked in GAO-07-907, dated July 20, 2007. A 1994 law guards the jobs of workers called to military service. The Labor Department investigates claims against employers. A trial project splits federal claims with the Office of Special Counsel. The split runs from February 2005 through September 2007. GAO sampled case files at both agencies. It traced records from databases back to source papers. The law ordering the study also set its questions.

Both agencies run intake and investigation processes, GAO found. Their caseload data cannot be trusted, though. Errors at Labor reached the annual report sent to Congress. Faulty figures cloud judgment about the trial project's success. Counsel's office works from one small central team. Labor uses over a hundred field investigators nationwide. GAO urged an internal review of every unresolved claim before closure. It also urged controls to keep the data accurate. Labor agreed with both points.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-407:
Military training and environmental law are the subject of GAO report GAO-08-407, released March 7, 2008. The Defense Department says environmental rules have limited some training on its ranges. Since 2003 it has won exemptions from three laws and sought three more. GAO visited 17 training sites for this review.

Some training events were canceled, delayed, or reshaped to meet the rules, and trainers used workarounds such as treating off-limits ground as mine fields in the exercise. Yet readiness data for active combat units did not confirm that the laws hurt overall readiness. Since 2006, the Navy has twice used a Marine Mammal Protection Act exemption to keep sonar training going. GAO saw no proven harm to the environment from the exemptions in use and told the department to build a sound business case before seeking more. The department partly agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-607:
Phone and data networks that once ran apart now share the same lines. A break in one can harm both. GAO-08-607, issued June 26, 2008, checks how the Department of Homeland Security is joining two watch centers. One center tracks phone networks, and the other tracks cyber threats to data.

The department took the first of three planned steps. In November 2007 it moved the two centers next door to each other and gave them shared tools. The last two steps are still undone, and the centers have not merged. GAO asked the department to finish its plan and set clear tasks and dates for the rest of the work.
gervase-tilbury-otia-imperialia-leibniz-:
Gervase of Tilbury wrote the Otia Imperialia, meaning imperial leisure, for his royal reader in the early thirteenth century. This text follows the edition prepared by Leibniz in 1707. Gervase mixed history, geography, and marvel into three parts, or decisions, meant to amuse and inform an emperor.

His book of marvels is the famous part. It tells of wonders from many lands, including a well-known tale of a werewolf. Gervase reports local legends beside sober chronicle without drawing a line between them. The result is the thirteenth century's own store of wonders. Kings were meant to enjoy it, and modern readers of folklore still do.
gurdon-the-khasis-1907:
Philip Richard Thornhagh Gurdon served as a colonial officer in Assam, and his 1907 study presents the Khasi people of the hills there. The Khasis stood out to early writers because descent and property passed through women, not men.

Gurdon describes Khasi villages, clans, and customs, along with their system of inheritance through the youngest daughter. He gives long attention to ancestor worship, divination by eggs and other signs, and the sacred forests where no tree could be cut. Myths and folk tales fill out the picture. The book remains a basic early source on a society ordered around the mother line.
hague-conventions-1899-1907:
Delegates from around the world met at The Hague in 1899 and again in 1907 to write rules for war. The two peace conferences produced a set of conventions that stand as the first broad attempt to bind warfare by law. Governments hoped that agreed rules could limit cruelty even when nations still went to war.

The texts ban weapons such as poison gas and expanding bullets, and set rules for prisoners, neutral states, and the sick and wounded. They also created a court for settling disputes between nations by arbitration. The rules did not stop the world wars, but much of their language still shapes the law of armed conflict today.
harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-volum:
Book Seven of Harold is titled The Welch King. It opens at sunset over the water where the Conway emerges, where no castle of Edward Plantagenet yet stands. A rude fortress rose above the stream of Gyffin, built from the wrecks of a greater Roman hold, and vast ruins of a former town lay round it. Opposite, on the ragged promontory of Gogarth, stood the forlorn wrecks of an imperial city destroyed by lightning.

The scene is Wales, whither the tale's feuds have carried Saxon arms. Harold's wars against the Welsh king, Griffith, form the matter of the part, with border raids, sieges, and the hard politics of mountain country. Lytton pours his learning into the landscape itself, reading Rome's ruin and Britain's fall in one view. The part is a somber interlude of war before the succession crisis closes in.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Thomas Carlyle built his huge life of Frederick the Great of Prussia volume by volume, and volume seven reaches a family crisis of 1730. Book seven bears the title Fearful Shipwreck of the Double-Marriage Project. Crown Prince Friedrich, bullied daily by his father King Friedrich Wilhelm, has secretly planned to slip away to England. His sister Wilhelmina faces a forced marriage of her own and refuses it.

Carlyle follows the pair to Dresden, where Friedrich confides his escape plan to Wilhelmina on the night before departure. Envoys, angry letters, and the English agent Hotham fill the rest of the book. Readers get Carlyle's loud, digressive voice at full stretch, turning court quarrels into high drama.
history-of-the-english-people-volume-i-e:
John Richard Green opens his eight-volume History of the English People with this first volume. Its spans are early England, the foreign kings, and the Charter. Green writes of peoples more than of courts and camps. William the Conqueror looms in these pages as the northern race's most terrible outcome.

Green grants William peerless knighthood even in his foes' words. Sea-robber blood and a statesman's cool temper meet in the man, he writes. The volume runs from the first settlements to King John's charter years. Green's gift is to make institutions feel lived. Readers get the birth of a nation told as the growth of a people.
hodgson-glen-carrig-1907:
Shipwreck throws a crew into a weird sea in William Hope Hodgson's first novel, from 1907. They find a vast swamp of weed in the far south seas. Strange beasts and lost ships wait in the gloom. The men must fight their way out by boat.

Told as a plain log, the tale keeps a tight grip. Fear comes from slime, rot, and things that lurk at the edge of sight. Hodgson knew the sea from his own years at sail. That grit gives the wild tale real weight. Weed men, crab beasts, and hulks of dead ships crowd the swamp. Each fight costs blood, which keeps the wild tale tense and grim.
hrdlicka-skeletal-remains-early-man-nort:
Ales Hrdlicka, the Smithsonian anthropologist, issued his survey of claimed early human bones in 1907. It appeared as Bulletin 33 of the Bureau of American Ethnology. Claim after claim of very ancient people in North America had reached the newspapers.

Hrdlicka examined each skeleton and site with strict skepticism. In case after case he found recent burials or weak evidence. His verdicts set the terms of debate about the first Americans for decades. Later discoveries moved the dates back, but his demand for proof endured. The bulletin became a standard reference for anyone claiming ancient American remains afterward.
james-pragmatism-1907:
William James published Pragmatism in 1907, the book that named a movement in philosophy. James gave the work first as lectures in Boston and New York. Pragmatism tests ideas by their practical results in experience. Truth, he argues, is what proves itself good in the way of belief over time.

He applies the test to God, free will, and the design of the world. The style is warm, vivid, and full of homely examples. Critics charged that he made truth mere usefulness, and James replied for years. The book shaped American thought far beyond philosophy. It remains the classic statement of the pragmatic method.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-07:
Volume 7, from 1897, spreads across Quebec, Huron country, and Cape Breton. Thwaites shows the mission pushing out in three directions at one time. Each front had its own risks, peoples, and hopes for new converts in the field.

Most weight falls on the new Huron mission in these pages. Its start opens the long road that ends in loss and death. Reports from the coast and the river round out the full picture. The pace of the whole chronicle quickens in this one volume. Readers feel the bold age of French America get fully under way.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abdon-207: Abdon is first the name of one of the last Ephraimite judges, a son of Hillel of Pirathon. He helped restore order in central Israel after the grim feud with Jephthah and the Gileadites, in Judges, chapter 12. The entry then lists three more bearers. One is a family of Benjamin, and one a family of Gibeon, both in First Chronicles. The last is a court officer in the days of Josiah. In Second Kings his name is given as Achbor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abimi-b-abbahu-:
Abimi ben Abbahu was a scholar of the third century whose home the entry can not fix. He is always cited as a son of R. Abbahu, and he loved to quote Baraitot. Those points make Bacher place him in Palestine, as Abbahu's son. Yet his name is missing from the Palestinian Talmud, and he settled debts in Babylonia. Frankel thus makes him a Babylonian instead.

His best known teaching is a riddle on honor owed to parents. One son feeds his father fine birds, yet wearies him of life with a rude word. Another yokes his father to a mill, yet readies him for the world to come, by taking the father's draft work on himself. Abimi's own father held him up as a model of a son's duty. He taught that the Messianic age would run seven thousand years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-of-bohe:
Abraham of Bohemia served as prefect of the Jews of Great and Little Poland at the start of the sixteenth century. In 1512 King Sigismund I named him to the post. One duty was to gather all taxes owed by the Jews and pay them into the royal treasury.

The king of Hungary and Bohemia and Emperor Maximilian backed him, praising his honesty. Polish courts had no power over him; he answered to the king's court alone. Polish Jews disliked their strong new prefect, and the king had to order rabbis to respect his rights. For them Abraham paid a yearly tax of twenty ducats.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-of-lune: Abraham of Lunel was a famed French philologist of the sixteenth century. He is said to have mastered twenty languages. He embraced Christianity, and about 1537 he was made professor of Hebrew at Avignon. As he grew older, love for his old faith revived in him. Unable to hide his true feelings, he was accused of being a secret Jew. In 1593 he was deprived of his office. To escape a worse fate he fled to Venice, where he openly returned to Judaism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abyss-707:
Abyss is a term for a deep place named in Genesis vii. 11. In later books it names a place of pain for the wicked. It is a kind of hell and a home for some demons. The Book of Enoch calls it a fire prison for impure angels. Luke and Revelation use it too. Revelation shows Satan shut in it with a seal set on him.

Rabbinic lore puts a spot below the Temple altar at Jerusalem. That spot was said to lead down to the Abyss of the world. In the rabbis' world picture, the Abyss forms part of Gehenna. It lies beneath the sea. It has three, or seven, stacked parts. Cabala gives the sealed pit of the lower world a twin in the upper world. There it works as a force in the making of the world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acosta-cristova: Cristoval Acosta was a Spanish doctor and plant scholar of the sixteenth century. He was born in Africa. His parents had fled there when cast out of Spain. He studied medicine and traveled for years in Africa and Asia. He knew the top doctors of Arabia, Persia, China, and Turkey. Back in Spain he settled at Burgos. In 1578 he put out a book on the drugs and plants of the East Indies. It was later turned into Italian and French. Death stopped a planned book on India's plants and beasts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adjiman-807: Adjiman was a Jewish family in Turkey. Some of its men served as cash keepers and head agents for the janizaries. Meir Adjiman lived under Selim III. His sway was so great that he raised a plain janizary to a high post. That same man had him strangled a few years later. The brothers Baruch and Jacob met a like fate. So did Isaiah Adjiman, the last named of the line here. He met his death under Mohammed II. Court wealth, in this tale, came with court peril.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agricultural-co:
Agricultural colonies in Palestine rest on a long wish to bring Jews back to farm the old land. Travelers of 1170 found small Jewish groups there. In 1481 a man of Florence found sixty Jewish families at Gaza on farms. They grew vines and grain. At the end of the sixteenth century Joseph Nasi rebuilt Tiberias. He planted mulberry trees to feed silk worms there.

Such notes show farm work, not true colonies. Those come in modern times. Sir Moses Montefiore held the plan dear for years. On his seven trips east he gave it much thought. His chief care was safety of life and goods for the men who would settle. In 1838 he met Boghuz Bey on the point. In 1854 the sultan took him in, and he spoke with the British envoy on land buys. The long entry then walks through the colonies that rose in the land in later years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aleksandria-110: Aleksandria is a district, town, and village in the government of Kherson, Russia. It stands on the Inguletz river. In 1897 its Jewish population was counted in three parts. The district held 3,857 Jews, the town 4,794, and the village 1,916. The town had two synagogues and two schools. The entry gives no history of the place, only these figures and facts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alfonsus-boniho: Alfonsus Bonihominis is the name on a Latin version of an anti-Jewish pamphlet. The pamphlet was first written in Arabic by Samuel of Morocco. The Latin version came out in the first half of the fourteenth century. Nothing is known about the translator himself. The entry reports a strong guess by Steinschneider. He held that the translator was Paul of Burgos. A second debate text is also linked to the same name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alpha-and-omega:
Alpha and Omega is a phrase found in the book of Revelation. It pairs the first Greek letter with the last. The voice in the verse calls itself the start and the end. The entry holds that the book grew from a Jewish work. It links the phrase to a rabbinic saying. That saying calls truth the seal of God.

Truth in Hebrew is spelled with three key letters. They are the first, the mid, and the last letters. A tale tells of a scroll that fell from heaven. The scroll bore that one word, truth. The entry reads the Greek phrase as a Greek dress for that old saying.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-andrew-1507:
Andrew is a name the entry treats in two parts. Saint Andrew, brother of Simon Peter, was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus. Both brothers were fishermen from Bethsaida, on the Lake of Gennesareth.

The Gospels, as retold here, make Andrew a former disciple of John the Baptist and one of the first called, with the words about becoming fishers of men. Tradition says he was martyred at Patrae in Greece, and that a relic of his arm reached Scotland, making him its patron saint. A second, brief item names a Jew of Crete who revolted against Rome under Trajan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aramaic-languag:
Aramaic language among the Jews starts from kinship: of all Semitic tongues, Aramaic stands closest to Hebrew. Yet ancient Hebrews counted it a foreign tongue, the entry says. A century before the Babylonian exile, only people of culture in Jerusalem understood it.

When an Assyrian envoy shouted insults in Hebrew at the crowd on the wall, King Hezekiah's officers begged him to use the Syrian language instead, which they alone knew. One Aramaic phrase survives in early Hebrew story. Laban named the stone heap of his pact with Jacob Jegar sahadutha, while Jacob called it Galeed in his own tongue. The entry follows Aramaic as it grew from a court language into the daily speech and study tongue of Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aron-emil-1807:
Emil Aron, a German physician, was born at Stettin in Pomerania on March 12, 1864. He studied at the Werdersche Gymnasium in Berlin. He then attended the universities of Berlin, Munich, and Heidelberg. He took his medical degree at Heidelberg in 1888. After travel to Vienna, Paris, and London, he set up practice in Berlin in 1890.

From 1891 to 1896 he worked as assistant physician in Berlin's Jewish Hospital. There he became a specialist in diseases of the throat. His writing appeared in leading medical journals of the day. He wrote on cervical ribs in 1892. He also studied the effect of compressed and rarefied air on pressure in the windpipe. A paper on the treatment of pneumothorax followed in 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ash-also-asch-1:
Ash, also written Asch, is a family name made by shortening longer names. It can stand for Altschul or for Eisenstadt. Such shortenings are common where a name's second part starts with the sh sound. Lasch for Lichtenstadt and Nasch for Nikolsburg follow the same pattern.

Meir Ash, rabbi of Eisenstadt, who died on June 7, 1744, carries the short form of that town's name. His descendant Abraham Zebi Hirsch, rabbi of Ottynia, died on August 21, 1868, yet signed himself Eisenstadt in full. A second Meir Ash, whose official name was Eisenstaedter, wrote Imre Esh, Words of Fire, at Unghvar in 1864 and died on December 27, 1861. The pun on esh, fire, may shape such book titles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashura-the-tent:
Ashura is a fast day among Muslims, kept on the tenth day of the month Muharram. It derives from the Jewish Day of Atonement, kept on the tenth of Tishri, as Leviticus states. The name is an Aramaic form of the Hebrew asor, the tenth, and it still lives in a prayer poem for the Day of Atonement.

Muslim tradition agrees that the Prophet knew nothing of the Atonement fast until he reached Medina in 622. There he saw the Jews fasting on Ashura. Told it marked the day God saved Israel from its enemy, the day Moses fasted, he claimed a nearer right to Moses, fasted himself, and ordered others to fast. Some followers disliked sharing a Jewish and Christian feast day, and a plan to move the fast to the ninth died with him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auer-leopold-21:
Leopold Auer was a Hungarian violinist. He was born in Veszprim, Hungary, on June 7, 1845, the son of a poor house-painter. His gift showed early: at four he marched before revolutionary troops beating a drum. He studied at Budapest, then at Vienna under Dont in 1857-58, and last with Joachim at Berlin.

Auer conducted at Düsseldorf from 1863 to 1865 and at Hamburg from 1866 to 1868. He then took Wieniawski's place as professor of violin at the St. Petersburg conservatory. In 1873 he became soloist of the imperial theaters, with the title of court-soloist to the Czar. He later led the concerts of the Russian Imperial Musical Society. The entry stresses his teaching. More than forty pupils of his won renown as soloists in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and beyond. His own works include a concert tarantelle and a Hungarian rhapsody for violin and piano.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azekah-2207:
Azekah was a city in the Shephelah, the plain of Judah. It lay about midway between Jerusalem and the Philistine border, to the southwest. It stood near Socoh, with which the Bible often pairs it. Its exact site was still unknown when the entry was written. Eusebius placed a village called Ezekah between two towns of his own day.

The city stood before Israel entered Canaan. Joshua chased the five beaten kings as far as Azekah. The Philistine army camped between Shochoh and Azekah when David fought Goliath. Rehoboam later walled the city. Four centuries on, in Zedekiah's reign, Judah's forces faced Nebuchadnezzar at Azekah. After the return from exile, men of Judah settled there again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bacher-wilhelm-:
Wilhelm Bacher, a Hungarian scholar of Eastern languages, was born in Liptó-Szent-Miklós on Jan. 12, 1850. He was the son of the Hebrew writer Simon Bacher. He studied at Budapest, Breslau, and Leipsic, and finished his degree in 1870. In 1876 he became a rabbi and soon after took a post at Szegedin.

From July 1, 1877, Bacher taught at the new national rabbinical school in Budapest. The entry lists a very long set of his books and papers. They cover Persian poetry, Hebrew grammar, Bible study, and the Agada, the non-legal part of rabbinic writing. He also helped found a Hungarian Jewish review in 1884 and a literary society ten years later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ballads-on-jewi:
Ballads on Jewish subjects are found in the folk poetry of Europe, and this entry surveys them. It opens with a Neo-Greek ballad on a Jewess. Most of the ballads it names, though, picture Jews as the popular mind of their day pictured them, in a hostile way. The death of Little St. Hugh of Lincoln lives on in ballads in French, English, and Scottish.

A second tale gets fuller treatment: a Jewish boy goes with Christian playmates to confession, turns Christian, and is thrown by his father into a furnace. The Virgin Mary saves him. Nearly forty versions are known, in Greek, Latin, French, Spanish, German, Arabic, and Ethiopic. The story is traced to Evagrius Scholasticus. Shylock appears too, in the "Ballad of Gernuto the Jew" from Percy's "Reliques."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barbary-states-:
Barbary States names the northwest of Africa from the Mediterranean to the Sahara: Morocco, Algeria, Tunis, and Tripoli. The words "Barbaria" and "Barbarians" occur in the Midrash. Later Jewish writers usually call the region "Africa." Its Jews are called Maghrebim, and the Moors call them "Yahoodi." No records survive of their first immigration. Legends say they came direct from Jerusalem.

By 1902 the majority of Africa's 400,000 Jews lived in the Barbary States. Many came from Spain and Portugal and form the better class in the cities. Others live as nomads in the Atlas mountains and beyond, far into the Sahara. They speak Berber, Spagniol, and Arabic, and by their languages they hold almost the whole commerce of the country. Their trades are butchery, silversmithing, engraving, tailoring, and shoemaking. They never work as masons, blacksmiths, or potters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-basch-victor-26: Victor Basch taught philosophy at the University of Rennes. Born at Budapest in 1863, a son of Raphael Basch, he moved to France as a child and studied at the Sorbonne. He held posts at Nancy from 1885 and at Rennes from 1887. During the Dreyfus affair Basch led the Dreyfusards at Rennes, where the case was tried. The entry says he faced persecution there but held to legal and social justice. His books include a study of Kant's esthetics from 1896 and work on the history of esthetics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belid-son-of-al:
Belid was a leading French Jew who lived in Toulouse early in the thirteenth century. Deeds name him with the title Dominus, a mark of high rank. His wife had to consent to his land sales, which shows the scale of his affairs.

With his brother Abraham, Belid took lands from the Templars in 1202 and bought more from the Knights of St. John in 1203 and 1207. A count seized his estates more than once. Each time, the entry says, he managed to win them back. His wife bears a lady's title of her own in the deeds that record those land sales at Toulouse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bendemann-rudol: Rudolf Christian Eugen Bendemann, a German painter, was born at Dresden on Nov. 11, 1851, and died in May 1884 at Pegli, near Genoa. He trained at the Düsseldorf Academy under his father, Eduard Bendemann. From 1877 to 1879 he lived at Munich, and he later made several visits to Egypt. His mural work in Berlin followed his father's plans. The entry lists his notable pictures, among them scenes from Egypt, a mosque exit at Cairo, and a well in Upper Egypt, and notes his success as a portrait painter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benoliel-don-ju: Judah Benoliel served as Moroccan and Austrian consul at Gibraltar and died in 1839. He led the Jewish community there and its chamber of commerce. In office he settled a clash between Sardinia and Morocco without war. His greatest credit came at Tangier, where the governor had torn down all the synagogues after a quarrel. Benoliel won the sultan's leave to rebuild them, asking no honor for himself. A memorial prayer for that act is still said each Day of Atonement at Tangier.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bern-olga-nee-w: Olga Bern, born Wohlbrück, was an Austrian author and the wife of Maximilian Bern. She was born at Vienna on July 5, 1865. She went on the stage under her own name and, while at the Odeon in Paris in 1887, married the German author Bern. In 1888 she left the stage for writing. Her books include short tales from three lands, several sets of stories, a drama on the right to happiness, and a novel named for two fathers, Chaïm and Benediktus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beth-hillel-dav: David de Beth-Hillel was a Beni-Israel author. He wrote a book of "Travels" printed at Madras in 1832. The entry gives it a notable distinction. It was the first work by a Jew published in India. The book describes his travels through India. Beyond that, the entry is brief. It calls him otherwise of little importance. Its only source is a catalogue of the Anglo-Jewish Exhibition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-binding-and-loo:
Binding and loosing is a rabbinical term. It means forbidding and permitting. "Asar" in Numbers describes a binding vow. The entry links it to a prohibitive spell. The Pharisees always claimed this power. Under Queen Alexandra they ran public affairs. They could banish, readmit, bind, and loose.

Schools could bind a day as a fast-day. Heaven's court ratified their rulings, tradition held. The entry then turns to the New Testament. Jesus used the same formula for his disciples. Peter received the power in Clementine writings too. John's version shifts it toward forgiving sins. That view shaped the Church's key-power.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blood-3407:
Blood holds a sacred place in Jewish teaching. Hunters and herdsmen saw life leave with blood. So Scripture calls blood the life itself. "The blood is the life" appears in Deuteronomy. Leviticus says the life of flesh is in blood. Hence eating blood is strictly forbidden. The ban repeats across the Torah.

The ban has one deeper reason too. God gave altar blood for atonement. So its place is the altar, not the table. Later rabbis hardened the commands further. They forbade any use of a corpse as well. Folk-lore, though, used blood for compacts and cures. Jewish practice abhorred those uses always.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brieg-3707:
Brieg is a town in Silesia, once capital of a duchy of the same name. Jews settled there about 1324. Its place on the trade route to Breslau drew them, the entry says.

Brieg Jews had their own place of worship from early times. Persecution over money lending claims struck them in the fourteenth century. In 1398 they bought a letter of protection from the duke. Two years after, most were driven from the city in 1401. A lender named Solomo later lent large sums to royal houses. By 1902 Brieg held a Jewish community of 310 souls, with three charitable societies for the poor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buffalo-3807: Buffalo, the animal, is a name shared by several kinds of cattle. The best known kind came from India, its native home. From there it spread into western Asia, Greece, southern Italy, and northern Africa. In eastern lands it is called jamoos, a Persian word meaning ram cow. Some writers once identified the buffalo with the re'em of the Bible. The entry says that idea is now generally given up. The re'em was far wilder and could not be tamed. It is now taken to be the wild ox.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cappadocia-gree:
Cappadocia was an old province of Asia Minor, running from the Taurus range to the Black Sea and from the Halys river to the Euphrates. Jews knew it by its Greek name, and the Talmud and Midrash cite it often. Josephus ties its people to the biblical tribe Meshech. Greek writers called them white Syrians, yet their speech was not Semitic.

Herod's house linked to Cappadocia by marriage, and Jews settled there in time. They came to Jerusalem for the feasts, and some moved to Sepphoris. Talmudic notes cover their Sabbath oil, their coins, and their sharp repute. The capital, Mazaca, held a large Jewish body: a Persian king's siege there cost twelve thousand Jewish lives, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caspari-charles: Charles Paul Caspari, a German Semitic and biblical scholar, was born at Dessau in 1814 and died in 1892. Raised in the Jewish faith by Jewish parents, he became a Christian in 1838. In 1847 he took a post at the University of Christiania and stayed there until his death. His Arabic grammar, issued from 1844 to 1848, became the standard work in its field. He also wrote commentaries on Obadiah, Micah, and Isaiah, studies on Isaiah's age, and a Norwegian version of the Psalter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castro-sarmento:
Jacob Henriquez de Castro Sarmento, a physician, naturalist, and poet, was born about 1691 at Bragança, Portugal. He died at London in 1761. He studied philosophy at Evora and medicine at Coimbra, taking his degree in 1717. To escape the Inquisition, he moved to London in 1720.

At London, Castro Sarmento studied medicine, physics, and chemistry, and passed his examinations. About 1725 the Royal Society elected him a fellow, honoring a new fever medicine he had brought in. His first book treated inoculation against smallpox, printed at London in 1721. Later works cover medical history, mineral waters, and the theory of the tides. Aberdeen gave him a medical degree in 1739. He also wrote Spanish sermons and poems for Jewish occasions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chaikin-moses-a: Moses Avigdor Chaikin, a rabbi and author, was born at Sklow in 1852. He moved young with his father to St. Petersburg and trained for the rabbinate. After the riots of 1881-82 he left for Paris, where he served Polish Jews as rabbi from 1883 to 1887. Back in Russia, he held a post at Rostov-on-the-Don, then was expelled in 1890. In England he became rabbi at Sheffield in 1892, and in 1901 rabbi of the Federation of Synagogues, London. His books came out at Paris in 1887 and Sheffield in 1889.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chernevtzy-4307: Chernevtzy is a town in the government of Podolia, in Russia. In 1898 it held about 15,000 people, including about 2,000 Jews. Of those Jews, 267 were artisans, and most of the rest earned a living as small tradesmen. The local sugar refinery employed 400 men, but only 14 of them were Jews. There were also 17 journeymen and 20 farm laborers. Jewish poverty in the town was very great. In 1898, 60 families received fuel from charitable organizations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-clay-homer-tit-:
Clay, in Old Testament use, covers several kinds of soil, from the clays of the East to the loam of the Nile valley. In strict terms it is a mix of broken-down minerals. Alumina, silica, and potash form its main parts, with lime, magnesia, and iron shaping its quality and color, the entry explains.

Three ancient uses structure the piece. Clay made bricks, sun-dried and kiln-burnt, for palaces and city walls across Babylonia and Egypt. Clay fed the potter's wheel, an image the prophets turned into a symbol of God's power over human fate. Most striking was clay as a writing surface. Tens of thousands of baked cuneiform tablets survive, some sealed as contract tablets.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-solomon-d:
Solomon da Silva Solis Cohen, an American physician, was born at Philadelphia in September, 1857. He studied medicine under his brother, Dr. J. da Silva Solis Cohen, and at Jefferson Medical College, taking his degree in 1883. Hospital and private practice in Philadelphia followed, and he still lived there in 1902.

Teaching posts came fast. He showed pathology at the Philadelphia Polyclinic, then lectured on therapeutics at Jefferson from 1889. For fifteen years he professed clinical medicine at the Polyclinic. Jewish life claims the second half of the entry. He helped found the Jewish Publication Society of America, the American Hebrew's first editorial board, and the Jewish Theological Seminary Association.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-conque-abraham-:
Abraham ben Levi Conque, a cabalist, lived at Hebron in Palestine in the later seventeenth century. His cabalistic studies swept him into the Shabbethaian movement. He became one of the most earnest apostles of the pretended Messiah. Even Shabbethai Zebi's apostasy did not shake him, and he stayed a loyal follower until death.

Traveling as a collector for Palestine's poor, he worked through Germany and Russia winning converts to the cause. In 1689, at a Frankfort friend's request, he wrote a life of Shabbethai Zebi full of miracles he firmly believed. Jacob Emden's history of the movement cites it. His printed works include Abak Soferim at Amsterdam in 1704, with homilies on the Pentateuch and sermons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-day-hebrew-yom-: In the Bible, a day means first the season of light, from dawn to the coming out of the stars. The word also covers a full period of twenty-four hours. The entry explains a legal habit: part of a day can count as a whole day. A funeral late in the afternoon still counts as the first of seven mourning days. A child is circumcised on the eighth day even if only minutes of day one remained. The day is reckoned from evening to evening, except for sacrifices.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-diniz-denis-520:
Diniz, also written Denis, ruled Portugal from 1279 to 1325 and was styled the father of his country. The entry presents him as one of the most tolerant rulers of his time. He was well disposed toward the Jews of his kingdom.

He kept judges from encroaching on Jewish rights and barred unlawful witnesses against them. He did not force Jews to wear special badges or pay tithes to the Church, though canon law demanded both. He ordered officials to honor every privilege granted by him or earlier kings. In 1295 he made Don Judah, the chief rabbi, his treasurer. The Portuguese clergy complained to the pope about these favors, but the king held his course.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-drama-hebrew-53:
Hebrew drama is traced here from biblical dialogue and song to modern plays. Miriam's song, with women answering in chorus, hints at early dramatic form. Many scholars read the Song of Solomon as a true drama. The Book of Job, with its speakers, is another early case.

Then, the entry says, no Hebrew drama is known until the seventeenth century. A Greek Exodus play by Ezekiel of Alexandria stood alone in the second century B.C. Amsterdam, free and bookish, birthed the modern Hebrew drama. The entry lists original plays from the mid-seventeenth century on. Translations from other languages joined them late in the eighteenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eber-ben-pethah: Eber ben Pethahiah was a Moravian scholar who lived at Ungarisch-Brod early in the eighteenth century. Steinschneider thought the name might be only a pen name, the entry warns. It stands on the title-page of one book. That book, Mar'eh ha-Ketab we-Rashe Tebot, is a guide to Hebrew-German and its short forms. The entry gives no date for the book and no other facts of his life. A cross-reference sends readers to Hayyim ben Menahem of Glogau for more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elah-5507: Elah was a king of Israel and a son of Baasha. His father had taken the throne of the northern kingdom after the killing of Nadab. Elah himself ruled for less than two years. A plot formed against him inside his own court at Tirzah. Zimri, who led half of his chariots, killed him there. The entry quotes First Kings, which says Elah was drunk at the time. He was at the house of Arza, the steward of his house. Josephus adds that the army was away fighting at Gibbethon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliakim-gottsch: Eliakim Gottschalk of Rothenburg was a German Talmudist. He lived in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. He traced his line back to Meir of Rothenburg. One view makes him a Swabian rabbi of the same name. In that view he signed a legal ruling in 1611 with Isaiah Horwitz. His known book glosses the Targum on the Five Scrolls. It came out at Prague in 1618 with no author named. In its preface he tells of a like work on the Targum to the Law. That work is not described here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-euphrates-heb-p:
The Euphrates is the great river of nearer Asia, named in Genesis as the fourth river of paradise. The entry forms it from two branches. The Kur rises north of Erzerum, and the Murad issues from Lake Wan. They join, cut through the Taurus range, meet the Tigris, and empty below Bassora into the Persian Gulf.

Floods from the river made the soil rich, the entry stresses. In old times it served as a trade highway, open to large vessels as far as Babylonia. Scripture makes it a border of Israel's promised land. In the prophets it stands for the Assyrian world empire. Necho and Nebuchadnezzar fought their deciding battle on its banks. One passage in Jeremiah may mean a smaller stream instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fiametta-joseph: Joseph ben Solomon Fiametta was rabbi of Ancona, Italy, and died in 1721. His name is spelled in several ways by later writers, the entry notes. He wrote atonement prayers of the Italian rite. Those prayers were printed at Venice in 1712. His book of prayers and penitential hymns came out at Venice in 1709. He also wrote an approval for a work printed at Berlin in 1713, a praise poem printed in 1719, and one responsum on a tax paid by a community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-foa-eliezer-nah:
Eliezer Nahman Foa was an Italian rabbi and author who died at Reggio after 1641. He was a pupil of Moses Isserles. He had wide knowledge in Talmud and Cabala. At Reggio he founded a society whose title means Association of the Modest Ones. His book is a commentary on the Passover Haggadah.

The society printed it at Venice in 1641, during his lifetime. A corrected edition came out at Leghorn in 1809. It added many new notes and a commentary on Hallel. He also left a manuscript of five sets of sermons on the Pentateuch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankfort-on-th:
Frankfort-on-the-Oder is a chief town in the Prussian province of Brandenburg, on the left bank of the Oder. Its fairs likely drew Jews there early. An organized community existed in the fifteenth century. In 1546 the elector ordered the town council to let the Jew Simon slaughter animals in the Jewish rite. In 1551 Jews won free access to a city fair. The council resented such edicts and taxed the Jews heavily despite them.

In 1573 all Jews were driven from Brandenburg, and none could stay at Frankfort even in secret. Rich Jews were allowed to found a new community there in 1671. The townsfolk petitioned for expulsion again in 1688, giving sixteen reasons. A dishonoring poll tax was then imposed, and repealed only in 1787. In 1890 the town had 775 Jews in a population of 55,738. A closing section treats Hebrew printing. Its high point was a Talmud edition of 1698.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gans-eduard-650:
Eduard Gans, a German jurist born at Berlin on March 22, 1798, died there on May 5, 1839. He was a banker son who studied law at Berlin, Gottingen, and Heidelberg. Hegel and Thibaut shaped his thought at Heidelberg. By 1820 he taught at Berlin and drew crowds of hearers. His attack on the historical school of law drew wide notice.

In 1819 Gans joined Zunz and Moses Moser to found a society for Jewish culture and science. Its aim was to stem mass baptism and to spur Jewish work in farms, trade, science, and art. The group faded for lack of support. In 1825 Gans himself took baptism. Berlin then made him a law professor in 1826 and full professor in 1828.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gerona-formerly:
Gerona, a walled city in northern Spain, shows Jews in a papal note of 1002. The pope thanked its bishop for the tax of the Jewish community. Jews held houses and lands without curb. Church councils of 1068 and 1078 took a tenth for the state from any land a Jew bought from a Christian. Jews lived in a set quarter by the Onyar river.

King Jaime the Conqueror ruled them with justice. In 1229 he set their interest rate at 20 per cent. He named Bonastruc de Porta as town bayle. That scholar is matched with Moses ben Nahman, who debated Christians at Barcelona in 1263. Later years brought long rounds of attack. Clergy-led mobs wrecked Jewish homes, vineyards, and the burial ground.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-glogau-6707:
Glogau is a town in Prussian Silesia, Germany, counted at 20,529 people, including 863 Jews. Jews lived there as early as the eleventh century, near the Breslauer Thor. In 1442 their street was plundered and the synagogue destroyed, and in 1485 Duke Hans drove them out, forcing worship in secret beyond the city limits.

A new congregation formed a century later under privileges granted to the Benedict family, which built a synagogue in 1636 used for 260 years. Under Prussia, Jews gained political equality, helped by the Stein-Hardenberg laws, and another synagogue rose in 1892 at a cost of 300,000 marks. The entry lists noted Glogau Jews, among them Solomon Munk and Michael Sachs, and a line of its rabbis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goose-pl-pl-680:
The goose entry is a Talmudic study of the bird. It opens by setting the domestic goose apart from the wild goose. Talmudic marks differ: beak length, organs, and eggs in the ovary at once. The bird, being a water-fowl, has a very thin brain-membrane. Sabbath rules follow: holding a goose by its wings differs from holding a hen. A goose returns home at night.

The entry also gathers sayings and uses. Seeing a goose in a dream may promise wisdom. Geese gave flesh, feathers, fat, and lungs to households. Fat and lungs served as medicine. Geese helped in threshing. Rabba bar bar Ḥana tells a tall tale of desert geese fat enough to drip rivers of oil. Those geese, the tale says, await the righteous at the Messianic meal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grunfeld-josef-: Josef Grünfeld was an Austrian physician and writer. He was born at Gyönk, Hungary, on Nov. 19, 1840. He studied at Budapest from 1861 and Vienna from 1863. He took his degree at Vienna in 1867. He became privat-docent there in 1881. In 1885 he headed a division at Vienna's Poliklinik. His eye compendium ran through four editions. He was the first to use the endoscope, the entry says. He led the Oesterreichisch-Israelitische Union for more than eight years as a founder and president.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haddad-isaac-70: Isaac Haddad was a Talmudic scholar of Gerba, an island near Tunis, where he died in 1755. He studied under Ẓemaḥ ha-Kohen. He wrote two works, both printed at Leghorn after his death. "Toledot Yiẓḥaḳ," printed in 1761, gives novellæ on Haggadah and Midrashim. "Ḳarne Re'em," printed in 1765, gives novellæ on Rashi's and Mizraḥi's notes to the Pentateuch. It is followed by "Zera' Yiẓḥaḳ," his own notes on Midrashim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halle-on-the-sa:
Halle on the Saale is a university town in the Prussian province of Saxony. Jews settled there soon after the city's founding, early in the twelfth century. They lived in their own quarter, the Judendorf, with a synagogue and cemetery. Like Jews across Germany they were plundered and harried again and again, in 1206, 1261, 1349, and 1492, and in 1493 Archbishop Ernst expelled them outright.

Two centuries later a new community formed, when exiled Halberstadt families were let in during 1692. Old bars held: no land, no university, trade fenced by special laws. In 1724 students wrecked the synagogue and Jewish houses. Full citizenship came from the Westphalian government in 1808. A new synagogue rose in 1864, and the school held 130 children in 1903. The town counts 156,624 people, 1,300 of them Jews. A long tail to the entry tells of Hebrew printing at Halle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanina-b-dosa-7:
Hanina b. Dosa was a first-century scholar and miracle-worker, a pupil of Johanan b. Zakkai. Almost no halakot and few haggadot survive from him; his lasting fame rests on saintliness and the power of his prayers. His maxims teach that fear of sin must come before learning, and that works must outweigh learning, for learning to endure.

The entry retells his healings: the son of Johanan b. Zakkai recovered after Hanina prayed, and so did the son of Gamaliel II., whose fever Hanina declared gone before the messengers returned. A lizard bit him mid-prayer and died while he felt nothing. He lived at 'Arab in Galilee, poor and famed for Sabbath observance, and was buried there with his wife, around whom legend also gathered.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyun-nehemiah:
Nehemiah Hiyya ben Moses Hayyun, born about 1650, was a Bosnian cabalist of Sephardic stock. He trained in the Talmud at Hebron and briefly served as rabbi of Uskup. Then he wandered as merchant, scholar, and beggar. In 1708 he surfaced at Smyrna with a bold book.

That book taught that God holds three persons, a claim drawn from hidden Shabbethaian sources. Jerusalem's rabbis banned him and ordered the book burned before he even arrived. He found backers at Prague and Berlin, where his sermons and books were printed. At Amsterdam a leading rabbi fought him hard. The entry follows his trail of bans, patrons, and printings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heine-maximilia:
Maximilian Heine, born at Dusseldorf in 1805 or 1807, was a German physician and the youngest brother of Heinrich Heine. He took his medical degree in 1829. That year he joined the Russian army as a surgeon. He marched over the Balkans in 1830 and served in the putting down of the Polish rising.

Heine then settled in St. Petersburg as surgeon to a military school. He left the army with the title of councilor of state. With partners he founded a Russian medical journal, which he edited from 1844 to 1859. His books cover the city's medical layout, plague at Odessa, and travel letters. His memoir of his brother's family drew a poor response. He died on Nov. 6, 1879.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herodium-7607: Herodium was a fortified city three leagues south of Jerusalem, founded by Herod I on a rocky hill. Its citadel held royal rooms of great strength and splendor. It also served as a tomb for Herod. In Roman times it headed a district and fell late to Vespasian's army. The entry identifies it with a modern hill called the Frank Mountain, where citadel remains can still be seen. A second fortress of the same name stood toward Arabia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hesse-4907:
Hesse was a former landgraviate of the German-Roman empire, treated here through the history of its Jews. Early Jewish families lived under heavy taxes and limits as servants of the empire. Philip the Magnanimous first proposed expulsion in 1524, then protected Jews in 1532, then restricted them again.

The entry follows three later divisions, chiefly Hesse-Cassel and Hesse-Darmstadt. It traces protection, harsh edicts, and slow gains across centuries. Full emancipation came in stages, in 1808 under Westphalia, then again by law in 1833. District rabbis, schools, and aid societies close the Cassel section. Population and four rabbinate districts are given for 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hillel-b-zebi-h:
Hillel Salauter, whose full name is given as Hillel son of Zebi Hirsch Mileikovsky, was a Russian rabbi born in Zareche, near Wilna, in 1819. At twenty-five he became rabbi of Kreve. He then served in Salaty, Ponyevyezh, Shklov, and Khaslavich in turn, moving from one community to the next over a long career.

His last post was at Mstislavl, where he died on June 1, 1899. He ranked among Russia's foremost rabbis, the entry says. In 1894 he sat on the rabbinical commission at St. Petersburg. He left a manuscript work that his grandson began preparing for print. Some of his responsa appear in another rabbi's published collection of answers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hoga-stanislaus: Stanislaus Hoga was an English convert to Christianity who lived in London in the nineteenth century. He printed a set of Zion songs in 1834, English and German hymns turned into Hebrew. A second edition with additions came in 1842. He also wrote a Hebrew grammar of English for Hebrew readers in 1840. Another work weighed Judaism and Christianity in 1845. He turned Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress and another Christian work into Hebrew. It is said he later returned to Judaism, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-host-of-heaven-:
Host of heaven is a Bible phrase with more than one sense. The Hebrew word for host usually means an army. In the phrase Lord of hosts it most likely points to the armies of Israel. Host of heaven at first suggests the stars drawn up in battle order.

Many passages show sun, moon, and stars worshiped under this name. Kings such as Manasseh and Ahaz favored that cult. Other verses use the phrase for angels who attend God. The entry traces a shift. Star gods with their retinues gave way, in later and purer religion, to an assembly of angels around God, while the old army image stayed in poetry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-migas-meir-: Meir ibn Migas was a Spanish rabbi and president of the school at Seville who flourished in the eleventh century. He was the son of Joseph ibn Migas and the father of Joseph ibn Migas ben Meir ha-Levi. Late in life he had to leave Seville and retire to Toledo. The entry is very short. It gives no dates and names only two sources for these few facts about his family place and his last move.
