The researchers wanted to know which measures matter most and whether patients fall into natural activity groups.

Using statistical methods that compress many measures into a few main patterns, the team sorted roughly two hundred fifty patients into clusters. Daily step counts stood out among the measures that best separated the groups. Grouping patients this way could help clinics tailor activity advice instead of giving everyone the same generic guidance.
pmc-11641407:
Gui Xiong, Qing Liu, and four co-authors mapped a gene family in oats, in work published in twenty twenty-four. The genes, called LecRLKs, sit in cell walls and help plants sense stress. Oats matter as food and feed, and they can grow on salty land where other crops fail. The team hunted these genes in oats and two wild kin.

They found three hundred ninety such genes in all, split into three types. Most sit in the outer skin of cells, as expected. When salt stress hit, one hundred seventy-three of the genes switched on or off. Some copies did the same job, while others took on distinct roles. The map may help breed tougher oats.
pmc-11641907:
Jing Ma, Xue Li, and Chunru Wang present a two thousand twenty-four review of nanomaterials for pancreatic diseases. Cancer, pancreatitis, and diabetes of the pancreas all lack gentle, effective treatments. Tiny engineered materials may deliver drugs precisely where they are needed.

The review first explains how particle properties change pancreas behaviour. Surface tweaks and smart loading help particles reach the organ past normal delivery barriers. Uses are then surveyed disease by disease, from boosting radiation in cancer to protecting insulin-making cells. Readers get a structured tour of a fast-moving treatment frontier.
pmc-11642307:
Michael Kosson and colleagues study how printed cement beams handle heat. Their materials paper from twenty twenty-four varies internal patterns and ink recipes. Printed cement can hold hidden structures that casting cannot make. Those structures may store heat or move it in useful ways.

Beams used straight, honeycomb, and curved chord infill patterns. Some inks included a small share of nanoclay additive. Heat applied at one end was tracked with thermal imaging. Internal pattern mattered far more than ink recipe. Void shapes created a clear ranking of heat behaviour. A simple fin-style model helped explain the cooling patterns. Builders gain design rules for printed walls with better thermal control.
pmc-11643807:
Zhiyi Liu leads a seven-author team building a biochar material that strips toxic chromium from water and soil, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Hexavalent chromium is a notorious industrial pollutant. Loading biochar with nano-sized zero-valent iron creates a powerful scavenger.

Their synthesis uses bioleaching followed by co-pyrolysis of biomass. Iron lands on the char as mineral compounds, then converts to reactive metal during heating. In water, the composite removed about ninety percent of chromium at test concentrations. Removal capacity beat plain biochar by roughly seventy percent. In soil, the material passivated chromium over forty-five days. Kinetic and isotherm models describe the process. The work explains the mechanisms behind the cleanup.
pmc-11645307:
Giovanni Taccetti and his team sift germ-drug care of germ lung ills in cystic fibrosis. Their 2024 review sets out the best plans now for the most oft-found germs of the air paths in this ill.

Germ ills of the air paths are the main cause of ill health and death in cystic fibrosis. Two germs are drawn out most oft, and joint ills from more than one germ come oft. Ways to take tests split in how sharp they are. Throat tests do less well, while drawn-up phlegm matches wash ways that cut in. Care tracks three ways for the main germ. They are early wipeout, long-term hold-down, and flare-up care. That plan is shown to work for one key germ but not for the rest. For more than one stock germ, no proof guide is there. Picks are left to care staff.
pmc-11645507:
Yannick Vander Zwalmen and three co-authors present a single-patient case report of cognitive control training taken to an unusual extreme: fifty-five sessions over a year against depression. The training exercises the brain's control functions, and its mechanisms and time course remain murky. This participant completed ten initial sessions, then forty-five more, with questionnaires tracking cognitive and affective change throughout.

Task accuracy climbed from twenty-four percent at baseline to sixty-one percent shortly after training, settling near fifty percent at follow-up. Depression scores fell from twenty-three to three after the initial phase, and burnout symptoms dropped in parallel. Maladaptive emotion regulation wobbled variably. One case proves nothing generally, but it maps how benefits can unfold and persist at high training doses.
pmc-11657007:
Hansen and co-authors review how push and pull forces shape the blood-brain gate. Brain vessel cells form this gate and bar most blood parts from the brain. Shear from flow and stretch of the base sheet tune how tight the gate stays. With age, and in ills such as stroke and MS, those forces change. Flow blurs, the base sheet stiffs, and flare-ups strain the wall. The gate then leaks more, reacts less, and lets white cells cross.

Much is known of the chem cues that guide white cells in. The force cues in that step have drawn note just of late. The review maps force types, the cell parts that sense them, and one key channel clan. That clan, the TRP channels, gets close care here. Clearer maps may point to new care paths for brain ills.
pmc-11657707:
Oscar González and colleagues piloted mosquito nets in Guna Yala, Panama in 2024. Panama sprayed homes against malaria for decades. Spraying was the primary control tool. Treated bed and hammock nets were alternatives. An indigenous region hosted the pilot. Feasibility and acceptance were the questions.

Distribution proved operationally feasible overall. Communities first accepted nets well. Care for nets also started strong. Use then dropped drastically over time. Two years of follow-up showed that fall. Future rounds need promotion resources badly. Reasons for low use need study. Cultural fit may decide success.
pmc-11667607:
Belayneh Dessie Kassa, Mebratu Libanos, Kumlachew Geta, and Natnael Moges audit triage at an adult emergency unit in Ethiopia. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Triage sorts who is seen first and steers scarce care. Done late or wrong, it wastes time and can cost lives.

They pull charts at random from three years of visits at Debre Tabor hospital. One in five charts lacks a triage sheet. The warning score is summed right for a tiny share of patients. Most are wrongly triaged, near all of them set too low a rank. Colour class, score notes, and the use of set clinical signs all track with the end call. The team calls the state of triage alarming.
pmc-11677207:
Diana Merida and co-authors review, in a set way, exposure to acrylamide and risk to the heart and vessels. Their 2024 review covers a food contaminant that forms when food is cooked at high heat. Diet is the main source of it for people who do not smoke.

Twenty-eight studies were let in. Most were cross-sectional, and most came, in large part, from a sample in a national survey in the United States. Higher exposure to acrylamide was linked to a raised risk of death from disease of the heart and vessels. In a paradox, it was also linked, in a reverse way, to glucose, to lipid levels, to diabetes, to obesity, and to metabolic syndrome. Its reactive metabolite showed the pattern in reverse, linked to higher glucose, lipids, blood pressure, and obesity. The team hints that harm may act through its shift to that metabolite.
pmc-11677407:
Antonio Rolando and six colleagues published a beetle study in two thousand twenty-four on dung choice in the Alps. Dung beetles clean pastures and enrich soil, and Alpine herds draw rich communities of them. Worry arose that exotic alpacas, newly farmed in the region, might not support the beetles.

Traps baited with alpaca or cow dung were set along mountain transects. Most species entered both trap types, and species counts per trap were similar. But total beetle numbers ran higher in alpaca traps, driven by one dominant species. Eight of nine indicator species preferred alpaca dung. Temperatures matched between traps, so taste, not climate, explains the pull. The authors call the exotic dung a surprise hit.
pmc-11679607:
Rena Ikeda and co-authors tested a DNA snippet that both builds bone and blocks bone loss, in twenty twenty-four. The snippet, named iSN40, was known to spur bone-forming cells, by a route that did not use the usual DNA sensor. Since like snippets often act through that sensor to block bone-eating cells, the team asked whether iSN40 does the same.

In mouse cell cultures, iSN40 fully blocked the making of bone-eating cells, silencing their genes and raising opposing ones. Blocking the sensor, or changing the snippet's key motif, erased the effect and stopped the snippet entering cells. The effect held when bone-forming and bone-eating cells were grown together. The authors say iSN40 works on both sides of bone turnover, which makes it a hopeful drug seed for osteoporosis.
pmc-11679707:
Alessandra Raffini and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four preliminary study of physiotherapy for swimmer's shoulder pain in competitive athletes. The overuse condition plagues competitive swimmers and cuts performance. Fatigue worsens shoulder mechanics during long training and raises injury risk further.

Five young male swimmers with the condition and years of training took part. Sessions mixed dry-land crawl exercises with one fatiguing swim between them. Wearable motion sensors tracked three-dimensional shoulder angles before and after treatment and fatigue. Rotation range jumped after fatigue before therapy began. Physiotherapy effects were then measured against that fatigued state. Small numbers mark this as groundwork for a fuller trial.
pmc-11693407:
Hana Kijima and four colleagues report a rare, dangerous kidney infection that arose during pregnancy. Their patient was a thirty-two-year-old first-time mother with type 2 diabetes and past kidney infections. At twenty-nine weeks she developed emphysematous pyelonephritis, a disease in which gas forms inside kidney tissue and death rates are high.

Her symptoms worsened on antibiotics, but ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging secured the diagnosis. Antibiotic therapy alone at last brought improvement. She avoided the drainage procedures or kidney removal the disease often demands. She delivered safely at thirty-nine weeks. Reviewing past reports beside the case, the authors stress early imaging and care tuned to balance mother and fetus.
pmc-11716207:
Julie Gonneaud and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on schooling and brain health in men and women across adult life. More schooling is often tied to lower dementia risk, but its link with brain scans has been mixed.

The team scanned two hundred seven healthy adults aged nineteen to eighty-four with three kinds of imaging. Across the whole group, years of schooling showed no clear link with brain measures. A closer look by age band told a narrower story. Only in the older group did schooling track a larger key brain region, and only in women. A second, larger sample hinted that mental engagement in midlife mattered more than early schooling. The authors say the reserve that schooling builds may work in unlike ways for men and women.
pmc-11728107:
Aleksandra Asaturova and four co-authors published a review in twenty twenty-four on catching endometrial cancer earlier without the biopsy suite. Diagnosis still leans on ultrasound, hysteroscopy, and tissue sampling, burdensome for the many women at low risk. The review surveys gentler routes through body fluids and molecular markers.

DNA methylation signatures and tumor-derived nucleic acids circulating in blood headline the new approaches, under the liquid biopsy banner. Sensitivity and specificity data are weighed study by study. One attractive prospect is piggybacking on existing cervical screening programs, adding a second cancer to a visit women already make. The authors frame the goal as personalized, less invasive diagnostics, while noting the validation distance still to travel.
pmc-12443007:
Gaines and co-authors survey whether race and ethnic group shape how therapy patients view referrals. Therapists vary in skill with set problems and with patients of varied backgrounds. Patients in general say they want such track records used in matching them.

The survey reached 308 adults who knew, used, or sought mental health care via Mechanical Turk. It compared people of color with white respondents on two fronts. One was their past path to finding a therapist. The other was their stance on using therapist outcome data for assignment. Results suggested broad difficulty in finding a therapist across groups.
pmc-12490507:
Gokhan Ceylan and colleagues chart which respiratory viruses send children to intensive care. Their study from twenty twenty-four reviews admissions at a tertiary hospital. Lower airway infections are a leading danger for young children. Knowing the local virus mix guides staffing and isolation.

Most admitted children were under two years old. A combined RSV type was the single most common virus found. Many children carried an underlying chronic disease as well. A minority needed invasive breathing machines during care. High-flow oxygen supported most of the sickest children. A few progressed to severe lung distress syndrome. Virus testing on admission helps units plan beds and precautions.
pmc-12664207:
Mehrdad Salehi, Fahimeh Hormozi, and three peers ask front-line health staff in Iran what blocks mind care in first-line health posts. The work came out in 2025. To fold mind care into first-line care is the world's stock plan. It aims to widen reach and cut cost. Iran has pushed that plan for years, yet the care still lags.

The team spoke at length with 16 pros in Hormozgan state in the south. The talks took place in 2024. They read the typed talks with a stock form of close read. The blocks they found come from folks who run the plan each day. Work load, skill gaps, shame marks, and thin funds are the kinds of drag such tales name. The tale of Iran counts past its own edge. Many mid-fund lands run the same plan on their own soil.
pmc-12692607:
Anna Díez-Betriu and colleagues asked what sets the smoke point of virgin olive oil, the heat at which it starts to break down and smoke. The smoke point guides cooks and fryers, but it is still judged by eye, a shaky test. The team measured forty-eight oils and used math models to weigh each trait. Free fatty acids ruled the result: the more of them, the lower the smoke point.

Oils richer in saturated fats, and those that resist oxidation, smoked later. That is because fewer breakdown fumes form early. With just two or three routine lab values, the models guessed smoke points well. The twenty twenty-five study points to a cheap, firm way to rate frying oils, replacing a cook's squint with numbers any quality lab already collects.
pmc-12703907:
Liqing Yang and co-authors mine gene data for phospholipid-linked markers that could flag idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and foretell its course. The disease scars the lungs step by step; its cause is unknown and its outlook poor. Phospholipids have been tied to its biology. The team merged gene datasets to find genes whose activity set patients apart.

A network method flagged a module of close to 1,900 genes. Crossing that module with the changed genes and a known phospholipid gene list left 50 hub genes. Machine learning then built two tools: an eight-gene model to diagnose the disease and an eleven-gene model to judge prognosis. Both were tested on fresh datasets. Key genes were checked in single-cell data and in an animal model. One tool could help spot a disease often found late; the other could sort patients by likely course.
pmc-12717707:
Johanna Tietavainen and colleagues measured iron handling in Finnish patients during and after a hantavirus infection that attacks the kidneys. Ferritin, the iron storage protein, tracks severity in several bleeding fevers, and stray iron can injure kidney tissue. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team analyzed blood from patients in the acute phase and again in recovery. Iron-related measures were compared with white cell counts, platelet counts, and kidney injury markers to see which aspect of illness they mirror.

In the acute phase, ferritin, the iron-regulating hormone hepcidin, and a kidney stress marker were all high, while circulating iron and its carrier protein were low. Ferritin and hepcidin tracked with high white cell counts and low platelet counts, signs of inflammation and bleeding risk. None of the iron measures tracked with kidney injury severity itself, a negative result the authors state plainly.
pmc-12729307:
Maluleke and coauthors gauge how often patients buy germ drugs without a script. Drug-proof germs are a grave risk in South Africa. Loose sales of germ drugs help drive that risk. Sales without a script occur most for bladder and sexual infections.

The team asked patients as they left rural drug shops. Shops fell into three types in one rural province. Forms asked if drugs were sold and if a script was shown. Forms also asked what drove each sale choice. Full facts on sales can guide rules that curb drug proof spread.
pmc-12731807:
Alisa Timiryasova and a large team study what happens after cancer in people living with HIV, in a twenty twenty-five paper. Cancer is a leading cause of death in this group, yet outcomes after diagnosis are less known. The team followed 2,485 people from two big cohorts with the five most common cancers. They counted deaths and new serious events such as heart disease, diabetes, and second cancers.

Lung cancer carried by far the highest death rate, while Kaposi sarcoma carried the lowest. The most common new events differed by cancer type, from AIDS events after blood cancers to diabetes after lung and prostate cancers. Newer diagnosis years and other factors shaped risk. The results guide follow-up care after cancer in this group.
pmc-12734907:
Cai, Kouznetsova, and Tsigelny build a diagnostic model for long COVID in a study from twenty twenty-five. Long COVID, the lasting illness after COVID infection, is poorly understood and hard to tell apart from similar diseases. Blood chemistry may hold a useful signal.

The team trained a machine learning model on metabolites, small chemicals, that shift in long COVID. Molecular traits of those chemicals were the inputs. In held out tests the model spotted shifted chemicals with strong accuracy. It split long COVID from several similar diseases, such as chronic fatigue syndrome and Lyme disease. It failed on one, fibromyalgia. The work is an early step toward a lab based test.
pmc-12736307:
Onita leads a large team studying stress and food craving in teens with virtual reality, in work from twenty twenty-five. Acute stress can push people toward rich, tasty foods. Classic lab stress tests feel artificial, which limits what they reveal about real choices.

Teens faced a virtual social stress test and a virtual supermarket. Heart signals from an electrocardiogram tracked body stress responses. Those signals were linked to eating traits and food cravings in the virtual shop. Immersive settings give a closer to life test of how stress shapes teen food decisions, with relevance for obesity prevention programs.
pmc-12737107:
Romana Schmiedt leads a large team in testing how barrier add-ons affect the recycling of polypropylene pack film. The paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Multi-stuff films block air well but jam recycling. Plain polypropylene recycles more cleanly, yet needs a barrier that does not spoil the stream.

They blend in a barrier resin, a coated layer, and printed labels with mixed glues, then re-melt and mould test pieces. Low label shares barely dent quality. The barrier resin stiffens the stock and guards it from air, but cuts film toughness hard. The coating weakens stretch and adds scent shifts. Caps on each add-on that keep quality are spelled out for pack designers.
pmc-12748707:
FatemehSadat Yazdiniya and GholamReza Ansarifar propose a new control scheme for aircraft, in work from twenty twenty-five. A plane must hold its tilt and pitch steady despite gusts and faults. Their scheme pairs two ideas: a watcher that gauges outside pushes and faults in real time, and a sliding control law that fights them off.

The watcher feeds its gauge into the control law, which cancels much of the push. A learning method tunes the strength of the response. The pair prove the scheme stays stable on paper, in strict math terms. The aim is tighter tracking of the flight path and less drift when the air turns rough or the model falls short.
pmc-12771207:
Jie Wang, Si-Li Jin, Jing-Hua Wu, and Kai Zhu build a survival prediction model for metastatic breast cancer. Their multicentre study from twenty twenty-five uses a large national database. Standard scoring systems predict survival with limited accuracy. Machine learning models can be accurate but hard to explain.

Over a thousand patients trained and validated the models internally. A small hospital cohort supplied external validation data. Key survival factors came from adjusted regression analysis first. Four learning algorithms then competed on prediction quality. A forest-based model performed best in training and validation. The authors stress interpretability alongside accuracy for clinical use. Doctors gain a tool that aims to be both strong and understandable.
pmc-12785607:
Nurullah Dag and four co-authors test whether belly CT scans can flag weak bones in liver transplant patients. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such patients face bone loss, and a CT done for other care could double as a bone check if its density reads track the standard DXA scan.

They pair scans and DXA reads taken close in time for hundreds of recipients. CT density at the spine and thigh neck falls in step as DXA class worsens, and tracks its scores. Skill at spotting the worst class, osteoporosis, is fair at best. The team calls CT a quick, cheap side aid that can flag risk, not a swap for DXA.
pmc-12801507:
Shiyu Zhao, Cuiping Yang, Linlin Gao, Xuemei Fan, and Shiwei Liu published a transcriptomics study in twenty twenty-five hunting blood-vessel-related biomarkers for diabetic nephropathy. The kidney damage is a common diabetes complication, and new vessel growth plays a part in it. Finding causal marker genes could sharpen diagnosis and treatment.

The team combined differential expression analysis of public datasets with Mendelian randomization, which tests whether genes plausibly cause the disease. Four genes passed: CD44, HSPG2, LPAR1, and PTGES, each raising risk. They built a prediction nomogram from the genes and mapped related pathways and immune differences. Lab tests then confirmed the markers' expression, grounding the computer findings in tissue.
pmc-12805507:
Kapralos and Rai report two courses that teach game-based learning for health care. Virtual worlds are used more and more in schools. Teachers often lack skill in how to design and use them well. Both courses aimed to close that gap for undergraduates.

One course sits in a game design program in Ontario, Canada. The next sits in a biomedical design college in Singapore. Each course blends design, build, and test of learning games. Students made games tuned for medical training needs. The report logs what worked and what fell short. It ends with advice for teams who launch like courses.
pmc-12808307:
Fan Zhang leads a large team mapping the genes of alfalfa in this twenty twenty-five study. Alfalfa carries four copies of its genome, which may help it adapt to harsh climates. Why such doubled-up genomes do better than normal ones was poorly understood.

The team built a full gene atlas from thirteen genomes across the alfalfa family. Only about a fifth of genes sat on all four copies in their test plant, and half of those were shared across the whole genus. These shared genes were rich in climate-response roles, yet they also carried many harmful changes. The atlas frames both the edge and the cost of the fourfold genome.
pmc-12819607:
Thalles Anthony Duarte de Oliveira and a large team of co-authors test a phosphate compound alone and with a sugar ring compound against melanoma cells, aiming at their energy hubs. Melanoma cells bend their metabolism to survive stress, backed by fat stores and tough mitochondria. The study was published in twenty twenty-five.

The team treated human and mouse melanoma lines and normal skin support cells, then read survival, growth, energy hub charge, cell cycle, and death marks. The phosphate compound killed melanoma cells at far lower doses than normal cells. The pair boosted each other, the authors report. Shape changes under the microscope and a synergy check round out the work.
pmc-12826407:
Andreia Sa Lima and three co-authors report a man in his early seventies whose lung and kidney harm proved to be IgG4-related disease. Their case report appeared in twenty twenty-five. This rare state swells and scars tissue and can mimic cancer, germs, or immune ills, which delays the right call. Lung and kidney hits are both rare.

The man came in for what looked like lung germs and sharp kidney loss. Drugs for germs failed, and scans showed lung clouds that grew. Blood tests flagged the state, and a lung cut proved it. Months on, kidney scans named the same state there. Steroids helped at first, then a stronger drug held the state down for good.
pmc-12830607:
Piotr Lewandowski and ten co-authors published an ophthalmology methods study in twenty twenty-five building an objective way to judge corneal damage in pigs. Limbal stem cell deficiency clouds the cornea, and testing new cell therapies needs a model with bias-free measurements. The team injured four pig eyes and tracked healing for a month.

Scans confirmed the surface layer was fully removed and swelling peaked around a week. Tissue analysis showed thickening, surface keratinization, inflammation, and new blood vessels. Computer measurements of roughness, thickness variation, and cell density separated injured from healthy eyes clearly. The authors offer the metric set, data, and code as endpoints for preclinical therapy trials.
pmc-12837907:
Aadil Manzoor Baba and colleagues study how chemical tags on DNA packaging proteins silence two blood-vessel-blocking genes in throat cancer. Their 2025 study links gene silencing to the tumour's ability to grow new blood vessels.

Available vessel-blocking drugs work poorly in this cancer, prompting a search for new angles. In tumour tissues and cell lines, the two protective genes were switched down while two tag-removing enzymes were raised. Acetylation marks on the packaging proteins were correspondingly reduced. Blocking those enzymes, silencing one of them, or restoring a protective gene changed vessel growth in laboratory and tissue assays. The inhibitor drug experiments began reversing the silencing pattern described in the results.
pmc-12843807:
Jun Chen and six colleagues review experimental research on micro pulsating heat pipes, a cooling technology for dense electronics. As chip power density climbs, heat becomes the bottleneck for performance and reliability. These pipes move heat through oscillating liquid slugs without any pump. They beat rival technologies on simplicity and safety, avoiding leaky microchannels and inefficient thermoelectrics. At micro scale, though, size, wall, and interface effects make their behavior erratic.

The review gathers experiments on the two-phase flow patterns inside the pipes and how heat transfer follows from them. Many groups have probed these mechanisms, but no thorough experimental review existed. Organizing the evidence helps engineers predict when a pipe will pulse stably. The twenty twenty-five synthesis targets designers of cooling for compact, high-power devices.
pmc-12860407:
Sean Louzon and seven co-authors study a histone form called H2BE in the brain, by age and by cell type. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Histones pack DNA, and swapped forms build up in the brain through life. Past work showed this form shapes DNA pack, nerve gene use, and mouse acts, but its roles past nerves were vague.

The form proved rich in astrocytes and rose with age in both astrocytes and nerves. In young cells of both kinds it boosted link genes and was key for link work. In old brains, its loss dulled age gene shifts in both kinds. Old mice that lacked it lost long recall but gained short task recall.
pmc-13126607:
Fromence Nyambu Mwachofi, Anthony Kebira Nyamache, and two co-authors pair zinc oxide particles with garlic extract against germs. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, targets two common disease bacteria. Drug resistance keeps growing worldwide, which drives the search for new germ killers. Garlic has long been known for germ-fighting compounds.

The team made the tiny zinc particles by a gel method. Lab checks confirmed the particles formed as planned. They then blended the particles with garlic extract. Tests on lab strains of both bacteria gauge the kill power of each mix. The pair may work better together than either alone, a common hope for such blends.
pmc-13136507:
Bita Bahrami Gholami and co-authors run a randomized trial of hippotherapy, therapy on horseback, to improve balance in older men. Aging brings loss of strength, balance, and coordination. Riding a horse forces the rider's body to adjust again and again, which may train balance. The team used a Biodex balance platform for exact measures, a first for this kind of trial in healthy older adults.

The men, aged 60 to 70, all moved on their own and had medical clearance to ride. The training group rode for 16 sessions over 8 weeks, two half-hour rides a week. The platform measured fall risk, stability, and sway front-to-back and side-to-side. Fall risk dropped sharply in the riding group next to controls, with a large effect size. The result backs horse riding as a potent balance trainer for older adults.
pmc-13155607:
Rehab Taha leads a team on gene faults in Thai bile duct cancer. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with cancer tied to liver fluke. That fluke is a major risk in Southeast Asia.

Groups held cancer folks, fluke sick folks, and healthy controls. Gene faults in key cancer and stress genes were typed. KRAS and CREBBP are named in the title as foci. Links to clinic traits and outlook were also checked. The study shows links, not proof of cause, they stress. A group specific gene sign may emerge.
pmc-13165907:
Vanchha Chandrayan and Ignacio Alvarez survey a young field: language models riding along in the car to watch and help the driver, in this survey from twenty twenty-six. Large language models can reason in words, which suits a job that depends on context: is the driver tired, distracted, or confused? Past work, though, came in scattered pieces, each tackling one slice.

The survey gathers the pioneers: the frameworks that chain reasoning steps, the test sets and data collections, and the designs that mix camera, sound, and text. It notes methods that keep a human in the loop to correct the model. The authors add a human-centered scorecard of their own, judging systems on trust and clarity, not just accuracy. They close with a roadmap: the field needs shared tests and open designs before such copilots earn a place in real cabins.
pmc-13171407:
Mukhsina Akhmadalieva, Gamze Talih, Aydın Tuncay, Isın Gunes, and Ayşe Ülgey compare two breathing strategies used while the heart-lung machine runs in heart surgery. Their observational study was published in twenty twenty-six. Lung problems after such surgery are common, and the energy a ventilator delivers may play a role.

In one group of one hundred and twenty-five patients, breathing was paused once the machine took over. In a second group of one hundred and twenty, gentle small breaths continued. The energy measure, called mechanical power, was read before, after, and in intensive care. It did not differ between the groups at any point. Patients were watched a week for lung problems. The study gives surgeons data on a debated detail of bypass care.
pmc-13185007:
Marco Krasselt reviews the shingles vaccine for people whose immune systems are damped by disease and drugs, in this solo review from twenty twenty-six. People with inflammatory rheumatic diseases catch shingles far more often than others, helped along by immune-suppressing drugs. The vaccine in question is a recombinant shot, not a live virus, and it guards healthy older adults for at least ten years.

Newer studies in these patients show strong protection, with one real-world cohort seeing relapses of shingles fall by about ninety-five percent after vaccination. The worry is flares of the underlying disease. One safety database flagged flares in a small share of patients, while trials found no clear rise against placebo. Major guidelines now back two doses for adults at risk, even on strong immune drugs. Krasselt's advice is to vaccinate, warn patients about short-term flares, and watch them briefly afterward.
pmc-13191807:
Marina Piergianni and a large team pool data on twin pregnancies where one twin dies in the womb and a blood disorder is in play. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The disorder, TAPS, makes one twin short of blood and the other rich in it. Most past work on a lone twin death came from plain cases or an other twin disorder.

They gather the small set of such cases in print. Death of the co-twin is rare after the first loss. No newborn deaths show. Early birth is very common, in most cases before the last weeks. Brain oddities show in a share of scans, both before and after birth. Data are too thin to split by type or stage.
pmc-13193707:
Jinglei Tian is first author on a 2026 systematic review of large language models in colorectal cancer care. Colorectal cancer is a leading cause of cancer illness and death, and guideline-based care is complex, with much clinical data buried in unstructured text. Language models promise help, but evidence specific to this cancer was scattered.

Searching six databases through April twenty twenty-six, the authors included thirty-seven original studies, mostly from China and the United States, with GPT models most often tested. Models helped extract data from clinical text, educate patients, aid diagnosis, and support decisions. Tailored and image-aware models sometimes beat general ones, and prompt design strongly shaped results. Quality, privacy, and generalizability concerns remain.
pmc-13197307: Yang An and colleagues are the authors of a study retracted in a 2026 note in Lasers in Medical Science. The study claimed green laser light helped orthodontic tooth retention in rats. After publication, an inquiry found overlapping and matching figure panels within the work and against another paper. The editor lost trust in the work as a whole, and the authors agreed to the retraction.
pmc-13202107:
Creams, gels, and biological dressings compete to heal diabetic foot ulcers, and a 2026 systematic review headed by Lihong Chen ranks them against each other. The review and network meta-analysis gathers randomized trials of topical therapies, a treatment area where direct head-to-head comparisons are scarce.

Searching three databases through early 2025, the authors included fifty-one trials with 6,161 patients and twenty-three different interventions. Twelve topical therapies improved healing rates over standard care, and placenta-derived products showed the largest benefit while also reducing adverse events in the analysis. Evidence quality was mostly low to moderate, so the authors urge better trials before firm treatment rankings.
pmc-13202907:
Finding one small overactive parathyroid gland before surgery decides how small the operation can be, and a 2026 study led by Felicitas Fries contrasts the imaging used to find it. The retrospective article reviews preoperative localization plans for primary hyperparathyroidism at a specialized thyroid center.

The cohort covers 325 patients who had minimally invasive parathyroid surgery between January 2015 and December 2023. Most patients began with neck ultrasound and scintigraphy, with MRI, CT, or specialized PET imaging added when first results were inconclusive. The study assesses how accurately each method and combination located the adenoma, and how thyroid disease, earlier surgery, and gland size influenced performance.
pmc-13207907:
Giulia Coco and six co-authors test how well lens power formulas work when cataract and glaucoma surgery are combined. Their twenty twenty-six article deals with phacotrabeculectomy, one operation that removes a cataract and adds a drainage channel for open-angle glaucoma. Picking the right lens power is tricky, since the combined surgery shifts the eye's measures.

Sixty eyes from forty patients were checked up to a year and beyond. Seven formulas were scored on their prediction error. Most leaned toward a long-sighted shift, while one leaned the other way. The absolute errors were close, with no formula clearly ahead. Most eyes landed within one diopter of target under every formula.
pmc-13211607:
Prescription apps could relieve crowded rehabilitation clinics, and a 2026 simulation study authored by Christoph Wallner prices that shift for German occupational rehabilitation. The multilevel simulation uses administrative data from five statutory accident insurers covering about twenty-six million people, modeling digital therapeutics inside physiotherapy pathways.

Ten thousand Monte Carlo runs produced average yearly net savings in the tens of millions of euros, with savings in about nine of ten simulated futures. Adjusting for how few users stay engaged long term trimmed the projected savings only slightly in the model. Break-even held unless app prices rose far above current levels, and waiting-time modeling suggested capacity relief for clinics.
pmc-13214107:
Lisa D. Hawke and a large team ask in 2026 what people with lived experience of mental illness and addiction, plus their caregivers, need in order to join research teams properly. Their voices improve studies, yet inaccessible meetings and processes shut them out.

Twenty experienced contributors joined five focus groups, guided throughout by a working group of peers and caregivers. Four themes emerged: keep accessibility an open, ongoing conversation; offer a range of supports; let people contribute in flexible ways; and pay fairly for their time. One participant's remark about truly discussing each member's needs gives the study its title. Planning access from the start, the authors say, makes engagement genuine.
pmc-13214207:
Nilmini Wijemunige leads a large Sri Lankan team piloting in 2026 a handheld eye camera whose artificial intelligence reads retinal photos taken by non-specialist health workers. Diabetes is exceptionally common in Sri Lanka, and eye specialists are too few to screen everyone at risk of blinding retinal damage.

Workers with brief training photographed both eyes of 119 clinic participants, before and after drops widened the pupils. Before dilation nearly half the participants had at least one unusable image, a share that fell sharply afterwards, especially among older people and those with cataracts. Against a specialist's examination, the device's referral calls reached moderate sensitivity and specificity, with poor image quality driving most errors.
pmc-13214407:
Hanna Wachten and Jana Strahler sort in 2026 the tangled overlap between obsessive healthy eating, exercise addiction, and disordered eating. Whether the first two stand as disorders in their own right is hotly debated, partly because they blend into eating pathology.

Six hundred sixty-one survey respondents completed standard questionnaires on eating, exercise, body image, and self-esteem. Statistical profiling found five groups, including two healthy ones. One troubled group mixed high scores on all three problems with the worst self-esteem and strongest body worries. Exercise addiction appeared alone in one mild group with favourable body image. Healthy-eating obsession never appeared alone, always intertwined with disordered eating, which questions its independence as a diagnosis.
pmc-13215207:
Marco Aviña and colleagues pool in 2026 the raw data from 100 past tests of which immigrants people prefer to admit. The set is the largest of its kind. It holds close to one and a half million fake profiles, judged by more than 140,000 people in 36 lands.

Traits tied to work, culture, aid, and legal steps all swayed the picks. Tastes looked much the same across lands and groups. Two faint shifts stood out. Work traits have grown in weight over the years. Also, how a person feels about immigration as a whole colours how they judge each single profile. A foe of immigration rates even strong profiles coolly. The work sharpens a decade of polls and shows where views might move.
pmc-13216207:
B. Presswell and co-authors present a 2026 species description of a parasitic roundworm new to science, found in the throat of sacred kingfishers in New Zealand. The worm belongs to a genus whose members almost always live in the stomach or gullet of birds.

Morphology and DNA sequencing together set the species apart, and the team names it Skrjabinoclava pharyngophila. Its throat-dwelling habit is unique in the genus. Infection was common in North Island birds and absent in South Island birds, which fits the kingfishers' sedentary habits and suggests a local intermediate host. The find is the first record of the genus in Australasia and supplies its first public DNA sequence.
pmc-13218007: Virology Journal issued this short correction in 2026 for an article by Alejandra Centurión and co-authors on furin as a target against mosquito-borne viruses. The notice is a correction only: in one background sentence, an arrow symbol in a protein cleavage motif was accidentally printed as the letter i, and the notice supplies the corrected sentence. The original article has been amended, and nothing else in it changes.
pmc-13218107:
Stéfanie Fréel and colleagues map the published research on mental health and psychosocial support during active armed conflict in a 2026 scoping review. More than two billion people live with ongoing war, and the mental health damage is well documented. Far less is known about which support programs actually run while fighting continues, and how well they are evaluated.

The review included 47 papers: 19 on children and adolescents only, 14 on adults only, and 14 covering both groups. Only 12 papers tested trauma-focused interventions, the approaches aimed directly at traumatic stress. Many studies reported significant improvements in post-traumatic stress, depression, and anxiety among adult civilians and former combatants, along with better day-to-day functioning. Results in children were mixed, as were results for aggression, drug dependence, and social skills in former fighters. Because studies used widely different designs and instruments, the authors call for stronger research standards in conflict settings.
pmc-13218507:
Maad S. Ytemi and colleagues characterize Commicarpus in Saudi Arabia in a 2026 taxonomic study. The genus, part of the four-o'clock family, holds thirty to thirty-five species across the tropics and subtropics, and five of them grow in Saudi Arabia, in the west and southwest. Distinguishing these species requires more than a glance at flowers.

Surveys collected the species, and the team examined them at three levels: outward form, anatomy, and pollen structure. Stem texture, leaf traits, flower structure, and fruit shape separated the species, while cross-sections of stems, leaves, and stalks revealed differences in layers and bundle arrangement. Pollen grains proved informative, differing in size, shape, pore diameter, and spine length; grains were very large in three species and merely large in the other two. The authors assembled two keys, one from outward characters and one from stalk anatomy, as a reference for the region's flora.
pmc-13218607:
Elizabeth Leung and colleagues present a 2026 case of a hard-to-treat infection caused by carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales, bacteria that shrug off carbapenems, antibiotics held in reserve for the toughest infections. A forty-five-year-old woman, previously healthy, arrived with a nonhealing arm injury. Six months earlier she survived a car crash in Nigeria that broke her right upper arm and forearm, treated with washouts and fixation hardware.

Two months after the injury she developed a surgical-site infection while in Nigeria, received surgery and antibiotics, and her forearm bones never united. After moving to Canada she presented to an emergency department, where the organism was identified. The authors use the case to underline how quickly bacteria acquire resistance and how such infections are rising. Newer beta-lactam antibiotics can treat these organisms, but getting susceptibility testing and starting the drug quickly remains difficult, shaping this patient's course.
pmc-13219107:
Mohammed Abrahim coins the term Midlife Wellness Medfluencers in a 2026 essay on doctors who share their midlife journeys online. Influencers, or medfluencers, speak to the public with the authority of credentials, and a subgroup are mid-career doctors telling of personal reinventions around diet, exercise, and lifestyle medicine. Their stories are compelling, and that is the problem the essay takes up.

Experience can generate hypotheses, Abrahim argues, but one person's transformation is not generalizable evidence, and blending the two undermines evidence-based practice. The essay traces the midlife crisis from Elliott Jaques in 1965 through challenges to its universality. It also reflects on why self-reflection in midlife, a normal passage, becomes a selling force when amplified by social media. The author urges teamwork between universities and credible physician influencers, so that experiential insight is tested against data while the line between anecdote and evidence stays drawn for audiences.
pmc-13219607:
Agneta Herlitz and colleagues test whether many sex differences add up to something large in a 2026 study. Taken one at a time, differences between men and women in cognition, personality, and interests are small, with distributions that overlap heavily, which has led some to argue they barely matter. The team asked what happens when thirteen measures are read.

Participants aged thirty-five to forty-five, 1,465 women and 1,302 men, completed cognitive tests and questionnaires on personality and interest in people versus things. Differences on the single measures ran in the expected directions and were modest alone. Combined in one model, they sorted eighty percent of participants by sex. The combined profile explained a substantial share of the variation in occupational gender segregation, the pattern of men and women clustering in different jobs. The authors argue that waving off small differences one by one misses their collective weight in shaping outcomes.
pmc-13220007:
Jung-Won Lim and colleagues report midterm results for replacement ankles, asking whether a crooked ankle before surgery dooms the outcome, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Total ankle replacement swaps a worn joint for a three-part mobile implant. Ankles tilted inward or outward have long worried surgeons.

The team reviewed one hundred twenty-four ankles treated at one center, followed at least two years, and sorted them by tilt: inward, neutral, or outward. Pain scores, function scores, and joint movement ended alike in all three groups. Most X-ray measures improved, though inward-tilted ankles kept some residual inward tilt at the heel. Extra corrective steps during surgery did much of the work, and revision-free survival was strong. The authors conclude that tilt, even marked inward tilt, need not bar replacement, provided the deformity is corrected as part of the operation.
pmc-13222007:
Zhikang Tang and colleagues argue for rebalancing, rather than blocking, a protein-folding chaperone in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2026 review. The chaperone Hsp90 sits at the center of the cell's protein quality network. Some partner proteins push it to stabilize toxic tau, while others help clear tau away.

Older drugs that shut down Hsp90 broadly showed limited clinical success. Newer ideas target single partner interactions, adjust the chaperone's tail region, or prompt immune cells to clear harmful proteins. Obstacles include crossing into the brain, choosing between chaperone forms, and proving long-term safety. Most evidence is still preclinical, which the authors state plainly while making their case.
pmc-13222407:
Loubna Taali and co-authors describe a parotid gland cancer that imaging made look like a harmless cyst, in a 2026 case report. A 49-year-old patient had a painful swelling behind the left ear plus partial facial paralysis on that side. Ultrasound and MRI suggested a well-defined benign cyst sitting apart from the parotid gland.

Facial nerve weakness is a warning sign that overrode the reassuring scans. Tissue examination after surgery pointed to mucoepidermoid carcinoma involving the parotid region, with spread into the skin. Treatment proceeded to total parotid removal, neck node dissection, and radiation. The authors warn that any mass near the parotid with nerve dysfunction counts as malignant until proven otherwise.
pmc-13222507:
Eyob Ayenew Engidaw and co-authors recount a bowel knot that masqueraded as a ruptured ovarian cyst, in a 2026 case report from Ethiopia. A 33-year-old woman arrived with sudden abdominal pain, vomiting, blocked bowels, and shock from internal bleeding. Ultrasound showed swollen bowel loops and bloody free fluid, which fit the gynecologic explanation.

Her instability ruled out CT scanning, so surgeons operated directly. They found two liters of bloody fluid, healthy ovaries, and one loop of ileum knotted around another, leaving a long segment dead. Removal of the gangrenous bowel and a stoma came first, with reconnection a week later and good recovery. Bloody fluid, the authors stress, does not rule out strangulated bowel.
pmc-13222607:
Sun Young Kang, Sanghyun Roh, and Jeong-An Gim scope Korean research on genes and lung function in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, in a 2026 scoping review. The source is the Korean Genome and Epidemiology Study. Most genetic evidence for this disease comes from European-ancestry populations. Seven databases were searched through April 2026 for Korean cohort work on genetics or epigenetics of lung traits.

Twelve studies qualified from the screened records. Most studied spirometry measures and decline over time rather than diagnosed disease. Genome-wide scans, exome arrays, gene-environment tests, and risk scores all appeared, with recurring signals near two genomic regions. Newer work follows lung function trajectories, giving population-specific evidence while clinical COPD genetics stays thin.
pmc-13223707:
Yu Li and co-authors test how superfine grinding changes forsythia fruit powder, in a 2026 study. Forsythia fruit has served Chinese medicine for centuries and feeds food and cosmetic uses today. Four sieved grades were compared, from traditional coarse powder down to particles under thirty micrometers across.

Finer grinding broke far more cell walls, multiplied surface area, and improved wetting. Active flavonoids and two marker compounds peaked in the 150-mesh grade, which also showed the strongest anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity in assays. Nineteen aroma compounds were shared across all grades. Grinding to that middle-fine grade, rather than the finest, gave the best quality and function for functional food development.
pmc-13224007:
Ting-Ling Ke and Linyi Chen present a study from twenty twenty-six on muscle cancer cells whose mitochondria bunch near the nucleus. The cells come from rhabdomyosarcoma, a rare cancer. They fail to mature into muscle as they should. Their power plants are swollen and stuck in a ring round the core. The team asks what transport flaw drives that bunching.

The cells lack much of a myosin motor that hauls cargo toward the cell edge. They hold too much of a dynein motor that hauls the other way, plus its adaptors. Adding the myosin back partly spread the mitochondria out. Blocking dynein spread them and let both cell lines mature. The work ties transport balance to muscle growth.
pmc-13224707:
Tatsuro Miyoshi and co-authors test a 2026 skincare delivery system built from tiny bubble-like carriers called niosomes. The carrier ingredient, GDS-23, also switches on the cell's antioxidant master switch, Nrf2. The team asked whether it could both push ingredients through skin and raise the skin's own uptake machinery for vitamin C.

In human skin cells, the ingredient raised production of two transport proteins, including the main vitamin C transporter, and blocking Nrf2 weakened that effect. A three-dimensional artificial skin model showed the carriers improved penetration. Vitamin C loaded into the carriers protected the model tissue best against chemical oxidative damage, beating cysteine-loaded carriers and supporting the dual-action design.
pmc-13225007:
Shuyun Zhao and co-authors present a 2026 emergency case of a perforated pyometra, a pus-filled uterus that ruptured in a 69-year-old postmenopausal woman. She arrived with severe abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, and septic shock, and scans suggested a burst gut. Surgery instead found a four-centimetre hole in the back wall of the uterus with infected fluid throughout the abdomen.

Surgeons removed the uterus and ovaries and drained the infection, and she went home after twenty-eight days despite breathing failure along the way. Reviewing sixty-six published cases, the authors found roughly eighty-four percent were misdiagnosed before surgery. They recommend keeping this rare cause in mind and favour removal plus thorough drainage.
pmc-13225307:
Hongwei Yang and colleagues published a 2026 study testing a cancer drug on retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma is an eye cancer of young children. The drug abemaciclib already treats some breast cancers. It blocks proteins that push cells to divide. The team asked whether it works differently here.

Gene data from patient tumors highlighted new targets. Lab tests measured cancer cell growth and death. The drug slowed tumor cells and triggered damage signals. Mouse models carried human tumor grafts for testing. Treated tumors grew less than untreated ones. The results suggest a second use for an existing drug.
pmc-13226507:
Le and colleagues edit a papaya gene to build resistance against papaya ringspot virus. The virus causes the crop's worst disease, cutting harvests across the tropics. In other plants, the gene eIF4E and its partner copy are known doors that such viruses use to infect cells, and blocking them can bring resistance.

Papaya's own versions had never been tested in a systematic way for this role. Using CRISPR and Cas9 editing, the team altered the gene and checked whether plants stood up better to the virus. Success would offer growers a built-in defence, bred into the plant rather than sprayed on it, for a fruit valued as food and medicine.
pmc-13232807:
Afua O Asare and colleagues examine in 2026 what shapes eye screening results and follow-through for schoolchildren in Kumasi, Ghana. An enhanced program screened more than eleven hundred children aged four to twenty-two for suspected eye problems. About a third were flagged, and about a third of those referred actually completed the referral.

Children in public schools showed lower odds of a suspected disorder than peers in private schools after adjustment. Family income shaped the second step more than the first, with the poorest children far less likely to complete referral. A screening that families cannot act on wastes its own findings. Referral support matched to local context is the gap this pilot exposes.
pmc-13235107:
Craig Paterson and colleagues reviewed in 2026 whether urine or spinal fluid tests could detect glioma brain tumours early. Gliomas cause many years of life lost, and diagnosis today depends on scans and tissue biopsy. Fluid samples could offer a less invasive route, since spinal fluid touches the tumour while urine is easy to collect. Searches of three databases gathered studies testing proteins, metabolites, loose DNA, or small RNA markers.

Twenty studies covering several hundred patients and controls met the review criteria. Most work used spinal fluid, while only five studies tested urine markers. Studies differed too much in markers, methods, and patients for a combined statistical analysis. Small samples and limited study numbers restrict firm conclusions about accuracy. The authors call for larger, well-designed studies before either fluid can support routine early detection.
pmc-13236107:
Kahn Rhrissorrakrai and seven co-authors test whether quantum computers can learn from very small health datasets. Small samples are common in medicine, where each test can cost a great deal. The team built several kinds of quantum ensemble models, which vote among many small learners. They ran them in simulation and on real quantum hardware with up to fifty-six qubits.

The models were tried on made-up data and on gene data from kidney cancer patients, to predict who would respond to immune therapy. A new cosine-based quantum model learned well from few samples. The quantum ensembles matched classical ones while using far fewer learners. The paper offers design lessons for learning on scarce data.
pmc-13236907:
Jia Tao and colleagues reported in 2026 a hospital bacterium, Providencia huaxiensis strain PR66, that resists every antibiotic tested, including carbapenems. Genome sequencing showed the strain had first been misidentified as a close relative. Its DNA carries many resistance genes spread across the chromosome and three plasmids.

The gene for the powerful NDM-1 carbapenem-destroying enzyme sits on a newly described mobile element built into the chromosome. Lab mating tests showed this element can jump into E. coli and stay there stably, passing the resistance on. The finding warns that mobile elements can move last-resort drug resistance into new species. Infection control teams may need to watch this genus more closely.
pmc-13237007: Hesamzadeh and colleagues publish an author correction to their paper on computer-designed antioxidant peptides. The correction fixes one methods sentence about the DPPH test, a standard lab check of antioxidant strength. The corrected sentence states that the peptide sample was mixed with the DPPH solution in ethanol, stirred in the dark for half an hour at room temperature. Small method details like solvent and timing decide whether other labs can repeat the test exactly, which is why journals correct them on the record.
pmc-13238007: Jiang and colleagues publish a correction to their review of selective autophagy in cancer. After publication, the authors found a large mismatch between the review's in-text citation numbers and its reference list, affecting more than half of all references. The correction realigns every in-text number with the reference it should point to. The authors also flag errors in several figures that had been reprinted from earlier sources, and put those right as well. Reference accuracy lets readers trace claims to sources, so journals fix such faults openly.
pmc-13239607:
Ibtissam El Harch and colleagues estimate how much lung disease in Morocco stems from household air pollution in a 2026 secondary analysis. Smoke from solid fuels burned indoors is a known hazard, and the team combined survey exposure data with pooled risk figures to calculate the share of illness it causes.

For adults over forty, indoor pollution accounted for roughly a quarter of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in women and a smaller share in men. Lung cancer showed a similar pattern by sex. Estimated case counts ran into the hundreds of thousands for the chronic lung condition, with yearly direct medical costs in the hundreds of millions of dollars.
pmc-13239907:
Jia Peng, Jing Liu, and Zhihuan Huang study wild plants growing among planted greenery in city housing areas in a 2026 survey. Residential green spaces in Hengyang, China, host both deliberate plantings and spontaneous herbs that arrive on their own, and the team asked how the cultivated layer shapes the wild one.

Across twenty-one sites they recorded 145 spontaneous species, most of them rare occasional visitors rather than common residents. Plots with no cultivated cover, or with a lawn grass dominant, held the richest wild communities. Dense ornamental plantings reduced diversity. Stability of the wild community depended more on its many occasional species than on total richness, a lesson for greener design.
pmc-13240207:
Fast and colleagues show that a newly found chemical switch tunes an enzyme modern humans inherited partly from Neanderthals. The enzyme, NAT1, processes certain drugs and cancer-linked chemicals and helps handle folate. Most people today carry one form of it, but some carry the older Neanderthal version, gained through ancient interbreeding, with two small amino acid differences.

Those differences alone, the team found, do not change the enzyme's activity. The real control is a phosphorylation site, a spot where a phosphate tag can be attached, newly identified in modern humans. Such fine control may matter because NAT levels are tied to cancer risk and birth defects, and this work shows where evolution actually adjusted the dial.
pmc-13241507:
Mahran and co-workers at Menoufia University tested whether human placental extract can shield rat kidneys from methotrexate damage. The chemotherapy drug is known to injure the kidney through oxidative stress. Male albino rats were split into four groups for the experiment. Treatments covered plain saline, the extract alone, the drug alone, and both agents together.

Methotrexate alone cut body weight and drained antioxidant defenses, including glutathione and protective enzymes. It also raised a lipid damage marker, thickened the blood, and visibly harmed fine kidney structure. Rats given the extract alongside the drug fared better on weight, chemistry, tissue structure, and electrical tissue measures. The team credits the extract's antioxidant support for the protection.
pmc-13241607:
Ogunbode and co-authors at Bowen University surveyed how households store water in Iwo Township, in Nigeria's Osun State. Seasonal supply swings make home storage essential in the tropical town. The survey reached seven hundred fifty-six households across four sections during 2023. Female household heads were prioritized, since they usually manage the water.

Steel and plastic drums led storage choices, followed by buckets and overhead tanks. Wells and boreholes supplied nearly nine in ten households. Factor analysis distilled eight drivers of storage choices, led by household age makeup and toilet count. The authors argue that family traits and assets shape storage more than supply alone, and they recommend affordable, safe storage support.
pmc-13242207:
Ping Li and co-authors report a 2026 randomized trial of a shoulder nerve block for scapular fracture surgery. Shoulder blade fractures cause strong pain around the back of the shoulder. The trial tested a block targeting the muscles behind the shoulder blade, given with ultrasound guidance alongside general anesthesia.

Patients receiving the block reported lower pain across the first two days than the sham group, with the advantage fading by the second day mark. They also needed less opioid during surgery and waited longer before asking for rescue pain relief. Recovery quality scores were higher at both follow-up points. Breathing muscle function on the treated side was unaffected. The authors present the block as an effective option with room for wider use.
pmc-13242307:
Liao and colleagues at Cornell mapped where the global land rush overlaps animal reservoirs of human disease. Large-scale land deals were overlaid on zoonotic host distributions worldwide. Administrative units were scored by hazard-exposure overlap. Investor and host country links completed the wider telecoupled picture.

Southeast Asia, Latin America, Eastern Europe, and Africa host most large deals. Spillover risk concentrates hardest in Southeast Asia and Latin America especially. High-risk units show more forest cover, bigger deals, and fewer roads and people. Domestic and intra-regional deals drive over half the total risk.
pmc-13242407:
Goetz Benndorf, a neurosurgeon, wrote this comment for Acta Neurochirurgica in 2026 in reply to a study claiming a previously unreported brain vein. Gurse and colleagues had described a “cuneus vein” found during surgery and urged preserving it during operations at the back of the brain. Benndorf questions whether the evidence shows that such a vein exists at all.

He notes the claim rests on one surgeon's retrospective review of 303 operations, with the variant reported in just 12 patients. His sharpest point is that the vein never appeared on preoperative MRI scans, even in those 12 positive cases. He also finds the published images and scan methods too thin to support the claim. The comment is a caution against naming new anatomy on surgical impression alone.
pmc-13242507:
Alexandra Israelsson and co-authors tested whether people can read blended emotions when face, body, and voice all speak at once. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. Actors portrayed pairs drawn from anger, disgust, fear, happiness, and sadness, mixing them in different proportions. In two preregistered experiments, viewers rated which emotions they saw and how strongly each one came through.

Viewers reliably picked out both intended emotions from the blends and ignored the ones that were absent. They could also tell which emotion in a pair was dominant and which was the minor note. Accuracy shifted a little with specific pairings, but the overall pattern held in both experiments, even when raters could choose any number of scales. The authors say this fine-grained reading helps explain how people manage a social world where feelings rarely arrive one at a time.
pmc-13242607:
Yalda Amiri Hezave, Rezvan Najafi, and Razieh Amini reviewed spiegelmers, mirror-image binding molecules, as a new platform against breast cancer. Their review appeared in Breast Cancer: Basic and Clinical Research in 2026. Ordinary aptamers, short synthetic strands that grip chosen targets, degrade quickly in the body. Spiegelmers are built from left-handed nucleotides, which enzymes barely recognize, so they survive far longer in blood while keeping tight, specific binding.

In breast cancer, the review sees spiegelmers serving both diagnosis and treatment. Tagged with fluorescent or radioactive labels, they could light up tumors on MRI or PET scans. They can also ferry drugs into tumors, support light-based therapies, and block harmful microRNAs such as miR-155, which drives aggressive triple-negative disease. Synthesis is difficult and the range of proven targets is still narrow. Even so, the authors judge spiegelmers a strong candidate platform for combined diagnosis-and-therapy tools.
pmc-13242807:
Fangsheng Xu and a large team report a 2026 randomized trial comparing sedation mixtures for digestive tract endoscopy. The standard pairing of propofol with fentanyl can drop blood oxygen. A newer opioid, oliceridine, is designed to spare breathing while keeping pain relief.

Adults having both upper and lower endoscopy were assigned to propofol with either drug, with neither patients nor staff knowing which. Mild oxygen dips were less common in the oliceridine group after adjustment, though the raw difference was borderline. Severe dips and airway rescues did not differ. Low blood pressure episodes and the need for pressure-raising drugs were fewer with oliceridine. Sedation depth and success rates matched, supporting the newer pairing as a gentler option.
pmc-13243107:
Chaohui Zhen and co-authors test computer vision methods for sorting colon images in this 2026 study. Correctly reading images from inside the colon helps doctors catch bowel diseases early, and newer artificial intelligence models can learn both wide image patterns and links between image parts.

Working with the Kvasir V2 image set, the team compared a fine-tuned Vision Transformer model with pipelines that link image features into graphs. The transformer scored best, at 94.6 percent correct, while the best graph setup reached 92 percent. A heat-map tool showed which image areas drove each call, helping users judge whether the models were looking at the right features.
pmc-13243307:
Turyalai Hakimi and Sultan Ahmad Halimi report an exceptionally young case of myxoid liposarcoma, a fat-tissue cancer. Their case report appeared in Oxford Medical Case Reports in 2026. The tumor usually strikes teenagers and young adults and is almost unheard of under age five. Their patient was a boy of three and a half admitted in Afghanistan with a large abdominal mass.

Surgeons removed the retroperitoneal tumor completely, with clear margins, and tissue analysis confirmed the well-differentiated myxoid type. He then received six cycles of cyclophosphamide chemotherapy at twenty-day intervals. Follow-up scans showed no return of the disease. The authors stress that such cases need a pediatric surgeon and oncologist working together, plus long-term surveillance. They also use the case to argue that policymakers should build stronger childhood cancer services, in Afghanistan and beyond.
pmc-13244507:
Masakazu Hamada and colleagues asked whether the look of a person's tongue predicts the microbes living in their mouth. Their study appeared in the Journal of Oral Microbiology in 2026. Ninety-three volunteers were grouped by tongue features from traditional exams: yellow coating, redness, fissures, swelling, geographic patterns, and tooth marks. Saliva and surface samples then went through diversity and composition analysis.

One feature stood out. People with fissured tongues carried less diverse oral communities, with more Firmicutes and sulfur-processing bacteria. Much of that signal faded once age was taken into account, since fissures and microbial shifts both grow with age. In age-restricted comparisons, two bacterial genera stayed lower in fissured-tongue saliva, an age-independent signature. The authors suggest tongue appearance could become a cheap, noninvasive marker of oral imbalance. Dentists already look at tongues; this study asks what else the look is telling them.
pmc-13245107:
Kristina Burić and co-authors compare numbing methods for lower molar surgery in a 2026 trial. The standard nerve block can fail when anatomy varies, leaving patients sore during drilling. A modified block near the mylohyoid nerve offers a backup route for the same area.

Sixty patients were split into three equal groups. Two groups got the modified block with articaine, one of them with an added steroid, and the third got standard lidocaine block. Pain scores, numbing quality, and numbing length landed close across all three groups. No gap reached statistical weight. The modified block thus stands as a fair stand-in when the standard block falls short.
pmc-13247307:
Kurtz, McKinley, Mullet, and co-authors catalogued small signaling peptides in sorghum, in this 2026 Plant Direct study. Plants coordinate growth with tiny protein messengers, but in sorghum, an important grain and bioenergy crop, these peptides were barely characterized. Starting from known peptide families in five other plants, the team identified two hundred nineteen sorghum genes encoding such signals and sorted them into nineteen families.

Twelve of the families had never been described in sorghum. Gene activity patterns varied sharply by organ: some families spoke mainly in roots, others in stem skin and pith or in the seed head. During stem growth, twenty-eight peptide genes switched on strongly in zones where cells divide, including relatives of a known stem-cell signal. The catalogue gives breeders targets for shaping sorghum stems, which carry most of the harvested biomass.
pmc-13248107:
Keitel-Gröner and co-authors fed farmed salmon extra vitamin D through a Norwegian winter, in this 2026 Aquaculture Nutrition study. Modern salmon feeds use less fishmeal and fish oil, so the fish. Eventually the people eating them, get less vitamin D, and winter darkness cuts the fish's own supply further. Under commercial conditions in southern Norway, salmon received either a standard diet or one with ten times the vitamin D for thirty-two weeks spanning winter into summer.

The enriched fish tolerated the dose without harm to growth or survival. Vitamin D levels in blood, liver, and muscle rose, offsetting the winter dip and approaching summer-like tissue levels, though seasons still left their mark. The authors conclude dietary boosting can raise the nutritional quality of farmed salmon fillets for human consumers.
pmc-13249607:
Kumar and colleagues measured partner violence and mental health among rural married women, in a 2026 Annals of Neurosciences study. One hundred sixty-nine women completed standardized questionnaires on violence by a partner, depression, and anxiety. The setting was a rural community where such problems are seldom studied or treated, and the team looked for the patterns behind them.

Nearly three in ten women reported partner violence during their lives, most often controlling behavior, then physical violence. About a quarter had depression and nearly a third an anxiety disorder, and both grew worse as violence increased. Violence was more common where husbands used alcohol or drugs and in poorer households. The authors call for coordinated action by health and community organizations.
pmc-13249907:
Tavassoli, Marco, and Puts review how autistic people experience the senses, in a 2026 article. Using a published framework, they sort recent studies by level: behavior, feelings, raw perception, body signals, and brain wiring. Sensory differences in autism are common, but the review stresses how much they vary from person to person.

Strong reactions to sensation predicted anxiety and inward-turning symptoms in children. Seeking out sensation looked more like a coping habit, tied to outward behavior. Lab tests found narrow quirks, such as sharper pitch hearing, rather than one global sensitivity, and surveys often disagreed with lab results. Brain studies pointed to an imbalance between excitation and inhibition, plus altered control of body arousal.
pmc-13250907:
Furubayashi and colleagues ask whether early growth on a two-drug immune therapy spells trouble for kidney cancer patients. Their 2026 Research and Reports in Urology study reviews Japanese patients with advanced renal cell carcinoma treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab at one cancer center since 2018. Early progression meant growth within twelve weeks or at the first scan.

Among thirty-eight patients reaching the twelve-week mark, the fourteen with early progression lived far shorter lives than the rest. Early progression and a poor-risk score each independently predicted worse survival. Tumors that were not the common clear-cell type were much likelier to progress early. The authors suggest watching tumor type closely when choosing first-line treatment and counseling patients.
pmc-13251107:
Mahmoud Gad and colleagues weigh surgery against watchful care for gallstones in this 2026 updated review. Gallbladder removal is the standard fix for painful gallstones, yet it costs money and can leave lasting symptoms, so the best choice for mild cases stays debated.

The team pooled four randomised trials with 677 patients comparing removal with conservative care. Surgery cut gallstone pain attacks and overall gallstone complications by more than half. Conservative care, though, brought fewer surgery-linked problems, largely since many patients never needed an operation during follow-up. Deaths and several specific complications did not differ between groups. The authors frame it as a trade-off to discuss per patient.
pmc-13251707:
Laura Mezquita and co-authors ask why personality shapes marijuana outcomes, studying college users in four countries in 2026. Traits such as emotional stability and openness are distant risk factors, while the reasons people give for using, their motives, sit closer to behavior. The team tested whether motives carry the effect of traits onto use and harm.

The sample held 1,031 students from the United States, Argentina, Spain, and the Netherlands who had used marijuana in the past month. Coping, enhancement, and expansion motives each tracked with more frequent use, and coping motives alone tracked with more negative consequences. Statistical modeling showed coping motives carrying the link from low emotional stability to worse outcomes. Expansion motives, the wish to broaden perception, carried the effect of openness onto frequency. Country differences were minor. The authors urge prevention programs to target motives, including the less-studied expansion pathway.
pmc-13252707:
Shiyi Bai and colleagues turn disaster nursing into a game for students in this 2026 study. Game-style teaching can lift motivation, but theory-based designs for disaster nursing in ordinary, low-resource classrooms were barely tested.

Third-year nursing students split into two groups of 66 by timetable. One group got 180 minutes of gamified teaching with points, team contests, and group work; the other got standard lessons. The game group scored higher on disaster nursing competence right after class, in both knowledge and practical skills, though the edge faded at one week. Self-directed learning was higher in the game group at follow-up, driven by teamwork skills.
pmc-13253507:
Xinzhou Huang and colleagues use network toxicology and machine learning to connect a persistent pollutant with osteoarthritis in a 2026 study. Perfluorooctanoic acid, a forever chemical found widely in the environment, has been linked to joint disease onset and progression without a clear mechanism. The team mined public gene expression datasets from joint tissue to find where the chemical's targets and the disease overlap.

Fifteen candidate genes emerged from the overlap, and six machine learning algorithms plus a network method narrowed the field to three core genes: IGFBP1, MKI67, and C9. Computer docking showed the pollutant binding strongly to each of the three proteins. A diagnostic score built from the genes separated patients from controls with high accuracy in both training and external validation sets. The authors propose that the chemical perturbs the joint's immune environment through these genes, stoking inflammation and cartilage breakdown.
pmc-13253607:
