Guanwei Wu and colleagues build explainable prediction models for a double diagnosis in this 2026 study. Metabolic syndrome and kidney stones increasingly arrive together, and diet's smallest ingredients, micronutrients, may hold clues to who is at risk.

Using a United States nutrition survey from 2007 to 2018, the team trained six learning models on 54 candidate features, trimmed to 33. With diet and personal data combined, a random forest model scored highest; on diet alone, a boosting model led. Explanation tools named the strongest dietary signals, including lycopene from tomatoes, magnesium, fibre, and vitamin K. The authors frame the models as a risk-sorting aid, pending checks in other populations.
pmc-13253807:
Limbani Kalumbi and colleagues draw lessons on sharing research results with communities from the Fuel to Pot project in a 2026 case study. Household air pollution from solid cooking fuels affects billions and kills millions yearly, yet interventions often fail because communities are handed findings rather than engaged with them. The project studied fuel use in informal settlements in Mukuru, Kenya, and Ndirande, Malawi, from 2020 to 2023.

After two years of hands-on work using walking interviews and photography by residents, the team rolled out a cascaded sharing model. Mobile poster shows carried local language versions, residents' photographs, and simplified charts into each settlement, sparking discussions that produced practical recommendations. From the experience the authors distill six principles, covering engagement, networks, access, capacity strengthening, trust, and budgeting. They argue sharing should be designed as collaborative action from the start, not performed at the end.
pmc-13254007:
Barbara Eichhorst and a panel of European experts issue 2026 guidelines for chronic lymphocytic leukemia, a blood cancer. For the first time, the European Hematology Association leads the guidelines, which will now update each year. Patient advocates joined the expert consensus for the first time as well.

The guidance takes a whole-course view, from diagnosis and watchful waiting to treatment choice based on both disease and patient traits. It also covers Richter transformation, where the cancer shifts to a faster form. New options include a time-limited drug pairing as first treatment and a continuous drug for relapsed disease after certain prior drugs.
pmc-13254207:
Matthias Hauptmann and co-authors follow gut bacteria in young children in a 2026 study. The first two years of life shape the microbiome and later immunity. Using the German LoewenKIDS cohort, the team analyzed 1,176 stool samples from 162 children, of whom 49 received antibiotics.

High levels of Bacteroides, a common gut genus, tied to getting antibiotic treatment 45 to 225 days later. Low Bacteroides before treatment tied to lower diversity after treatment and more varied gut makeup. The authors suggest this genus plays a key role in infection risk and in how the young gut bounces back.
pmc-13254507:
Sapir Gershov and colleagues detect distress in health care workers from fleeting changes in behavior during interviews in a 2026 study. Burnout and trauma stress are common in this workforce, yet stigma and weak self-report tools hide many cases. The team focused on microbehavior intervals, brief unplanned shifts across face, gaze, posture, and gesture that surface when questions touch emotional ground.

Workers recorded a video interview answering five charged questions about their jobs, then completed validated burnout and trauma surveys. Computer vision converted the recordings into time series for each channel, and an unsupervised anomaly model flagged those intervals without human labels. About twenty intervals appeared per interview on average. Features from those moments trained a classifier that sorted workers into four profiles: moderate to severe burnout, subthreshold trauma symptoms, both together, or resilient. An explanation analysis then identified the features driving each prediction.
pmc-13254707:
Han Cai, Zhiming Wang, and Xiu Jin examine how using artificial intelligence at work relates to employee creativity in a 2026 survey study of Chinese small and medium enterprises. The sample held 316 employees, and the analysis tested a model built on resource and social exchange theories.

AI usage showed its association with creativity running through work engagement: employees who used AI more were more engaged, and engagement carried the creative benefit. Attitude toward the technology changed the strength of the whole chain. When technology acceptance was high, the interaction between acceptance and AI use amplified effects on both engagement and creativity; when acceptance lagged, the boost faded. The authors offer practical guidance for smaller firms in digital transformation: supply the tools, but also win employees over to them. Training and involvement, they imply, are part of the technology investment.
pmc-13254907:
Johan Dahlberg and colleagues study mental health in women with lipoedema in a 2026 paper. Lipoedema is a chronic disorder of painful fat build-up, almost only in women, mostly on hips and legs. Participants filled in tested scales for stress, anxiety, self-compassion, perfectionism, and impostor feelings, plus a life quality survey.

Results are reported for 18 women. One third showed signs of raised stress, and 16.7 percent had raised anxiety. Yet 88.9 percent reported moderate or high self-compassion, with nine at a high level. Life quality scores were low, mainly for physical roles and pain, with no clear gaps by disease stage.
pmc-13255207:
Reichardt and colleagues tested whether probiotic bacteria can tame oral biofilms grown from human saliva in the laboratory. They compared two Streptococcus salivarius probiotic strains, K12 and M18, against a lactobacillus probiotic and no treatment, under low and high sugar conditions. The team tracked acidity at microscopic scale, mapped the biofilm matrix, and sequenced the microbial community.

Effects were modest. Under low sugar, the M18 strain kept biofilm pH higher, while the lactobacillus treatment lowered it, and no probiotic changed pH under high sugar. Community shifts were minor and the biofilm matrix was essentially unchanged. The authors conclude these probiotics barely dent biofilm virulence in this model.
pmc-13255607:
Yu Xue and colleagues report a 2026 analysis of cell partnerships inside colorectal tumors, using single-cell and spatial gene-readout methods. Tumor cells trade signals and nutrients with nearby immune cells, and those exchanges can help cancers grow and hide. The team hunted for pairs of cell types whose metabolism seemed linked.

One pair stood out: epithelial cells marked by SLC6A20 and macrophages marked by SPP1. Both showed shifted handling of energy, vitamin B6, and amino acids, and they appeared in the same tumor neighborhoods. Patients whose tumors carried strong signals from the pair tended to fare worse. The team built a gene-based risk model from the findings. They suggest the partnership as a research lead for metabolism-focused treatment ideas.
pmc-13255807:
Catherine Powers-James and a large team report a 2026 randomized trial of a whole-person lifestyle program for women treated for breast cancer. The program blended healthy eating, exercise, stress management, and emotional support, starting during radiation and running for a year. Few earlier trials had combined all these elements in one package.

Women in the program improved body composition and cardiovascular fitness compared with the comparison condition. They also ate more fiber and reported better quality-of-life outcomes across several measures. The authors argue that structured lifestyle support deserves a place inside standard breast cancer care rather than as an optional extra. They call for larger trials to confirm the gains and test whether they translate into longer survival.
pmc-13255907:
Ravi Kumar Paluri and colleagues report a 2026 biomarker study using tiny vesicles shed into the blood by pancreatic tumors. Patients had locally advanced or borderline removable cancer treated with chemotherapy first, then focused radiation. Doctors lack good tools to watch tumor response during such therapy, so the team sampled blood at several points.

They isolated small extracellular vesicles and measured cancer-linked surface proteins and microRNAs riding on them. Marker patterns shifted during treatment, and the shifts differed between chemotherapy regimens. The authors say these vesicle fingerprints can describe how a tumor is responding without repeated biopsies. The work is exploratory, pointing toward blood tests that track pancreatic cancer in something close to real time.
pmc-13256907:
Xinqi Wang and co-authors offer a 2026 genetics study that maps metabolic pathways across types of ovarian cancer. Ovarian cancer is not one disease, and each histotype behaves differently. The team uses Mendelian randomization, a method that uses inherited variants as natural experiments.

Screening covered about 1,400 blood metabolites in two large data sources, and amino acid and energy pathways stood out. Alanine raised risk for one serous type, while glutamate looked protective for endometrioid cancer. Lactate-related traits pointed most often to low-grade serous disease. Drug-target tests highlighted PPARG as protective and a potassium-channel target as risk raising for invasive mucinous cancer. Lab experiments in mucinous models matched that pattern, which strengthens the case for follow-up work.
pmc-13257807:
Ke Hu and co-authors spray graphene over silver nanowires to make a clear conductive film in a 2026 study. Silver wire networks beat brittle indium tin oxide for flexible screens, yet they oxidize in air and lose performance. A reduced graphene oxide coat on plastic film was tested as protection and stabilizer.

The finished film passed about seventy-seven percent of visible light while keeping very low electrical resistance. Powered at low voltage, it heated evenly to near boiling-surface temperatures and held steady. It also blocked electromagnetic interference by a solid margin. Device makers gain a dual-purpose skin for heaters and shielding in bendable electronics. Long service life, the usual weakness of nanowire films, is the property this design most directly defends.
pmc-13258307:
Sławomir Liberski and colleagues scan deep optic nerve structures in adults with cystic fibrosis in a 2026 case-control study. Thirty-four patients and thirty-four matched healthy controls received swept-source eye tomography, and patients were rescanned after a year or more on modulator therapy. Nerve fiber thickness, ligament-like lamina thickness, and lamina depth were compared.

Surface nerve fiber thickness matched controls after adjustment, yet the deep lamina was far thinner in cystic fibrosis. Eye pressure also ran higher in patients. Over follow-up on therapy, nerve fiber thickness slipped slightly while lamina measures stayed stable. Eye specialists gain a new watch point in a disease better known for lungs and digestion. Deep support tissue thinning may flag vulnerability long before surface measures move.
pmc-13258507:
Mohamed Abu El Asrar Afify leads a 2026 crossover trial of oat flakes in teenagers with type one diabetes. Sixty adolescents took part, eating oat flakes daily for three months in one study phase and a usual diet in the other. Continuous glucose monitors tracked daily swings, while blood tests covered cholesterol and a pancreatic marker.

During oat phases, glucose variation and long term sugar control both improved. Cholesterol, triglycerides, and harmful LDL cholesterol fell, while protective HDL cholesterol rose. The pancreatic marker also increased during oat intake. Most gains faded after oats stopped, which suggests steady intake matters. Families and clinicians get measured evidence for a simple food based support.
pmc-13259007:
Yingshan Jiang and coauthors test fermented deer bone extract against arthritis linked bone loss in a 2026 rat study. Rheumatoid arthritis often thins bone through chronic inflammation. Deer bone carries a traditional reputation for bone support, and fermentation may unlock more active peptides.

Fermented extract eased arthritis signs and raised bone density in treated rats. Bone internal structure also looked healthier under the microscope. In cell tests the extract slowed formation of bone eating cells. Signaling proteins that drive that formation showed reduced activation. Results support development of the extract as a functional food ingredient for inflammatory bone disease.
pmc-13259407:
Aiping Chen and coauthors profile pyrolysis products from mixed plastic waste in a 2026 study. Six polyolefin rich waste streams underwent high resolution chemical analysis after rapid heating. Three consumer plastics also faced vapor and water migration testing.

Heated products were dominated by mid range hydrocarbons suited to fuel or feedstock recovery. Polyethylene rich feeds gave straight chains, while polypropylene rich feeds gave branched products. Additive breakdown traces appeared at low levels in most streams. Weathered plastic kept low level oxygenated compounds from prior oxidation. Recyclers learn which quality targets matter before chemical recycling scales up.
pmc-13260707:
Jasper Okoro Godwin Elechi and colleagues present a 2026 lab study of how digestion in the mouth and upper stomach affects wheat-based baked foods. Many lab digestion models skip the oral phase, where saliva's starch-cutting enzyme starts working. The team simulated oral and proximal gastric digestion for bread and cookies. They tracked particle size, the release of plant phenolic compounds, and sugar release over sixty minutes, relating digestion rates to estimated glycemic index.

The longer saliva phase broke food into small particles under two millimetres through starch breakdown. Phenolics and flavonoids were released irregularly at different stages and differed between samples. Sugar release rose swiftly in a nonlinear pattern, and all breads ended with similar glucose release despite different recipes. Starch digestion rates in this phase correlated strongly with a standard glycemic index protocol, highlighting saliva's role.
pmc-13261007:
Thomas J Whitford and Judith M Ford wrote a 2026 primer on corollary discharges, brain signals that help distinguish self from world. When the brain issues a motor command, a copy of that signal, called an efference copy, is sent to sensory areas. It tells them what sensation the movement should produce. That allows the brain to dampen self-caused sensations and credit the rest to the outside world, supporting the feeling of controlling one's own actions.

Such signals are found across the animal kingdom, from crickets, where one identified neuron suppresses hearing during chirping, to bats, songbirds, primates, and humans. In humans they are inferred from suppressed brain responses during self-produced sounds, especially vocalizations. Disruption of this mechanism has been implicated in schizophrenia symptoms, such as mistaking one's own thoughts or actions for external events. The primer reviews how these signals are measured.
pmc-13261407:
Daniel Walter and colleagues built in 2026 a machine learning tool that finds peaks in chromatography traces for antibody medicines. Size-exclusion chromatography checks antibody quality, but overlapping peaks and drifting baselines make human reading slow and variable. Their system, PFE-1, uses an attention-based transformer trained on millions of simulated traces.

The simulator was tuned to match real routine data for antibodies and related large molecules. The model flags likely peak regions and events, and transparent rules then draw the final peak boxes. On both simulated and real test sets it beat convolutional networks and classic derivative methods. The margin grew largest where peaks overlapped or took odd shapes. It also needs no hints about where peaks should appear. The authors offer the framework as a reproducible base for routine analysis.
pmc-13262007:
Zhijian Wu and co-authors offer a 2026 journal article on spotting mild cognitive impairment, an early stage of memory and thinking loss, in older adults in urban China. Their test was whether adding movement, body, and neighborhood measures could improve screening beyond standard survey questions. Cases were set by scores on the MoCA thinking test, adjusted for schooling.

The study covered 309 adults aged 60 or older in Nanjing, of whom 110 met the case definition. Six computer learning models were trained on 216 people and tested on 93 others. A model called LightGBM did best, correctly sorting cases with strong scores. Movement habits, waist-related body measures, age, and local area features carried the most weight.
pmc-13262207:
Keyi Huang and co-authors study tech-based elder care and life satisfaction in China in a 2026 journal article. Smart elderly care uses internet tools to deliver support to older adults at home and in their communities. The authors asked whether users feel better about life, and whether health and social activity help explain any link.

They used a 2021 national survey of 8,950 people aged 65 and older. Smart care use was linked to higher well-being, with a small but clear statistical effect. Better health explained 38.47 percent of the link, and social activity explained 2.65 percent. The pattern held in city and country areas, and was stronger among older adults with lower digital skills.
pmc-13263307:
Tarık Kutlu and Abdurrahman Durmuş report a 2026 journal article on blood markers around kidding in Saanen goats, a dairy breed. They followed twelve goats from three weeks before birth to four weeks after. Six goats lost kids at birth, and six did not.

Blood samples were tested for oxidant and antioxidant measures, which show chemical stress inside the body. Goats that lost kids had higher total oxidant status and a higher oxidative stress index across the period. Their superoxide dismutase, a protective enzyme, also ran higher. The authors stress that these are early associations only. The small group size means the markers cannot yet be called causes of kid loss.
pmc-13263407:
Naylya Djumaeva and Baisakhi Banerjee present a 2026 case report on seizure change in a girl with Rett syndrome, a severe developmental disorder usually caused by variants in the MECP2 gene. The girl developed normally at first, then around age two lost speech, began repetitive hand movements, and started having seizures.

Her seizures resisted standard anti-seizure medicines. Doctors added long-term low-dose prednisolone and methotrexate, two drugs that calm the immune system, suspecting that brain inflammation helps seizures spread. Over follow-up, her whole-body seizures became less frequent and were replaced by brief partial seizures. The authors caution that one case cannot prove cause, but the shift supports testing immune-based treatment further.
pmc-13264107:
Manuel Mello and colleagues show that babies already pick out social interaction with their brains in a 2026 study. Infants in the first year watched people facing and moving toward each other, as if interacting, or moving away. A gentle light-based brain method recorded activity over the back and side of the head, areas also used by adults for social perception.

Both six-month and ten-month babies showed stronger responses to the interacting pairs. Older infants showed the effect over a wider area and looked longer at interacting people. Responses differed from those for simple body motion, pointing to separate systems. Early tuning of this kind may steer attention toward relationships and support later social learning.
pmc-13264207:
Yeqin Fu and colleagues review materials that block a form of cell death in worn spinal discs in a 2026 article. Disc degeneration drives much back pain in aging populations, and surgery remains the main option once damage advances. A death pathway called ferroptosis, driven by iron buildup and fat oxidation in cell membranes, has emerged as a key driver that damages disc cells and speeds breakdown.

Functional biomaterials can deliver protective drugs directly to the disc and also shield cells through their own chemistry. The review maps how ferroptosis is controlled inside disc tissue and compares material designs built to interrupt it. Organized guidance of this kind may help engineers create injectable treatments that slow degeneration without major surgery.
pmc-13264307:
Yue Sun and colleagues review plant-derived vesicles as treatments for brain degeneration in a 2026 article. Alzheimer disease and related disorders resist treatment because causes are many-sided and most drugs reach the brain poorly. Tiny vesicles shed by plants carry fats, proteins, small RNAs and plant chemicals. They hold healing activity of their own. They also form a natural delivery shell that survives digestion and travels through the body.

Possible actions include calming brain inflammation, correcting energy failure in cells, clearing toxic protein clumps and supporting repair through the gut and brain connection. The review also weighs routes of administration, distribution evidence and barrier-crossing claims critically. Production, purification and engineering advances are covered alongside the gaps blocking clinical use.
pmc-13264407:
Rajesh Shetty and colleagues examine whether lens position affects vision after cataract surgery with an extended depth of focus implant in a 2026 observational study. About two hundred eyes received the standard or astigmatism-correcting version of the lens. Assessments took place at least a month after surgery. Vision at distance and intermediate range was measured, along with refraction, lens decentration and tilt, pupil size and corneal aberrations. No intervention was assigned by the study team.

Average decentration was small and tilt modest across the cohort. Distance vision results were strong overall. Unadjusted analyses found no significant links between corrected distance vision and either decentration or tilt. Tolerance to slight misalignment supports the lens design, though larger shifts seen in complicated surgery were outside this selected group.
pmc-13264607:
Leonie Goelz and co-authors report early data in 2026 from the G-MEMBRANE trial on chronic subdural hematoma, a slow bleed on the brain surface common in older people. Surgery alone often sees the bleed return. The trial tested adding a vessel-blocking step, which seals the artery that feeds the bleed.

Ninety-three patients were assigned by chance to surgery with or without the added step, and 64 could be judged at three months. Bleeds returned in 19.2 percent of the added-step group and 23.7 percent of the control group, a small gap. No harm was tied to the added step. Dropout was high, mainly in the treated group. With so small a gap, the team stopped the trial early and call the results not conclusive. A review of eight past trials is included.
pmc-13264807:

Their patient was a seventy-seven-year-old woman with sudden left-sided weakness. Scans showed moyamoya vessel changes plus a small stroke deep in the brainstem. A heart test found a small shunt between heart chambers. She received two antiplatelet drugs and rehabilitation care. The case urges broad thinking when older patients arrive with stroke.
pmc-13264907:
Ellen Maj-Britt Brinkmann and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a scoping review on what shapes data quality in electronic health records in hospitals. Good records guide good care, and health staff create most of the data, yet the human and workplace factors behind quality are poorly mapped. Past reviews covered single professions or topics only.

The review will follow a standard scoping method and search five sources, including Google Scholar. Two reviewers will screen and chart studies on their own. Results will be sorted by six quality traits: accuracy, completeness, consistency, fit to context, currency, and access. Findings will be compared across staff groups and hospital settings. The plan is logged in a public registry, and results will go to journals and conferences.
pmc-13265007:
Matthew Justyn and colleagues published a 2026 review of the genetics of fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction in Asian populations. The disease is rising fast in Asia, strikes younger people, and varies greatly between patients. Genes help explain who stores liver fat, who progresses to liver inflammation, and who scars.

The review groups variants by pathway: fat handling, insulin resistance and new fat making, cholesterol handling, inflammation, and scarring. One variant in the PNPLA3 gene stood out as the strongest driver of liver fat and harsh tissue features across studies. Other variants raised or lowered risk. Frequencies and effect sizes differ between Asian and Western groups. The authors back adding genetic markers to risk models so high-risk people are found earlier.
pmc-13265707:
Chris Broeckhoven, Bryan Minne, and Cang Hui present ArmourTraits, a dataset on skin armour in lizards and relatives (2026). Bony armour plates evolved on their own in two distant lineages. Measurements cover 131 species, drawn from 272 scanned samples. Micro-CT scans gauged armour and hindlimb bones. Habitat, life-history, and climate data accompany the measures. pmc-13266307:

Recurrent tumors were selectively enriched in large neutral amino acids, the building blocks ferried by a transporter called LAT1. Pathway analysis pointed firmly at amino acid metabolism. In the validation group, staining showed LAT1 clearly higher in recurrent tumors than in first-time ones, while a sister transporter showed no difference. The authors call the amino acid shift a metabolic weakness of recurrent tumors that deserves further study as a treatment angle.
pmc-13266407:

The acute crisis settled once the drugs were stopped, but new nerve symptoms slowly appeared. Tests found a gene change and raised porphyrins, yet gene testing for porphyria was negative. pmc-13266607:

A 3D body scanner measured spine curves while people stood and walked at three speeds. The forward-head group had a more rounded upper back and more side-to-side imbalance while standing. At the slowest walking speed, their front-to-back imbalance was also higher. The authors say both standing and walking checks matter when this posture is treated.
pmc-13266707:
Tengfei Kang and the team work on catalytic rearrangements that break aromaticity with handedness control (2026). Making such rearrangements selective is hard because losing aromatic stability costs energy. That penalty has limited catalytic, mirror-selective versions that use pendant aromatic groups. The challenge is recognised as significant in the field.

The title frames the advance: divergent products from one rearrangement family. Three product routes are named, covering two Wittig-type shifts and a Sommelet-Hauser type. A catalyst-driven, enantioselective approach is the stated goal. Work of this kind aims to widen the chiral building blocks available for complex compound synthesis.
pmc-13266807:

Later placement, though, was much more common in the atrial enlargement group, which also slipped more often into a slow junctional rhythm. Survival and major heart events did not differ clearly. The pattern suggests gradual decline of the heart's natural pacemaker, so the authors advise long-term rhythm checks for these patients.
pmc-13267707: Sona Zare and colleagues' 2025 review of stem cell secretions for skin care is the subject of a 2026 retraction note in Stem Cell Research and Therapy. As a result, the editor states, confidence in the paper has been lost. The note records that all of the authors disagree with this retraction. No part of the review's content is re-argued in the note itself.
pmc-13267807:

Each held a consent talk with an actor playing a patient in severe pain who awaited urgent stomach surgery.

Most invitations were closed yes-or-no questions. Few residents used the patient's name, though most kept eye contact. Neither gender nor training year changed the pattern. pmc-13269507:

Kids from leaf-fed mothers weighed more at weaning. That group also gave the best financial return.
pmc-13269607:

pmc-13270607:

Working with BALB/c mice, the team perfused, or flowed, a labeled form of L-arginine through the brain in place and varied time, dose, salt levels, and acidity. They also added blocker chemicals and related amino acids to test which carrier system moves L-arginine and how strongly other substances compete with it. The paper stays focused on that measurement work.

The statement gives evidence-based advice to help doctors choose which patients with a suspected inborn error should get genomic testing, meaning a broad read of their DNA. It offers practical tips meant to improve choices, the delivery of testing, and patient outcomes.
pmc-13271107:

Case mix or surgeon preference, the writers argue, could explain gaps in operating time, failures, and bowel symptoms.
pmc-13271307:

The authors call for education built into pregnancy care.
pmc-13272207:

Capture rates peaked near an average temperature of twenty degrees Celsius in the same month. Higher current humidity and rain three months earlier both linked to lower capture rates, and greener vegetation scores linked to a fluctuating decline.
pmc-13272307:

pmc-13272607:

Participants wore the tracker for 21 days and gave nightly saliva samples. In the suspected group, 16 confirmed cases and 13 excluded cases showed similar sleep, apart from an earlier daily rhythm in confirmed cases. In 23 patients in remission, sleep was also similar across subgroups. Night cortisol varied a lot and showed no steady link to the sleep measures.
pmc-13273107:

They argue that payment delays should be seen as a system and fairness problem, not only a household money problem. Weak public funding and reliance on user fees push clinics to collect first. The authors admit direct bedside evidence from Somalia is thin, so they frame the harm as a reasoned policy concern. Their reform plan puts triage and stabilization first, with waivers, billing kept apart from urgent care, and tighter rules.
pmc-13273207:

The dashboard pulls daily extracts from the trial management system, checks data quality on its own, and forecasts enrollment over time. Access is shaped by role, and the tool sits inside existing oversight routines. The team judged the rollout with a standard implementation framework, using system logs and staff feedback. From May 2022 to May 2026 the system served the whole institution and logged 1,605 user sessions. The authors share lessons for other academic centers.
pmc-13273407:
Ibtissam Ait Azzi leads a 2026 survey of French medical residents and their confidence in infection control and careful drug use. Among 151 residents, confidence was higher for drug choices than for infection control. Training in infection control linked to higher confidence in that area, but drug training showed no such link. Only 17 percent knew of the national action plan on resistance. The authors call for earlier, practical training that joins both areas through residency.
pmc-13274107:

The team compared women whose migraine began in that window, women whose migraine began earlier, and women without migraine.

Each group held twenty-two women, and all gave hormone blood tests and headache scores. Migraine starting in perimenopause tended to throb, switch sides, and strike often at moderate to severe strength, with light and sound sensitivity. Painkiller overuse was common and relief often poor. Both migraine groups reported more fatigue, poor sleep, and anxiety than controls, and women with migraine had lower estradiol levels.
pmc-13274307:
