The listed problems include scope mismatches, data that did not match the research described, inappropriate citations, incoherent content, and compromised peer review. The notice warns readers the content is unreliable, and says the authors did not respond when told.
pmc-13274607:
Huaxing Liang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on fully recycling the multilayer plastic membranes used to purify water and chemicals. These composite sheets mix several plastics, so shredding or melting recovers little of value. Their stage-based plan instead unbuilds the membrane step by step with solvents and chemistry.

Starting from real worn-out membranes, the process pulls the layers apart, breaks one layer down chemically, then recasts fresh membranes from the recovered material. The regenerated membranes matched commercial ones in strength and separation performance. Life-cycle and cost analyses found substantial cuts in environmental harm and material cost versus making membranes from scratch. The authors pitch it as a scalable route for membrane waste.
pmc-13274907:
Miren Aldasoro and co-authors present a 2026 journal article quantifying how many farm pests common bats eat across varied landscapes. The team studied six colonies of horseshoe bats, three each of two species, within the bats' best range. Droppings and diet analysis revealed what the colonies consumed through the breeding season.

The bats steadily ate a wide range of pest insects, and consumption rose and fell with pest outbreaks, showing they track boom prey. Some pest species in the diet were previously unknown in the area or not targeted by farmers, making bats early detectors of emerging pests. Across the study area, the colonies' breeding-season pest consumption totaled nearly three tons of insects.
pmc-13275307:
Ruairidh Macleod and a large team present a 2026 journal article reporting lethal plague outbreaks among Siberian hunter-gatherers about fifty-five hundred years ago. Early plague strains lacked the genes for flea-borne bubonic spread, so whether they could kill en masse was disputed. The team recovered ancient bacterial genomes from burials near Lake Baikal in southeast Siberia.

Across four cemeteries, thirty-nine percent of tested individuals carried plague infection, in two outbreak phases. Family pedigrees showed small kin groups hit within a single generation, pointing to person-to-person spread, and children aged eight to eleven died acutely in high numbers. The strains split off before all known plague lineages, pushing the bacterium's emergence back beyond roughly fifty-seven hundred years ago.
pmc-13275407:
Alfred J Simmons and colleagues describe a 2026 laboratory study of a shared vaccine target for colorectal cancer. Most of these cancers involve faults in the APC gene, which normally restrains cell growth. The team looked for mutated APC fragments shared across patients that could anchor a single vaccine design.

Computer analysis pinpointed shared altered fragments in the gene region where disease-linked mutations cluster. The group built a virus-like particle carrying self-amplifying RNA that encodes those fragments. Tests in cells showed T-cell activation, and mice given the vaccine produced strong antibody responses against the altered fragments. The results offer early proof of concept, well before any human testing.
pmc-13276507:
Vladimir Shlyakhover and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review on a puzzling overlap: heart attack and Takotsubo syndrome happening at once. Takotsubo, a stress-triggered weakening of the heart, was long defined by the absence of blocked arteries. The authors name the overlap STAMI and gather every published case.

Their search found forty-eight patients reported between 2000 and 2025. The average age was sixty-seven, and about seven in ten were women. The telltale sign was a mismatch: wall motion damage spread beyond the territory of the blocked artery, often ballooning at the heart's tip. Heart strain markers ran disproportionately high. Initial pump failure was often severe yet largely reversed later. Shock hit about one in ten patients, and about six percent died in hospital.
pmc-13276607:
Fei'e Liu and colleagues catalogue the interferon regulatory factor genes of spotted sea bass in a 2026 study. These genes switch on interferon defences, the first line of protection against viruses in vertebrates. Fish lineages carry their own expansions of the family, which had not been fully mapped in this species.

Nine IRF genes were identified, each carrying the family's characteristic functional motifs. The genes were active across many tissues at baseline. Two duplicated copies, IRF4a and IRF4b, had diverged in where and when they switched on. Viral-style stimulation strongly raised IRF6, IRF7, and IRF10, while bacterial challenge favoured IRF8 and IRF11. IRF9 answered both, hinting at a broad immune role.
pmc-13276807:
Fouad Sakr and colleagues present a 2026 study that builds a short survey for rating community pharmacies in Lebanon. Their nine-item Patient Satisfaction Questionnaire, called PSQ-9, grew out of a longer eighteen-item survey. An online survey of 501 adults from all Lebanese districts ran from February to May 2025.

Tests split the sample in two and found two themes: personal care and work engagement, plus cost and clear information. Scores held up well on repeat testing and across groups. Longer talks with a pharmacist, easier access to care, and fewer barriers to communication were linked to higher satisfaction. Pharmacies could use the short form for routine checks.
pmc-13277207:
Aakash Pandey and colleagues present a 2026 study that uses travel patterns to predict how respiratory epidemics spread. Knowing where an outbreak arrives next helps officials act early, yet case data are often sparse. Their models use an idea called effective distance, which shrinks between places that exchange many travelers.

The team tested the approach on COVID-19, flu, and RSV at county level in South Carolina and at state level nationwide. Effective distance beat plain map distance at predicting the order of arrival. A model based on how people spread out from home areas worked best in tests. Larger, well-connected places were hit earlier. The tools could aid early planning without rich case data.
pmc-13278407:
Feiping Xu leads a 2026 study of a computer model that predicts traffic conditions on highways inside roadwork zones. Lane closures, detours, and changing road shapes during rebuilding make traffic hard to forecast, yet good forecasts help cut congestion, emissions, and noise. The proposed model blends road shape data and changing traffic rules into a graph-based neural network, a program that learns from connected road points.

A dynamic Bayesian layer first infers how road points influence each other over time. The network then fuses that map with traffic flow data to predict conditions. Tests on the Wuxuan highway beat benchmark models on accuracy, the authors report. The model also produced readable diagrams of how congestion spreads through the work zone.
pmc-13278807:
Hou and colleagues built a retrofit system in 2026 that lets ordinary MRI machines image several atomic nuclei at once, rather than one at a time. Nuclei beyond hydrogen reveal extra biochemistry, but their signals are faint, so serial scanning takes long. The team's add-on mixes multiple transmit and receive channels with a flexible four-channel tone source, keeping the radio chain phase-stable without later correction.

Bench tests showed channel separation better than thirty decibels, a measure of isolation. In test objects the system captured hydrogen, deuterium, and sodium signals together, and ran water-suppressed hydrogen and phosphorus spectra at the same time, with no signal loss against single-nucleus work. It supports two to four nuclei, simultaneous or interleaved firing, and receive arrays of up to sixteen channels. The authors present it as a low-cost upgrade path for multinuclear studies on standard scanners.
pmc-13279407:
Oscar Victor Cardenas Alegria and colleagues report a 2026 study of germs and drug resistance in pig waste. Waste ponds on pig farms can spread resistance genes to soil and water. The team tracked germ groups and resistance genes in waste ponds and in soils spread with manure. They used shotgun metagenomics, a method that reads all DNA in a sample at once.

Eighty samples came from twenty pig farms, with waste before and after pond care and soils with or without manure past. Waste held mostly three large germ groups, while soils held more soil germs such as Streptomyces. Pond care cut germ diversity and shifted groups toward stress hardy types. Manure spread soils showed changed germ mixes as well. Pond and soil steps both shape where resistance genes move.
pmc-13280407:
M. Zalabardo and colleagues report a 2026 multicentre study of antibiotic use and chemotherapy response in breast cancer. Antibiotics are often prescribed during neoadjuvant chemotherapy, given before surgery for localized breast cancer. Their impact on pathologic response was uncertain. Charts covered women treated at three university hospitals in Spain from 2009 to 2024. Exposure meant at least one systemic course in the month before or during chemotherapy to surgery.

Of one thousand three hundred sixteen patients, five hundred sixteen, about thirty nine percent, got antibiotics. Optimal response, judged by a Residual Cancer Burden index, was less frequent in exposed patients: about thirty six versus forty nine percent. Complete response rates were checked as a second endpoint. Joint models adjusted for clinical, pathologic and treatment factors, plus dose intensity and performance status. Antibiotic timing in chemotherapy may merit care, though germ needs still rule.
pmc-13280807:
Sergio Alexandre Gehrke and colleagues tested dental implant length in a 2026 lab study. Dental implants are metal posts set in the jaw to hold false teeth. How firmly a post grips at first helps predict whether it will fuse with bone. The team placed posts of four lengths, from five to eight millimeters, into foam blocks. The blocks mimicked bone from dense to soft, with thin or thick hard shells.

In dense foam, longer posts gripped harder and scored higher on a shake test. In soft foam the longest post also gripped best, and the shortest gripped worst. The authors say length counts most when bone is poor. Short posts can still grip well in dense bone and may lower surgery risks there. In weak bone, added length is key, they conclude.
pmc-13282707:
Ming Tai-Seale and co-authors report a 2026 evaluation of a patient-facing artificial intelligence chatbot built into a health portal's test results page. Many patients struggle to interpret lab and diagnostic findings on their own. The assistant aimed to explain results in plain terms inside a secure test version of the portal. One hundred thirty-one adults used it to view their results, then completed a survey.

Usability scored high, at eighty-one on a standard hundred-point scale. About seventy-seven percent said they were very or extremely likely to use it again, and the loyalty score was strongly positive. Patients with more diagnoses showed the strongest intention to reuse it. The authors conclude that a portal-embedded assistant can be usable and satisfying, especially for patients managing more illness, while secure design keeps the tool inside clinical systems.
pmc-13283207:
Goldenrod leaf tea freezes root-knot worm juveniles in dishes yet behaves differently in pots, Abdullah A Abdel-Rahman's 2026 assays find. The worm Meloidogyne incognita harms crops worldwide and cuts farm yields. Plant extracts offer a greener path than harsh chemical worm killers.

Water extracts froze young worms better than extracts made with other solvents. Column sorting split the water extract into 11 parts for testing. The raw extract froze all young worms at every dose tested. Three parts worked best in dishes, led by parts F5, F7, and F9 in the assays. In pots, one part with weak dish results cut root galls the most. Dish and pot tests must both guide product choice.
pmc-13283407:
Two crossed wires fused a neglected thumb joint without imaging guidance in Tadesse Debrye Belay's 2026 low-resource case. The patient had a long-standing thumb joint dislocation with worn joint surfaces. Delayed care and prior bone-setter treatment shaped the late presentation.

The patient was a 21-year-old right-handed man injured 11 years earlier. X-rays confirmed chronic dislocation with degenerative arthritis in the thumb joint. Surgeons opened the joint from two sides and fused it with two crossed wires. No live X-ray guidance was used during the operation itself. At six months he had pain relief, stable fusion, and kept grip and pinch. The authors call it a low-cost, workable option.
pmc-13283607:
Fiona Tierney authored a 2026 commentary on family caregivers of people with restless legs syndrome. The piece responds to an interview study by Odzakovic and colleagues from 2026. Family needs often go unseen when care focuses only on the patient.

Interviews covered 25 partners and adult children of people with the syndrome. The syndrome causes pain and a strong urge to move the legs, often at night. Sleep loss and daily strain spread to family members in clear ways. Nurses are well placed to inform, involve, and advocate for families. Family-centered nursing care is the central call of the commentary. Findings can empower nurses to support whole households.
pmc-13283807:
Yiqing Zhang and co-authors presented in 2026 a case of stubborn glaucoma treated with electroacupuncture on top of standard drops. The patient was a 76-year-old woman with primary open-angle glaucoma, a slow optic nerve disease, whose eye pressure swung despite four kinds of drops. Twice-weekly electroacupuncture began in late March 2025.

Eye pressure in her worse eye fell from 29 into target range after the first two sessions and stayed steady. Vision sharpness improved in both eyes, and no major side effects appeared. The authors are careful: her drops continued throughout, and one case cannot prove cause. They frame the method as a workable short-term add-on for patients who are poor candidates for surgery, pending proper trials.
pmc-13284007:
Mapping rules for alpine river habitat diverge sharply between Bavaria and Austria in a 2026 study by Wiebke Winkelhues and colleagues. The protected habitat centers on a shrub, Myricaria germanica, along mountain rivers. Dynamic rivers need maps that track pioneer growth and shifting channels.

Guideline maps were compared with habitat suitability models for the species. The Bavarian method labeled most of the study area as protected habitat. That area far exceeded modeled suitable ground by a wide margin. Austrian mapping tracked current occupancy and mapped far less land. The authors urge tracking young successional patches beside known populations.
pmc-13285407:
Shunyun Wang and colleagues propose a computer framework that predicts epileptic seizures from brain-wave recordings before they happen. The 2026 study addresses a real danger: seizures strike without warning and can injure patients or catch them while driving. A warning about half an hour ahead could let people reach safety and reduce fear.

Brain signals were split into frequency bands, and features describing their shape and complexity were extracted. A layered model then combined local pattern detection, attention across channels, and memory of signal sequences. Testing on a public children's hospital dataset gave accuracy near 96 percent. Event-level checks also showed few false alarms, at roughly one false alarm every three hours.
pmc-13285907:
Dandan He and co-authors describe ultrasound signs of a rare nail growth in a 2026 report of two cases. Acquired periungual fibrokeratoma is a harmless lump beside the nail that can bend the nail plate out of shape. Doctors often confuse it with other lumps in the same spot, so clear imaging signs could help before surgery.

Both patients had growths confirmed under the microscope after removal at a Hangzhou hospital in 2025. High-frequency scans showed neat, dark nodules rooted in the nail matrix with very little blood flow inside. Scan measures matched the removed tissue closely, which supports mapping the lump before cutting. The authors urge routine use of such scans to shield the nail matrix and keep the nail working well after surgery.
pmc-13286207:
Yitian Ou and co-authors trace a growth signal from tumor-friendly immune cells into prostate cancer cells in a 2026 laboratory study. Crowds of M2-type macrophages inside prostate tumors release a factor that makes cancer cells bolder, but the receiving end of that message was unclear. The team dosed prostate cells with the factor and scanned their full protein output for what switched on.

One protein, PCLAF, rose under the factor's push and no other top candidate held up on retesting. Tumor data banks and a tissue grid of 79 patients both tied high PCLAF to worse grade and shorter freedom from disease. Mice grew larger tumors when cancer cells carried extra PCLAF or extra factor shots, in step with protein levels inside the growths. The axis now stands as a named target for slowing prostate spread.
pmc-13286307:
Evan Fang and co-authors audit how the literature names the blood-vessel growths of Maffucci syndrome in a 2026 systematic review. The rare condition pairs cartilage tumors with vessel anomalies, but old reports lumped very different lesions under one loose label. The team read definitions across 265 articles since 1950 and charted diagnoses in 220 reported patients against the modern naming standard.

Over half the definitions still leaned on the vague old label, and only two matched the current standard wording. Barely one patient in six carried a vessel diagnosis precise enough to fit a modern category. A small group held one specific lesion type with none of the expected partner lesion, hinting either lesion alone might define the syndrome. Until naming tightens, the authors warn, doctors risk mismatched treatment for patients already hard to classify.
pmc-13286707:
Laura Bock Paulsen and colleagues test whether the brain's visual code drifts while perception stays put in a 2026 brain imaging study. One woman was scanned with magnetoencephalography across many days spanning six months, viewing the same pictures each session. Decoders trained on one day's signals were then asked to read another day's, and the pattern was checked in a public dataset with four more people.

Which scanning day produced a recording could be guessed from brain activity alone, proof the signals genuinely drift over months. Yet telling living from nonliving objects worked just as well across days as within them, and accuracy never decayed as the gap widened. The drift, the authors argue, runs sideways to the category code: sensory responses wander while the stable structure behind object recognition holds its shape.
pmc-13287107:
Fengmei Li and colleagues run a genome-wide search for DNA regions controlling panicle number in rice, the count of grain-bearing branches that anchors yield. The 2026 study uses two rice diversity collections scored under two day-length regimes across three Chinese agroecological zones, producing twelve datasets. Over three million markers fed the analysis.

One hundred thirty-eight regions linked with panicle number, several containing already-known genes. Helpful versions stacked up additively, raising panicle counts as they accumulated, while landraces carried more losing versions than improved varieties. Follow-up work pinned two known genes as regulators and found a hormone receptor gene in a finely mapped region that also shapes height and branching. Stable small-effect regions suit breeding best, the authors argue.
pmc-13288107:
Jung-Sik Joo and colleagues map how two stress proteins shape gene activity in cells, in a 2026 study. The endoplasmic reticulum folds new proteins, and overload there triggers a stress response. Two factors, ATF4 and CHOP, turn on gene programs that can either rescue the cell or push it toward death. The team combined several genome-wide methods in cells lacking each factor.

Removing ATF4 sharply weakened stress-driven enhancer activation, the DNA switches that boost gene output. It also broke loops that link those switches to their target genes. CHOP acted as a selective partner, tuning only some ATF4-driven enhancers and gene sets. Its strongest influence fell on death-linked programs, with little effect on core survival responses. The authors describe a layered system in which ATF4 builds the network and CHOP narrows its output.
pmc-13288207:
Mai Yasumoto and colleagues compare brain networks in autistic children during a sound test, in a 2026 study. Children heard a steady 40-hertz tone pattern while a magnetic scanner recorded brain activity. That rhythm probes how brain cells sync in the gamma range, tied to the balance of excitation and inhibition. Earlier work on single regions gave mixed results, so the team analyzed whole networks instead.

The study included 19 autistic children and 34 typically developing children aged five to eight. Network maps built from the recordings showed one clear group difference. Autistic children had a shorter characteristic path length, meaning signals could cross their networks in fewer steps. Clustering and small-world measures did not differ between groups. Across all children, shorter path length linked to higher scores on a social responsiveness scale. The authors suggest network measures add information beyond standard response strength.
pmc-13288307:
Cassidy M Van Stiphout and co-authors review in 2026 how cancers of the food pipe, stomach, bowel, and anal canal can increasingly be treated without removing the organ. Cure once demanded major surgery plus drug treatment, with lasting costs to daily function and quality of life.

Stronger drug and radiation courses given before surgery now clear tumours fully in some patients. For carefully chosen cases, close watching can replace the operation while keeping cancer outcomes steady. The review weighs proof and open questions site by site, from gullet to anus. The authors frame organ sparing as a growing standard option, not a compromise, when follow-up is tight.
pmc-13288607:
Emanuele Amore and colleagues present a crowded skin case in 2026. Their patient was a 17-year-old girl. She held five severe skin diagnoses at once. They were atopic dermatitis and scalp psoriasis. Inverse psoriasis and pustular acne also featured. Hidradenitis suppurativa completed the set.

Single-disease plans fit her case poorly. The strain on her life quality was heavy. Mind health suffered as well. The authors urge a whole-picture view. One shared process drives harm at many levels. Skin, heart, nerves, and psyche are all touched. Her case may guide care for tangled skin disease. Such cases need joint, not split, planning.
pmc-13289007:
Alberto Leardini and colleagues draft a 2026 trial plan for diabetic foot care in Italy. The trial is a no-profit, multi-site study. Foot sores strike many people with diabetes. Such sores cost a great deal to treat. Early checks may stop sores from forming.

Two patient groups will take part. One group has mid-level sore risk and no past sores. The other had sores that healed six months ago. Sites will run clinical and metabolic checks. One site adds gait and foot pressure tests. Scans will rebuild foot bones in 3D. Checks repeat after 12 months.
pmc-13289107:
Mumbi Chola and a large working group argue for African-led HIV control in 2026. The piece is a call to action. Gains in the HIV fight are at risk. Outside models and funds still dominate. African nations invest too little, they say.

The group has twelve members in all. It wants locally built and funded plans. Teamwork across the continent is key. Values include justice, dignity, and openness. Care should fit local cultures, not one mold. World bodies should back African aims. Fund blocks must be faced head-on. The ethos of Ubuntu guides their stance.
pmc-13289407:
Geovana S F Leite headed a 2026 lab and mouse study on whether blinatumomab still kills leukemia when a graft-versus-host drug blocks T-cell help signals. After donor cell transplant for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, relapse and graft-versus-host disease drive failure. Abatacept calms graft-versus-host disease by blocking CD28 signals, but it might also blunt graft-versus-leukemia effects.

Donor immune cells treated with abatacept were tested against leukemia lines with and without blinatumomab, which links T cells to cancer cells directly. Killing, activation markers, and cytokine output held up despite blockade in the assays. Humanized mice carrying leukemia then got single or combined therapy, with burden, graft symptoms, and survival tracked. Results support keeping antileukemia power while calming transplant harm.
pmc-13290107:
Research trends in smart bioelectronics from 2020 to 2024 are mapped by JiWon Bae and co-authors in a 2026 topic modeling study. These devices pair electronic hardware with artificial intelligence software, reading body signals and delivering stimulation meant to treat disease without drugs.

Bae and colleagues gathered 92 publications indexed in PubMed and applied latent Dirichlet allocation, tuned with coherence scores, to pull out the field's main themes. Three topics emerged: bio-signal-based neuromodulation, AI-driven analysis of neurological disease, and implantable devices and biomaterials, the last being the largest group. Output grew steadily over the five years, and the focus moved from sensing and materials toward AI analysis and disease-specific uses, pointing toward adaptive therapeutic systems.
pmc-13290207:
Tiny vesicles shed by stem cells could calm the immune storm after a heart attack, Ali Raza and colleagues argue in a 2026 review. A heart attack triggers a fast immune response that clears dead tissue, but inflammation that runs too long deepens the damage and pushes the heart toward failure.

The review covers vesicles from mesenchymal stem cells, induced pluripotent stem cells, and cardiac progenitor cells, and the signals they carry, including microRNAs and proteins. Reported effects include softening neutrophil-driven injury, steering macrophages toward a repair-oriented state, and rebalancing T-cell activity. Raza and colleagues also weigh engineering tricks to improve delivery, plus the hurdles of large-scale production, uneven cargo, and missing standard protocols that still block clinical use.
pmc-13290507:
A mental health scale built for Latin American workplaces gets its first psychometric workout in a 2026 study by María José Rosas-Carmona and colleagues. Existing tools in the region rarely capture distress and positive functioning together, so the team designed the 30-item LA-Mental Health Scale around sleep problems, anxiety, stress, and subjective well-being.

A sample of 308 workers from several Latin American countries completed the scale online. Confirmatory analysis supported the four-factor structure with acceptable fit, and reliability was excellent for anxiety and stress but weak for sleep. A 12-item short form also fit acceptably, though the authors warn it may be overfitted to this sample, and exploratory work hinted at a three-factor shape. They call for refinement and fresh validation before wider use.
pmc-13290807:
Cold-tolerant wheat for Himalayan valleys gets a genomic shopping list from Mukesh Rathore and colleagues in a 2026 breeding study. Prolonged cold in the Kashmir Valley delays wheat growth and cuts yield, so the team hunted DNA markers tied to both cold survival and productivity under cold.

A panel of 340 wheat lines carrying diversity from wild and durum relatives was grown across three temperate sites and genotyped on a 35K marker array. Association mapping found 152 stable marker-trait links, several passing strict significance thresholds, and haplotype analysis grouped them into 32 blocks where favorable versions boosted tolerance and yield together. Candidate genes inside the best intervals fit known cold-response biology. Rathore and colleagues offer the markers for breeding programs building hardier, higher-yielding wheat for rice-wheat systems.
pmc-13290907:
A fat-tagging enzyme partners with a polarity protein to set cilia length, Csenge Kata Rezi and colleagues show in a cell study from 2026. Primary cilia are sensory antennae whose length and contents are tightly controlled, and the team mapped the interaction network of DLG1, a cilia regulator, in mouse kidney cells.

Proximity labeling found 46 high-confidence DLG1 partners, most already tied to cilia or centrosomes. Among them, the enzyme ZDHHC5 was confirmed as a direct partner, and it reaches cilia with or without DLG1 present. DLG1 also binds SCAMP3 and STXBP1 and is needed to park STXBP1 at the cilia base. In zebrafish missing both zdhhc5 copies, embryos showed brain swelling, curved bodies, enlarged kidney filters, and overlong cilia. Rezi and colleagues model DLG1 as a hub whose partner web keeps cilia the right size.
pmc-13291107:
Color changes and flipping a picture upside down shift how natural and pleasing art looks, in a 2026 experiment by Xiao Wang and Yannan Zhang. Earlier work showed such basic visual features sway liking, but whether pictures of real things respond the same way as abstract works with no clear subject was unknown.

Paintings were shown in original or rotated hues, upright or inverted, across both concrete and abstract categories, and viewers rated naturalness and preference for each version. Both hue and orientation changes moved ratings far more for concrete works than for abstract ones. Naturalness also seemed to carry part of the effect into preference, yet the two judgments partly split apart, which suggests liking is not just a by-product of looking natural.
pmc-13291807:
Luca Cerniglia, Silvia Cimino, and Sherif Badawy wrote a 2026 theoretical paper extending Daniel Stern's motherhood constellation for the smartphone era. Stern's mid-1990s model describes a mother's mental organization through three relationships and four concerns, from keeping the baby alive to remaking her own identity. The authors argue that phones and AI now act inside that system rather than sitting outside it.

Drawing on attachment theory, mentalization research, and studies of technoference and online parent groups, they describe digital tools as actors that widen access to help yet also interrupt mother-infant contact. Algorithmic feeds form part of a mother's support matrix. The authors sketch a spectrum, from constellations strengthened by technology to ones it disrupts, and draw lessons for clinicians, designers, and policy makers.
pmc-13292307:
Junjie Wang and co-authors run a 2026 target trial emulation asking whether amino acid infusions after aortic surgery protect the kidneys. Acute kidney injury strikes many cardiac surgery patients and raises deaths, and amino acids might improve renal blood flow. Using a Shanghai aortic surgery database, the team mimicked a randomized trial with overlap weighting across 1,816 patients.

Kidney injury hit 37.8 percent of patients overall, and 30-day mortality was 1.6 percent across the cohort. Low-dose amino acids showed no clear link with either outcome. One subgroup stood out: patients aged 65 and older had lower injury odds with amino acids, at an odds ratio of 0.71 in the analysis. The authors label that finding exploratory and say it needs a real trial.
pmc-13293307:
Karianne Forcier and colleagues study, in a 2026 field paper, fungi living on plant roots at a site harmed by acid mine drainage. Acidic, metal-rich ground makes plant recovery hard, and root fungi may help plants settle in such soil.

Four plant types were sampled at the harmed site and a nearby clean site, across bulk soil, root-zone soil, and roots. Fungal counts rose toward the roots on one growth medium, hinting at close root ties under stress. Most finds were Ascomycota, many of them dark septate endophytes. One genus thrived on plants in wet, acidic metal soils, while another favored calmer ground.
pmc-13293807:
Hugues Duffau argues, in a 2026 viewpoint, that the future of brain tumor surgery lies in cognitive neuroscience, not in better surgical tools alone. Glioma care has long prized longer survival, sometimes at the cost of quality of life, with trial endpoints that may not serve patients.

Duffau notes that earlier radiation lengthened time without tumor growth yet not overall survival in a major trial, and questions short follow-up for new drug claims in slow tumors. Patients with low-grade gliomas now live over 15 years after wide removal in cited series. Balancing tumor control with brain function needs a shift toward how the brain processes thought.
pmc-13294307:
Paolo Pecere examines plant cognition debates through history and philosophy in a 2026 article. Some botanists credit plants with sensing, learning, memory, and even awareness, while many peers reject such claims for thin evidence and the lack of nerves. Pecere returns to Darwin's 1880 book on plant movement, which likened root tips to brains and spoke of plant sensation.

Present quarrels reuse Darwin-era moves: appeals to continuity among living things and reasoning by analogy. One side warns against projecting human traits, while the other allows cognition in non-neural forms. Animal ethics and non-Western views on living nature now enter as tie-breakers, shifting the balance of debate.
pmc-13295007:
Yan-Nan Cao and co-authors use genetic methods to ask how lung disease raises lung cancer risk in a 2026 study. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and lung cancer often occur together, but shared smoking habits cloud the picture. Blood chemicals were tested as possible go-betweens on the causal path.

Genome study data fed two-sample and two-step analyses, checked by reverse and sensitivity tests. Results supported a causal effect of the lung disease on cancer, with no effect running the other way. Three blood metabolites partly carried the effect, while inflammation factors showed no such role for the disease itself, sharpening ideas about mechanism.
pmc-13295507:
Dong Zhang reports airway gene patterns and a little-known signal protein in asthma in a 2026 letter. Bronchial lining cells grown at an air surface can show how dust mite exposure mimics asthma changes. Cells brushed from eight healthy volunteers were grown, exposed, and read by gene sequencing.

Comparisons found 1,506 asthma-linked genes changed after differentiation and exposure, split evenly between rises and falls. One rising gene, C10orf99, tied closely to immune and inflammation themes and makes a receptor ligand protein. Its mouse counterpart also rose in mite-driven asthma models but not in a different model type, singling it out for airway study.
pmc-13295907:
Zuraifah Asrah Mohamad and colleagues set out a 2026 study protocol on gut microbes and major depression in Malaysia. Evidence links gut bacteria to mood through the chemicals they make, yet Malaysian patients have barely been profiled.

The planned study in the Klang Valley will compare stool samples from clinic patients on one drug, patients on several drugs, and healthy community members. Bacterial DNA testing will map which microbes each group carries. Approval is in place, results will go to journals and policy makers, and the team hope the profiles guide future care.
pmc-13296007:
Matt M. Mallette and co-authors test heated massage delivered from a car-style seat against chronic low back pain, in a 2026 study. Back pain is very common, and heat and massage each help, yet the two are rarely paired in a handy form. Seventeen adults with long-term, non-specific back pain near six out of ten in strength tried two heated styles in random order: smooth stroking and rhythmic tapping.

Each visit paired a quiet control stretch with twenty minutes of heated massage to the low back, upper thighs, and seat muscles. Both styles cut pain by ten and twenty minutes and eased felt tightness at twenty minutes, while skin warmth and comfort rose. Tapping eased tightness sooner and more, and it raised tissue elasticity. The authors offer seat-based heated massage as a handy aid on commute-length trips.
pmc-13296107:
Yan-Wu Yang and colleagues pool studies on two blood and spinal fluid marks of brain injury as warnings of delirium after surgery, in a 2026 meta-analysis. Delirium is a common, grave muddling after operations that flags acute brain trouble and foretells later decline. The marks are neurofilament light chain, from nerve fibers, and glial fibrillary acidic protein, from support cells. Three databases were searched to January 2026.

Fourteen studies with 2,604 people qualified, and near thirty percent developed delirium. Higher levels of the nerve mark tied to higher delirium odds in both blood and spinal fluid, and delirious patients carried more of it. The glial mark's link was weaker and less steady. Each mark alone sorted patients only fairly, so the authors say neither is ready to stand alone as a test.
pmc-13296507:
Bo E. Zweedijk and a large surgical team measure, in 2026, how clearly a glowing tracer outlines mouth cancers during operations. Clear edges matter for cure, and the tracer targets a molecule common on these tumours, so the team compare brightness ratios across mouth sites in living tissue and removed samples.

Every sample cleared the contrast bar needed for reliable outlining, and final tissue checks confirmed accurate edge calls. One rear upper site glowed less in the body, blamed on camera angle and natural background glow. The authors say the method separates tumour from healthy lining across the mouth.
pmc-13297407:
A count of mutations per tumor might help sort a rare gland cancer into risk groups, a 2026 study led by Karan Patel hints. The team worked with people whose adenoid cystic cancer had spread or come back and could not be cured.

In two groups of patients, they counted mutations and set the counts next to gene types and survival time. Counts were low in most tumors. Cancers with switched-on NOTCH genes tended to score higher. The team says counts like these could sharpen how doctors group patients by risk. That step could help match people to immune drugs, which tend to work best when mutation counts run high.
pmc-13297707:
Hard exercise may blunt the effect of obesity-linked gene variants, suggests a 2026 pilot study led by Jenni Chambers. Fifty-six adults aged 18 to 65 were sorted by activity level, genotyped for variants in the FTO and MC4R genes, and checked for methylation of a third gene, SREBF1.

Among vigorously active participants, the FTO risk allele tracked with lower body fat (p = 0.0387), while the MC4R risk allele tracked with higher body mass index (p = 0.0256). The vigorous group also showed higher SREBF1 methylation, a first look at that link. The authors conclude that activity patterns may help predict how these variants play out in body composition.
pmc-13297807:
Drone swarms fighting an unseen adversary must invent their own task lists on the fly, and Wenxin Li with Yongxin Feng offer a method in a 2026 paper. Their system turns local observations, target beliefs, and each aircraft's remaining resources into structured task graphs for mixed fleets.

An offline search program first grades possible futures and teaches a graph attention network what good task structures look like. A manager module then filters tasks, repairs broken dependencies, and checks resources before anything flies. In simulations with heavy observation noise and unfamiliar enemy tactics, the method beat a Graphormer baseline on task-graph utility and edge accuracy, and cut the share of impossible tasks by 35.14%.
pmc-13299607:
An oxygen-sensing enzyme fine-tunes cell division by editing a chromosome manager protein, show Jimena Druker and colleagues in a 2026 cell biology study. The enzyme PHD1 adds a hydroxyl group to proline 604 of RepoMan, a regulator that guides the phosphatase PP1 during mitosis.

Removing PHD1, but not its sibling PHD2, left a key histone mark over-phosphorylated during division. Cells carrying a RepoMan version that cannot accept the edit bound its partner phosphatase PP2A weakly, then lagged in finishing mitosis, misaligned and mis-segregated chromosomes, and died more often. The authors place this oxygen-linked edit among the controls keeping chromosome distribution accurate.
pmc-13299707:
Compounds from the ashwagandha herb do reach the urine after swallowing a supplement, though only a small share, report Alex B Speers and colleagues in a 2026 pharmacokinetic study. Healthy older adults took 240 or 480 mg of a commercial root-and-leaf extract, and urine was collected for twelve hours.

Sensitive mass spectrometry found four withanolides in urine, including withaferin A and an abundant metabolite not present in the product itself, apparently created by the body. Recovery of the other detected compounds stayed under 3% of the ingested amount. The authors say urinary data add a missing piece to how these plant chemicals are absorbed and processed.
pmc-13300007:
Eating insects could help meet rising protein needs with far less land and water than cattle farming. Mohd Suhail Banday and nine colleagues published a 2026 review that pulls together current knowledge on edible insects as food and feed. Their survey covers nutrition, safety, processing, rules, and shopper attitudes in one place.

The authors compare insect protein quality with standard scores and note how species, feed, and rearing change nutrient content. They also weigh allergy risks, uneven safety rules across countries, and steps that could win over hesitant consumers. Farming advances such as automation and nutrient enrichment get attention too. The review argues insects can support steadier food supplies if standards and public trust improve.
pmc-13300307:
Hanna Witoszek and co-authors review how melatonin and nitric oxide work together in plant defense, in a 2026 article that reaches from classic stresses to new pollutants. Melatonin is a signaling molecule that limits oxidative damage, and nitric oxide acts as a key partner inside its signaling network. The authors synthesize known evidence on drought-like and other abiotic stresses before extending the discussion to microplastics, nanoparticles, and surfactants.

The review traces how the two molecules shape each other's levels and jointly manage reactive oxygen species, stress enzymes, and ion balance. That partnership helps plants keep growth going under harsh conditions. Evidence for the newer pollutants is still thin, which the authors flag as the main gap. They argue the established stress pathways offer a plausible route for protecting crops as these contaminants build up in soil and water.
pmc-13300707:
Mhd Nawar Alachkar and co-authors test a tweak to a tricuspid valve risk score in a 2026 prospective study. The TRI-SCORE predicts death after tricuspid procedures, and one of its inputs grades right ventricular function by a simple motion measure. The team proposed swapping that input for a coupling ratio that also accounts for pulmonary pressure, then compared both versions in 109 patients undergoing catheter based tricuspid treatment at one center.

At twelve months, about nineteen percent of patients had died, and the combined outcome of death or cardiovascular rehospitalization reached about forty percent. Each extra score point raised the odds of death similarly under both versions, and discrimination was identical on the standard curve measure. The combined outcome showed the same near tie. The authors conclude the physiologically appealing substitution adds nothing in practice, and they keep the original score's simpler input.
pmc-13301507:
Pushing an antibiotic in by hand instead of dripping it through a bag worked just as well, Mary Fronrath and colleagues report in a 2026 retrospective study. Across a five-hospital system from 2014 through 2021, 254 adults treated with cefepime for Gram-negative bloodstream infection split evenly between intravenous push and piggyback infusion. A ranked outcome blended cure with nerve side effects.

The composite showed no difference between the routes. Push patients did need vasopressors more often, at 22.0 percent against 10.2, and stayed a median of ten days against seven in hospital. Other endpoints matched, and ward admission plus a urinary source predicted cure. The authors endorse push dosing as a shortage-era substitute.
pmc-13301707:
Vein grafts begin failing on the operating table, Benedetto Ferraresi and colleagues argue in a 2026 narrative review of graft preservation during bypass surgery. Harvest handling, storage fluid, and the shock of arterial pressure injure the vein's lining and set up later narrowing. The review weighs local defenses applied while the conduit sits outside the body.

Protective storage solutions, external support sleeves, drug-eluting biodegradable wraps, and RNA therapies aimed at the graft wall all show early promise. Studies link them to calmer inflammation and less wall thickening, but durable gains in patency or patient outcomes stay unproven. The authors sketch a combined strategy and call for trials that test it whole.
pmc-13303007:
Ufuk Karabacak and co-authors ask, in a 2026 single-centre study, how much healthy tissue must surround a removed non-invasive breast tumour to keep recurrence low. Guidelines accept two millimetres, yet narrower margins might spare women repeat surgery. The analysis centred on the one-millimetre line.

The cohort held 107 women treated with breast-conserving surgery plus radiotherapy between 2009 and 2025 for ductal carcinoma in situ. Seven patients saw the tumour return in the same breast over a median four years of follow-up. Survival without recurrence looked similar whether the two-millimetre line was used or not. Margins under one millimetre, however, carried clearly worse outcomes, suggesting the one-to-two millimetre band deserves case-by-case judgement.
pmc-13303607:
Mioara-Calipsoana Matei leads a 2026 review of antibiotic use and hospital-acquired infections in a Romanian emergency hospital. Busy emergency settings rely heavily on antibiotics given before test results return, which can breed resistant germs.

Use from January 2021 to October 2025 was measured in defined daily doses per 100 bed-days and sorted by the World Health Organization AWaRe groups. Use varied widely among units, with medical wards highest, and the Watch group overtook the Access group from 2023 onward. Only 27 hospital infections were recorded over the period. The patterns give stewardship teams clear targets for closer oversight.
pmc-13305307:
József Janszky and Réka Horváth pool 375 published cases of epilepsy tied to GAD65 antibodies in a 2026 patient-level analysis. Seizures in this immune condition often resist standard drugs and respond unevenly to immune therapy.

Cases came from 132 papers drawn from a checked register of studies. The typical patient was female with temporal lobe seizures and other immune illness. Treatment timing groups split at six and twelve months after symptoms began. Early immune treatment showed a signal that varied by drug class rather than helping across the board. Timing and drug mix both deserve weight in care planning.
pmc-13305807:
Huirong Lv fed shrimp-derived peptides to obese mice during a return to normal food in a 2026 animal study. Peptides from Solenocera crassicornis were first profiled in detail, then tested for added benefit beyond diet change alone.

After seven weeks on a high-fat diet, male mice switched chow and received vehicle, orlistat or peptides for four weeks. Peptide groups showed less belly and kidney fat, better blood fats and liver appearance, plus stronger antioxidant and gut barrier markers in the reported checks. Gut microbe shifts and cell tests supported a possible gut and liver pathway worth further study.
pmc-13305907:
Muhammad Idrees made copper cobalt sulfide particles to clean dyed wastewater with sunlight in a 2026 study. Particles formed by a mixing and precipitation route were checked with several imaging and light-based tools before testing.

Measured band gap was 2.06 eV, average crystal size was 28.23 nm, and surface charge balance point was pH 7 in the reported values. The catalyst cleared Eosin B more strongly than Rhodamine B when each dye stood alone, while mixing dyes changed little for the second dye. Higher dye load lowered efficiency, and dose, acidity and heat all shaped performance.
pmc-13306507:
Dong Zhao devised a satellite method for finding oil slicks at sea in a 2026 study using China's Zhuhai-1 imagery. Older methods used only a slice of the rich colour information in each pixel, blurring slicks into uneven ocean backgrounds.

A spectral DNA encoding scheme captures fine colour detail, and two extraction routes pull out signature genes that separate oil from seawater. Three satellite scenes tested the full approach in the reported experiments. Results described slick spectra precisely and located spills well, offering a sharper watch as spill risk grows with global tensions.
pmc-13307707:
Xudong Lan and colleagues clean oilfield wastewater in 2026 with water hyacinth plants helped by tough local microbes. Produced water from a Pakistani oil field carried heavy metals and high salt, and baseline chemistry was measured first. Plants with added microbes worked on the water for fifteen days in the laboratory.

Plants grew rather than wilted, with shoots and roots lengthening and wet weight rising slightly. Acidity settled from strongly alkaline toward neutral, and dissolved solids fell by about half. Metal removal varied widely by element, peaking for silver and running lowest for mercury. Microbe partnership appeared to raise plant tolerance and overall performance. The authors present plant-microbe treatment as a sustainable option for petroleum wastewater, though the trial stayed at bench scale.
pmc-13308207:
Abdulaziz M Alodhailah and co-authors explore in 2026 the emotional labour of emergency nurses in Saudi Arabia, and how burnout and resilience sit side by side. They spoke with 17 nurses from three sites in Riyadh, in talks that ran from 38 to 67 minutes each during the study span.

Five themes arose, from the strain of hiding feelings during high stakes care to peer backing and finding meaning in the work. Burnout signs such as drained energy and distance from patients arose alongside coping, not in place of it. Ward leadership, staffing, and mind health support tipped the balance most. The authors urge system fixes over calls for nurses to toughen up alone.
pmc-13308507:
Mohammad Asim introduces a 2026 virtual special issue of Translational Oncology built around reading tumours cell by cell. Twenty-eight peer-reviewed papers make up the collection, and the editorial treats the single review separately from twenty-seven original studies. Cancers covered range across gut, lung, kidney, brain, skin, bone, and blood.

Methods run from single-cell mapping and combined omics to laboratory perturbation studies and drug discovery driven by systems pharmacology. One strand builds cell atlases of tumour surroundings and squeezes them into survival signatures. Another anchors computer findings in tissue staining and animal models before claims are made. A clinical strand embeds biomarker analysis inside a randomised phase three trial. Asim arranges the papers along a discovery-to-clinic path. The issue's promise, he argues, is measurement precise enough to change individual patient decisions.
pmc-13308907:
Tak Wing Yu and co-authors ask in 2026 South African health teachers what they think of virtual reality for training, at one university with tight means. They spoke with 18 teachers across physio, nursing, dentistry, and allied fields after each tried three immersive apps of rising clinical depth.

Teachers liked the pull and hands on feel, though some first saw the gear as a game like novelty for class. Gripes spanned visual overload, queasy heads, and the hassle of kit, rooms, and timetables in real terms. Safe room to err won praise, as did a stair plan from basic anatomy to full tasks. Gear alone will not do, the group warned, without teaching support.
pmc-13309507:
Thi Hoa Vu and co-authors survey how small tea farmers in northern Vietnam rank risks from nature in a 2026 study. Small farms tend much of the world farmland and face climate swings, worn soil, scarce water, and pest pressure. What farmers fear most shapes what they do next, so views matter beside hard measures.

Face-to-face interviews with 312 farmers covered ten kinds of nature risk. Sharp weather and pests ranked as the most pressing threats, while soil and water decline loomed as slower worries. Heavy fertilizer use tied to greater soil worry, and watering systems tied to lower felt climate risk. The authors urge farm support that matches these ranked fears.
pmc-13310407:
Mingjing Gao and co-authors review targeted biologic drugs for immune kidney diseases in a 2026 article. In these disorders, misdirected immunity scars the kidney filters and drives chronic kidney failure. The review frames the disease chain in three steps: innate alarm, adaptive misfire with self-attacking antibodies, and end-stage scarring injury.

Drugs are sorted by the step they interrupt across eight named diseases, from IgA nephropathy to lupus nephritis. Options include cytokine blockers, B-cell depleting antibodies, plasma cell agents, and complement blockers aimed at set points in the chain. Trial and clinic evidence is weighed for each class. The authors argue for matching drug to disease step rather than blanket immune suppression.
pmc-13310707:
Xiaoyu Yang and co-authors describe a 2026 case of a rare tumor inside the skull of a 2 month old baby girl. Tumors of this type, called angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma, usually grow in arms, legs, or the trunk. A growth inside the head at such a young age is highly unusual and hard to manage.

Scans showed a mass behind the ear, and surgery removed a lump that measured about 4 cm across at its widest point. Lab tests and gene checks confirmed the diagnosis. Full removal is the main treatment, but care in tiny infants needs close control of bleeding and close work with lab doctors.
pmc-13310807:
Ezgi Yavasca led a 2026 study on filling pressures after heart transplant in children and long term graft survival. Survival has improved, yet late graft loss still occurs. High pressures inside the heart in early years, without rejection on biopsy, may warn of later harm, but proof past ten years was thin.

Records covered 114 grafts from 1986 to 2020 in children who survived five years. Fourteen grafts showed high pressures in the early window. Those grafts had far worse survival at ten years and a much higher risk of graft loss. Heart related events also trended higher. Early pressure checks may flag grafts that need closer care.
pmc-13311007:
Cesar Nadala and colleagues trace a toxin germ in powdered infant formula during a 2025 outbreak study reported in 2026. Infant botulism struck across states and was linked to formula powder. Sealed product tubs and bulk base powder were screened with a tiered lab method that joins enrichment, gene tests, and genome reading.

The germ Clostridium botulinum was found in both finished product and base powder. One lot isolate matched base powder exactly, while another lot strain differed. Standard indicator counts missed the germ in positive samples. Makers should treat the germ as a likely hazard in some inputs and build direct controls.
pmc-13311107:
Brandon D. Howell and colleagues argue for hospitality as a formal health design field in a 2026 viewpoint. Health grows not only from medical care but from the spaces and service people meet in clinics, care homes, and rest lodging. Privacy, sound control, and kind service can cut stress, aid sleep, and lift safety.

Viewing care spaces as linked healing settings opens joint work across design, mind science, and systems fields. Shared courses and studies could spread gains to staff health and firm performance while cutting gaps in dignity and access. Formal status for the field is the next step proposed.
pmc-13311307:
Ding Xiaoli and colleagues offer a 2026 analysis of two conditions, premenstrual syndrome and uterine fibroids, and their world burden in women aged 15 to 49. Data come from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023.

In 2023 the study counts about 233 million new cases of premenstrual syndrome and about 10 million new fibroid cases worldwide. Rates of both conditions rose from 1990 to 2023, as did the years lived with disability from each. Forecasts to 2050 see premenstrual rates easing slightly while fibroid burden keeps rising. The numbers give planners a base for women's health services over the next decades.
pmc-13312407:
Emiliano Paradiso and Žiga Jakopin offer a 2026 perspective on the medicinal chemistry of CD1d ligands, the glycolipids that switch on invariant natural killer T cells. The prototype compound, alpha-galactosylceramide, has anchored this immunotherapy field for years, and chemists have spent two decades reshaping its parts to steer the immune response it triggers.

The authors walk through changes to the sugar headgroup, the phytosphingosine base, and the fatty acyl chain, and explain how each edit tilts the response toward inflammatory Th1 or calmer Th2 patterns. They assess pairing these agonists with other adjuvants. They also highlight a newer direction: fully synthetic self-adjuvanting vaccines that fuse antigen and glycolipid into one molecule so both reach the same cell together. The piece frames tailored glycolipid design as a route to precise, durable immunity against cancer and infection.
pmc-13314407:
Haiyan Peng and ShaoXue Li compare two styles of coping therapy for stomach ulcer relapse in their 2026 study. Ulcers of the stomach and upper gut come back often, and how patients handle stress may shape that risk over years.

The team looked back at 167 patients treated in hospital from January 2021 to March 2025. One group of 84 patients got problem-focused sessions that taught spotting problems, making answers, setting goals, and acting on plans. The other group of 83 patients got emotion-focused sessions built on awareness of feelings and relaxation. Each course ran as 6 monthly group sessions of 90 minutes, by the design given in the report. The four-year follow-up lets the authors weigh which coping style better keeps ulcers away.
pmc-13314507:
Yao Wang, Yu Yue, and Xu-Chen Cao build a survival model for breast cancer that has spread to the liver, in a study dated 2026. Outlook in this group varies widely and is often poor, and old staging tools give weak personal forecasts.

The team drew on the SEER database for patients from 2010 to 2021 and used four machine learning methods to pick steady predictors. Ten variables made the cut. Among them were age, tumor size, spread to brain, bone, or lung, tumor grade, and chemotherapy, plus the three receptor marks ER, PR, and HER2, as listed in the report. The cohort was split into a training share of 70 percent, as stated, and a test share. The resulting chart aims to give each patient a fairer, personal survival estimate.
pmc-13314607:
Mayadhar Sethy and co-workers hunt the drivers of health system performance in poorer countries in a study from 2026. Low- and middle-income states still struggle to reach health care for all, and the COVID-19 shock laid bare weak governance, funding, and facilities.

The team built a data set for 135 such countries from 2000 to 2023, drawn from world health, bank, and survey sources, filling gaps by set rules. Fixed-effect, dynamic, and path models sorted which factors drive performance. From those numbers they built optimization models that seek the best spend of scarce funds toward universal coverage. Their pathways aim to turn stalled progress on world health goals into a workable plan for states with tight budgets.
pmc-13314807:
Zuping Wu and colleagues review moving mitochondria between cells as a therapy for bone disease, in work published in 2026. Faulty mitochondria run through osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and bone tumors, driving inflammation, breaks, and pain.

Cells can hand whole mitochondria to neighbors, a newly found natural process that can reset energy work in the receiving cell. The review centers on transfers tied to mesenchymal stem cells and how they steer growth, division, death, and immune action in bone and joint cells. It then weighs transplant and delivery tactics for putting fresh mitochondria where they are needed. Turning a natural cell-to-cell gift into a drug-like tool could open a new class of bone care.
pmc-13314907:
Xinyue Yang and colleagues pool animal studies of stem cell therapy for Sjögren syndrome in work published in 2026. The autoimmune disease dries the mouth and eyes and stiffens joints, and mesenchymal stem cells can calm immune attack, yet their true worth here was unproven.

The review, logged in PROSPERO as stated in the report, searched five databases to May 2025 and kept 25 studies. Pooled math gauged changes in saliva flow, gland inflammation, and immune signal levels. A clear tally before human trials is the point: it shows whether effects hold across labs and where study designs clash. If the animal gains prove steady, the case for careful first human tests grows much stronger.
pmc-13315807:
Naoki Takahashi and co-authors used deep learning in 2026 to guess the causative gene in lissencephaly from 3D brain MRI scans. In this migration disorder, faulty genes leave distinct marks on brain shape, so image patterns might point to which gene is at fault.

The team extended standard network designs to handle 3D inputs and sorted scans into three classes, the main genes LIS1 and DCX plus other genetic causes. A 3D-ResNet18 model reached mean accuracy above 78 percent. A probability threshold step then sharpened calls for the primary genes. Image-based gene hints could speed confirmatory testing.
pmc-13316207:
Haifu Sun and a large team built a conductive fiber scaffold in 2026 to heal diabetic bone defects. In such defects, lasting inflammation, metabolic trouble, and scar-like repair block the path from injury to regrowth. Their scaffold joins local electrical cues with fixed and slowly released peptide signals aimed at the mTOR pathway.

Single-cell sequencing showed the scaffold reshaped macrophage and fibroblast states early in repair. Macrophages cut mTORC1 activity, burned more fat, and turned calmer, while fibroblasts eased activation through KLF4 and made less scar protein. In diabetic rats with 5 millimeter skull defects, mature layered bone grew better.
pmc-13316607:

Three patients with reflux disease and mixed germ sinus infections, including drug-resistant staph, had failed years of standard therapy.

All three cleared their infections on the oral drug and tolerated it well, according to the report. The cases matter because resistant germs increasingly drive sinus flare-ups that cycle despite long, rigorous treatment. An oral option that covers resistant strains could spare patients stronger hospital drugs. Pugliese stresses that three successes only justify a proper trial, not a change in routine care yet.
pmc-13317607:
Lijin Wang, Aiwei Tang and Jingbi You review, in 2026, blue-emitting quantum dots based on zinc selenide that avoid toxic cadmium. Blue is the hardest colour for quantum dot displays, and zinc-based dots offer narrow emission, bright output and good stability. Adding tellurium extends the colour range into the blue needed for screens.

The review covers material properties and synthesis first, then strategies for improving the dots themselves. Core-shell versions have reached near-perfect light efficiency in the laboratory. Device sections examine the emitting layer and the layers that carry charge. Reported zinc selenide telluride devices now rival cadmium-based ones on efficiency and can last tens of thousands of hours at display brightness. Remaining barriers to commercial use close the discussion.
pmc-13317807:
Armando Viramontes and colleagues describe, in 2026, an 87-year-old woman whose bowel was blocked by a gallstone, a rare complication called gallstone ileus. A stone escapes from the gallbladder into the gut through an abnormal channel, then lodges and obstructs. Diagnosis is hard because symptoms are nonspecific, and older patients often fare poorly.

She arrived with obstructive pain, poor appetite and vomit resembling coffee grounds, plus unstable blood pressure and kidney failure. Computed tomography showed the classic trio of obstruction, air in the bile ducts and a stone outside the gallbladder. Surgery found the stone lodged well down the small bowel. Surgeons milked it to a suitable point and removed it through a simple opening. She recovered well and went home on day six.
pmc-13318207:
Abdulmalik Alhuwaymil and colleagues formulate, in a 2026 food study, low-calorie date snacks padded with psyllium or oat fiber. They built them for regions where dates are beloved but blood sugar control is a growing worry. They profiled the snacks' nutrition and then tested blood sugar responses in volunteers.

Bars mixing two date pastes with nuts carried fiber at set levels up to ten percent. Fiber-rich versions packed up to 17.55 percent fiber against 7.86 percent in the plain control, with fewer available carbs and less energy per bite, plus strong antioxidant readings. In 20 healthy adults and 20 patients with type 2 diabetes, the favored fiber bars blunted post-meal glucose climbs, with the psyllium version ahead. Sweet snacks, they show, can be redesigned, not just banned.
pmc-13318707:

Patients had cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy, meaning nerve root or spinal cord pressure. The team tracked short-term complications and their risk factors.

Records covered 107 patients treated at one centre between June 2021 and June 2024. Overall in the series, complications struck 12.1 percent of the patients treated. The rate was 7.4 percent for radiculopathy cases and 20.5 percent for myelopathy cases. Myelopathy complications were also more severe, including bleeding needing another operation. Age 65 or older, other illnesses, and laminectomy each raised risk. Early cases in the learning curve fared worst, with complications in 40.0 percent of them.
pmc-13318907:
Shiyu Li and Hongyu Liu review, in 2026, the gut-bone axis and Chinese botanical drugs for osteoporosis. Weak, porous bones raise fracture risk as populations age. Microbe imbalance disturbs bone through short-chain fatty acids and hormone signalling. Immune balance between Th17 and regulatory T cells also matters. The review explains how botanical drugs reshape microbe communities. They can strengthen the gut barrier and retune gut-bone signals. Evidence for specific preparations and their pathways is summarised. The authors frame the work as support for microbe-targeted bone therapies. Clinical application and new drug research both stand to gain.
pmc-13319007:
Mingchang Pang and co-authors review, in 2026, a chemical protein modification driven by hydrogen sulfide and its grip on fat metabolism. The review maps effects on fatty acid turnover, triglyceride handling, and cholesterol balance. It gathers newly identified protein targets from recent studies. The modification links redox signalling with lipid stability across the body. That pairing may explain part of several metabolic diseases. The authors discuss treatments built on sulfide donors or on drugs aimed at modified proteins. They frame the pathway as a fresh therapeutic module for lipid disorders.
pmc-13319707:
Yang Fang and co-authors comment on a new mapping method for spread tumors in a 2026 article about a study by Wang and co-authors. The method pairs gene edits inside living tumors with fine sampling of thin tissue slices, so cause and local effect can be read in place. Spread tumors resist immune care in ways that flat lab tests miss.

Blocking it changed scaffold buildup and the local immune mix, and tumors then answered better to cell based immune care. Gene losses in one growth control path also drove immune escape. The platform gives a shared way to test such links at scale.
pmc-13320007:
Dipendra Pant and co-authors mine 25 years of drug records in child and teen mental health care in Norway in a 2026 study. A step by step pipeline was built to pull clean counts from those records.

From records of patients age 19 or younger, 7214 visits with at least one drug were mapped by diagnosis and drug class. Behavior and mood type diagnoses led the counts, and extra diagnoses on the same visit were rare on the main layer but near universal on the side layers. The maps show which drugs pair with which diagnoses at visit level.
pmc-13320107:

Five domains cover access, readability, ease of use, acceptability and overall evaluation, with twenty-five items in total. Each item is scored on a five-point scale, higher meaning more usable. The author intends the framework to support wider uptake of syndrome criteria in daily practice.
pmc-13320407:
Geetika Vadali and co-authors present a data set for reading print through paper with terahertz waves in a 2026 data article. Reading text on both sides of a sheet that cannot be flipped, where print may be hidden or faded, stays an open puzzle with uses in archives and forgery hunts. Sheets of plain copy paper carry test grids and letters in four inks, toner, jet ink, iron gall ink, and pencil lead, on front, back, both, or none. Scans ran in bounce mode under dry nitrogen, logging a full wave shape at each spot. Files give spot maps and wave data with hand labels for each ink setup.
pmc-13320507:

In mice with colitis, the treatment eased weight loss, colon shortening, and tissue damage. It lowered harmful oxygen and swelling signals, cut immune cell inflow, and supported the bowel mucus barrier.
pmc-13320707:
Nami Suzuki and co-authors compare two dosing plans for an overactive thyroid drug in a 2026 records study. Propylthiouracil, or PTU, is used less now due to side effects, but some patients with Graves disease cannot take the main alternative. The study weighed a high dose alone against a low dose paired with potassium iodide.

Records covered 1171 patients treated from 2005 to 2024, all of them women, and the median age was 32 years; matching was used to balance the groups. Side effects occurred in 294 patients, almost all in the high dose group. Thyroid hormone levels fell faster by week 2 in the low dose paired group, though the gap later closed.
pmc-13321307:
Abdalla Ibrahim and a large team check whether plaque fat measures repeat reliably with a current imaging catheter in a 2026 study. The Dualpro catheter pairs near-infrared light with ultrasound to map both plaque makeup and vessel shape during heart procedures. Its fat scores guide judgements about risky plaque, yet real world repeatability was unknown.

Paired repeat scans of the same artery stretch were compared in 87 cases across procedure stages. Both the overall fat burden score and the peak four millimetre score repeated strongly, with correlation values of 0.95 and 0.90 in the report. Key risk cut-offs agreed in about nine of ten repeat runs, supporting trust in the readings.
pmc-13321807:
Jun Morita and his team run, in 2026, a drug interaction study in healthy Japanese adults for a new antibiotic helper called nacubactam. The drug blocks enzymes that bacteria use to destroy beta-lactam antibiotics, so it will be given alongside them. Whether the partners change each other's blood levels needed checking before wider use.

Thirty-two men in four cohorts each received nacubactam alone, then one of four partner antibiotics alone, then both together, all as single intravenous doses. Blood exposure values for every drug were basically unchanged by combination treatment, with statistical ratios inside the accepted matching range in all cohorts. Side effects were all mild and resolved without treatment. The authors say the results support developing nacubactam pairings with cefepime, aztreonam, meropenem and piperacillin.
pmc-13322407:
Wang and Cao built an interpretable prediction model in 2026 for adverse outcomes in older heart patients who take many medicines at once. Their retrospective study covered 1,200 patients aged 65 and over with cardiovascular disease and at least five medicines at a Chinese hospital from 2021 to 2024. The team trained an extreme gradient boosting model, a tree-based learning method, and used a standard explanation tool to show which factors drove each prediction.

About 19 percent of patients suffered an adverse drug event during follow-up. The model predicted such events well, clearly beating plain logistic regression, and also forecast 30- and 90-day readmission and one-year death with similar strength. Age, kidney function, medicine count, blood albumin, and overall illness burden ranked as the top drivers, with sharp risk jumps below set kidney and albumin cutoffs. The authors say the blend of accuracy and openness suits bedside risk checks.
pmc-13322907:
Lingshuai Meng and co-authors review the two-way link between the gut barrier and gut microbes in sepsis, in a 2026 article. Sepsis brings whole-body inflammation, organ damage and high death rates, and the intestine sits close to its course.

A leaky gut lining lets microbes and their products drive local and wider immune responses, while a disturbed microbial mix changes disease progress through its chemical output. The authors build a framework for gut-driven body-wide inflammation and note that some standard supportive care can itself harm the intestine. Treatments aimed at gut function, from microbial repair to barrier support, close the review as routes worth testing in practice.
pmc-13323007:
Yanhu Ji and co-authors link daily air pollution to non-accidental deaths in Shantou, China, in a 2026 study of a subtropical coastal city. Daily records from 2016 to 2020 covered deaths, weather and six pollutants, and a Poisson model estimated short-term effects by sex, age and season.

Deaths rose with PM2.5, PM10, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide and ozone over lags of several days, but not with carbon monoxide in their models. People aged 65 or older showed added sensitivity to ozone alone among the splits tested. Burden estimates used World Health Organization and Chinese air standards as reference levels. The authors argue for tighter control of particle and gas pollution in similar coastal cities.
pmc-13323407:
Anna Carolina Batista Dantas and her co-authors looked back at 335 adults who had a first weight-loss operation from 2020 to 2023. The operations were sleeve gastrectomy or gastric bypass, and each patient was graded with the Edmonton Obesity Staging System, which rates how far obesity-related illness has advanced. The 2026 study asked whether a higher stage meant more trouble in the 90 days after surgery.

Major problems within 90 days affected 5.4% of the group, and the rate rose steeply with stage, from 1.8% in stages 0 to 2 to 12.5% in stages 3 to 4. Repeat surgery was needed by 1.5% of patients, and no one died. Adjusted models linked a higher stage to higher odds of overall and major problems. The authors read this as proof that staging can flag high-risk patients, but warn against using it alone to judge surgical risk.
pmc-13323807:
Joon-Tae Kim leads a Korean registry study on how well stroke risk factors were controlled before an ischaemic stroke, published in 2026. Records from 2011 to 2022 held 63,570 patients with at least one major risk factor among hypertension, diabetes, lipid disorder and atrial fibrillation.

Patients were classed as well, partly or poorly controlled by set treatment and biomarker rules, with roughly a third in each group. Good recovery at three months, meaning independence on the Rankin scale, fell as the number of risk factors rose. The authors test whether fuller pre-stroke control also predicts better recovery within each group, making a case for tighter risk management long before stroke strikes.
pmc-13324307:
Tae-Il Jeon and co-authors show that copper import through CTR1 powers heat production in fat, in a 2026 mouse study. Cold exposure and beta3-adrenergic stimulation raised CTR1 levels and copper build-up in thermogenic fat, linking the metal to the calorie-burning programme.

Mice lacking Ctr1 only in fat cells spent far less energy and turned severely cold during acute chill. Their brown fat showed suppressed oxygen-based energy pathways and weaker fat breakdown signals, and white fat depots also cleared lipid poorly. Brown-fat-only deletion still caused cold intolerance despite near-normal acute drug responses. The copper carrier elesclomol partly restored mitochondrial capacity and cold tolerance in the fat-wide knockout mice.
pmc-13324907:
Islam Younis and team report a 25-year evolution from systemic mastocytosis to mast cell leukemia, traced through skin clues. Their 2026 case report follows a earlier healthy 52-year-old man with persistent, intermittently itchy, red-brown macules on the lower legs, consistent with telangiectasia macularis eruptiva perstans. Systemic mastocytosis is a rare clonal proliferation of mast cells whose varied skin and systemic signs often delay care and diagnosis.

Over 25 years, the man's skin disease progressed to mast cell leukemia, an advanced form of the disease. His course included antihistamines for itch and rash, topical steroids alternated with tacrolimus, and later systemic drugs for flares, including prednisone tapers. The authors highlight the diagnostic challenge of mast cell disease and argue for early recognition and consideration of targeted therapy once disease advances, before skin clues give way to systemic crisis.
pmc-13325907:
Joyce Rops and colleagues expose a counting trap in blood vesicle research and offer a fix, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Doctors measure tiny cell-shed vesicles in blood plasma as disease markers. A standard counter needs the plasma diluted, but each sample is diluted by a different amount, and in thin samples the machine mistakes glowing background for vesicles.

The team calls this the dilution paradox and built a model that estimates the background glow and flags measurements it dominates. Applied to two past clinical studies from their group, the model judged nearly half the measurements unreliable. Removing them forced changes to both studies' conclusions. The authors recommend rechecking older work with the model, and using one fixed dilution in future studies, so vesicle counts can be trusted and compared.
pmc-13326107:
Zhimei Sun and colleagues compare how stir-frying changes the scent of white and yellow mustard seeds in a 2026 food study. Heat work is a classic step for spice seeds, yet its flavor chemistry is rarely mapped side by side.

Tasters, an electronic nose, and chromatography with ion mobility checks covered raw and fried seeds. Frying shifted the aroma from sharp and mustard-like toward toasted and oily, strongest in yellow seeds. Instrument strength ranked fried yellow first, then fried white, raw white, and raw yellow.
