Counseling is where a gene panel becomes decisions, yet here it is required only after positive results. Their 2026 study speaks with twenty nine customers of a 59 gene cancer and heart risk panel. A survey asks whether they used counseling and what stopped them.

Most never spoke with a counselor. Half of those who had not done so wanted a session, an unmet demand behind low uptake. People who did use counselors rated them helpful for grasping results, clarifying risk, and choosing steps. Time pressure was the barrier named most. The gap, the authors argue, is a design flaw rather than disinterest. Counseling should be woven into the testing path, not left as an extra most customers never reach.
pmc-13401307:
Rehab Elmeazawy and co-authors published a 2026 prospective study comparing lung ultrasound with chest X-ray for children with lower respiratory tract infections at a tertiary hospital. X-ray is the usual tool but involves radiation and can miss disease, while ultrasound is quick, radiation-free, and done at the bedside.

The study enrolled 338 children aged one month to 18 years with suspected infections, and every child received clinical assessment, X-ray, and ultrasound on admission and again at follow-up. Ultrasound sensitivity for lung pathology was high, at just under 96 percent on admission and a similar level later. Its specificity was weak at first, under 30 percent, but improved to about 63 percent at follow-up. Agreement between the two methods rose from fair to substantial over the same span.
pmc-13401407:
Scott Fong and co-authors wrote a 2026 database study of results after acromioclavicular joint reconstruction. That surgery rebuilds the joint between collarbone and shoulder blade, and the study takes a close look at differences between women and men. They drew on the TriNetX national database.

Patients treated between January 2015 and October 2022 were followed for 90-day and two-year results. The revision rate was just under 4 percent, while loss of reduction affected about 13 percent and distal clavicle fractures about 16 percent within two years. In propensity-matched comparisons, women reported postoperative antidepressant use more often than men, at about 16 versus 11 percent, and female sex carried a higher fracture risk. A Kaplan-Meier analysis compared revision probability by sex across the two years.
pmc-13401607:
John Chwen-Yu Chen and a large team report a 2026 study giving fast pain fibres, the myelinated A-nociceptors, a central role in mechanical pain behaviour. Slow unmyelinated C fibres have led pain research, while their fast cousins stayed unexplored.

In mice, light-based switching of these fibres on triggered rapid, precise withdrawal reflexes plus place aversion and facial changes consistent with pain feelings. Switching them off strongly blunted withdrawal from mechanical stimuli. Prolonged activation produced lasting mechanical pain that is easily triggered, plus a wound-up central response. Human evidence aligned: a rare person lacking thick A-beta fibres, and healthy volunteers under a nerve block favouring those fibres, both lost mechanical withdrawal reflexes and felt less mechanical pain. The findings redraw the wiring diagram of pain that protects.
pmc-13401707:
Maedeh Amini and co-authors analysed sex differences in the burden of diarrhoeal disease among children under five in a 2026 population study using Global Burden of Disease 2021 data. Global burden has fallen sharply over three decades, but gaps between boys and girls and across Asian regions remain poorly charted, especially for non-fatal outcomes.

The team extracted sex-split data on incidence, prevalence, deaths, and disability-adjusted life years from 1990 to 2021 and measured trends with estimated annual percentage changes. For Asian countries, three-level statistical models hunted for factors tied to burden, and forecasting models projected sex-specific patterns thirty years ahead to 2050. Burden fell substantially for both sexes on every measure across the study window, although boys carried the heavier share. The projections aim to steer child health policy toward fairer outcomes.
pmc-13402707:
Jiyuan Piao and colleagues isolate a dormancy factor from hibernating snails, copy it in the lab, and show it shields mouse hearts from the damage that follows restored blood flow. Hibernators remodel metabolism and switch on autophagy, the cell recycling system, to survive oxygen starvation that wrecks other animals. Named SNAP for its activation of the phosphatase PHLPP1, the molecule pushes stressed cells toward a protected dormant state.

In snail tissue and mouse cells alike, SNAP moved PHLPP1 signaling onto mitochondria, quieted growth pathways, raised autophagy, and helped cells resist death after oxygen returned. Perfused hearts gained protection too, with a key enzyme of fuel burning preserved and membranes holding their charge. Hearts lacking that enzyme in heart cells lost the benefit entirely. The authors float SNAP as a guard for donor hearts awaiting transplant.
pmc-13403007:
Thinh Tran Xuan and colleagues rank cheap prognostic markers for sepsis in central Vietnam, where costly tests cannot be assumed. Their cross-sectional study covered 146 adults meeting Sepsis-3 criteria at two Hue hospitals; average age was 67, about 62 percent had septic shock, and overall mortality reached 51.4 percent. Candidate markers included the lactate to albumin ratio, platelet count, and standard blood values.

The lactate-albumin ratio at a cutoff of 2.1 forecast death best, with an area under the curve of 0.76, sensitivity of 58.7 percent, and specificity of 88.7 percent in the reported results, beating lactate, albumin, platelets, and several rivals that scored near chance. Adjusted models kept the ratio, platelet count, and SOFA score as significant predictors. The authors recommend the ratio as a bedside tool matched to resource-limited wards.
pmc-13404107:
Elizabeth McKiernan and team used ultra-high-field MRI to spot subtle brain shrinkage in dementia with Lewy bodies. Their 2026 work weighs 20 patients with probable Lewy body dementia, 25 with probable Alzheimer's disease, and 19 healthy controls. Standard MRI may lack detail to reveal hippocampal and amygdala subfield loss in Lewy body dementia, though such loss is known in Alzheimer's.

Seven-tesla scans showed four of 13 hippocampal subfields and five of nine amygdala subfields clearly smaller in Lewy body dementia than in controls, after allowing for age, sex, schooling, and head size. Hit hippocampal zones included the molecular layer, subiculum, presubiculum, and entorhinal cortex, while amygdala losses spanned basal, central, medial, and cortical nuclei. The work gives Lewy body dementia a finer structural fingerprint for diagnosis and research.
pmc-13406707:
Alexander S Atalay, Benjamin T Newman and T Jason Druzgal link screen time to brain development paths in a huge teenage cohort, in a 2026 study. Scans from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study were taken at two time points across thousands of young people. Advanced diffusion imaging measured cell-level structure beyond standard scans.

More screen time tracked with faster maturation in reward-linked cortex and slower maturation in control-linked cortex, the authors report. The sensitive imaging method picked up links that grey matter density and standard diffusion measures missed or showed weakly. The findings raise the possibility that heavy screen use bends normal teenage brain trajectories. Association is not proof of cause, a limit inherent in the design.
pmc-13407407:
Yao shi mapped RAS route activity types in lung adenocarcinoma using machine learning. His 2026 work weighs transcriptomes from 624 patients in two GEO groups, checked in TCGA data, to map variety in a route central to lung cancer growth. RAS activity types and their immune and outlook meanings had stayed poorly mapped.

Consensus grouping on 238 RAS-linked genes revealed two distinct activity types. A three-gene signature, MAPK10, PLA2G12B, and SHC3, formed a solo outlook risk score, with high-risk tumors rich in DNA copying, cell cycle, and repair routes and showing distinct immune cell patterns. All signature genes rose with resting mast cells, while two fell with activated memory CD4 T cells. The model offers an outlook and immune-aware sorting tool for lung adenocarcinoma.
pmc-13407707:
Katie Hutchinson and co-authors report, in 2026, fourteen patients whose breastbone infections surfaced long after heart surgery, treated with combined orthopaedic and plastic surgery principles. Late sternal infection with non-union is poorly understood. It is also handled inconsistently. A specialist bone infection unit applied the pathway used for infected fractures. That means radical cleaning, deep sampling, stabilisation, and reconstruction. Targeted antibiotics complete the package.

Patients averaged about 64 years and carried heavy other illness; the gap from original surgery to definitive cleaning ranged from 25 days to nearly nine years. Eleven were rebuilt in a single operation and three in stages. Skin staphylococcus species and acne bacteria dominated the cultures, often mixed. Single-stage patients stayed about ten and a half days, and only one recurrence appeared over roughly 410 days of follow-up.
pmc-13407807:
Konstantinos Triantafyllias and co-authors test, in 2026, shining light through fingers to detect hand osteoarthritis. Optical transmission imaging promises a fast, examiner-free read on joint inflammation. The team measured thousands of finger joints with a dedicated hand scanner. Ninety-seven patients and 100 healthy controls took part. A subset also had examinations, blood markers, and ultrasound.

Light values ran clearly higher in patients, 10.39 against 7.51 on average, and the gap survived adjustment for other influences. At the small end joints of the fingers, values correlated weakly but significantly with both ultrasound types, and a discrimination analysis reached moderate accuracy for separating patients from controls. Hand size itself correlated moderately with readings in both groups, a caveat for interpretation. The authors offer the scan as a possible adjunct, not a replacement.
pmc-13408007:
Simone Cerciello and co-authors describe, in 2026, a step-by-step arthroscopic stitch, nicknamed the tie stitch, for anchoring the long head of the biceps tendon during shoulder surgery. Fixing that tendon is often added to rotator cuff repair in younger, active patients when the tendon is worn or inflamed. The same tendon has lately been drafted to rebuild the shoulder's superior capsule after massive, irreparable cuff tears. There, rock-solid initial fixation is mandatory.

Existing stitches can slacken a degenerated tendon or prove fiddly through the scope. The tie stitch is presented as easy to perform while gripping firmly enough to prevent slackening during healing. The technique paper walks through the procedure in sequence for surgeons weighing tenodesis against simply cutting the tendon.
pmc-13408507:
A correction notice for a pediatric dental pain study fixes errors in the published version of a split-mouth crossover trial of the Buzzy Bee device during local anesthesia in children. The notice, issued in 2026, corrects the abstract sample size from 39 to 38, along with Figure 1, Table 5, and procedure text where group labels had been reversed. Such corrections matter because group labels determine which results belong to intervention versus control.

Corrected materials include a revised abstract, flowchart, table with first-visit parental scale values, and procedure description clarifying that group A and group B swapped interventions after a seven-day washout. The corrected abstract reports significant pain reduction in the test group at both visits, with parental and SEM scale gains significant only at the first visit. The notice states that the corrections do not change the study's interpretation or overall conclusions.
pmc-13408607:
Riya A Pursnani and colleagues compared smart polymer burs with diamond points for removing decay in children's primary molars. Their 2026 double-blinded randomized trial addresses a minimally invasive goal: polymer burs selectively remove soft decayed dentin by hardness, preserving healthy tissue and reducing discomfort, versus traditional high-speed drilling that can overcut. Efficiency and completeness had not been head-to-head compared in this setting.

Among 60 pediatric patients, diamond points worked faster, averaging 112.93 seconds versus 128.40 for smart burs, and revealed caries completely in 76.7 percent of cases versus 43.3 percent for smart burs. The authors conclude that smart burs aid minimally invasive dentistry by preserving healthy structure, despite slower and less complete removal. The paper suggests pairing smart burs with careful checking rather than using them alone for complete excavation.
pmc-13408807:
Wenhan Li, Craig Peeples, Juan Rey, Juan Perilla, and Reidun Twarock bring geometry to bear in 2026 on the cone-shaped shell that packages HIV's genome. Textbook models draw such capsids as perfect fullerene lattices, like a football's panels. Real HIV cores, the authors show, only approximate that tiling: the boundaries of their hexamer and pentamer building blocks form a pseudo-tiling with measurable local deviations.

A triangular criterion quantifies how far any spot on an atomic model strays from the ideal lattice. Applying it shows the deviations are not cosmetic: they shift the shell's physical properties. The same measure may predict where helper molecules bind and how the surface deforms in response. For antiviral designers targeting capsid assembly, and for engineers borrowing the shell as a delivery vehicle, geometry becomes a functional variable rather than decoration.
pmc-13410607:
Abhiram Manda and colleagues review in 2026 how eye doctors tell apart three kinds of dark spots at the back of the eye. One kind appears alone by chance, another signals an inherited bowel condition with many polyps, and a third forms grouped tracks nicknamed bear tracks. Mixing them up can trigger needless worry or missed screening.

Features compared span the eye exam view, tissue studies, and several scan types. Spots tied to the inherited condition tend to be many, on both sides, and free of small holes or swelling. The grouped type follows a wedge pattern and keeps the outer retina intact under scans. A side-by-side framework in the review helps clinicians decide who needs gene testing.
pmc-13410807:
Zhimeng Yao leads a team reporting in 2026 a delivery trick that eases memory problems caused by cancer treatment in mice. Chemo-brain, as patients call it, blights life during and after therapy, and no effective medicine exists. Their target is a brain enzyme long deemed undruggable, locked behind the blood-brain barrier.

Tiny cell-made parcels were fitted with a rabies virus tag that homes to neurons, carrying a small RNA that switches the enzyme's gene on. One vein injection raised brain levels of the enzyme for at least 28 days. Treated mice showed better neuron survival, more new neurons, and stronger connections, with milder cognitive symptoms. Safety checks in cells and animals supported further work.
pmc-13410907:
Yuanzheng Ye and colleagues test in 2026 whether a simple blood ratio flags risk for hospital patients with high pressure in the lung arteries. The ratio joins uric acid, a waste product tied to stress in tissues, over albumin, a protein tied to nutrition. Both values come from routine blood work.

Records covered 8,763 patients at one center, grouped by ratio level. Death in hospital climbed step by step across the groups, from the lowest share to nearly three percent at the top. Each rise in the ratio also tracked with worse recorded disease grade, weaker heart pumping, and a wider right heart chamber. The cheap ratio may help staff sort patients by risk on arrival.
pmc-13413307:
Paschalis Theotokis, Soultana Meditskou, and Maria Eleni Manthou open a 2026 special issue that links how humans grow before birth with the health of whole groups. The set of papers runs from stem cells and embryo growth to birth defects and newborn health. Their editorial walks through the main themes. Stem cells come first, as tools that might one day mend fertility and help women have children.

Other papers trace how harm before birth can seed birth defects and later disease. One line of work ties placenta health to the fetal heart, a link the editors call a heart-placenta axis. More papers weigh the mother's vitamin D, gut germs, and swelling in slow fetal growth. Screening and registry work rounds out the set.
pmc-13415207:
Ricardo Lopes and colleagues stretch the World Health Organization fungal priority list toward animal health, in a 2026 review of Portuguese lab records. They checked every yeast positive find sent to one veterinary lab from 2019 onward. Naming used looks, an automated system, and mass spectrometry.

Of 2,033 fungal finds, 219 grew yeast, and 82 matched critical or high priority types. Candida albicans led the priority group, then came other Candida kin and Cryptococcus. Priority yeasts came mostly from ornamental birds, plus dogs, cats, and marine mammals. Routine animal testing already catches fungi that threaten people, supporting shared surveillance.
pmc-13415607:
Diego Romano Perinelli and colleagues sort out which factors matter when making nanoemulsions with high energy ultrasound, in 2026. These are tiny oil drops in water, used in foods, skin creams, and drugs. The team screened oil traits, soap type, heat, and machine settings, then let a neural net rank each one.

Oil thickness ruled both drop size and size spread, with thick oils fighting breakup into tiny drops. More heat helped, since warm oil thins. Sound strength and pulse mode counted most in hard runs, while soap type and oil share counted for less. The net forecast results well and flagged the oil thickness cap for good runs.
pmc-13415707:
Mohammed AlSarhan and colleagues review dental implant outcomes against patient traits and surgical choices, in a 2026 retrospective study. Records held 218 implants in 109 adults treated between 2015 and 2023, each with X-rays at least six months after the crown was fitted. Bone loss around implants was judged by whether implant threads showed on X-ray.

Most implants were bone level type placed in native bone. Grafting clustered at sites where decay had destroyed the tooth and in patients with good oral hygiene. Age tracked with poorer hygiene, while education and smoking did not. Bone loss and complications were rare overall, and grafting showed no link to bone loss.
pmc-13417707:
Gouli and colleagues present a 2026 study on how pulling force breaks carbon-carbon bonds in polymers, and how side groups change the force needed. In stretched plastics these bonds often snap even when weaker-looking bonds are present. The team used a computer method that mimics applied force to compare many side groups on plain bonds.

The calculations showed which side groups lower or raise the force at which a bond breaks, through electronic effects and crowding around the bond. That map can help chemists pick plastics whose bonds break on cue for recycling, or hold firm in use. pmc-13418207:

pmc-13418507:

Adding sulfur beside each iridium atom shifted its electronic centre and lowered the energy barrier for activating oxygen, according to computer models.

pmc-13418707:

Field injury, lab assays, and molecular markers can each mislead through confounding factors.

pmc-13419307:
Mulu Negesse and colleagues chart how Boutourlini's blue monkeys divide their day across two zones of Saja Forest in southwest Ethiopia. pmc-13419607:

pmc-13420207:
Xu and co-authors test a blood biomarker in this 2026 study of rheumatoid arthritis, an autoimmune disease where responses to the drug etanercept vary in ways no one can predict. pmc-13420307:

Heart injury from this drug can surface during treatment or years later, and no settled prevention exists.

Those three routes match the main ways the drug injures the heart in the first place. The authors sort cell types and delivery routes by strength of support. pmc-13421207:
Bassant Ehab and Ekram Saleh review, in a 2026 paper, how pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma rewires its use of fatty acids to survive in a harsh, oxygen-poor tumour environment. They also describe how surrounding tissue supplies extra lipid and supports the cancer's metabolism. The review ends with drugs that interfere with these pathways, presented as a route to weakening the tumour and improving response to existing therapy.
pmc-13421307:

Thousands of patients have been treated in trials over two decades. The review weighs strong anti-tumour activity and off-the-shelf manufacturing against stubborn limits, notably poor persistence and weak antigen targeting. pmc-13421607:

pmc-13421807:

pmc-13422107:

Fekete suggests the cytokine may illuminate how this disorder works.
pmc-13422307:
Jialiang Han and colleagues tracked gut microbes across seasons in 2026 among endangered Francois langurs in China's Mayanghe reserve, sampling feces in all four seasons. Species richness dipped in fall while overall evenness held, Faecalibacterium enriched in fall, and fine-scale microbial functions shifted seasonally even as broad carbohydrate metabolism stayed stable. Conservation teams gain evidence that microbial flexibility buffers these langurs against seasonal food change in the wild.
pmc-13422807:
Charlotte Lambrechts leads a seven-author team setting out, in a 2026 protocol, a non-invasive work-up of calf muscle in children with spastic cerebral palsy. Grip-style dynamometry and functional tests add strength. The authors plan to compare groups property by property and then examine the relations among properties within the same muscle.
pmc-13423907:

pmc-13424007:
Montgomery and Harcourt interviewed in 2026 eighteen adults with inheritable conditions that visibly affect appearance, such as neurofibromatosis and craniofacial conditions, about deciding whether to have children. Memories of stigma shaped views on natural conception, embryo screening, and ending a pregnancy. Testing offered a sense of control but raised ethical strain. Participants asked for unbiased counseling and peer contact. The authors urge counselors to name stigma openly in such talks.
pmc-13424607:

pmc-13424907:

pmc-13425007:

Delivery mode, birthweight, breastfeeding, smoke exposure, pet type and timing, and living conditions all entered the exposure list.
pmc-13425607:

Oil from red-quinoa-fed larvae held the most protective plant compounds and scored best on three antioxidant tests, with rice bran oil close behind. pmc-13425807:

pmc-13426007:

pmc-13426407:

pmc-13426507:

pmc-13426707:
Chad G. Ball, Sean Gregg, and Edward J. Harvey examine Canada's unregulated private health care market in a 2026 French-language commentary on Alberta's new law. Legislation in force from 18 December 2025 created a legal framework for dual practice, letting Alberta physicians work in both private and public sectors. Debate was heated, with many Canadian health coalitions calling the bill a violation of the Canada Health Act.

Supporters see a chance to improve access and expand system capacity, while critics warn of drift toward a two-tier system shut to citizens who cannot pay. The authors situate the fight within wider frustration among patients who already feel poorly served.
pmc-13427907:

pmc-13428107:

pmc-13428407:

pmc-13428707:

pmc-13430207:

pmc-13430607:

pmc-13430707:

pmc-13432907:

pmc-13434007:

pmc-13434607:

pmc-13434707:

pmc-13434807:

pmc-13435107:

pmc-13437507:

pmc-13437607:

pmc-13437807:

pmc-13437907:

pmc-13438607:

pmc-13439307:

pmc-13439607:

pmc-13440107:
Shi and colleagues followed in 2026 the gut microbes of ovarian cancer patients through chemotherapy, asking whether change over time links to later relapse. Past work mostly took single snapshots in other cancers. In a prospective cohort of 91 patients, the team sequenced stool samples from 33 patients across early, middle, and late chemotherapy, one hundred samples in all, and modelled the trajectories against recurrence.

Shi found gut diversity rose steadily through the course, with fringe species turning over faster than core ones. Severe side-effect burden did not predict relapse. The clear signal was one genus, Fusicatenibacter, draining away over time in patients who later relapsed, a pattern that survived every sensitivity check the team ran. Predicted pathway shifts and a microbe network tied to those pathways added support. The authors flag the disappearing genus as a candidate early marker of relapse risk.
pmc-13442007:
Moritz A Knolle and colleagues audit medical AI models patient by patient and find privacy risk hiding beneath reassuring averages, reporting in 2026. Membership inference attacks ask whether a given person's records trained a model, a direct privacy threat when training data are sensitive scans. Past audits averaged attack success across whole datasets. Across varied medical datasets, the team instead scored the attack separately for every contributing patient.

For individual patients, attacks often succeeded almost perfectly, even where the dataset average hovered near coin-flip level. Patients contribute multiple similar records, which is part of what exposes them. Bigger models widened the exposed group further. Underrepresented patients, sorted by sex, insurance, self-reported race, disease status, or imaging protocol, faced disproportionately high attack success. The authors warn that average-case privacy metrics can badly understate the risk borne by the most exposed patients.
pmc-13442607:
Joel Ravichandar and colleagues report use of a new sleep drug, remimazolam, for a heart scan in a 16-month-old girl in a 2026 case report. Her heart muscle worked poorly due to a primary muscle illness, so standard sleep drugs posed real risk to her breathing and blood flow. She needed a CT vessel scan while fully still and calm.

Care ran remimazolam as a steady drip, topped with small ketamine doses as needed. The drug wears off in minutes, since body enzymes break it down fast, which limits pile-up in the blood. The report walks through her course and then weighs past reports of the drug in heart-sick patients. The authors present the pairing as a workable path for scans in small children with weak hearts, while case counts stay low.
pmc-13442807:
Rawane Bellemrrabet's team mapped drug failure in 2026 in chronic blood cancer, the most common lymph cancer, where BTK and BCL-2 aimed drugs changed care but drug failure persists. Standard BTK blockers and drug letdowns were mapped alongside newer options: loose-binding BTK blocking, BTK breakdown, CAR-T cells, and dual-target drugs, plus surroundings drivers like white-cell rewiring and blocking myeloid cells.

The review argues drug failure is a system problem, not only a tumor cell problem, requiring combos guided by early markers. Clinicians get a current drug-failure atlas for lining up therapies after relapse. Its advice rests on shifting trial evidence, so treatment choices need single trial and rule checks.
pmc-13443107:
Cristina Antich and colleagues print a living placenta model in 3D to mimic pregnancy stages in a 2026 paper. The placenta feeds the unborn child, yet faults in it drive early birth and growth harm. Real tissue is hard to get, and animal models predict human faults poorly.

Their printed tissue joins primary human trophoblasts with stroma cells and blood vessel paths. Builds in a 96-well plate copy early and late pregnancy states. Tests show wall guard duty, food uptake, carrier work, and hormone release like the real organ. The team offers the plate as a screen for drugs and for goods that may harm the unborn. Deep trait checks back the claim that stage marks match human pregnancy well.
pmc-13444007:
Alakram and Hedding measure how a South African port coastline is moving and what a major surge would flood. Their 2026 study of Richards Bay integrates satellite analysis and modelling. It uses 45 years of shoreline positions, from 1977 to 2022, through the standard digital shoreline analysis system. The trends are then extrapolated ten and twenty years forward.

The harbour splits the coast's behaviour: persistent erosion to its north, and accretion, shoreline growth, to its south. About eighty percent of South Africa's coast is erodible sandy beach, much of it sensitive dune, which makes the pattern consequential for planning. The storm surge analysis delivered the starkest figure: a ten-metre surge would inundate 82 percent of the study area. The authors offer the shoreline history and flood mapping as an information base for flood risk analysis and disaster management around the port.
pmc-13444607:
Danielle P. Uhl and colleagues present a single-cell atlas of blood immune cells in dogs at each stage of leishmaniosis, a parasite disease spread by sand flies. Published in 2026, the work maps dogs with no infection beside dogs with mild through severe illness from Leishmania infantum. Dogs matter here because they carry the parasite and pass it on to people, so their illness mirrors a wider public health risk.

The team used single-cell RNA sequencing to track how cell types shift as disease grows worse. Blood moved from a lymphoid-heavy mix toward a myeloid-heavy one, helper T cells showed growing signs of exhaustion, and monocytes took on more inflamed states. Readers gain a shared reference, named the LeishDog Atlas, for comparing immune change across stages and for later work on treatment.
pmc-13445507:
Dominik Hlauschek and colleagues warn of common traps in studies that track tumor DNA in the blood over time, in a 2026 viewpoint. Such DNA can flag cancer that lingers after treatment, guide care, and track response. Yet the numbers these studies report can mislead when time itself is mishandled.

Three traps get close looks: how lead time before relapse is defined, test accuracy that shifts as months pass, and a bias that creeps in when patients are classed by later results. Worked toy cases, computer runs, and fresh looks at past data show each trap in action. The authors offer design and reporting guidance, while noting that firm fixes await more proof.
pmc-13445707:
Yolanda Andres-Lopez and nine co-authors present a living clock built into cells, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. Biology runs on timing, but catching change as it happens is hard. Their method pairs gene editing with single-cell reading: barcodes in the DNA gather edits step by step, stamping each cell with a record of elapsed events.

They tested the clock in mouse stem cells as some cells slipped into a rare two-cell-like state. Barcode drift showed that state is brief and passing. In a model of early embryo growth, the edit pace held steady across many cell types. The team says the clock can log other time signals too, opening a way to watch cell histories unfold from inside.
pmc-13446107:
Anna Kubota and colleagues test whether work performance sits between sleep quality and wellbeing in high-stress office workers in Japan, in a 2026 survey study. Poor sleep is known to drag wellbeing down, yet the steps in between are less clear. Showing up sick or drained, called presenteeism, was their candidate middle step.

One hundred twenty-nine workers filled tested scales for sleep, performance loss, and wellbeing. Poor sleep went with both worse performance and lower wellbeing. Mediation checks found performance loss carried part of the sleep effect, and the indirect path held after adjusting for age, hours, rank, smoking, and drinking. The authors say sleep programs at work may pay off twice, lifting both output and felt health.
pmc-13446307:
Savvas Teloni and Yiorgos Apidianakis present a protocol for counting odd features of gut stem cells in the fruit fly, meant as early warnings of later tumors, published in 2026. The adult fly gut renews itself through stem cells that can cluster wrongly when a key signal weakens. Such clusters grow with age and track rare true tumors late in life.

Steps cover labeling the clusters, staining, and counting cell number and size by gut region as flies age. Further steps give division rate and DNA content per clustered cell. Scores can then be set across gene types and conditions and matched to each group's late tumor rate. The authors offer the counts as a forecast tool for gut aging studies.
pmc-13447307:
Ana Isabel González-Hernández and fellow editors introduce a 2026 collection on polyamines in plant stress and development. Polyamines are small nitrogen-rich molecules found in all living cells, where they steer growth and buffer plants against drought, heat and attack. Climate change makes that buffering role urgent for crops facing harsher conditions.

One study covered here built a precise measurement toolkit that tracks two key enzyme routes and related compounds in a single run. Gene-edited tomato plants showed one route is essential for flower formation, since plants lacking it made no buds at all. Another line of work shows a specific polyamine fine-tuning wood vessel growth through two balancing proteins. Further papers cover chemical priming and nano-delivery ideas aimed at multi-stress resilience in the field.
pmc-13447407:
Hendrianus Hendrianus and co-authors test if blood clot tests can flag heart and vessel events that come after surgery that is not on the heart. Their 2026 piece is a prespecified analysis of the PANDA study.

The work tracked, in advance, one hundred twenty patients set for surgery with a mid to high risk. Clot traits were gauged before surgery. Coronary artery disease was checked by computed tomography angiography. Sixteen patients had heart or vessel events in the span of thirty days. Coronary disease, D-dimer level, and platelet-fibrin clot strength were each linked to events on their own. The team says these tests do more than the old clinical risk models. Those models have weak power to flag problems that come after surgery.
pmc-13447707:
Sommer reviews how purified and reshaped cellulose, the fiber that stiffens plant walls, serves modern winemaking and wine testing. Cellulose is a chain of glucose, a simple sugar, and makers can tune its water behavior by chemical tweaks. His 2026 review covers plain cellulose as a filter aid, treated forms that pull unwanted compounds from wine, and cellulose gums used to keep wine stable in the bottle.

In production, cellulose filters wine and helps stop crystals and haze that form in cold or heat. Carboxymethyl cellulose, a treated gum, guards against cold instability, a cloudy fault in white wines. Methylcellulose is barred as a wine additive but earns its place in the lab, where it measures condensed tannins, the bitter plant compounds that shape red wine taste. Sommer closes on a green note: plant based cellulose can replace several mined or animal based aids.
pmc-13448507:
Kizilkilic and colleagues use a special MRI method to look at the walls of brain arteries in neuro-Behçet syndrome, an inflammatory disease long known for vein problems. Standard scans show the channel inside a vessel, not its wall, so early wall disease can hide. Their 2026 study scans 39 patients, some during an attack and some between attacks, and rates 1,170 artery segments for wall thickening and contrast uptake, a sign of active inflammation.

Wall involvement appeared in 16 patients, about two in five, and sat mostly in the back of the brain's circulation. The common pattern was even, ring like thickening without contrast uptake. Patients scanned during attacks showed wall changes far more often than patients scanned in quiet periods, and contrast uptake appeared only during attacks. Worse disability scores tracked with wall disease across three or more back circulation segments, a clue for grading severity.
pmc-13448707:
Peijin Li and colleagues present in 2026 a flat optical device that creates and measures complex states of light. The states mix polarization with orbital angular momentum, giving photons a larger space of possible forms. Such high-dimensional states could carry more information for communication and quantum uses.

A single-layer metasurface built from four-atom unit cells shapes amplitude, phase, and polarization at once to make any chosen state in a four-dimensional space. The team also reads back the full state from just three interference patterns. Their analysis reveals a parity rule in the patterns that holds regardless of how the modes are weighted, plus controlled transformations driven by geometric phase.
pmc-13448807:
K. A. Yashaswini and co-authors propose in 2026 a phone-based framework for flagging bipolar disorder near its onset. Called IDMBD, the system collects five kinds of information through a mobile computing device and profiles each participant in fine detail. A standard severity scale anchors its forecasts of how critical a person's state may be.

The profiled features pass through several analysis steps before reaching a deep neural network that learns patterns linked to the disorder. The team tested many pairings of machine learning and deep learning methods against standard performance measures. The framework performed best when random forest and decision tree models were integrated with it. The authors frame the tool as a faster alternative to repeated questionnaire and interview visits, which can delay early detection.
pmc-13449307:
Xiuquan Shi and coauthors track a 2026 path study of early blood-chemistry shifts after spleen removal in 935 patients with Wilson disease liver scarring from 2001 to 2019. Liver enzymes, bile pigment, and albumin taken before surgery and on days 1, 7, 14, and 21 fed group-based path models sorting good versus poor patterns.

Poor rates ran 20.3 percent for ALT, 12.7 percent for AST, 13.6 percent for bile pigment, and 46.1 percent for albumin, with higher Child-Pugh class strongly calling poor albumin and bile pigment patterns. The paths capture short-term shifts rather than final liver healing, so signs need checks against long-term results.
pmc-13449507:
Yousafzai and co-authors test whether teaching nurses suctioning technique changes what they know and do. Their 2026 single-group study covers sixty intensive care nurses in three public hospitals in Peshawar, Pakistan. Knowledge was measured by questionnaire and practice by an observational checklist. Both were assessed before and after training on endotracheal tube suctioning. That is the airway-clearing procedure for ventilated patients.

Both measures jumped. Knowledge scores rose from about 6.6 to about 10.2, and practice scores from about 12.7 to about 16.4, each with very large effect sizes and strong statistical significance. The authors conclude the training was associated with substantial improvement, a result relevant to preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia. They also flag the design honestly: with no control group, some of the gain could reflect testing effects or concurrent changes, so controlled confirmation is needed.
pmc-13449807:
Saima Armana and colleagues report in 2026 a case of Lemierre syndrome whose damage kept unfolding months after the initial infection. The syndrome classically follows a throat infection with sepsis, a clot in the jugular vein, and infection seeded around the body, usually by Fusobacterium bacteria. Their patient, a previously healthy seventeen-year-old, arrived with a week of sore throat and worsening neck pain, then developed a retropharyngeal abscess.

The infection ate into the skull base and cervical spine, injuring the twelfth cranial nerve and loosening the junction where skull meets spine. Five months after hospitalization, scans showed atlanto-axial instability and the skull settling downward, a combination that threatens the spinal cord itself. The patient is being managed without surgery for now and has been told to avoid contact sports. The authors urge long follow-up imaging whenever this syndrome touches the skull base.
pmc-13449907:
Shangyi Fu, Danny Huynh, and Milcah Poothakary write in 2026 to estimate how many people in the United States live with myelodysplastic syndrome. The bone marrow disorder is sometimes called preleukemia because its faulty blood-cell production can precede leukemia. They mined the national SEER cancer registry, which held records for nearly 44 million people at the time of collection. Their calculation put the number living with primary disease of this type at roughly 5,747.

Prevalence climbed steadily with age and peaked in people aged eighty-five and older. By race, the estimate ran highest in White individuals, at 0.03 percent, against 0.02 percent in Black, American Indian and Alaska Native, and Asian or Pacific Islander groups. The authors caution that the registry's own mix skews Whiter and more Asian than the country. Patients missed by the census or by healthcare access could push the true count higher.
pmc-13450507:
Yu Bo and colleagues compared two ways of teaching dental students about non-cavity hard-tissue diseases in 2026, testing a digital case-based blend against lectures. These diseases pose a growing clinical challenge, yet lecture teaching often fails to build diagnostic skill or lasting knowledge. The team combined Rain Classroom, a digital teaching platform, with case-based learning.

Two cohorts at Nankai University's medical school took part, one with traditional lectures and one with the integrated approach. Knowledge tests measured learning, while surveys captured satisfaction and perceived effectiveness. Students in the blended group performed better and reported stronger engagement in the reported results. Dental schools gain a tested blend for teaching a tricky diagnostic area.
pmc-13450607:
Jipeng Huang and a large team probe in 2026 how hearing and attention grow in children with ADHD, using brain wave tests. They enrolled 80 children with ADHD and 80 peers with typical growth, all aged seven to twelve. Each child did a listening task with rare odd tones while scalp sensors traced fast brain replies.

One early brain reply grew steadily with age in typical children, yet in the ADHD group it stayed weak in the older years and traced a U shape. A later reply tied to focus was weak in the youngest ADHD children. The team reads the pattern as a late-stage effort to catch up, and they offer the brain marks as leads for longer studies.
pmc-13451407:
Attiq ur Rehman and co-authors test in 2026 gene-based forecasts of mildew resistance for strawberry breeding stock. They crossed two wild strawberry kin and scored the young plants for leaf and fruit resistance to powdery mildew. Forecast models used gene markers from thirteen families.

Leaf resistance was easier to forecast than fruit resistance across years. Close family ties lifted accuracy a lot, and a training set of two fifths of the plants proved steady. Adding the big known resistance spots as fixed parts of the model raised accuracy for both traits. Field and greenhouse checks held up, so the team gives breeders working rules for set size and marker counts.
pmc-13451807:
Junchao Xu and co-authors lay out in 2026 a plan to build mRNA vaccines as one joined system, carrier and message tuned together. Most work tunes the fat carrier and the message ends apart, yet only a sliver of a shot reaches the cells that spark immunity. Their summary draws on a study that screened both parts at scale.

A search of 96 carrier fats picked a lead fat that homes to the immune starter cells. Fine-tuning the mix routed the shots through lymph paths, while a screened message frame lifted output and tilted immunity toward a virus-fighting type. The joined design aims for strong shots at lower doses, with less soreness as a hoped gain.
pmc-13452107:
Kazem Habibi-Tanha and co-authors scan in 2026 work on learning models fed with body marks to guess which mouth sores will turn to cancer. Mouth cancers often grow out of such sores, yet the shift is hard to call and tissue grading wobbles between readers. The review gathered ten past studies that paired machine learning with marks from genes, proteins, or tissue images.

The models showed strong promise, and image-based tissue traits looked most ready for clinic use. Yet methods varied, no study had tested its model on fresh patients ahead of time, and age and sex reporting was patchy. The authors urge mixed-mark models, trials that run forward in time, and checks across wider groups.
pmc-13452307:
Gutierrez-Aguirre and colleagues compare in 2026 drugs that speed blood recovery after autologous stem cell transplantation. That procedure returns a patient's own stem cells after high-dose chemotherapy, done here as an outpatient treatment for lymphoma or myeloma.

Thirty transplant patients were randomly given a single dose of either the original pegfilgrastim or its biosimilar version. Their results were set against 53 earlier patients who received daily filgrastim instead. White cell recovery took a median of ten days with the original drug, nine with the biosimilar, and eleven with filgrastim. Platelet recovery took ten days against twelve in the same comparison across the groups. Fever with low white cells struck far fewer pegfilgrastim patients than filgrastim patients. The original drug cost the most and filgrastim the least.
pmc-13452407:
Meseret Bekele and seven co-authors survey how homes in Harar, Ethiopia handle chicken and tomatoes safely in the kitchen. Their 2026 study visited 252 urban households and built a hygiene index from 39 habits and conditions. The index gives town programs a single score for how safely a home prepares food.

Risky habits were common: 74 percent of homes used one cutting board for both meat and vegetables, and 35 percent cleaned surfaces only now and then. Homes with better scores tended to sit in areas with stronger services and to get food safety news from television. Scores for chicken and for tomatoes tracked each other closely, which suggests the same daily habits shape safety for both foods. The authors back TV campaigns and better local services as the next steps.
pmc-13453507:
Aiyang Tong and six co-authors build a nanoparticle that floods cancer cells with calcium until they die in a fiery, immune waking way. The death mode, called PANoptosis, blends several cell death paths and rouses the immune system against the tumor. Their 2026 particle stacks a calcium peroxide core inside a manganese oxide shell, coated with hyaluronic acid to home in on tumor cells.

In the tumor's acidic, glutathione rich setting, the shell breaks down and frees a drug, fingolimod, that jams calcium channels. Calcium then floods the cell while a Fenton like reaction, a burst of chemical stress, wrecks its inner balance. Manganese freed in the process also trips an immune alarm that helps immune cells mature. Tumors shrank hard in tests, and pairing the particle with a checkpoint drug spread the effect to distant tumors.
pmc-13453607:
Itzick Nahmoud, Karli Monahan, Eric A Woodcock, and Alana C Conti review a tryptophan breakdown path that may link brain injury to lasting pain and depression. The path, named for its first product kynurenine, is stirred up by the swelling that follows a traumatic brain injury. Their 2026 review weighs the path's products in blood, spinal fluid, and brain tissue from patients.

Two products pull in opposite directions: quinolinic acid, which can excite and harm nerve cells, and kynurenic acid, which calms them. Injury skews their levels, and the same skew shows in depression and in pain states such as fibromyalgia and nerve pain. The review maps which enzymes steer the path at each fork. The authors point to those enzymes as drug targets that might ease two of the heaviest burdens after brain injury.
pmc-13453707:
Yuxuan Qi builds a prediction model to tell whether a lone lung nodule is cancerous, using scans, personal facts, and blood tests. Their 2026 study reviews 516 patients seen between December 2022 and August 2025, of whom 402 had benign nodules and 114 had cancer. Two modeling methods competed to pick the strongest warning signs.

Five signs stood on their own in the classic model: older age, smoking history, larger nodule size, a lobed edge, and spiky strands reaching out from the nodule. A second method swapped in a blood marker, carcinoembryonic antigen, for age and lobed edge. The classic model won on both accuracy and fit, so Qi turned it into a nomogram, a chart that gives each patient a personal risk score. The tool aims to spare benign cases from needless surgery.
pmc-13453807:
Zhiyue Zhu and four co-authors ask how extraordinary landscapes restore national park visitors, tracing the path through awe. Their 2026 study surveys 457 visitors at Sanjiangyuan and Qinghai Lake parks in China. A chain model links how striking the scene feels to awe, then to how broadly people think, then to felt closeness with nature.

More extraordinary scenes came with more awe, more closeness to nature, and stronger restoration. Awe itself lifted broad thinking and closeness, and closeness in turn lifted restoration. Statistical resampling backed the chain, with the direct scene effect only partly explained by the links. The authors advise park designers to stage the moments that spark awe, since awe starts the whole chain. The study extends earlier work from plain green space to grand wild settings.
pmc-13454007:
Aleksandra Dmitrowicz, Mariusz Sacharczuk, and Dominik Skiba put out a full review in 2026. They looked at how microplastics are found in human tissues. Tiny plastic bits now draw wide medical interest. Meanings and size rules still lack standard form. Write-up methods differ greatly between studies too. Such gaps make matching studies very hard. The review focused on lab methods for human samples. Most covered studies were very recent papers.

Placenta, kidney, liver, lung, and heart samples showed up often. Urine was another often tested sample. Microscopes and light-based tests were the main tools. Sample prep varied widely between labs. Storage, breaking-down, and filtering steps all varied. Control of stray plastic also varied a great deal. Particle sizes and units were given in unlike ways. The authors call for shared standards fast. Without them, health claims rest on shaky ground.
pmc-13454107:
Lili Wang and five co-authors profile the cardiology voices who lead opinion on Xiaohongshu, a Chinese social platform. Their 2026 study screens accounts by set rules and scores them on 14 signs of credibility, reach, and style. In all, 150 accounts with 46,616 posts form the set, and clustering sorts them into four types.

Public Health Educators share plain language prevention posts, while Clinical Narrators mix case stories with emotional support. Academic Interactors won the highest engagement and pushed research news hardest. Authoritative Experts held the largest followings and the strongest credentials, yet drew lower engagement per post. The authors describe the four types as a complementary ecosystem that spreads heart health facts, comfort, and debate. The map could help health agencies pick the right partners for campaigns.
pmc-13454207:
Yan Guo and nine co-authors sort the causes of chest pain in children and teenagers in the Shihezi area of Xinjiang, China. Their 2026 study reviews 243 patients aged 8 to 17 seen at one university hospital in 2023 and 2024 with non traumatic chest pain. Each case is classed as heart related, non heart related, or unexplained.

Non heart causes led at 47.7 percent, heart causes took 20.6 percent, and 31.7 percent stayed unexplained. Work and rest patterns, pain scores, shortness of breath, and palpitations differed across the three groups. Heart markers ran higher in the heart group, though the authors warn those markers helped make the class call, so the link is partly circular. Lung tests ran most abnormal in the non heart group. The authors back careful history and exams, with tests chosen by risk signs.
pmc-13454307:
Elena Papamichael, Irene-Chrysovalanto Themistocleous, Stelios Hadjisavvas, and Christina Michailidou published a 2026 review of game-like exercise programs for people with dementia. Most earlier work covered mild memory problems, leaving open how such programs serve people with deeper decline. The team gathered randomized trials from three databases and pooled their results.

Nine trials with 717 people in total met the entry rules. Pooled results showed a clear gain in overall thinking scores on one common test. Gains on a second thinking test, daily living skills, and a short physical test did not reach clear levels. Programs differed widely in length and intensity, and most used flat-screen rather than immersive systems. The authors call the thinking benefit real but the body benefits unproven.
pmc-13455307:
Halliday and co-authors interviewed women and physiotherapists inside a feasibility trial of a bespoke elastic fabric support garment. The garment targets chronic pelvic girdle pain after pregnancy. That pain lingers beyond three months in roughly 10 to 30 percent of postpartum women. The parent trial randomized women across three English trusts to standard advice and exercise, with or without the garment.

Seven of the 24 trial participants, five from the garment arm and two controls, plus five of seven physiotherapists, gave interviews for the sub-study. The web-based data collection and remote delivery were broadly acceptable, though both groups would have preferred at least one face-to-face session during the trial. Women said the garment held them together, heightened body awareness, and enabled more physical activity in daily life. Physiotherapists found fitting acceptable but wanted a wider range of garment options available.
pmc-13457007:

Surveys of two major conferences found most papers lean on such scales.

A shared, searchable home lets researchers find a scale's source, its items, and what it truly measures before adopting it. The authors frame measurement hygiene as a foundation for cumulative science: if the field cannot agree on how it asks people about robots, its claims about better robots rest on sand.
pmc-13457107:

Classic statistics first singled out the factors that matter on their own.

Tumor size, node surgery, hormone receptor levels, a growth index, and HER2 status each predicted disease-free survival independently. Among the seven algorithms, random forest and a boosting method led the field with steady accuracy. The forest's discrimination scores in validation ran from about 0.76 to 0.85 across one, three, and five years. Error scores stayed low and calibration looked honest. Explanation values showed which inputs drove each forecast. The authors offer the winning model as a decision aid, pending outside testing.
pmc-13457307:
Huihua Tang and colleagues ask why nurses who feel backed by their hospital also behave more safely at the bedside. Their 2026 cross-sectional survey gathered 753 nurses from four top-tier hospitals in China's Guangxi region. It measured organizational support, feelings that the job is decent work, job embeddedness, and self-reported safety behavior with validated scales. Structural equation modeling then traced how the pieces connect.

Support, decent-work feelings, and embeddedness each correlated positively with safer behavior. The pathway analysis showed much of the support effect traveling through the two middle factors: the total indirect effect reached 0.297, just over half the whole association. Feeling the work is decent accounted for about 14 percent, embeddedness for about 24 percent, and the chained path through both for about 14 percent. The authors advise managers that visible support, fair and decent conditions, and reasons for nurses to stay rooted should together lift patient safety.
pmc-13458507:
E. Jeba Saral Darling and Velmathi Guruviah solve a matching problem for millimeter-wave 5G antennas that must live on two bands, 27 gigahertz and 39.8 gigahertz, the higher one. The strip lengthens the path cavity currents travel and loads the resonator with inductance and capacitance, reshaping how the two resonances couple.

Against the cavity design, the strip improved the reflection coefficient by 7 and 9 decibels at the two bands while holding gains of 9.03 dBi and 7.81 dBi across the pair. Bandwidths came to 5.74 and 1.97 percent, with radiation efficiency between 83 and 94 percent. The authors frame it as a deliberate trade: some gain surrendered for better impedance control in a compact footprint.
pmc-13459007:
Maxim Wilkinson and a team of Scottish public health researchers used linked hospital records in 2026 to ask how often blood-borne viruses are diagnosed late. Late HIV meant a low CD4 count soon after diagnosis, while late hepatitis meant cirrhosis or liver cancer appearing near diagnosis. The cohort covered 543 people with HIV and several thousand with hepatitis B or C.

Many late cases had already passed through emergency departments or hospital wards in the five years before diagnosis, often more than once. Among late HIV cases, 44 percent had attended an emergency department earlier, and late hepatitis C cases reached 61 percent on that measure. The authors argue that secondary care visits are missed chances to test earlier.
pmc-13459207:
Stephanie Shiau and co-authors examined DNA methylation, chemical tags on DNA that tune gene activity, in young people who acquired HIV around birth. Their 2026 study compared 32 such youth with seven peers who were exposed to HIV before birth but not infected. Blood samples were taken twice, at least three years apart, and the team searched genome-wide for tag differences linked with the virus, drug treatment, or inflammation markers like C-reactive protein.

No genome-wide methylation differences separated the groups at either time point. One targeted gene involved in immune protein processing, PSMB9, did differ at both visits, however. Within the HIV group, neither viral load nor immune cell counts explained methylation patterns. Inflammation did: C-reactive protein tracked with seventeen sites at the first visit and eighteen at the second. The authors frame inflammation as a possible early intervention target.
pmc-13459407:
Jonathan Annan-Asare and co-authors looked at nutrition and mental health among adults living with disabilities in Accra, Ghana's capital, a group facing layered disadvantage in low income settings. pmc-13463707:

pmc-13463907:

pmc-13465007:

pmc-13465307:

pmc-13465507:

pmc-13467007:

pmc-13468507:

pmc-13473107:

pmc-13473507:

pmc-13474807:

pmc-13478507:

pmc-13478607:

pmc-13479407:

pmc-13480107:

pmc-13480507:

pmc-13482007:

pmc-13482307:

Six months later patients were split by whether their corrected vision had improved, 39 in the improved group and 13 not.

pmc-13482607:

pmc-13483407:

pmc-13483607:

pmc-13483707:

pmc-13483907:

A weighted ranking method then picked a single compromise setting for the factory floor. The recipe transfers to other curved molded parts.
pmc-13486507:

Sharma says fractal pretreatment deserves a place in agricultural forecasting for climate-stressed regions.
pmc-13486707:
Ke-yu Liu and others search human heart failure data for a new drug target and land on a transporter gene called SLCO5A1. In 2026, the study joins gene network analysis, machine learning, and genetic causal analysis across human data sets, finding the gene consistently reduced in failing blood-starved heart muscle. Mice tests then test whether restoring it helps.

pmc-13487607:
Jos Borkent simulates what happens to vitamin and mineral intake when Dutch older adults eat less or no animal food. Published in 2026, the modeling uses two-day food diaries from 607 community-dwelling seniors in the national consumption survey. Five scenarios replace meat and fish at forty and eighty percent, then remove seafood only, all animal flesh, or all animal products.

Gentle forty-percent replacement added no new problem nutrients. Deeper cuts made niacin low across scenarios, while the fully vegan pattern left nearly every micronutrient low. Sustainability advice for older adults must pair protein swaps with deliberate micronutrient cover.
pmc-13487907:
Gad Murenzi and colleagues examine HIV viral load testing in Rwanda in a 2026 observational study. Paired blood samples from the same people were sent to two laboratories that used different test kits. Participants were adults aged 40 years or older who had received HIV care for many years, most of them on modern treatment.

Results agreed well at higher cutoffs used for clinical decisions, yet they differed sharply near the lowest measurable levels. One laboratory reported far more low-level quantifiable results than the other did on the same samples. The authors conclude that very low thresholds can misclassify people, so higher cutoffs for judging viral suppression are safer in routine programs.
pmc-13488007:
Reneigh Morley-Hart and colleagues run a sham-controlled trial of joint manipulation for squat strength in a 2026 crossover study. Twenty-four resistance-trained adults with limited ankle bend, measured as dorsiflexion range, received quick thrust manipulations of lower limb joints and, on another occasion, a sham procedure that mimicked the treatment. Each person served as their own comparison, with squat one-repetition maximum and ankle motion captured by three-dimensional cameras.

Strength rose slightly after both real and sham sessions, with no clear difference between them in the reported tests. Ankle range also failed to change more after real treatment. The authors conclude that a single manipulation session does not meaningfully boost squat performance in this group.
pmc-13490407:
Xiuxiu Liu and co-authors study a ribosome-building protein in fruit fly development in a 2026 genetics investigation. Ribosomes are the cell's protein factories, and a nucleolar protein called nucleostemin helps assemble them in growing cells. The team depleted its fly version, Ns1, in the wing imaginal disc, a growing tissue that becomes the adult wing, and tracked protein production, ribosome parts, and cell death signals.

Loss of Ns1 triggered widespread cell death without using the classic p53 route seen in mammals, and global protein production fell in the reported measures. Sixty-five ribosomal proteins dropped in abundance, while a stress-sensing complex rose and switched on a death signal pathway. The authors name Ns1 a guardian of ribosome supply in growing tissue.
pmc-13490507:
Kazymbetova and team built a lithium-sulfur battery cathode from buckwheat-derived carbon threaded with carbon nanotubes, attacking the chemistry's notorious shuttle problem. Their 2026 cathode traps those species in porous hard carbon baked from buckwheat at high temperature, while a small nanotube share wires the structure electrically.

The cathode delivered an initial capacity near 1,250 milliamp-hours per gram at a gentle discharge rate in the reported tests. After one hundred cycles it kept about sixty percent of that capacity, with charging efficiency near one hundred percent throughout. Six percent nanotubes proved the sweet spot among the loadings varied. Kazymbetova pitches the biomass-based design as cheap, scalable, and sustainable compared with engineered carbon hosts.
pmc-13491607:
Ali Tadayon and nine colleagues present a 2026 case series on aortopexy, an operation that lifts the aorta away from a soft, collapsing windpipe in infants. The condition, tracheomalacia, often stems from blood vessels pressing on the airway. All six infants also had several other birth defects, which made their outlook hard to separate from the surgery itself.

Symptoms began between six days and one year of age, and diagnosis rested on direct airway inspection. Surgery used chest incisions in five babies and a neck incision in one, each paired with removal of some or all of the thymus gland. No major early complications occurred, though two children later needed further procedures and two died from their other conditions. Survivors often kept lasting problems, so the authors credit underlying defects more than the operation.
pmc-13491707:
Richmond Balinia Adda and five colleagues measure in 2026 how strongly pregnant women in northern Ghana react to one piece of a malaria parasite protein tied to pregnancy infection. The team focused on one such region, called DBL5, in blood from 156 women.

Responses to DBL5 tracked closely with responses to the whole protein, suggesting the fragment captures much of what the immune system sees. Computer predictions also flagged conserved stretches likely to be recognized widely, though the authors call for longer studies with functional tests.
pmc-13491807:
Ziliang Yu leads a fourteen-author team overturning in 2026 assumptions about interleukin-35, an immune signal usually described as purely calming in rheumatoid arthritis. The route ran through an internal alarm pathway, cGAS-STING, and blocking that pathway erased the effect. Lowering the body's own IL-35 worsened disease unless an activator of the same pathway was added. Turning pathogenic fibroblasts senescent, the authors argue, is a new therapeutic lever.
pmc-13492407:
Megan E LaBreck and four colleagues evaluate in 2026 the safety of giving dofetilide through a feeding tube instead of as a swallowed capsule. Dofetilide is a rhythm-control drug with a notoriously narrow safety margin. Some patients who need the drug cannot swallow, because of ventilation or other illness. Opening the capsule and flushing the contents through a tube could change how the drug is absorbed or how fast it acts, and no earlier study had examined the practice.

The report walks through why caution is warranted: the drug stretches the heart's electrical recovery time, and excess effect can trigger a dangerous rhythm called torsades de pointes. Risk depends on the patient's own repolarization traits, on drug levels, and on interacting medicines. Standard care starts the drug in hospital with continuous monitoring for the first doses, a safeguard the authors carry into their tube-administration evaluation.
pmc-13493107:
Amirhossein Jamshidi, Baharak Akhtardanesh, Mehdi Rasekh, Dariush Vosough, and Mohammad Behzadi follow cats with an inherited kidney disease over eighteen months. The disease fills the kidneys with cysts, which slowly wreck their function. The team tracked twelve affected cats with ultrasound scans and blood tests. Cyst volume grew by fourteen percent and kidney length by seven percent in that time.

Blood markers of kidney strain rose in step, and the cats grew more anemic as the disease advanced. The decline went on despite careful care from owners and vets. The paper urges routine scans and blood work so the disease is caught and managed early.
pmc-13493807:
Zheng and colleagues address a practical tunnelling problem: knowing rock quality ahead of a tunnel boring machine helps crews build safely and quickly. Their 2026 approach computes features from boring machine data in a knowledge-guided way, then feeds them to learning models trained across projects.

The authors compared five algorithms and found CatBoost strongest on accuracy and F1-score, a combined measure of precision and recall. Tested on three separate tunnel projects, the method predicted rock class with accuracies in the mid-to-high eighties. Because the features transfer between sites, a new tunnel can borrow strength from finished projects instead of gathering its own long history. That supports real-time decisions at the tunnel face.
pmc-13493907:
Ticha and colleagues developed a three-dimensional cell model for toxicity testing, growing human nerve-like cells as hundreds of tiny balls called spheroids instead of flat sheets. In their 2026 work, coating wells with poly-D-lysine coaxed SH-SY5Y cells into forming spheroids. Flat-grown cells suffered more on every measure, including energy stores and protective glutathione levels, while spheroids resisted better. Spheroid numbers per well settled over a week of growth, from roughly three hundred down to about half that count. The authors offer the model as a more tissue-like tool for safety testing.
pmc-13494407:

In 2026, the imaging report concerns an infant with trisomy 21, prenatally diagnosed with tetralogy and lung atresia, born at thirty-seven weeks by urgent cesarean section. Prostaglandins maintained ductal blood flow to the lungs.

pmc-13499607:

Pet reptiles are known germ hosts, but yeast loads and drug strength had not been gauged in them. The set held nine species of lizard. Lab growth and gene tests named each yeast found, and drug tests checked how well antifungal drugs could stop them.

Three in four lizards grew yeast, and more than half of all swabs did too. The lab named 113 yeast strains from 17 species. One kind, Arthrographis kalrae, made up more than a third of finds. The authors urge hygiene and routine checks in zoo reptile houses.
pmc-13499807:
Sun and coauthors test a signal protein that may cut brain harm in stroke. Signal proteins are known for calling immune cells to swelling. New work hints they also steer brain cell states in a direct way. The team asks if one such protein calms brain immune cells.

Lab brain immune cells shifted toward repair marks with the protein. Those treated cells also helped nerve cells live and cut cell death. In mice with stroke, the protein shrank the dead brain zone. Mice moved and acted better after that care. Cell death in the brain fell in treated mice too.
pmc-13500707:

Both compounds lowered the damage marker and improved the other readings in the reported results, yet quercetin clearly outperformed its partner. pmc-13500807:

pmc-13501607:

pmc-13501807:

pmc-13503107:

pmc-13503507:

pmc-13503707:

pmc-13504007:

pmc-13504207:

pmc-13505007:

No safety problems appeared. The team judges the tracer ready for patient studies.
pmc-13506107:

pmc-13506507:

pmc-13506607:

pmc-13507107:

pmc-13507307:

The catalog holds 4708 viral enzymes targeting plant fiber, lignin, and pectin, including newly found oxidative types. pmc-13508007:

pmc-13508207:

Tests on flowering time, flower color, and seed protein showed the population can locate trait genes. Filling in missing markers from the map produced millions of extra data points and sharpened gene hunts. The datasets are public for breeders and researchers.
pmc-13508307:

The authors call the trade worthwhile but say reach and duration need work.
pmc-13509407:

pmc-13510707:

pmc-13515807:

pmc-13516207:

pmc-13516907:

pmc-13518107:

pmc-13518707:

pmc-13518907:

pmc-13520007:

pmc-13520407:

pmc-13521907:

pmc-13522107:

pmc-13522307:

pmc-13522507:

pmc-13522607:

pmc-13522807:

pmc-13523207:

pmc-13523307:

pmc-13523407:

pmc-13523507:

pmc-13525507:

pmc-13526307:

pmc-13530707:

pmc-13531207:

pmc-13531807:

pmc-13531907:

pmc-13532007:

pmc-13534507:

pmc-13534807:

pmc-13534907:

pmc-13536507:

pmc-13536707:

pmc-13537607:

pmc-13540807:

pmc-13540907:

pmc-13541807:

pmc-13542107:

pmc-13543007:

pmc-13543607:

The authors name this fast local storm as a target for calming drugs added to clot removal.
pmc-13587407:
Ignacio Ventura and colleagues review a rare X-linked syndrome and argue that one of its forms deserves its own name. Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome begins with early deafness and moves on to movement and vision loss, driven by faults in a gene called TIMM8A. In some patients the damage also wipes out a neighbor gene, BTK, which the immune system needs to make antibodies. Their 2026 review gathered 75 confirmed patients from three decades of reports.

Every patient with the double deletion had the immune failure, and none with the single-gene form did. Language delay was far more common in the double form, while progressive blindness was far more common in the classic form. The authors name the double form XLA-MTS and urge wider gene testing for children with syndromic deafness and slow development, so the immune side is never missed.
pmc-13587507:
Beibei Zhang and colleagues compare two ways of clearing cysts from the jaw in a randomized trial. Jaw cysts hollow out bone and loosen teeth, and the standard fix scrapes the cyst out through an opening in the bone. The rival bone lid method lifts that bone plate off, cleans the cyst, and sets the plate back, keeping the jaw's outer wall. Sixty patients were assigned by chance, thirty to each method, and followed with 3D scans for nine months.

The bone lid group refilled their defects faster, with bigger drops in hole volume and surface area and denser new bone on scans. Gum measures around nearby teeth also improved more, and teeth steadied sooner, with a clearly higher chance of stable teeth at nine months. The authors add one caution: the groups differed a little in starting lesion shape, which softens the surface-area result.
pmc-13588807:
Bin Chen and eleven colleagues test whether a parent's gut microbes can echo into the next generation's brain. Autism is known to involve both genes and environment, and gut bacteria have been linked to its risk. In their 2026 mouse study, adults given antibiotics were colonized with stool microbes from children with autism or from typically developing children, then bred, and their pups were watched for autism-like behavior.

Parents stayed behaviorally normal, but pups of the autism-microbe group showed autism-like changes, plus gut inflammation and neuron loss in two brain regions. Chemical tags on DNA, called methylation marks, shifted in parents' brain, blood, and colon, and a subset of those shifts appeared in the pups. The patterns ran through sex-specific networks tying microbes to genes and behavior. The authors read this as a route by which unaffected parents might pass risk along.
pmc-13590007:
Yan Xing and six colleagues lay out a trial testing an antidepressant to prevent shingles' most dreaded aftermath, in a protocol published in two thousand twenty-six. Postherpetic neuralgia afflicts roughly thirty percent of shingles patients, mostly older adults. Treating acute pain rarely prevents it.

Over eight hundred patients with acute shingles and significant pain will be randomized. Half add venlafaxine, started low and titrated, to conventional therapy; half receive conventional therapy alone. The multicenter design uses open labels but blinded outcome assessment. Prevention aims at the early nerve injury mechanisms while the rash is fresh. A cheap generic preventing months of nerve pain would change shingles care substantially; the protocol pins the test down in advance.
pmc-13590607:
Jeremiah John and Darryl Shibata built mitotic clocks for male childhood tumours, set by conception itself. Gene clocks rebuild tumour history, but adult cancers lack firm age anchors. Childhood tumours ease the problem: their age is bounded by conception and a minimum of about 30 cell splits. Their 2026 study built clocks from flickering CpG methyl tags on the X chromosome, using a two-state Markov model.

Across blood cancers, nerve tumours, and baby brain tumours, model and seen methyl tags matched closely. Tag-change rates ran near one per thousand splits, and tumour ages ran from 30 to several hundred splits. The clocks also untangled relapse moves, tracing returns to small numbers of mixed dormant leftover cancer cells. The authors present conception-set clocks as a window on hidden tumour history.
pmc-13591207:
Ying Huang and colleagues tested a traditional plant extract against rheumatoid arthritis cells in 2026. Clerodendrum japonicum has reported anti-inflammatory use, but its action against rheumatoid arthritis was poorly characterised. Overactive joint-lining cells drive lasting inflammation and joint damage in the disease, so those cells were the test target for the extract.

Treatment calmed the harmful behaviour of the activated cells. The effect ran through a pathway where an enzyme adds chemical marks to a messenger molecule, altering its fate. Animal arthritis also eased under treatment. The authors caution that the active ingredient, direct target, body handling, and full safety picture remain unknown, so chemical and drug studies must follow.
pmc-13592007:
Zhimin Wan leads a twenty-author team reporting newly emerged H6 bird flu viruses in Chinese poultry, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Six viruses, five H6N1 and one H6N2, were isolated from chickens with respiratory symptoms. Reassortant flu viruses carrying H9N2 internal genes have repeatedly infected humans.

Genetic analysis traced the surface genes to goose H6 viruses and to H9N2 or H5N1 sources. All six internal genes came from the G57 genotype of H9N2, the cassette linked to cross-species jumps. Laboratory studies examined the viruses' behavior in cells. The authors warn these reassortants pose a potential zoonotic risk. Surveillance of poultry flu, their work argues, must watch gene combinations, not just surface types.
pmc-13592307:
Lee and colleagues report in 2026 a reaction that builds tetrahydrofuran rings, five-membered oxygen rings common in natural products and drug candidates. The reaction controls the rings' three-dimensional shape precisely. Shaping four stereocenters, the atoms whose arrangement defines handedness, in one step is a prized result.

The reaction joins allylsilanes with glyoxal partners through a formal cycloaddition followed by a hydrogen shift, steered by a chiral catalyst that acts as a Lewis acid, an electron-pair acceptor. Yields reached the high eighty percent range at their best. The desired handedness was produced almost exclusively, and one ring shape was favored more than twenty to one over its rival in the best cases. Earlier versions of this reaction relied on chirality already built into the starting materials; this one creates the asymmetry from scratch.
pmc-13592607:
Md Parvej Hussain leads a team linking low birth weight to child malnutrition across five South Asian countries. Survey data from Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal, and the Maldives gave 147,332 complete child records. Matching methods paired similar children who differed mainly in birth weight, then compared five outcomes: stunting, wasting, underweight, any malnutrition, and several forms at once.

About one child in six was born underweight, with Pakistan highest and Nepal lowest. Matched comparisons tied low birth weight to every malnutrition form in the pooled data and in nearly every country. Wasting alone broke the pattern in Bangladesh and the Maldives. Hussain and the team press for country specific action on birth weight as a lever against early childhood malnutrition.
pmc-13592707:
Amanda R. Young leads a team asking how myelin sheaths know how long to grow. Sheath length tunes signal timing in the brain, and thicker axons carry longer sheaths, yet the sensing trick was unknown. Using lab grown fibers and mice, the group tested whether each sheath reads its own fiber's width locally. A pressure sensing channel called Piezo1, found in the sheath making cells, stood as the prime suspect.

Each sheath did respond to its own fiber's diameter alone. Mice lacking Piezo1 in those cells grew sheaths too short on thick axons, matching the dish results, while sheath thickness stayed normal. Young and the team propose that Piezo1 turns width into length, hard wiring timing patterns across circuits.
pmc-13593707:
Mathias Busch, Gerrit Bredeck, Hans Bouwmeester, and Roel P. F.
