Schins review how inhaled or swallowed particles and fibers switch on the NLRP3 inflammasome, a protein assembly inside immune cells that drives inflammation. Their 2026 review gathers laboratory and animal work on materials from asbestos and quartz to microplastics and desert dust.

The chain from particle exposure through inflammasome activation to disease is firmly established for workplace mineral dusts. For the low-level environmental exposures people meet daily, that chain is still being traced. The authors argue that testing whether a new material activates NLRP3 should become a routine part of hazard assessment. The response appears across very different materials, and it sits upstream of lasting harm. Emerging materials such as nanocomposites could then be screened before wide use.
pmc-13595707:
Julia Naganuma-Carreras and co-authors analyzed survey data from 1,360 post-9/11 American veterans to see which post-deployment struggles predict arrest and charge, and whether the pattern differs for women and men. Their 2026 study defined justice involvement as arrest after deployment and tested mental health, substance use, anger, and housing factors together.

Fifteen percent reported justice involvement overall, with men higher than women. Younger age and a probable alcohol use disorder raised the odds in both sexes. Other risks split by gender: problematic anger mattered for women, while a history of homelessness mattered for men. The authors argue for gender-responsive prevention that treats mental health, drinking, and housing as one tangle, with the mix tuned to the different risk profiles they found.
pmc-13598007:
Madelaine Hettler leads a seventeen-author pilot study combining two imaging lenses on high-grade soft tissue sarcoma. One lens is a PET tracer. It lights up fibroblast activation protein, a marker of the tumor's supporting tissue. The other is MRI diffusion measures of how crowded the cells are. Nine patients underwent thirteen combined scans, some after treatment.

Every tumor took up the tracer distinctly. Neither tracer uptake nor diffusion separated grade two from grade three tumors, disappointing one hope. Two measures did talk to each other: denser cell packing on diffusion went with stronger tracer uptake, an inverse correlation. Tissue staining agreed with imaging, since stained-positive tumors showed far higher uptake. Responders to treatment showed steep uptake falls and looser diffusion before size changed. The authors call the pairing complementary and worth larger study.
pmc-13599907:
Mukhethwa Netshiombo and four colleagues map how African health systems are responding to climate change, and how far global climate pledges have entered national law in southern Africa. African health services produce few emissions yet face heavy climate shocks. The scoping review gathered research from six databases plus policy documents, keeping 78 research papers and 15 grey publications for analysis.

Most research clustered on training a climate-ready health workforce and on greener buildings, technology, and supply chains. Among Southern African Development Community members, only South Africa and Mauritius had passed a Climate Change Act. Four countries had a national health adaptation plan, and Madagascar alone had measured emissions across its public hospitals. Because immediate threats dominate, adaptation clearly outweighs emission cutting in both research and policy. The authors urge planners to weave climate goals into everyday health system planning so resilient, low-carbon care can actually be built.
pmc-13600107:
Nagendra Verma and Swati Arora review rules for cell and gene therapy world wide. Their review from twenty twenty-six compares three big drug agencies. It also covers five growing markets, named as the BRIC-M group.

Cell and gene cures have moved from test stage to goods for sale. Yet rule books still differ a lot from place to place. Four gaps show up in all eight places they checked. Those gaps deal with strength tests, change checks, and proof for small groups. Some lands are far more ready to align than others. The review maps where rules could meet.
pmc-13601507:
Ramya Lakshmi Rajendran and colleagues review in 2026 a cell-free approach to healing wounds that refuse to close. Chronic wounds stall amid lasting inflammation, poor blood vessel growth, and faulty tissue rebuilding. Stem cells can nudge these processes along, yet their use is held back by poor survival after transplant, uneven quality, and safety worries. Tiny parcels released by stem cells, called extracellular vesicles, might deliver the benefit without the cells.

The review weighs natural vesicles against artificial nanovesicles built to imitate them. In animal wound models, vesicle treatments calmed inflammation, encouraged vessel growth, and improved closure and tissue appearance. Proof is still missing for harder endpoints: lasting function, less scarring, and wounds staying closed. Delivery route, dose, and trial endpoints all remain unsettled. The authors supply a framework for the studies needed before vesicle therapy can claim a place in routine wound care.
pmc-13604207:
Fatemeh Soheili and ten co-authors study a saliva test that counts white blood cells from the mouth. These cells show how much inflammation the gums carry, but counts today need lab work. The method rests the cells on a coated surface that holds them while mouth skin cells wash away. In the team's tests, the step cut skin cell contamination by ninety-one in each hundred while keeping nearly all the white cells.

A smart image model then counted the cells, matching a standard lab method across thirty test days. The paper explains why the surface method works and where it beats filters.
pmc-13610407:
Sake Wang, Hassen Dakhlaoui, and Bryan Wong present a study from twenty twenty-six on a layered quantum dot that traps light in set bands. The dot is a ball with an indium arsenide core in a shell of aluminum antimonide. A lone donor atom sits at its heart. Size limits and a magnetic field both tune how the dot takes in light. The team works out the light response in full.

One jump between levels sets the main take in peak. A stronger field shifts that peak by a wide span of energy. A larger core shifts it too, but in a lower band. The split ranges hint at detectors that span two light bands and tune by magnet.
pmc-13611007:
Aisha Khaled Chaudhri and six co-authors test a treated charcoal for cleaning polluted farm soil, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. The soil held phthalate esters, chemicals used in plastics, which build up near e-waste sites and harm crops and soil life. The team made charcoal from coconut shells, with and without added zinc, and grew wheat in treated pots.

The zinc version had a richer surface and grabbed more of the two chemicals tested. Wheat in zinc-treated soil grew taller, with longer roots and more mass, than wheat in plain polluted soil. After harvest, that soil showed better acidity balance, more carbon, and stronger enzyme activity. The authors present the zinc charcoal as a green fix for such soils.
pmc-13612207:
Junlin Pu and three colleagues map five years of publishing on brain fog after COVID-19. Cognitive dysfunction is among the most disabling features of post-COVID-19 condition, and work on it has exploded. Their analysis pulled papers from 2021 to 2025 out of Web of Science and Scopus, screening to 746 and 1,117 papers respectively. Output, teamwork, and themes were then charted with standard mapping tools.

Publication counts climbed steadily across the five years. The United States produced the most, the University of London led the institution list, and the Journal of Clinical Medicine stood out on publication and citation measures. Keywords clustered into three domains: psychological factors, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation. Burst detection flagged the blood-brain barrier, the choroid plexus, and endothelial cells as emerging frontiers where attention is suddenly concentrating. The authors offer the map as a guide for newcomers and hypothesis fodder for researchers choosing where to dig next.
pmc-13613007:
Lucía Casares-Crespo and colleagues map two groups of astrocytes, the star-shaped support cells of the brain, in the adult hippocampus, a region central to memory. The groups are told apart by pairs of surface markers, proteins named ACSA and ATP1B2 among them. Sorting the cells and reading their active genes showed that each group carries its own gene signature and ages in its own way.

The most common group, positive for both ATP1B2 and GLAST markers, looks like a stable, specialized set of support cells with high protein sugar-coating activity. A second group, positive for ATP1B2 alone, switched on genes for cell energy and cholesterol handling as the animals aged. Other gene sets tied to cell sticking were switched off in the common group. The work shows that brain support cells are far from uniform.
pmc-13615107:
J. Bergqvist leads a team using the long-running RHINE study of respiratory health in northern Europe to ask whether childhood factors predict chronic rhinosinusitis, lasting sinus inflammation, in adult life. The study drew 7,686 people, average age about 51, from seven centres in five countries. Health data were first gathered in the early 1990s. Sinus outcomes came from the 2020 follow-up round.

A serious lung infection before age five nearly doubled the odds of adult sinus disease. Parental asthma raised the odds more than fivefold, and parental chronic lung disease nearly doubled them. Growing up in an inner city carried more risk than a farm childhood. Some crowded-household measures pointed the other way. The results suggest the roots of a stubborn adult condition can reach back to the family home and the air of early childhood.
pmc-13615207:
Piero Barbanti and colleagues tracked long-term real-world response to eptinezumab in migraine over 48 weeks. Evidence beyond 24 weeks was thin for this preventive antibody. Their prospective multicentre study gave 261 adults with frequent episodic or chronic migraine, each with at least three failed preventives, intravenous eptinezumab every 12 weeks, with optional dose doubling after week 12.

At week 48, about 82 percent had halved migraine days, about 52 percent had cut them by three-quarters, and about 10 percent were migraine-free. Monthly migraine days fell by about 16, painkiller use by about 15, and disability scores improved sharply. Barbanti and colleagues present eptinezumab as durably effective in hard-to-treat migraine.
pmc-13616007:
Rocha and colleagues reported in 2026 on five new selenocyanate compounds, chemicals that combine selenium with a cyanate group and differ in their side chains. Selenium helps control redox balance, the balance of damaging and protective reactions in cells, so such compounds may protect the brain. The team tested the compounds in computer models, in lab assays, and in live mice.

Rocha found that computer models predicted good drug-like traits and binding to two brain enzymes, acetylcholinesterase and the monoamine oxidases, which shape nerve signalling. Lab tests showed antioxidant power, strongest in compounds 1, 4, and 5, and all five slowed the target enzymes. Compounds 2 and 4 were then given to mice. Neither was toxic at a low oral dose. At a higher dose, compound 2 caused signs of harm while compound 4 stayed non-lethal, making it the lead candidate.
pmc-13616307:
Gyurin Kim and colleagues hide a secret optical fingerprint inside an ordinary-looking coloured surface, using two stacked kinds of light cavities. Surfaces with structural colour look the same every time, while random nanoparticle scatter gives a unique fingerprint that is hard to copy. Joining the two in one material is hard because order and disorder fight each other. Their stack separates the jobs by depth.

Flat layered cavities on top set the visible colour. Below them, a disordered spray of copper nanoparticles in tiny gaps scatters light in a random pattern that barely affects the look. The whole device is laid down in one vacuum process, with a cooled angled spray keeping particles from merging. Such a tag could certify goods: a public colour anyone can see, and a hidden pattern only a reader can verify.
pmc-13618207:
Makoto Tanaka and eight colleagues publish the protocol for a randomized trial of an app-based fatigue program for people with inflammatory bowel disease whose gut inflammation is in remission. Fatigue often persists even when Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis is quiet, draining quality of life, and scalable psychological help is scarce. The intervention centers on a seven-week cognitive behavioral therapy course delivered by mobile app, backed by support messages.

Adults in remission with at least mild fatigue were randomized evenly against a waitlist control, with fatigue scores as the main outcome and disease self-efficacy as a secondary measure. Recruitment ran from July 2025 to February 2026: five hundred two patients were assessed, three hundred fifty-one were randomized, and follow-up is still ongoing. No effectiveness results exist yet; the team expects to submit them in 2027 and hopes engagement data will refine the program for larger rollouts.
pmc-13619107:
Jinze Jiang and six colleagues introduce HADD, a method for estimating three-dimensional human poses from a single camera view. Their framework splits a pose into bone lengths and bone directions, adds noise to each part, and then removes that noise step by step. A denoising module built around the skeleton's hierarchy is meant to stop errors from growing at joints far from the body's center.

Experiments used two large motion datasets, Human3.6M and MPI-INF-3DHP, which record people moving in laboratory settings. On the second dataset the method reached a mean joint error of under thirty millimeters with very high accuracy scores under a single-guess setting. The authors present the gains as help for sports training, rehabilitation checks, and animation work that need fine motion detail.
pmc-13620407:
Narongrit Tipcompor and five colleagues built a smart extractor that pulls vanillin, vanilla's main flavor compound, from cured pods using microwaves in pulses rather than a steady blast. Their rig links an infrared temperature sensor, a small controller board, and a web dashboard, so the run can be watched and programmed in real time. A statistical tuning method then searched for the best settings.

The sweet spot combined moderate microwave power, about seventeen minutes, a small dry sample, and strong ethanol. Two validation runs at matched energy landed within a few percent of the predicted yield. Computer simulations put error bounds around the result and showed microwave power and ethanol strength mattered most. Pulsed operation cut the calculated energy use by about a sixth against a continuous baseline. The authors offer the platform as a template for energy-aware plant extraction.
pmc-13621707:
Mohaned A Hameed and co-authors present a 2026 review of medical records asking which signs at diagnosis predict who will later start strong biologic or targeted drugs. The two joint diseases are spondyloarthritis and psoriatic arthritis. Both are long-term inflammatory conditions, meaning the immune system attacks the body's own joints and tissues. The records came from one rheumatology centre.

The study followed 119 people with psoriatic arthritis and 120 with spondyloarthritis who were diagnosed between 2012 and 2016. About four in ten in each group started the stronger drugs, sooner for the spine-related group. In that group, high levels of a blood marker of inflammation and swelling seen on scans of the sacroiliac joints predicted a start. Older age lowered the chance for the psoriatic group. Background factors such as schooling and birth country showed no link, which the authors read as a sign of fair access.
pmc-13622407:
Greta Gerdes joins a large team reporting genetic findings from a founder population in Colombia, where a small group of ancestors left some gene variants unusually common. The team studied serious mental illness, including schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, in the Paisa region using the Mision Origen biobank. Such isolated populations can reveal variants with strong effects that stay hidden elsewhere.

The team read the protein-coding parts of the genome in nearly 22,000 cases and about 19,800 controls. Seven genes showed links that crossed diagnostic lines, and five had not been tied to serious mental illness before. The strongest signal was a small insertion in a gene called ADAP1 that more than tripled risk and also shaped symptoms and thinking test scores in carriers. Because several risk variants grew common only in this population, the study fills a gap between rare, powerful variants and common, weak ones.
pmc-13623007:
Garyoung Lee and four co-authors look for universal laws hidden in freeway traffic jams. Physicists have suspected that traffic, like water turning to ice, passes through a tipping point with patterns that repeat at many scales. Proof at the level of single vehicles was missing, so the team used detailed trajectory data from the I-24 MOTION testbed, which tracks cars on a real highway.

Their analysis found that jam clusters grow in the scale-free pattern expected near a phase transition. The authors link that state to self-organized criticality, where a system tunes itself to the edge of disorder. The wobbles in traffic flow matched a growth model known as the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang class, which describes many rough, growing surfaces. If traffic follows shared rules, forecasts and control systems could borrow the maths. The authors present the results as a new base for traffic science.
pmc-13623507:
Laura Biondi and three co-authors update the word lists used to test hearing in Italian speech audiometry, the clinic test that measures how well a patient understands spoken words. Italy's standard lists date from the 1950s and no longer match everyday language. The team built fresh two-syllable lists balanced for sound and modern word use, then validated them under international standards.

Twelve young native speakers with normal hearing listened to the lists at falling loudness levels, in quiet and in party-like background noise. Scores behaved as a good test should: understanding faded as volume dropped, and every list hit perfect scores at the test's top level. Lists matched each other, and results a week later were nearly identical, showing excellent repeat reliability. Performance in noise stayed steady. The authors offer the workflow as a template other languages can copy to refresh their own test materials.
pmc-13624007:
Hiroaki Watanabe and colleagues published a 2026 head-to-head test of two commercial artificial intelligence systems against radiologists for spotting lung nodules on routine chest CT scans. Screening studies flatter AI, since their images are standardised; daily hospital scans vary in quality and carry other diseases. The team wanted a real-world scorecard.

The retrospective study covered 102 patients holding 353 nodules or masses, judged against an expert-made reference standard. Two radiologists found more of the lesions than either AI system, with sensitivity in the low nineties against the low-to-high eighties. The humans also raised far fewer false alarms per scan, so their positive calls were right more often. Weaknesses differed by reader type: radiologists struggled with faint ground-glass nodules, while AI faltered on complex cases, central locations, and large masses. The authors position current AI as a helpful second reader, not a replacement.
pmc-13624307:
Hai-Lian Bi leads a study tracing atrial fibrillation, the rhythm disorder, to a protein-cleaning enzyme that protects a calcium-handling kinase from destruction. The enzyme, called UCHL1, was raised in heart tissue from fibrillating patients and in mice given a hormone that provokes the rhythm. The team bred mice lacking the enzyme only in atrial cells, and others making extra amounts of it.

Mice without the enzyme resisted the provoked rhythm, showed less scarring and enlargement, and kept steadier calcium control. Extra enzyme flipped every result the other way. The mechanism ran through a link: the enzyme strips disposal tags off the kinase CaMKII-delta at one site, sparing it from the cell's shredder. The surviving kinase then over-activates a calcium channel that leaks and sparks abnormal beats. A drug blocking the enzyme lowered rhythm inducibility in mice, which the authors offer as a treatment lead.
pmc-13625807:
Eva Maria Schleicher and colleagues, with the German cirrhosis study group, ask how long doctors should give albumin before starting a key drug for a failing liver-kidney syndrome. Albumin infusions help confirm hepatorenal syndrome, yet waiting delays terlipressin, the drug that can reverse it. Twelve German centers contributed 145 patients, split by whether albumin ran under a day or one to two and a half days before the drug began.

About four in ten patients responded fully to treatment, and the response rate matched between the two timing groups. Longer albumin time also failed to change the odds of avoiding dialysis and transplant or of surviving. Shorter workups, the authors conclude, do not seem to cost patients their chance of response, which may speed treatment where beds and albumin are scarce.
pmc-13627707:
Qi Tang and colleagues run the first clinical trial of gum-derived stem cells for type 1 diabetes. Insulin manages the disease but cannot stop the immune attack that kills insulin-making beta cells. Mesenchymal stem cells from human gums calm immunity in many settings. So eighteen patients received four vein infusions of the cells or a placebo, three weeks apart. The trial was double-blind and phase 1, and all patients stayed on routine insulin.

By week twelve the treated group showed better leftover beta cell function and needed less daily insulin, and one patient stopped insulin entirely after the first dose. Blood sugar control matched between groups, and side effects, including low blood sugar, were no worse with the cells. Blood markers hinted the cells tire out attacker T-cells, a lead the authors offer for larger trials.
pmc-13627807:
Abdul Kader Natour and four colleagues, publishing in 2026, report the redo of a redo: fixing a ballooned weak point on an aorta bypass, for the second time. Middle aortic syndrome narrows the body's main artery in youth, and bypass grafting is its standard cure, yet the graft's stitched joints can slowly bulge into pseudoaneurysms that threaten to burst. Their patient, a 55-year-old woman, arrived with a growing recurrence at the lower joint of her earlier bypass.

The team opened the site, cut out the false sac, and rebuilt the lower aorta and both iliac arteries that feed the legs. The operation succeeded in a case the authors call surgically complex, with scarred planes and little margin for error. Their report adds a worked example to the thin literature on late graft failure in this rare syndrome.
pmc-13628507:
Panagiotis Zymaris and seven co-authors report a life-threatening case, published in twenty twenty-six, of a rare vessel disease that surfaced during treatment for hives. The disease inflames small and medium blood vessels and often comes with late-onset asthma and high counts of a white blood cell type. The patient was taking a biologic drug for chronic hives.

The woman, in her late sixties, arrived with trouble breathing, nosebleeds, coughing of blood, and deep tiredness. Scans showed cloudy patches in both lungs, and a lung wash confirmed bleeding inside the air sacs. Blood tests backed the vessel disease diagnosis. Strong steroid treatment and other immune drugs were not enough at first, and she needed a breathing machine. Plasma exchange and a stronger drug followed, and she slowly recovered. The authors ask whether the drug hid, caused, or revealed the disease.
pmc-13630307:
Isabel Schwaninger and six colleagues asked what patients can learn about health app quality from app store pages and user reviews. They analysed nearly twelve hundred Apple and Google apps aimed at Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, combining statistics, content analysis, and language-model-assisted classification of descriptions and feedback.

Only about two percent of the apps claimed certified medical device status, and many patient-facing apps sat outside the medical category altogether, clustering around care support, wellness, and monitoring. Reviews carried genuinely useful signals about usability, perceived health benefit, and cost, buried in personal opinion. The authors argue that store information should be made more trustworthy and readable, and that review mining deserves development as a complementary quality signal.
pmc-13630707:
Şeyma Halaç and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six qualitative study of pharmacy academics in Türkiye and public health. Pharmacists could do more for community prevention, the authors argue. The study asked teachers how they see that role and its training.

Eleven academics from Istanbul pharmacy faculties gave in-depth online interviews. They described public health as prevention built on teamwork. Community pharmacies looked like easy entry points for advice and chronic disease help. Weak training, low public health literacy, and poor official recognition held the role back. The authors urge curriculum and policy change.
pmc-13631107:
Katrina Portelli and two colleagues comment on a mouse study of temporal lobe seizures. The study reframes where such seizures get their power. The piriform cortex, a smell-processing region, is notorious as a seizure trigger. It was the starting point here. The commentary stresses the circuit the study uncovered, not the single hotspot.

The first team worked across stimulation, imaging, and tracing methods. They showed piriform activity drives seizures through a relay. It runs into the lateral entorhinal cortex and onward to the dentate gyrus. The relay reorganised activity brain-wide. Breaking either link suppressed the seizures. Portelli's group sets this against the limits of focus-based surgery. That surgery frees only about half of patients long term. Network targets, they argue, deserve the field's attention.
pmc-13633807:
Alblooshi and nine co-authors assess patient safety culture among healthcare professionals in the United Arab Emirates, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The team used the standard Hospital Survey on Patient Safety Culture. They also examined how job traits and reporting barriers relate to safety scores. Over six hundred physicians, nurses, and allied professionals responded.

Reporting of near-miss events was limited, at about forty percent. Felt respect between people, by contrast, was high. Oddly, respondents who seldom reported barriers scored higher on safety culture across most domains. Group comparisons used standard statistical tests across job categories. The authors recommend system-level fixes. Making reporting simpler, building a nonpunitive culture, and giving better feedback should raise reporting and safety.
pmc-13635007:
Sarè and a large international team publish in 2026 a reference dataset for mapping farmland in central and northern Benin. There, small, varied plots and scarce ground data make satellite land cover maps unreliable. The data article describes how the reference set was built.

The dataset holds 33,065 hand-labeled polygons covering more than eighteen thousand hectares across six pilot sites, each a fifty-by-fifty kilometer window. Annual field campaigns from 2022 to 2024 documented crops on the ground, while other polygons were drawn from high-resolution satellite images and open map data, then checked by experts. Thirteen classes cover the local farming reality, from cereals, cotton, and roots to orchards, forests, savanna, and built-up land. The authors offer the set for training deep learning models and for producing yearly agricultural maps.
pmc-13638707:
Takero Shindo and Mami Shindo analyzed real-world treatment of chronic graft-versus-host disease after donor stem cell transplant in Japan, a 2026 claims study of a burdensome complication. Chronic graft-versus-host disease inflames and scars multiple organs, yet practical data on drug sequences and outcomes remain thin. The authors mined anonymized insurance claims for 1,090 patients, tracking systemic therapy, complications, and survival patterns by age and donor cell source.

Eighty-one percent received systemic immune suppression, most often tacrolimus plus steroids at first. Second-line therapy reached 44 percent and third-line 23 percent, with steroid-only treatment most common at third line. Treatment was paused in 79 percent and restarted in about half, while younger recipients and cord blood recipients restarted less often and died less often. Most complications eased over time, except chronic bone, eye, and breathing disorders.
pmc-13639007:
Andrew A Butler and eleven colleagues report a 2026 monkey study on adropin, a blood peptide, and thinking in old age. Finding blood markers that flag weak cognition early is a major goal in aging research, and adropin has been linked to metabolism and blood vessel health.

Aged rhesus macaques with low adropin made poorer decisions on a food-choice test that grew harder over time. Monkeys with higher levels improved their reaction speed faster and varied less, while simple task performance stayed intact. The pattern suggests adropin signals resilience under challenge rather than basic ability, making it a candidate marker for cognitive aging.
pmc-13649507:
Kaiyuan Zhao and Xiongying Niu build a framework for why game-like work design delights some staff and grates on others. Points, badges, and leader boards are now common in offices, yet research has leaned on drive and output to explain the split. Their paper draws on feeling-based judgement theory and 52 past works.

They sort what staff judge into five fields: the system itself, the task, the self, peers, and the wider meaning of the firm. The same design cue can read as support to one worker and as a threat to another, and those first feelings shape later results. Eight testable claims turn the framework into a plan for future studies.
pmc-13651107:
Kun Qin and one colleague review what aerobic exercise, whey protein, and creatine each do for adolescents. Adolescence is a developmental window when training and nutrition can set lifelong patterns for muscle, bone, metabolism, and brain. The three are often studied separately in adults, leaving their combined use in teenagers poorly charted.

The narrative search covered major databases through May 2026, favoring studies in adolescents and borrowing mechanism evidence from adults and animals where needed. Aerobic training builds the cell's energy factories and metabolic flexibility. Whey supplies amino acids that drive muscle repair and remodeling signals. Creatine speeds energy recycling in muscle and may support brain energy and growth-factor pathways tied to learning. Shared messengers from muscle, bone, and brain suggest the systems talk to each other during training. The authors caution that much mechanism evidence is indirect and that direct trials of combined programs in adolescents are still scarce.
pmc-13651607:
Jason D Eckmann and one colleague test whether isotope ratios can tell one white cotton T-shirt from another. That is a forensic headache because bleached cotton is everywhere and ordinary chemistry sees all of it as identical. Fibers from a crime scene are only useful if they can be tied to a source, or cleared from one.

Using elemental analyzers feeding a continuous-flow isotope ratio mass spectrometer, the team measured several stable isotopes in cotton samples of varied manufacturing origin. Each garment proved internally uniform, while garments from different sources separated clearly, especially when multiple isotopes were combined and plotted in three dimensions. Even sewing thread and cloth from the same item carried distinguishable signatures. Statistical testing confirmed the separations. The authors present the pilot as evidence that isotope fingerprinting deserves a place in the fiber examiner's toolkit.
pmc-13651907:
Yulin Du and four colleagues investigate how a soybean protein called AATRhg1 helps plants resist the soybean cyst nematode, a worm that causes heavy yield losses. The protein sits in the Rhg1 region of the genome, a major source of nematode resistance, yet its exact job was unclear. Experiments with silenced and mutant plants let the team watch what changed when the protein was missing, altered, or restored.

Microscopy placed AATRhg1 in the tonoplast, the membrane around the plant cell vacuole. Silencing it raised levels of several amino acids in roots and weakened defense responses involving hormone and energy pathways. While one mutant form of the protein restored resistance and another did not. Simply adding extra copies of the gene was not enough to help, which suggests the protein must work in step with partner pathways.
pmc-13659507:
Xi Xu and twelve colleagues describe a surgical method that joins two partial liver grafts before putting them into the recipient. Dual-graft transplantation lets an adult receive enough liver tissue when no single graft of safe size is available. The usual sequence implants one graft while the second waits in cold storage, lengthening its time without blood flow. The team's approach assembles both grafts outside the body and implants them as one unit.

The en bloc piggyback technique aims to shorten that waiting time and simplify the connections once inside the patient. Reports of technique matter in transplant surgery, where small gains in preservation time and reconstruction order affect whether scarce organs succeed. The paper gives other centers a described, repeatable version of the procedure to evaluate against their own sequential practice.
pmc-13681407:
Shibo Liu and six co-authors show that activating the longevity protein SIRT1 helps aged bone rebuild itself, in a two thousand twenty-six stem cell paper. SIRT1 declines with age alongside the special type H blood vessels that support bone formation.

In dishes, boosting SIRT1 improved both blood vessel tube formation and bone differentiation in co-cultures of aged marrow stem cells and endothelial cells. In animals, a SIRT1 activator significantly improved regeneration of osteoporotic bone defects in femur and jaw. The mechanism runs through beta-catenin, which SIRT1 deacetylates and sends into the nucleus to switch on Wnt signaling. The authors propose SIRT1 as a target for rejuvenating elderly bone.
pmc-1994707:
Leek and Storey address hidden variation in gene expression studies using surrogate variable analysis. Gene activity is shaped by genes, environment, daily life, and lab technique, all at once. Alongside the factor a study cares about, unknown or unmeasured factors add their own signals.

Their method estimates those hidden factors from the data itself, so they can be accounted for in analysis. Without that step, stray signals can fake a finding or hide a real one. Surrogate variable analysis became a widely used guard against false claims in large gene studies.
pmc-3065307:
Stephens, Greenman, Fu, and co-authors report massive genome rearrangement acquired in a single catastrophic event in cancer. Cancer is driven by mutations and chromosome rearrangements gained during a person's life. Such changes were conventionally thought to accumulate gradually over many years.

Using next-generation sequencing, the team characterises a phenomenon they name chromothripsis. In it, tens to hundreds of rearrangements appear to happen in one crisis, shattering and restitching chromosomes. The discovery changed how scientists think about some cancers, showing evolution inside a tumour can jump rather than creep.  Single-event shattering also explains some tumours whose genomes look unusually scrambled overall.
pmc-3084507:
Polman, Reingold, Banwell, and co-authors publish the 2010 revisions to the McDonald criteria for diagnosing multiple sclerosis. Multiple sclerosis is a disease in which the immune system attacks the brain and spinal cord. Diagnosis rests on showing damage spread across place and time in the nervous system.

The revised criteria update how scan and clinical evidence may be used to reach that judgement sooner. Earlier, more certain diagnosis lets patients start treatment while it can do most good. The McDonald criteria are the field's shared standard, so each revision shapes neurology practice worldwide.
pmc-3190407:
Ondov, Bergman, and Phillippy present a tool for interactive viewing of metagenomic results inside a web browser. A critical output of metagenomic studies is estimating how abundant each group of microbes is. Assignments of DNA pieces to groups carry real uncertainty, though.

Good tools must show both the tree context of each group and how sure each assignment is. Their browser-based approach makes such exploration hands-on, without special installs. Letting users inspect doubt directly helps prevent too bold claims about which microbes lead a sample.  Tree views let users zoom from broad phyla down to single genera by hand.
pmc-5605707:
The GBD 2016 DALYs and HALE Collaborators reported in 2017 on disability-adjusted life-years and healthy life expectancy worldwide. Measuring changes in health across locations helps compare epidemiological patterns against health system performance. It also shows where research money, policy effort, and program funds are most needed.

Using the Global Burden of Disease 2016 framework, the team estimated DALYs, which combine years lost to early death and years lived in poor health, for hundreds of diseases and injuries. They also estimated HALE, the years a person can expect to live in full health. Gaps between lifespan and healthy lifespan show where added years come with heavy illness.
pmc-5912207:
Nicholas Kassebaum and Global Burden of Disease colleagues estimated the toll of oral conditions in 2017. The work uses the GBD 2015 data to count how common mouth diseases are worldwide. Tooth decay and gum disease rarely kill, but they disable many people.

Estimates cover new and existing cases plus years lived with disability from 1990 to 2015. Untreated decay in permanent teeth ranks among the most common conditions on Earth. The burden falls heavily where dental care is scarce. These numbers press health systems to treat oral health as part of general health, not a luxury.
pmc-6602507:
Guangyan Zhou, Othman Soufan, Jessica Ewald, and coauthors described NetworkAnalyst 3.0 in 2019. Gene expression data make most sense inside networks of interacting genes and proteins. NetworkAnalyst was first released several years earlier for that purpose.

The new version offers a visual analytics platform that starts from raw counts or gene lists. It builds protein interaction networks, finds key hub genes, and maps pathways. Support now spans many species beyond human and mouse. The point-and-click design serves biologists who need network insight without writing code. Built-in tutorials walk a new user from a sample file to a finished network figure.
pmc-6899507:
Ashkan Afshin and the GBD Diet Collaborators measured the health effects of diet worldwide in 2019. A poor diet is a major preventable cause of chronic disease. Its total impact across countries had never been fully tallied.

The study estimates intake of key foods and nutrients in nearly two hundred countries and links them to deaths and disability. Too little whole grain and fruit, and too much salt, rank among the top problems. Diet-related deaths exceed those from smoking in their accounting. The findings argue that food policy deserves a central place in health planning.
pmc-7199907:
Mart Lamers, Joep Beumer, Jelte van der Vaart, and coauthors showed SARS-CoV-2 infects human gut cells in 2020. COVID-19 was seen mainly as a lung disease spread by breathing. Yet many patients had gut symptoms, and virus turned up in stool.

Growing human intestinal organoids, tiny gut models in a dish, the team watched the virus infect the lining cells and multiply. Both entry receptors were present and used. Productive gut infection may explain symptoms and a possible fecal spread route. The work widened the picture of where the virus can live in the body.
pmc-7615407:
Yongyue Wang and a team including Kebin He map fine particle air pollution across Beijing at street-level detail to judge what people actually breathe. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three. As regional pollution falls, local sources drive more of the differences in exposure between neighborhoods.

The team built a thirty-meter mapping method that blends many helper data sources, and it proved far more accurate than standard transport models. Phone signal data gave hourly population maps at the same fine scale. District average pollution levels hid real exposure gaps between people. Indoor levels, judged from indoor-outdoor ratios, differed from outdoor readings as well. The work gives a sharper basis for health risk work in dense cities.
poincare-value-science-halsted-1907:
Henri Poincare was a French mathematician whose work touched nearly every branch of math and physics. His Value of Science, in Halsted's 1907 translation, asks what science is for and how it earns trust. He writes as a working scientist speaking to general readers.

Poincare argues that some truths of science rest on handy conventions, chosen because they make the world easier to describe. He defends the role of intuition, the sudden flash that comes before formal proof. The book remains a clear, calm guide to the aims and limits of physics. He also asks why the public trusts science, and what that trust should rest on.
raffles-further-adventures-of-the-amateu:
Raffles: Further Adventures of the Amateur Cracksman, by E. W. Hornung, opens with the story No Sinecure, told by Raffles's companion in crime. A telegram, handed in at Vere Street at eight in the morning of May 11, 1897, tells the narrator to see Mr. Maturin's advertisement in the Daily Mail and earnestly begs him to try for the post.

The narrator, unwashed in a Holloway attic, is writing paid articles on prison life and must cash his first check to buy the paper. The post is male nurse to an elderly gentleman in feeble health, and the knighted relative who once called him a disgrace now offers to speak for him.
rapaport-tales-maxims-midrash-1907:
Samuel Rapaport gathered Tales and Maxims from the Midrash in 1907 for English readers new to rabbinic storytelling. The Midrash is the body of Jewish tales and comments that grew up around the Hebrew Bible over centuries. Rapaport retells its best-known pieces in plain prose.

Readers meet Abraham smashing idols, Moses pleading for Israel, and rabbis arguing points of mercy and law. Short maxims, crisp sayings on pride, study, and kindness, stand between the longer tales. The collection remains a classic English gateway into the humor and wisdom of the tradition. The book assumes no Hebrew, only curiosity about an old and lively literature.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: Volume seven of The Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte is preceded here solely by the standard header of its plain-text publisher. That header names the work, credits Constant as its author, and gives English as its language. It is followed by no text of the memoir at all: no first page, no preface, no list of chapters. All that can fairly be said is that this is the seventh part of Constant's account of Napoleon, presented in English under that title.
richard-carvel-volume-07:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel opens its seventh volume with My Friends Are Proven, at the door of Richard's lodgings. His man Banks stands red with indignation: Mr. Dix, his agent, has sat in possession since noon, smoking Richard's tobacco in the chair Dolly chose. Richard faces him from the threshold.

He tells Dix the news by packet is known, and that he shall have his money though it take a lifetime. Ten per cent more is promised if Dix will not press Lord Comyn. Asked what security he will give, Richard answers, my word, never yet broken. The volume's chapters lead back to Annapolis and a house of memories.
scheible-das-kloster-vol07:
Band seven of Das Kloster reached buyers in 1847, holding cells twenty-five through twenty-eight. Editor Johann Scheible had kept his anthology growing for two full years by then. Its German subtitle, worldly and spiritual, named the two great shelves of his cloister of books.

On those shelves, grimoires and Faust books rub covers with Höllenzwänge and homely folk charms. Chapbooks of wonder and warning, once sold for pennies, gain a second life in sturdy print. Scheible cut nothing and softened nothing, which is why workers in the field trust his pages. Band seven carries the stock past the set's midpoint in undiminished bulk.
schiller-studies-humanism-1907:
Four years after Humanism, F. C. S. Schiller issued Studies in Humanism in 1907 as a second series of essays. The Oxford pragmatist returned to his central claim with fresh cases. Human thought, he held, is an active tool shaped by human aims. The new essays test that claim on new ground.

Schiller applies his view to logic, knowledge, and the disputes of his day. He answers critics who charged that pragmatism makes truth a matter of whim. His replies stress testing, results, and the slow work of inquiry. The volume shows a system in mid fight, still growing. It pairs directly with the 1903 essays.
schnitzler-the-dead-are-silent-1907:
Love, death, and self-deception in anxious, glittering Vienna fill The Dead Are Silent, Schnitzler's story collection in English from 1907. The title tale follows a man's guilt after a fatal carriage accident kills his lover, while her husband knows nothing. Secrecy poisons every scene that follows the accident's first shock.

Other stories in the set cut into Viennese society with the same fine blade. Schnitzler anatomized his city like no one else, and these pieces show the scalpel at its sharpest. Doctors, officers, and actresses all discover what their arrangements with truth really cost. The collection suits readers meeting Schnitzler for the first time. Its best pages rank with the finest short fiction of the period.
sidgwick-methods-ethics-1907:
Henry Sidgwick published The Methods of Ethics in 1874; the text here is the 1907 edition. Sidgwick studies three methods by which people judge right and wrong. Egoism pursues one's own good, intuition follows common moral rules, and utilitarianism seeks the greatest general happiness. He tests each with unmatched care and fairness.

Sidgwick finds deep merit in both common-sense morality and utilitarian reform. His honest puzzle is that reason seems to support both self-interest and universal good without full harmony. The book is often called the greatest work of English moral philosophy. Philosophers still study its final chapters. It set the agenda for modern ethics.
spr-proceedings-vol19-1905-1907:
Parts fifty through fifty two and an appendix form volume nineteen, for 1905 to 1907. The Society for Psychical Research marks twenty five years of work in these pages. Telepathy trials take modern forms, with targets chosen by lot. Reports on trance mediumship remain the longest and most contested items.

Sitters test Piper and her peers with false names and sealed facts. Apparition reports, gathered by the old census standards, keep arriving. The appendix tidies society business and stray evidence. Volume nineteen shows a research society in settled middle age. Its files joined the primary archive of the long evidential debate. The mix of rigor and wonder persists.
stirner-ego-and-its-own-byington-1907:
Steven T Byington published his translation of Max Stirner's The Ego and His Own in 1907. Stirner, a German schoolteacher named Johann Kaspar Schmidt, issued the work in 1844. It vanished, then returned as the founding text of individualist anarchism and egoism.

Stirner declared war on every abstraction set above the self: state, church, humanity, and morality itself. Only the Unique, the single ego owning itself, escaped his scorn. He urged each person to take their own cause as the only cause. Byington's English, the first full version, shaped American individualist anarchism for decades. The book still startles readers with the reach of its refusal.
suzuki-outlines-mahayana-buddhism-1907:
Suzuki's Outlines of Mahayana Buddhism, published in 1907, was his first major work in English. Mahayana, the Great Vehicle, is the branch of Buddhism that spread through China, Korea, and Japan. Suzuki wrote the book while living in America and working on Eastern texts.

He sets out the bodhisattva ideal, the saint who delays final bliss to help all beings, and the doctrines of emptiness and Buddha-nature. His chapters draw on Sanskrit and Chinese sources he was among the first to open to Western readers. The Outlines prepared the audience that his later Zen books would win.
synge-aran-islands-1907:
John Millington Synge spent parts of four summers on the Aran Islands, off Ireland's west coast, at the urging of William Butler Yeats. Yeats told him to go where life had not yet been expressed. Synge's prose account of those visits appeared in 1907.

Synge records island life in plain, beautiful prose: fishing in frail curraghs, funerals with wild keening, fairy tales by the fire, and evictions resisted by whole villages. He learned Irish and listened more than he talked. The islanders' speech, half English and half Irish in rhythm, later shaped his plays. The book is a classic of Irish travel writing and a key to Synge's art.
synge-playboy-western-world-1907:
J. M. Synge's The Playboy of the Western World opened in Dublin in 1907 and caused riots in the theater. Audiences took offense at its picture of Irish country life and at a mention of women's underclothing. Synge had built the story from tales he heard on the Aran Islands and in County Mayo.

Christy Mahon stumbles into a Mayo shebeen claiming he has killed his father. The villagers, bored with dull routine, treat him as a hero, and Christy grows bold and poetic in their praise. Then his very alive father arrives. The play's rich, musical language and its dark joke about fame have made it a cornerstone of modern Irish drama.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Love and loss join the two tales in the seventh volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels. They are The Falcon and The Little Dog. Both come down from Boccaccio through the stream of Italian story that La Fontaine loved to retell.

The Falcon opens with the poet correcting himself: he had lately blamed the miserly sort of lover, and now, by the rule of opposites, the generous lover should stand in paradise. In Florence, he tells, a gentle youth loved a beautiful lady with his whole heart, and would have sold his soul to please her, spending freely on whatever amusements she wished. Readers of Boccaccio know where such spending leads: to a last treasure, a falcon, given up at the moment it could have won everything.
the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-07:
Volume 7 of The Bride of the Nile, by Georg Ebers, starts its chapters over at one, as a note on the numbering warns. Philippus found no sleep that night, and Orion slept no better. He no longer doubts Paula, but he longs to hear her say once more that she loves him and him alone. At first dawn he springs from bed, glad the night is past.

Orion crosses the Nile to place half of Paula's fortune with Salech, who is brother to Haschim, a merchant in Memphis. In Memphis all is still, and the old town strikes him as worn-out and fit for ruin. Across the river, in the new town of Fostat, busy new-born life meets his eyes on all hands. The old capital of the Pharaohs strikes him as a mummy eaten by time. Amru's new city, by contrast, seems a youth in full vigour.
the-canadian-brothers-or-the-prophecy-fu:
This copy of The Canadian Brothers opens directly with Chapter I, where an American party including the Major and Miss Montgomerie embarks in Gerald's schooner for Buffalo. Gerald must rejoin the flotilla at Amherstburg, and the voyage puts the travellers on the water together under the shadow of the late war's loyalties.

Family feeling runs across the plot. Gerald's brother Henry Grantham disapproves of his attachment. The narrative also refers back to adventures already detailed. The opening thus reads as a sequel in motion rather than a cold start. War service, kinship, and a contested courtship are all in play before the schooner clears the shore, and the frontier setting binds the three together from the first page.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-07:
In Part VII of The Caxtons, Pisistratus goes on with the story of his house. The novel calls itself a family picture, and the frame holds: one son's first-person account. His bookish father and a lively uncle share the stage in this stretch.

Uncle Jack hangs puddings in the chimney, and the narrator wishes he had warned his father with a tale from Luther's Table Talk. That tale tells of Dr. Gode, whose pudding talk was read as a sign of short life. The narrator grants that Uncle Jack hung the puddings himself, without coaxing his father to tell of them. Half of them, he guesses, will feed Uncle Jack, and the rest will feed young Pisistratus.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau:
Book VII of Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions stands here as volume VII of the twelve-book set, privately printed for members of the Aldus Society at London in 1903. After two years of silence and patience, Rousseau takes up his pen again, against his own resolutions.

He asks the reader to suspend judgment on the reasons forcing this step, since no one can judge them before reading the book. His peaceful youth, he notes, has been seen passing calmly and agreeably. It brought no great disappointments and no remarkable prosperity. That mediocrity, he argues, came mostly from his own nature: ardent yet feeble, slower to undertake than easy to discourage. He quit repose for violent agitations, then returned to it from weariness and inclination. Such a nature placed him in the idle, tranquil state he felt born for.
the-crisis-volume-07:
Volume 7 of Winston Churchill's novel opens at Chapter VII, With the Armies of the West. The scene is Memphis as Christmas nears, though war, the narrator says, honors no holiday. The brown river runs high between yellow clay banks, and the city has never seen such activity.

A restless spirit named William T. Sherman possesses the place. He prods Memphis awake and peoples it with running men in blue uniforms. Gunboats built by a man named Eads ride the river, loyal Southern citizens get leave to depart while their houses and slaves are hired for the Federal government. Cotton speculators flock in with trade permits, giving the Confederates the gold they need for bales they cannot use.
the-disowned-volume-07:
Volume seven of The Disowned opens at chapter sixty-eight with a tense letter. Lord Ulswater writes to Lady Westborough, asking that Clarence Linden be kept away until Wednesday at noon. Then, face to face, he will prove Clarence a fraud, or yield Lady Flora to his rival without a fight. Lady Westborough agrees and writes to Clarence, who accepts the meeting with thanks.

A trial of character is now fixed. The chapters ahead turn on proof, pride, and a young woman's future. Lytton builds suspense through polite letters that hide sharp threats.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-h:
Part seven of Hell in Dante's Vision covers cantos eighteen through twenty-two, in the Rev. H. F. Cary's English verse. Dante names a place called Malebolge, a field of dark, iron-hued rock cut by ten deep trenches. Bridges cross the ditches toward a vast pit at the center, like the moats and paths around a castle.

Each trench holds a kind of fraud: flatterers, fortune-tellers, and grafters sunk in pitch. Devils patrol the bridges with hooks and jeers. The part shows deceit sorted into neat, cruel rows, each with its own fitting pain.
the-emperor-volume-07:
Volume seven of Georg Ebers's The Emperor opens at part two, chapter five, amid festival noise in Alexandria. While Pollux waits, grieving, for his father's return, Papias curries favour with the emperor by feigning to take Hadrian for a mere Claudius Venator. Meanwhile Aurelius Verus, mocked as the sham Eros, calls on the Empress Sabina to lure her to the gay streets.

Sabina, low and unwell, pleads that the crowd's noise and dust would kill her. Clara Bell keeps Ebers's contrast sharp: a bright court, a sour empress, and a city drunk on show.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
The Ormsby Don Quixote, Cervantes' tale in English, opens Volume 1, Part 07 here. Chapter eighteen relates the discourse Sancho Panza held with his master, with other adventures worth relating. Sancho reaches Don Quixote limp and faint, hardly able to urge on his beast after his tossing.

Don Quixote insists the inn must be enchanted, since phantom beings amused themselves with Sancho while some spell kept him from mounting the yard wall or leaving Rocinante. Sancho disagrees in plain terms. The men who tossed him, he says, were flesh and bone with names he heard, among them Pedro Martinez, Tenorio Hernandez, and Juan Palomeque the Left-handed.
the-history-of-the-rise-progress-and-acc:
Thomas Clarkson, M.A., wrote The History of the Rise, Progress, and Accomplishment of the Abolition of the African Slave-Trade. The book is dated 1808. Chapter one carries a long summary of one year. The year runs from June 1788 to July 1789. Topics include travel to collect evidence and committees formed on tour. Privy council examinations and a Commons report also appear.

Matters had now become serious, Clarkson writes. The challenge had been issued and taken up. The contest would be decided on the great theatre of the nation. The committee had pronounced the slave-trade criminal by its founding. Those concerned in the trade denied the charge. A sibling record, dated 1839, shows only front matter.
the-inside-of-the-cup-volume-07:
Volume 7 of Winston Churchill's novel opens with chapter XXIII, The Choice. Hodder ponders Alison's note and frames his reply. Phrases from Harnack's History of Dogma guide him. Treating faith as simple submission is irreligious, Harnack holds. Faith honestly won must be striven for. What we think we possess is soon lost. Her admitted doubts set Alison apart. Others accepted their creed and went their ways.

His trials pile up beside his longing to talk with her. A newspaper prints a garbled account of his sermon. Black headlines make him a hero of the poor. The socialistic champion label nauseates him. He refused the reporter and got fame anyway. He would not trade his problems for the old false peace. Compromise had bought that peace, he now sees. The volume proceeds to the vestry meeting. The current of life closes it.
the-last-of-the-barons-volume-07:
Edward Bulwer Lytton labels the portion in this record Book Seven, called the popular rebellion. Hastings joins the King squires in the White Tower council chamber after a courier arrives from the north. Lords Rivers, St John, and Scales already wait with Edward IV.

Edward stands in a tight tunic, open letters and a dagger on the table before him. His clear, loud voice and bright eye tell Hastings that war news has come. Lytton shows a king who drops soft court manners when action calls, while rebellion gathers beyond London.
the-memoirs-of-count-grammont-volume-07:
Volume 7 of Anthony Hamilton's Memoirs of Count Grammont, edited with notes by Sir Walter Scott, opens at Chapter Eleventh. The Chevalier returns to France, is sent back to England, and the chapter promises marriages for most of the heroes of the memoirs. On the road, Grammont regrets England more with every mile toward the French court. Thoughts of friends' congratulations pass quickly through his head.

Love allows him no other subject than Miss Hamilton, left behind in London. Between Montreuil and Abbeville his heart protests that he tore himself away only to return the sooner. Hamilton teases his own trade, calling such passages the way a trifling writer abuses a reader's patience. He insists, though, that the memoirs record only what Grammont himself dictated. Readers close the series with a lover's journey home and an author winking at his own storytelling.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, November 24, 1827, No. 284, presents a view and plan of the Bay of Navarino and the island of Sphagia. The editors disavow interest in what Burke called the mystery of murder and the perfection of modern gunnery. The recent event at Navarino has revived interest, and readers are presumed familiar with it already.

Turning from ephemeral glory, the article describes the bay itself as a place famous in ancient and modern warfare. It borrows from Pouqueville's Travels and quotes Sir William Gell's Journey in the Morea. Gell calls Navarino's port certainly one of the finest in the world, shut in by a long island. That island, ancient Sphacteria, saw the defeat and capture of the Spartans in the Peloponnesian War. A naval battle of 1827 is thus framed by a shore where Athens humbled Sparta.

Lisbon, capital of Portugal, is described in No. 569 of The Mirror, dated October 6, 1832. The ancients called it Ulyssippo, and legend credited its founding to Ulysses. The city crowns hills on the north bank of the Tagus, and its harbour ranks among the finest in the world.

Entering the river means passing the forts of St. Julian and Bugio at the mouth. Villas thicken along the shore toward Belem, where arriving ships had their papers examined and warships exchanged salutes with the castle guns. The great aqueduct above Alcantara carries the capital's chief water supply across its valley. The palace of Necessidades and the new quarter of Buenos Ayres, thought the healthiest spot near the city, are also noted.
the-parisians-volume-07:
Volume 7 of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's The Parisians opens with Book VII, in the first week of May 1870. Gustave Rameau has won the place he sighed for. His journal grows in public hold, his profits rise, and critics of his own clique praise his poetry above Musset and Hugo. Yet his verse has won no wide public audience.

Trouble follows. Articles in the Sens Commun under the name Pierre Firmin, on the plebiscite question, have angered the government. Rameau is warned that, as editor, he answers for his contributors. If Pierre Firmin is a pen name, the real author must be proved, or Rameau pays the penalty. The poet-editor faces a suspended journal and prison.
the-poisoned-pen-pg5007: Arthur B. Reeve's The Poisoned Pen belongs to the Craig Kennedy series, its frontispiece drawn by Will Foster. Here only the title page, contents, and first line of the opening story appear, so the cases themselves are absent. Twelve chapters are listed: the title case, then The Yeggman, The Germ of Death, and The Firebug. The Confidence King, The Sand-Hog, The Forger, and The Smuggler follow. The Invisible Ray and The Campaign Grafter close the list. The opening line finds Kennedy's suit-case lying open on the bed.
the-spell-of-egypt-pg3407:
Robert Hichens tours Egypt's ancient sites in chapters named for the Pyramids, the Sphinx, Sakkara, Abydos, the Nile, Karnak, Luxor, the Tombs of the Kings, and Philae, among others. The text was prepared from a 1911 edition published by the Century Company of New York, and a companion record carries the same book in a contents-only state.

The Pyramids chapter opens by asking why the traveller comes to Egypt at all. Does he come to gain a dream, regain lost dreams, or gild life with romance? Does he come to forget sullen grey hours? Hichens warns that the Sphinx will not ask and the Pyramids keep their secrets, while temples and tombs answer only with brooding silence.
the-wandering-jew-volume-07:
Volume seven of Eugene Sue's Wandering Jew contains book seven, its contents running from The East Indian in Paris through doubts, consultations, Mother Bunch's diary, and a trysting-place of wolves. Chapter forty installs Prince Djalma in Paris, three days after Adrienne de Cardoville left Dr. Baleinier's care.

Djalma's little dwelling in the Rue Blanche is hung with Indian drapery, purple figures on a grey ground relieved by threads of gold. Matching hangings hide the ceiling, tied by a silken cord ending in tiny gold filigree lamps. Those lamps also burn perfumes, while blue crystal plates glow like sapphires in the arabesque openings. Sue furnishes the room as an oriental jewel box inside Paris.
thomson-corpuscular-theory-matter-1907:
Three years after Electricity and Matter, J. J. Thomson gave his corpuscular theory its full form in 1907. The Corpuscular Theory of Matter pushes the electron account as far as he could take it. Thomson asks how many corpuscles an atom holds. He also argues that mass itself may have an electrical origin.

New evidence from positive rays joins the older cathode ray work in these pages. Thomson weighs rival readings and defends his own atomic picture. The book stands as a sequel that tests the theory's limits. Soon other models would pass it by. Still, it records a great physicist thinking at full stretch. Its care rewards close study.
titus-andronicus-pg1507: William Shakespeare's Tragedy of Titus Andronicus is mapped here in a contents list of five acts, with a cast list. Saturninus and Bassianus are sons of Rome's late emperor. Titus Andronicus, a noble general against the Goths, heads the family with his brother Marcus, a tribune. Lavinia is Titus's daughter, and Lucius, Quintus, Martius, and Mutius are his sons. Scenes range across Rome, a forest lodge, plains, and Titus's gardens. A scene list and cast alone are given in this record, so Shakespeare's lines themselves are not shown.
tob-0007:
Farmers and priests of Sumer, in what is now Iraq, pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay about five thousand years ago. Their tablets are the oldest writing on earth. Temple accounts, hymns, law lists, school exercises, and early forms of the Gilgamesh tales all survive in baked mud.

No single edition unites the thousands of tablets, and the evidence notes none is attached to this entry. Scholars still piece the record together shard by shard from museum stores. What the tablets prove is large: writing began with accounts and stories together, and literature is as old as the ledger.
tob-0107:
Basil Valentine, a monk said to have lived in the fifteenth century, hid the stages of the Great Work inside twelve pictures and texts called keys. Each key is an allegory: a king, a queen, a wolf, a dragon. Together they map the path toward the philosopher's stone.

Readers must decode the images, since plain speech would betray the secret. The emblems are among the most beautiful in all alchemical books, copied and reprinted for centuries. This entry draws on a verified pre-1930 edition. Chemists of the time read real laboratory steps in the riddles; artists simply loved the pictures.
tob-10407:
Thomas Aquinas organized the Summa Theologica as questions with objections, answers, and replies, and this volume holds Part II-II, the second half of his moral theology. Aquinas treats the virtues and vices one by one in systematic order. Faith, hope, and charity come first, as the theological virtues.

Prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance follow, each shadowed by opposing sins and each broken into precise cases. A reader can look up anger, usury, war, or lying and find a reasoned verdict. The result remains the most systematic ethics in Christian thought, and a reference theologians and philosophers still argue with today.
tob-10807:
Otto Henne am Rhyn chronicled the secret doctrines of the ages in Mysteria, moving from ancient mystery cults through Gnostics, Templars, and Rosicrucians to Freemasons. His guiding curiosity asks what was really hidden behind their veils of secrecy and symbol. The flavor is encyclopedic and nineteenth-century.

Rather than treating each movement separately, Henne am Rhyn presents esoteric history as one continuous underground stream, surfacing in different costumes across centuries. Rites, grades of initiation, and legendary founders fill the pages. Modern scholars would dispute the single-stream picture, but as a period survey it preserves how an earlier age organized its fascination with hidden knowledge.
tob-11107:
Eiríkr Magnússon and William Morris translated the Volsunga Saga, the Norse prose saga of the Volsung clan. Sigmund and Signy open the line's grim history, and Sigurd the dragon-slayer stands at its center. The cursed gold of the dragon Fafnir poisons generation after generation, and Brynhild's tragic love completes the pattern.

Morris, a poet devoted to the North, worked to keep the saga's stark music in English. The telling is swift and pagan to the bone: oaths, vengeance, and fate bind every character. Wagner drew raw material for his Ring cycle from these same legends, and readers can compare the colder original with the opera.
tob-13507:
John Wesley's collected Works open with volume one, Sermons on Several Occasions, the preaching that fueled the Methodist revival. Wesley, an Anglican priest who took his message outdoors, preached on salvation by faith, the new birth, and Christian perfection. His audiences ranged from coal miners to, on occasion, the well placed and powerful.

The sermons are plain, urgent, and practical, built to be understood by unlettered hearers and to press for a decision. Wesley revised and republished them as standards of Methodist doctrine. Readers hear the voice that changed England's religious landscape, and they can watch a revival leader define his movement in its own pulpit language.
tob-14507:
F. Max Müller's classic translation presents the Buddha's 423 verses in the Dhammapada, drawn from his Sacred Books of the East series. Müller's version introduced Victorian readers to Buddhist scripture. The mind as master, hatred never conquered by hatred, and the path of diligence stand among its most quoted teachings.

Chapters proceed by topic, pairing fools and wise men, anger and kindness, craving and release. Müller renders the Pali verses in plain, dignified English that stays endlessly quotable. Readers who want the Dhammapada in the form nineteenth-century Britain first received it, with a great scholar-translator's care behind every line, will find this edition historically central.
tob-4007:
Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa published his Three Books of Occult Philosophy in 1533, and Western occultism took its lasting shape from them. The entry uses a checked 1919 public-domain printing. Agrippa, a restless scholar and soldier, set out to organize all magic into one system.

Book one treats the natural world of elements, stones, and herbs. Book two climbs to the heavens, numbers, and stars. Book three reaches ceremonial magic, divine names, and spirits. Charms stand beside high philosophy without apology. Later magicians from Barrett to the Golden Dawn worked from Agrippa's plan. His three books remain the Renaissance summa of the occult arts.
tob-4107:
Purity law fills the Vendidad, the Zoroastrian book at the head of Darmesteter's Zend Avesta in the Sacred Books of the East. Darmesteter translated part one of the Avesta from the ancient tongue with Max Muller editing the series. Ancient Persia's rules for keeping demons and corruption at bay fill the chapters.

Corpses, sickness, and unclean acts require set cleansings, some lasting days. Priests, dogs, and sacred fires all play their parts in the system. The Vendidad is law, ritual manual, and myth at once, with tales of Yima's golden age woven through. Verified from the 1919 edition, it opens the Avesta for English readers.
topsell-historie-four-footed-beastes-160:
Edward Topsell, an English clergyman, published The Historie of Four-footed Beastes in 1607. It was the first great English book of animals, built from older writers like Conrad Gessner. Topsell wrote for readers who wanted the whole animal kingdom set out in their own language.

Lions, apes, horses, and stranger beasts fill its pages, each with a woodcut picture. Topsell reports habits, uses in medicine, and tall tales, all told straight. He rarely doubts what his sources say, so fact and fable stand side by side. The book shows natural history before it learned to doubt. Shakespeare's England read its beasts here.
traite-de-la-poudre-de-projection-divise: A French treatise on the powder of projection, printed at Brussels in 1707, fills the opening pages here. Its title page divides the work into two letters. One part promises an analysis drawn from Holy Scripture. The other promises means of reaching the powder by a moist, substantial first principle. Only the title page and the start of a historical address to philosophers are present here, so the letters themselves do not appear. No author is named on the page.
uarda-a-romance-of-ancient-egypt-volume-:
Chapter twenty-nine opens volume seven of Uarda, with Paaker sending his dead dog to Kynopolis for embalming. Dogs were sacred there above all animals, a footnote explains, and its people once feuded with Oxyrynchos over eaten fish and sacrificed dogs. Paaker's mother travels with the pioneer's boat.

Paaker himself returns to the House of Seti for the priests' grand banquet, an honor he owes to the Regent's favor. His mother has bound his hand, hurt by Rameri, and it pains him badly. Yet his ancient family's pride sits uneasily among superior company. He is scribe and warrior, at home in neither priestly hall nor royal hero's rank.
un-sc-res-107:
Tension along the armistice line between Egypt and Israel drew the Council's attention on 30 March 1955. The chief of staff of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization had reported on conditions there. His report also covered the causes of the strain between the two sides. The Council acted under the General Armistice Agreement that Egypt and Israel had signed.

The resolution asks the chief of staff to keep consulting both governments. He had already offered concrete proposals to calm the border. The Council calls on Egypt and Israel to cooperate with him. It notes his view that cross-border infiltration could shrink to a minor nuisance. That gain would follow if both sides accepted his plan.
un-sc-res-1307: Under number 1307, the catalog lists a Security Council resolution dated to 1999 in the official UN record. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1407:
Weapons kept flowing into Somalia despite a decade-old embargo. On 3 May 2002 the Security Council moved to give that embargo teeth. The chairman of its Somalia sanctions committee planned a visit to the region. The Council noted the continued flow of arms with serious concern. That flow, it said, hurt peace and reconciliation in Somalia. A presidential statement in March had set up this step.

The Secretary-General had one month to set up a two-person expert team. The team would work for thirty days. Its job was an action plan for a full panel of experts. The plan would list the skills and resources needed to track embargo breaches. The Council promised to weigh the findings by the end of July.
un-sc-res-1507:
Ethiopia and Eritrea's border mission was renewed by the Security Council on 12 September 2003. The peace process had reached the key phase of marking the border on the ground. The Council voiced concern at delays in demarcation and at the cost of the mission while demand for peacekeepers grew elsewhere. Hunger crises in both countries also threatened the process.

The Council extended the United Nations Mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea, UNMEE, at its authorized troop and observer levels to 15 March 2004. It called for demarcation to begin on the Boundary Commission's schedule. Both parties had to name field liaison officers and give the commission full cooperation. The Council repeated its demand that UNMEE move freely, with all restrictions lifted at once. It also pressed the two governments to open political dialogue, saying lasting peace needed more than a marked line on a map.
un-sc-res-1607:
The Council dealt with Liberia in Resolution 1607, adopted on 21 June 2005. No illegal timber exports had shown up in the expert reports. Yet few of the needed forestry reforms were in place. Unlicensed diamond mining and shady exports were on the rise. The interim government still lacked control over the diamond and timber areas.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the diamond ban for six more months. The arms, travel, and timber measures stay in force until 21 December 2005. The asset freeze on the old regime's circle also stands. The government must build a clear certificate system for rough diamonds and fix its forestry body. The Panel of Experts serves until 21 December 2005.
un-sc-res-1707:
ISAF's authorization was renewed amid a Taliban resurgence on 12 September 2006. Violent and terrorist attacks by the Taliban, Al-Qaida, illegal armed groups, and the narcotics trade had grown. The Afghanistan Compact, launched at London, set the frame for work between Kabul and its partners. Security, governance, and development were judged to rise or fall together.

The Council extended the International Security Assistance Force's authorization for twelve months beyond 13 October 2006. The states serving in the force could take all necessary measures to carry out its mandate. The need to strengthen the force further was recognized, and states were called to give staff, funds, and equipment. The force had to keep working in close consultation with the Afghan government and the Secretary-General's representative. Its leadership owed the Council quarterly reports. The text covered the year in which the force took charge of security across the whole country.
un-sc-res-1807:
Council members took up the Democratic Republic of the Congo and adopted Resolution 1807 on the Democratic Republic of the Congo on 31 March 2008. The Goma conference and the Nairobi statement had raised hopes for peace in the east. Weapons still flowed to armed groups, and stolen minerals still paid for them. The old embargo treated the government and rebels much the same.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council rebuilds the sanctions to run until 31 December 2008. The arms embargo now binds only non-government groups and people. The government may receive arms again, but every shipment must be reported to the committee in advance. Travel bans and asset freezes stay in force for listed violators. Aircraft checks and customs controls also continue.
un-sc-res-1907:
Eritrea received the Council's formal attention in Resolution 1907, adopted on 23 December 2009. United Nations monitors said Eritrea had given money, arms, and training to Somali armed groups. Eritrea also still held ground seized from Djibouti in June 2008. It refused all talks and mediation on that border clash.
